text:
There is a sheet of paper in Vienna that is more than three hundred years old. It is brittle, stained at the edges, and written in a cramped hand by someone whose name almost nobody remembers. It holds a recipe for a pastry that the entire world now believes it knows.

But here is the thing that should bother you. That recipe is not for apple strudel. And the dough it describes did not come from Vienna. It did not come from Austria at all.

So who first stretched a ball of flour and water until it was thinner than a love letter? Who looked at that translucent sheet and decided to wrap it around fruit and roll it up like a scroll? And how did a dessert that begins in the kitchens of one empire end up as the proud national treasure of another?
The answer involves a conquered city, a stubborn cook, a tablecloth, and a fruit that nobody expected to matter. And if you have ever pulled a strudel from the oven and heard that crackle of golden pastry, you are about to find out that you were tasting five hundred years of history.
Stay with me. Because the story of strudel does not begin with an apple at all.
Chapter One: The Paper-Thin Secret
To find the beginning, we have to leave Europe entirely and travel east, far to the east, to the wide grasslands where Turkic peoples moved with their herds long before anyone dreamed of Vienna's coffeehouses.
Life on the steppe was built on portability. You could not carry a brick oven on horseback. But you could carry flour, and you could carry a rolling pin, and with those two things you could make bread that cooked in minutes over a flat metal plate. The simplest of these breads was a thin, unleavened sheet of dough called yufka. Flour, water, a pinch of salt. Rolled out wide, cooked fast, stacked in piles.
As those peoples migrated west over the centuries, they carried the technique with them into Anatolia, and there it met something new: the sophisticated palace kitchens of the Seljuks, and later the Ottomans. In those kitchens, cooks asked a dangerous question. What if the dough could be thinner?
Not thin like a flatbread. Thin like a veil.
The best pastry masters of the Ottoman court did not simply roll their dough. They rolled it with a long, slender pin, dusted it with starch, and worked it outward and outward until it spread across a huge wooden table, so fine that you could see the grain of the wood through it. Sheet after sheet, they brushed these veils with butter and layered them with nuts and honey syrup. The result was a family of pastries that we still love today. Baklava is the most famous. But there were savory versions too, filled with cheese and greens and minced meat, and sweet versions filled with cream and fruit.
This was not home cooking. This was a craft, passed from master to apprentice, guarded like the secret of a blacksmith's forge. A young apprentice might spend years just learning to roll a single sheet without tearing it. Palace records from the empire show that pastry cooks formed their own specialized ranks, and that the sweet kitchens of the great Topkapi Palace in Istanbul were busy places indeed.
Now, hold that image in your mind. A master standing at a table, his hands under a sheet of dough so fine it floats. Because in the middle of the sixteenth century, that skill was about to travel north on the boots of an army.
The world of the steppe had made the sheet. The Ottoman palace had perfected it. But it would take a collision between empires, in the heart of Central Europe, to turn that sheet into something nobody had ever seen before: a roll.
Chapter Two: Buda, 1541
In the late summer of 1541, the Ottoman army entered the Hungarian city of Buda, high on the hill above the Danube. The medieval kingdom of Hungary had been shattered fifteen years earlier on the battlefield of Mohács, and now its old capital passed into Ottoman hands. It would remain there for almost a century and a half.
Imagine what that meant for an ordinary kitchen. Overnight, the city filled with new officials, new soldiers, new merchants, and new cooks. They brought spices that Hungarians rarely saw. They brought coffee. They brought paprika's cousins and the habit of stuffing vegetables. And they brought, in the saddlebags and the memories of their craftsmen, the art of the thin dough.
Let us follow one imagined kitchen on the Buda hillside. We will call the master of this kitchen Hasan, a pastry cook in the household of an Ottoman official. He is in his fifties, with flour permanently settled into the lines of his knuckles. And we will call the kitchen girl, the one who carries water and scrubs the tables and watches everything with sharp eyes, Ilona. She is fourteen. She is Hungarian. And she is about to learn something that will outlive them both.
Every morning before dawn, Hasan began the same ritual. He mixed a dough of flour, water, and a little salt, kneaded it until it was smooth as a polished stone, and let it rest under a warm bowl. Resting, he told his assistants, was not laziness. Resting was when the dough forgave you. A dough that has been kneaded is angry, tight, ready to snap back. A rested dough relaxes and agrees to be stretched.
Then came the part Ilona loved. Hasan would flour the great table, roll the dough out with a long pin, and then, when it was as wide as a dinner plate, he would stop using the pin. He would slide his hands, backs up, underneath the sheet, and begin to pull gently outward with his knuckles. The dough thinned. It widened. It rippled like water. Soon it hung over the edges of the table, and Hasan would walk slowly around it, tugging a little here, a little there, as if coaxing a sleeping animal to roll over.
"Do you see the table?" he asked her once in the rough Hungarian he had picked up in the marketplace. "Through the dough?"
She did. She could see every scratch in the wood, every ring in the grain. She could see the colors of her own sleeve moving beneath it.
"That is how you know," he said. "If you cannot see through it, it is not finished. If you can see through it and it has no holes, then you are a pastry cook."
Ilona did not become a pastry cook that year, or the next. She tore sheet after sheet. Hasan did not shout. He simply gathered the torn dough into a ball, set it aside to rest, and told her to begin again. In that kitchen, failure was just dough that needed more time.
By the time she was seventeen, she could stretch a sheet as thin as any of the men.
But Ilona was Hungarian, and she had a Hungarian's instincts. In her mother's village kitchen, she had grown up with different ingredients: sour cream, soft white cheese, poppy seeds, walnuts, sour cherries, and above all, the fat of the pig and the cow, which Hungarian cooks used generously. Ottoman pastry was built on layers, sheet upon sheet, flat as a book. And Ilona found herself wondering, in the quiet hours before dawn, what might happen if she did not stack the sheets at all.
What if she simply rolled them up?
Chapter Three: The Roll
We do not know who first rolled a thin sheet of dough around a filling and baked it as a spiral. No document records the moment. That is the frustrating beauty of food history: the greatest inventions are usually made by people too busy cooking to write anything down.
But historians of food generally agree on the outline of what happened. Under Ottoman rule, the technique of stretched dough took root in Hungary. Hungarian cooks adapted it to local tastes and local pantries. And somewhere in that blending, the layered pastry of the Ottoman tradition gave rise to a rolled one. In Hungarian, it was called rétes. In German, the word that eventually stuck was Strudel.
That word is wonderful. In German, Strudel means a whirlpool, an eddy, a swirl of water. Cut a strudel crosswise and you will see exactly why. The thin dough wraps around the filling again and again, dozens of translucent turns, like water circling a drain. The name is not poetry. It is a plain description of what the cook sees.
So let us imagine Ilona's experiment.
One morning, after the household had eaten and the great table was nearly empty, she stretched a fresh sheet, finer than anything Hasan had asked of her that week. She brushed it lightly with melted butter, the way he had taught her. Then, instead of cutting it into squares to layer, she did something else. Along one edge she spread a line of soft white cheese mixed with a little sugar and an egg yolk, the kind of filling her mother used. She lifted the edge of the sheet and folded it over the cheese. And then she kept lifting, slowly, with the backs of her hands, rolling the whole sheet over itself the way you roll a rug, until it formed a long, fat log.
She laid it in a pan, brushed it with more butter, and slid it into the oven.
Hasan came in when the smell reached him. He stood over the pan with his arms crossed. The surface of the roll had gone the color of amber, blistered into a thousand tiny crisp bubbles. Ilona was sure she was about to be scolded.
He cut it open instead. The pastry shattered with a sound like dry leaves. Inside, the spiral of layers was as clean and even as the rings of a tree.
He ate a piece. He said nothing for a long moment.
"The layers," he finally said. "You did not have to stack them. The rolling made them for you."
It was the cleverest thing about the whole idea. A baklava maker spends hours cutting, brushing, and stacking sheet after sheet. But a strudel maker stretches one sheet, one enormous sheet, and the act of rolling creates all those layers at once. The technique was faster, cheaper, and, because a single piece of dough could wrap a very generous filling, perfect for feeding a crowd.
Whether or not it happened on a particular morning in a particular kitchen, this is the logic that made strudel possible. A technique from the East. An appetite from the West. And a cook, somewhere, brave enough to try something that was neither one nor the other.
In the years that followed, Hungarian households filled their strudels with whatever the season offered. Sweet cheese. Poppy seed ground with honey. Walnuts. Sour cherries from the orchards that would later become famous. Cabbage, in a savory version. Pumpkin, in the autumn. And yes, here and there, apples.
But apples were not the star yet. They were just one filling among many, a modest guest at a very crowded table. They would have to wait for another city to make them famous.
Chapter Four: The Road to Vienna
The Ottoman presence in Hungary did not end quietly. In 1683, an enormous Ottoman army besieged Vienna, the capital of the Habsburg monarchy. It was one of the most dramatic moments in European history. The siege failed. A relief force broke through in September, and the Ottoman tide began to turn. Three years later, in 1686, a coalition army retook Buda after a long and brutal campaign. By 1699, the Treaty of Karlowitz formally ended Ottoman control over most of Hungary.
But notice what happened to the pastry. Wars end borders. They do not end recipes.
By the time the Habsburgs governed Hungary, the stretched-dough tradition had been alive in Hungarian kitchens for generations. It was no longer an Ottoman import. It was Hungarian, as Hungarian as paprika, which had also arrived from the same complicated history. And Hungary was now part of a vast, multilingual empire that stretched from the Alps to the Carpathians, and that kept its capital in Vienna.
The Habsburg lands were a giant, ongoing conversation between kitchens. Bohemian cooks, Hungarian cooks, Austrian cooks, and cooks from Moravia, Croatia, and Galicia all worked in the great households of the empire. Noble families moved between their estates. Armies moved. Merchants moved. Servants married across regions, and a girl from one valley might end up stirring a pot in another.
In that restless mixing, a recipe was never really owned by anyone. It was carried. A Hungarian cook who took a position in a Viennese noble house brought her rétes with her, just as she brought her hands and her memory. Bohemian pastry traditions, with their own love of yeasted dough and fruit, mingled in. And Viennese cooks, who were already famous for their pastry skill, took the technique and began to make it their own.
Let us imagine Ilona's great-granddaughter, a woman we will call Katalin, born in a village near the Danube long after the siege smoke had cleared. She is twenty when she takes a position as a kitchen maid in a prosperous household in Vienna. She carries her bundle on her back, and in her head she carries something more valuable: the exact feel of a dough that is ready.
The Viennese kitchen, she discovers, is a different world. It is louder. It is more ambitious. The head cook has opinions about everything, including the proper temperature of butter and the correct angle at which to hold a whisk. But when Katalin quietly stretches her first sheet on a floured cloth, the kitchen goes silent.
She does not use the pin for long. She learned from her grandmother, who learned from her mother, who learned it from the old tradition: roll the dough out, then lift it onto a cloth, a clean linen tablecloth dusted with flour, and stretch it with the backs of your hands. The cloth is a secret weapon. It grips the dough, spreads the weight, and lets you lift and roll without tearing.
The head cook watches her work the dough until it covers the whole table, thinner than paper. She is a proud woman, and she does not hand out compliments. She says only: "Again."
Katalin does it again. Then again. By the end of the week, the household has a new dessert on the table, and the cook who once said "again" is quietly asking Katalin to teach the girls how to do it.
This is how a recipe moves through an empire. Not by decree. Not by cookbook. But by one cook watching another, one dough passing between hands, one quiet kitchen at a time.
Chapter Five: The Paper of 1696
And now we arrive at the paper from the beginning of our story.
In the collections of the Vienna City Library, the Wienbibliothek, there is a handwritten manuscript dated 1696. It is a recipe for a strudel. Not an apple strudel, but a Millirahmstrudel, a milk-cream strudel, filled with a rich, sweet dairy mixture. It is widely cited as the oldest known strudel recipe in the German-speaking world. And it is one of the reasons historians can point to the late seventeenth century as the moment when strudel was already settled in the Viennese kitchen.
Sit with that date for a moment. 1696. The siege of Vienna had ended only thirteen years before. Buda had been recaptured just ten years earlier. The ink on the Treaty of Karlowitz was still three years away from being written.
The empire that had fought a desperate war against the Ottomans was already, quietly, eating their pastry technique, transformed into something its own cooks could claim.
There is a delicious irony in that. The recipe survives in a Viennese library, written in German, belonging to the Habsburg world. But the method it describes, that thin, stretched, rolled dough, carries a long journey inside it. From the steppe to the Ottoman palace. From the palace to the Hungarian hearth. From the hearth to the Viennese kitchen.
We should be honest about what we do not know. We do not know exactly who wrote that manuscript. We do not know whether the author invented the recipe or simply recorded what the kitchen already did. And we cannot say that strudel was born in a single moment. The truth is better and messier than that. Strudel is a recipe that emerged from a thousand hands over several generations, and the 1696 manuscript is simply the first time anyone we can still read decided to write it down.
But the manuscript tells us something important. Strudel, by the end of the seventeenth century, was not a curiosity. It was a recipe worth preserving. And the person who wrote it down was trusting that someone, someday, would want to make it again.
They were right. Three hundred years later, someone is still reading that page.
Notice, too, what the filling is. Cream. Not fruit. For a surprisingly long time, strudel was not primarily an apple dessert. It was a vehicle, a clever way of wrapping a dough around whatever was good and abundant. If the apple had not become the favorite, strudel might today be known as a cheese pastry, or a cherry one, or a poppy-seed roll. The history of food is full of near misses like that.
So what changed? Why did the apple, a fruit that every orchard on earth produces, rise above all the others to become the face of strudel?
The answer lies in the Austrian landscape, and in one very clever trick of the kitchen.
Chapter Six: The Apple Arrives
Picture the Austrian countryside in autumn. In Styria, in Lower Austria, in the Wachau valley and along the slopes above the Danube, orchards are heavy with fruit. Apples are the great harvest. They are stored in cool cellars through the winter, packed in straw, wrapped in paper, kept until spring. In a household without refrigeration, the apple was the dependable fruit, the one that was always there when the others were gone.
And apples have a gift that most other fruits lack. A good cooking apple holds its shape under heat. It softens without dissolving. It balances sweetness and tartness. It pairs beautifully with the warm spices that traveled into the Habsburg lands through trade: cinnamon, clove, and a little lemon.
When cooks began to put apples into the stretched dough, they ran into a problem that every baker still knows. Apples are full of water. Slice them, sprinkle them with sugar, and they release juice. And juice is the enemy of a paper-thin dough. A wet filling turns that delicate, translucent sheet into a soggy, tearing, miserable mess.
So somebody, somewhere, invented the solution. Breadcrumbs.
Fry fresh breadcrumbs in butter until they turn golden and fragrant. Scatter them over the stretched dough before the apples go on. The crumbs act like a sponge, soaking up the juice as it escapes, keeping the pastry crisp and the filling rich. It is a brilliantly frugal trick, born of the habit of using stale bread, and it gives the strudel a gentle toasted flavor underneath the fruit. To this day, a classic Viennese apple strudel is made exactly this way.
Let us picture a late autumn afternoon in the kitchen of a Viennese household, perhaps in the middle of the eighteenth century. Katalin's own granddaughter, a woman now called Theresia, is at the table. The apples have been peeled and sliced thin, tossed with sugar, cinnamon, a handful of raisins that have soaked in rum, and a squeeze of lemon. The breadcrumbs sizzle in a pan, smelling of toast and butter.
She has already stretched the dough. It hangs over every edge of the floured tablecloth, and the dim afternoon light shines straight through it. Her young apprentice, wide-eyed, leans in close.
"Do you see the pattern on the cloth?" Theresia asks.
The girl nods.
"The old people say it is ready when you can read a letter through it. A love letter, they say, because a love letter is the one you will read twice."
The apprentice laughs. Theresia does not. She brushes the sheet with melted butter, scatters the crumbs along the near edge, and spoons the apples in a long, loose line. Then she does the thing that always makes apprentices gasp. She lifts the corners of the tablecloth itself, and uses the cloth to roll the strudel over, as smoothly as folding a blanket. The thin dough wraps the apples once, twice, again and again, a spiral so fine it looks like a seashell.
She seals the ends, curves the roll into a crescent so it fits the pan, brushes it with butter one last time, and slides it into the oven.
Forty minutes later the whole kitchen smells of caramelized apples and warm cinnamon, and the pastry has the glassy, bubbled, golden surface that only a properly stretched dough can create. When Theresia cuts it, the sound is the sound of autumn leaves.
They eat it warm, dusted with powdered sugar, perhaps with a spoonful of vanilla sauce or a dollop of whipped cream. And the apprentice, with a mouth full of crisp pastry and soft, spiced fruit, understands in a single bite why this recipe will never die.
The apple had arrived. And it would not leave.
Chapter Seven: The Cloth and the Empire
By the nineteenth century, apple strudel had become a fixture of Austrian cooking and, increasingly, a symbol of it. Viennese cookbooks of the period include strudel in many forms, and the stretched dough became a kind of test of a cook's skill, the way a perfect omelette is a test in a French kitchen. A girl who could stretch a strudel dough was a girl who could run a household. Many a young woman was judged by her ability to cover a table with a sheet of dough so thin that she could read a newspaper through it.
This was also the era of the Viennese coffeehouse. Those grand, marble-topped, newspaper-strewn cafes became the living rooms of the city. Writers, composers, politicians, students, and gossips settled in for hours over a single cup of coffee. And on the little plates beside those cups sat the pastries of the empire: Sachertorte, kipferl, Gugelhupf, and, of course, a warm slice of apple strudel.
The coffeehouse did something important for strudel. It made it public. A dish that had lived in private kitchens, taught from one pair of hands to another, was suddenly served to thousands of people every day in the most fashionable rooms in Europe. It became part of the city's identity.
Meanwhile, the multicultural empire kept feeding the tradition. Hungarian rétes continued as its own beloved cousin, filled with sour cherry, poppy seed, or sweet cheese. Czech závin and Slovak štrúdľa appeared in their own kitchens. Croatian and Slovenian cooks made their own versions. Jewish families across Central Europe made strudels with their own fillings and their own holiday traditions. Each region kept the basic idea of the whirlpool and wrote its own flavors into it.
What I find most moving is that nobody in this story ever truly owned the recipe. The steppe baker gave it to the Ottoman court. The Ottoman court gave it, by conquest and by trade, to Hungary. Hungary gave it to the Habsburg lands. Vienna gave it to the coffeehouse, and the coffeehouse gave it to the world. Every handoff changed it, and every change made it more delicious.
When the empire finally dissolved after the First World War, the borders were redrawn once again. But the strudel stayed on every table. It had survived sieges, treaties, and the collapse of kingdoms. It would survive anything.
And then it crossed an ocean.
Chapter Eight: The Whirlpool Goes Global
In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, millions of people left Central and Eastern Europe for the Americas. They carried very little. A trunk, a few photographs, a prayer book, and the recipes held in their memories. In the crowded kitchens of immigrant neighborhoods in New York, Chicago, Cleveland, and beyond, grandmothers stretched dough over kitchen tables, and the smell of baking apples rose through tenement stairwells.
In those new countries, strudel changed again. Ingredients were different, ovens were different, and the old cloth-stretching method was often replaced by shortcuts. Store-bought phyllo dough, a descendant of the very same Ottoman tradition that began this story, became a convenient substitute. There is a lovely circularity in that. A sheet of dough that began in the East traveled to Europe, became a roll, crossed an ocean, and then, in a supermarket freezer aisle, returned to something very close to where it began.
Today, apple strudel appears on dessert menus from Vienna to Vancouver, from Budapest to Buenos Aires. It is served in Christmas markets, where it steams in the cold air beside mugs of mulled wine. It is sold in mountain huts in the Alps, where hikers eat it after a long climb. It is baked in home kitchens by people who have never stretched a dough in their lives and who still understand, instinctively, that this is a dessert that carries love.
And in a few stubborn kitchens, there are still cooks who do it the old way. They flour a clean cloth. They rest the dough under a warm bowl. They slide their hands underneath and pull gently outward, outward, until the dough has covered the entire table and the pattern of the cloth is clear beneath it.
Those cooks are doing something extraordinary. They are repeating a gesture that was already old when Ilona first tried it in a kitchen on the Buda hillside. They are connecting their own hands to a chain that reaches back through centuries of bakers, of conquered cities and crowded coffeehouses, of grandmothers who taught granddaughters without ever writing anything down.
And at the end of that chain, there is you. In your own kitchen, with your own apples.

text:
The Economist reports that US negotiators are considering redrawing Donetsk and Luhansk oblast boundaries. The idea is to let Putin claim he has “liberated Donbas” without Ukraine surrendering the cities it holds. The front line would stay where it is. Only the map would change.

THE MAP TRICK

Under the idea being discussed, the Ukrainian-held parts of Donetsk get assigned to other regions. These fairy-tale real-estate agents around Trump are treating an invasion as a dispute over property listings.

Russia currently demands all of Donetsk oblast as a condition for a ceasefire. Ukraine will accept only a freeze along the present front line. Renaming the territory does not resolve that disagreement. More importantly, Putin’s demands have never stopped at a neat piece of land on a map. Moscow also wants Ukraine neutral, its armed forces reduced and foreign troops kept out. A plan to leave the whole country vulnerable to the next attack goes far beyond a compromise over an oblast boundary. Europe would be foolish to imagine Russia’s ambitions end at Ukraine’s western border.

THE OTHER CARROTS

The Economist also reports that Washington is offering to reconnect Russia to European energy markets. So the package pairs a paper victory for Putin with a potential economic reward, while Moscow continues its winter campaign against Ukrainian infrastructure. Kyiv’s assessment is that negotiations are Russia’s Plan B; destroying that infrastructure remains Plan A.

Russia has reportedly become more flexible about freezing the current front line since the US offered talks on the security of Europe as a whole. That gives Moscow a much bigger table on which to pile demands. Every new condition can buy it more time.

THE CLOCK IN WASHINGTON

The Economist links the haste around the Abu Dhabi talks to US domestic politics: Republican election losses and the prospect of investigations involving Witkoff and Kushner from January. That pressure is no excuse to sell a theatrical fix as peace. It makes the incentives of the people designing it worth scrutinising all the harder.

Ukraine is asking for support to maintain an 800,000-strong army for at least ten years. US negotiators consider that too expensive and argue that American security guarantees would suffice. Ukrainians have reason to doubt Trump would enforce them. A changed map cannot defend a city; an army can.

text:
My father gripped my arm outside a White House reception and told me to pretend I had never met him. Twenty-six years earlier, he had cut me off for choosing the Army. Now he called me a “mall cop”—until the agent beside us looked past his expensive suit and asked whether I needed help.

“Take your hand off me, Conrad,” I said.

His face tightened. The last time we had stood this close, I had still called him Dad.

My stepbrother, Simon, had started it. He shoved my shoulder and told me to clear the VIP lane. When I turned, my father caught my arm, recognized me, and looked more embarrassed than surprised.

“Mara? What are you doing here?”

“Attending the reception.”

My stepmother gave a small laugh.

“Conrad, she's working. They all dress up for these things.”

I was forty-eight years old. I had led soldiers, delivered news no family should have to hear, and helped younger officers speak about things they were afraid to report.

Still, my hand shook when I smoothed my sleeve.

For a moment, I was twenty-two again, sitting across from my father while he offered to pay for business school and give me a future at Ellison Signal Systems.

“I commission next week,” I had told him.

“You can decline.”

“I made a commitment.”

He said that if I walked out, there would be no allowance, no company position, no inheritance, and no rescue when my “experiment” ended.

I left the company car in his driveway and took the train.

Later, I tried a letter. Photographs. An invitation to lunch.

He offered me a job instead.

Eventually, I stopped asking him to be my father on terms he hadn't written himself.

Now, at the reception entrance, he finally released my arm when he noticed the agent watching.

“Family,” he explained with a smile.

The agent looked at me.

“Ma'am?”

“He has released me,” I said. “I need some space.”

My father had to move away.

He checked his watch and told me about the fifty thousand dollars his company had contributed to a foundation luncheon earlier that day. He was hoping this evening would bring him a conversation with General Harlan Reed.

Ellison Signal Systems wanted a major communications program.

“This isn't a business meeting,” I said.

“Every room is a business meeting if you belong in it.”

Then he looked down at my uniform.

“Try not to make a scene.”

I had people waiting inside: Major Lena Ortiz and retired Sergeant First Class Owen Price. We had come for work that belonged to an entire team, including people who would never stand in that room.

I wanted to reach them.

A reception aide checked the arrival list, recognized me, and spoke to a colleague. An agent asked the next group to wait.

My father straightened his jacket.

General Reed appeared beyond the entrance, four silver stars catching the evening light.

My father moved forward immediately, his hand extended.

“General Reed. Conrad Ellison, Ellison Signal Systems. I'm delighted you could come out to welcome us.”

The general gave him a brief nod.

Then he looked past my father's shoulder, directly at me, and began to speak.

Type EAGLES and I’ll continue.

text:
This rhetorical cliche, to still remain viable, presupposes a binary in which free speech, voting choice, and religious practice exist in pure form in the United States and Australia and are simply “denied” in China. It treats the Freedom House categorisation as self-evident proof rather than as one institutional index with its own methodological assumptions. 

The claim that Australians “can speak, vote, and worship as they choose” embeds the assumption that existing legal and administrative limits do not meaningfully constrain these activities.  This is increasingly evident to be not the case.

As an official US Embassy account, the post advances the institutional narrative that the US–Australia alliance rests on shared values of unrestricted freedom. This framing positions closer alignment with US strategic priorities as an extension of domestic liberty rather than as a separate policy choice involving force posture agreement military subordination, AUKUS industrial dependence, and risk of US provoked military entanglement with China.

The post omits documented Australian restrictions on speech and political communication, the absence of a constitutional free-speech right equivalent to the US First Amendment, and the bipartisan lock-in on major foreign-policy questions that limits meaningful electoral alternatives.

Australia does not have an individual constitutional right to free speech. The High Court has recognised only a narrow implied freedom of political communication.  Section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act makes it unlawful to engage in speech reasonably likely to “offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate” on racial grounds; the provision remains in force and is currently under High Court challenge (Hanson). 

The eSafety Commissioner holds statutory powers under the Online Safety Act 2021 to issue removal notices for content meeting the adult cyber-abuse threshold and has used informal alerts that courts have found can operate outside the formal statutory process. 

Additionally, Australia has implemented a social-media minimum-age ban for under-16s on major platforms, currently subject to High Court challenge on implied-freedom grounds. Proposed Digital Duty of Care legislation would require platforms to proactively mitigate “harm,” with critics arguing it incentivises over-removal of lawful speech under the threat of large fines. 

These mechanisms constitute real constraints on what Australians can say online and in public; they are not equivalent to the absolute denial asserted for China, but they contradict the Embassy’s unqualified claim that Australians “can speak… as they choose.”

On "democratic elections": Major-party consensus on core strategic policy has narrowed the range of electoral alternatives on offer to Australian voters (the @Greens and @DavidShoebridge being the notable exception). Both Labor and the Coalition have maintained support for AUKUS Pillar I, the Force Posture Agreement’s unimpeded US access arrangements, and the framing of China as a primary security challenge requiring forward military integration. Former prime ministers from both sides (Keating, Turnbull) and the recent public inquiry have criticised this consensus as subordinating sovereignty and risking entanglement, yet no major-party platform offers a decisive break from the US-aligned model.  Voting therefore offers rotation of personnel within a relatively fixed strategic framework rather than a genuine choice between competing models of regional engagement.

China operates a different political system that prioritises stability, economic development, and party-led governance; public political speech is more tightly regulated. Australia, however, has also erected specific legal and administrative barriers to certain categories of speech (racial offence, online “harm,” age-restricted platforms). The binary map collapses these differences into a single free/not-free contrast and ignores Australia’s own restrictions.  

China does not offer multiparty electoral competition of the Western type. In Australia the major parties present limited divergence on the central foreign-policy questions that define the US relationship (AUKUS, basing access, China-threat framing). The practical range of choice on those questions is narrower than the Embassy’s language implies.  

Both societies regulate religious practice to varying degrees; China maintains tighter control over organised religion and unregistered groups. Australia’s legal framework is more permissive, but the Embassy’s claim of unrestricted choice is again absolute rather than comparative.  

The post equates alliance membership with domestic liberty. The Force Posture Agreement, AUKUS industrial and basing arrangements, and the absence of a major-party alternative to the US-aligned model are structural features independent of the free-speech or voting differences between Australia and China. China’s primary engagement with Australia remains economic (largest trading partner); kinetic hostile intent toward Australian territory has not been expressed. The Embassy’s framing converts a strategic policy choice into a values binary while omitting the sovereignty and entanglement costs documented by Australian diplomats and the public AUKUS inquiry.

The map and text therefore function as alliance messaging that projects an idealised domestic freedom onto the United States and Australia while erasing both Australia’s actual speech constraints and the limited electoral alternatives on the strategic questions that define the relationship.

What to Delegate, What to Preserve: Human Preferences for Agentic AI Across Everyday Life and Work : https://t.co/0MGgKNV2Nw

"06 Nov 2026
What to Delegate, What to Preserve: Human Preferences for Agentic AI Across Everyday Life and Work
DOI: XXXXXXX.XXXXXXXConference: Make sure to enter the correct conference title from your rights confirmation email; June 03–05, 2018; Woodstock, NYISBN: 978-1-4503-XXXX-X/2018/06CCS: Human-centered computing Empirical studies in HCICCS: Human-centered computing HCI theory, concepts and modelsSarah Wheelerswhee5@illinois.eduUniversity of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, Illinois, USAVeronica Rammouzveronica.rammouz@utsa.eduUniversity of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, Texas, USAYaoyao Qianqian.ya@northeastern.eduNortheastern University, Boston, Massachusetts, USAZexuan Liuzexuanl5@illinois.eduUniversity of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Champaign, Illinois, USAMengyi Weimengyi.wei@tum.deTechnical University of Munich, München, GermanyAnthony Riosanthony.rios@utsa.eduUniversity of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, Texas, USATianzhi Hetianzhi.he@utsa.eduUniversity of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, Texas, USAKyrie Zhoukyrie.zhou@utsa.eduUniversity of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, Texas, USA2026Abstract.
AI agents can execute multi-step tasks on users’ behalf, yet the boundaries of acceptable delegation remain unclear. We report a scenario-based survey of 289 U.S. adults with prior AI experience covering 45 use cases across nine life domains. Each respondent evaluated one scenario per domain, producing repeated measures of automation preference, trust, collaboration, AI leadership, privacy concern, and willingness to pay. Automation preferences varied substantially across domains. Generalized estimating equation models showed that greater trust in the AI agent, desired AI leadership, prior task-specific AI use, and anticipated financial savings were associated with greater automation preference. In contrast, concerns that automation would reduce personal fulfillment predicted lower automation preference. Open-ended responses further revealed a preference for bounded autonomy, with participants often favoring substantial AI execution while retaining human involvement, oversight, or final authority. We argue that delegation is best understood as a configuration of execution, collaboration, leadership, and authority.Agentic AI, Task delegation, Automation preferences, Human-AI collaborationKeywords:

1.Introduction
It is 7:40 AM on a Tuesday morning. Before Maya finishes her coffee, an AI agent has drafted a reply to her landlord’s recent email, rebooked a cheaper flight for her sister’s wedding, flagged a streaming subscription she forgot to cancel, and proposed a dinner recipe built around the vegetables wilting in her refrigerator. She approves all four with a tap. But when the same agent offers to turn yesterday’s bullet-points in her therapy journal into a full entry, adjust her blood-pressure medication schedule from last night’s readings, and negotiate a pay adjustment with her manager, she hesitates. The delegation that felt like relief just moments earlier now feels like a loss of judgment, of privacy, and of something that was supposed to be hers to do.This scenario is no longer confined to speculation or science fiction. Large language model (LLM)-based agents can already plan and execute multi-step tasks such as booking travel and completing online payments (He et al., 2025), and they are being deployed in socioeconomic roles, from autonomously operating a small store (Anthropic, 2025) to negotiating purchases on consumers’ behalf (Zhu et al., 2025). Meanwhile, generative AI has become a technology of everyday life rather than of work alone as more than 70% of ChatGPT conversations now concern non-work matters such as practical guidance and personal writing (Chatterji et al., 2025). Yet, the public is deeply ambivalent about this trajectory. Half of U.S. adults report being more concerned than excited about AI in daily life, and a majority say they want more control over how AI is used in their lives (Pew Research Center, 2025). Early evidence on the psychosocial consequences of everyday AI use, such as shifts in loneliness and emotional dependence (Fang et al., 2025; Heffner et al., 2025), as well as changed perceptions of one’s own productivity and accomplishment (Kobiella et al., 2024), suggests that this ambivalence is not irrational caution.Prior research offers partial answers to the question of which parts of life people are willing to hand over to AI agents, and why they might do so, though from each specific domain respectively. Prior work shows that reliance on AI agents depends strongly on the task, tending to be higher for objective tasks and lower for subjective or personally consequential ones (Castelo et al., 2019; Dietvorst et al., 2015; Logg et al., 2019; Longoni et al., 2019). Much of prior work, however, predates AI agents capable of completing entire activities end-to-end. The trust-in-automation literature explains when people rely on machine assistance (Lee and See, 2004; Hoff and Bashir, 2015), but focuses on settings where the human remains the decision maker and the AI advises (Bansal et al., 2021; Sivaraman et al., 2023). Task-level audits of automation preferences are confined to occupational work (Shao et al., 2025; Lubars and Tan, 2019). Privacy research documents how users navigate disclosure to LLM-based systems (Zhang et al., 2024; Leon et al., 2013), and technology-acceptance research examines perceived usefulness, effort expectancy, and price value (Davis, 1989; Venkatesh et al., 2012). However, privacy risks and economic benefits are rarely measured together, for the same task, from the same person. Delegating an activity to an AI agent, however, is precisely a joint decision as it bundles beliefs about competence and trust, exposure of personal data, economic value, and the meaning of doing the activity oneself into a single choice (Lubars and Tan, 2019; Draxler et al., 2024).To address these gaps, we ask three research questions:•RQ1. How do preferences for AI automation vary across everyday and work domains, and which task-level and respondent-level factors are associated with greater willingness to delegate tasks to AI?
•RQ2. How do people compare AI agents, human workers, and human-AI teams in terms of trust, and how do preferences for collaboration and AI leadership relate to desired levels of automation?
•RQ3. How do people want AI involvement to be configured when they are willing to delegate a task, particularly with respect to execution, collaboration, oversight, and decision authority?To answer these questions, we conducted a scenario-based survey (N=289) covering 45 AI-agent use cases across nine domains of daily life: household management, workplace, travel, physical health, mental health and emotional support, learning, creative work, communication, and personal finance. Each respondent evaluated one randomly selected scenario from every domain under an identical set of measures, including prior experience and enjoyment, automation desire and preferences, required collaboration, comparative trust, willingness to pay, and privacy and interest-alignment concerns, yielding a repeated-measures design that supports comparisons across domains, tasks, and individuals.Based on the quantitative and qualitative analysis of collected responses from the survey, we found that across domains, automation preferences were task-dependent, with greater willingness to delegate communication and travel activities and lower preferences in mental health, physical health, and professional contexts. In multivariable analyses, greater trust in the AI agent, desired AI leadership, prior task-specific AI use, and anticipated financial savings were associated with greater automation preference, whereas concerns that automation would reduce personal fulfillment link to lower automation preference. Although privacy concerns varied substantially across domains, they were not independently associated with automation after adjustment. Open-ended responses further showed that participants often favored bounded autonomy: AI could execute substantial portions of a task while humans retained involvement, oversight, or final decision authority.This paper makes three contributions. First, we contribute what is, to our knowledge, the first systematic within-user comparison of AI-agent automation preferences spanning both work and everyday life, extending task-level auditing beyond occupational settings (Shao et al., 2025) to the domains where most generative AI use now occurs (Chatterji et al., 2025). Second, we provide an empirical account of delegation as a comparative choice, measuring trust in AI agents against human workers and human-AI teams and the division of agency people prefer within those teams. Such dimensions were not yet observed in prior decision-support studies (Bansal et al., 2021; Lee and See, 2004). Third, by jointly eliciting willingness to pay, anticipated financial consequences, and privacy concerns for each task, we provide a task-level account of how economic value and privacy considerations accompany AI delegation, with implications for how such agents should be designed and priced across different domains of everyday life.
2.Related Work
We organize the related work around three areas. First, we review work on how AI systems are entering everyday life and how automation preferences vary across tasks and domains (Section 2.1). Second, we examine prior work on trust, delegation, human-AI collaboration, and the value of continued human involvement (Section 2.2). Lastly, we investigate the privacy and economic considerations that shape people’s willingness to delegate activities to AI agents (Section 2.3). Each subsection concludes by identifying the gap that motivates our study.
https://t.co/E7DyrHDV91 Agents in Everyday Life and Task-Dependent Automation Preferences
Generative AI has moved rapidly from a workplace novelty into the fabric of daily life. Analyzing ChatGPT usage at scale, Chatterji et al. (2025) report that non-work messages now account for more than 70% of all conversations, dominated by practical guidance, information seeking, and writing support. Public sentiment, however, has not kept pace with adoption: in a 2025 Pew Research Center survey, half of U.S. adults said they were more concerned than excited about AI in daily life, and a majority wanted more control over how AI is used in their lives (Pew Research Center, 2025). Empirical studies have also examined how AI use affects different areas of everyday life. Longitudinal and experimental studies link chatbot use to changes in loneliness, emotional dependence, and momentary well-being  (Fang et al., 2025; Heffner et al., 2025), and AI assistance has been shown to reshape interpersonal communication  (Hohenstein et al., 2023), enhance creative ideation (Lee and Chung, 2024), affect teaching and learning (Singh and Hiran, 2022), and alter customer-service experiences (Nguyen et al., 2022).On the other hand, people’s willingness to delegate activities to AI varies considerably by task. Classic work on algorithmic judgment shows that people become less willing to rely on algorithms after seeing them err, even when the algorithms continue to outperform humans (algorithm aversion (Dietvorst et al., 2015)), while other studies document the opposite tendency, with people weighting algorithmic advice more heavily than human advice (Logg et al., 2019). Task characteristics reconcile much of this tension: people rely less on algorithms for tasks they construe as subjective rather than objective (Castelo et al., 2019), and they resist medical AI in part because they fear it will neglect their unique circumstances (Longoni et al., 2019). Attitude surveys echo this context dependence. Risk and opportunity perceptions, and consequently willingness to use AI, differ markedly across domains such as medicine, mobility, and media (Schwesig et al., 2023); use intention is predicted better by context-specific evaluations than by global attitudes or familiarity (Potinteu et al., 2023); and the public separates into distinct attitudinal segments with different perceptions of AI’s risks and benefits (Bao et al., 2022).Recent work has extended this task-level approach to larger sets of activities. Shao et al. (2025) audited automation and augmentation preferences across 844 occupational tasks in 104 U.S. professions, finding that workers most often prefer an equal partnership with AI agents and want higher levels of human agency than experts consider technically necessary for nearly half of the tasks. Such audits demonstrate the value of comparing many concrete tasks under a common instrument. However, its focus remains confined to paid work and occupational settings, while usage data indicate that most engagement with generative AI now occurs outside of work (Chatterji et al., 2025).Prior work has characterized either broad attitudes toward AI within single domains or task-level preferences within occupational settings, using instruments that vary from study to study. What is still missing is a systematic, within-user comparison of concrete AI-agent use cases across multiple domains of everyday life. Our survey addresses this gap by eliciting evaluations of 45 scenarios spanning nine life domains, from household management and travel to mental health and personal finance, under a common set of measures, enabling automation preferences to be compared across domains and tasks while accounting for differences between individual users.
https://t.co/qbVlok5rLH, Delegation, and Human-AI Collaboration
Trust has long been treated as a critical factor shaping the reliance on automation. Foundational accounts describe trust as the mechanism by which people decide when reliance is appropriate under uncertainty (Lee and See, 2004), shaped by dispositional, situational, and learned factors that vary across users, systems, and situations (Hoff and Bashir, 2015), as well as by the perceived humanness of the technology itself (Lankton et al., 2015). Previous HCI research has broadly examined how system design affects reliance in AI-assisted decision-making: Explanations can increase reliance on AI recommendations without improving joint accuracy, particularly when users follow erroneous AI advice (Bansal et al., 2021), while cognitive forcing functions can mitigate such overreliance at some cost to user experience, making the interaction less convenient or satisfactory (Buçinca et al., 2021). Domain studies further complicate a binary picture of acceptance, that reliance is often selective rather than all-or-nothing. Clinicians “negotiate” with AI treatment recommendations, adopting some components while rejecting or deferring others (Sivaraman et al., 2023), and a deployed LLM-driven care-call chatbot both eased public-health workloads and surfaced mismatches between system capabilities and stakeholder needs (Jo et al., 2023). In healthcare more broadly, scenario-based surveys show that acceptance rises when AI is framed as assisting rather than replacing human professionals (Antes et al., 2021; Longoni et al., 2019).Delegating an entire task to an agent, however, is a different act from taking advice, as the system may also plan and carry out actions on the user’s behalf. Frameworks of task delegability propose that motivation, difficulty, risk, and trust jointly determine which tasks people are willing to hand over (Lubars and Tan, 2019). As LLM-based agents become capable of planning and executing multi-step tasks, researchers have begun to probe such delegation empirically: in a study of 248 participants using an LLM agent as a daily assistant for tasks ranging from flight booking to online payments, the quality of the agent’s plan and the user’s involvement in execution shaped trust, trust calibration, and team performance (He et al., 2025). Recent deployments also illustrate the risks of autonomous execution. When an LLM agent autonomously operated a small store for a month, it hallucinated payment details, priced items below cost, and was easily talked into unwarranted discounts (Anthropic, 2025). Agent-to-agent negotiation experiments likewise show that consumers who delegate transactions to weaker models can incur systematic financial disadvantages (Zhu et al., 2025).Delegation also carries consequences for the delegator. Users who publish AI-ghostwritten text report a diminished sense of ownership over it (Draxler et al., 2024). Young professionals describe ChatGPT-supported work as undermining perceived productivity and accomplishment when it removes challenge and authorship (Kobiella et al., 2024). Generative AI imposes new metacognitive demands of monitoring, prompting, and verification (Tankelevitch et al., 2024); and knowledge workers who place more confidence in AI report investing less critical-thinking effort (Lee et al., 2025). These findings resonate with long-standing evidence that intrinsic motivation and the experience of performing an activity are themselves sources of value (Amabile, 1996). Delegation may therefore reduce some of the value users derive from an activity even when the task is completed successfully.Most prior work has examined trust and reliance in settings where the human remains the decision maker and the AI assists on researcher-selected tasks. Comparative judgments, i.e., how much people trust an AI agent versus a human worker versus a human-AI team performing the same activity, and preferences over the division of agency within such teams, have rarely been elicited and received limited attention, particularly outside the workplace settings. Our survey addresses this gap by measuring, for every scenario, trust in an AI agent, a human worker, and a human-AI team; the desired degree of AI leadership in collaborative execution; the amount of human collaboration respondents believe the task requires; and concerns that automation may reduce the value or fulfillment derived from performing an activity oneself.
2.3.Privacy, Economic Value, and the Costs of Delegation
Delegating everyday activities to AI agents often requires giving them access to personal information, making privacy an important part of the delegation decision. Privacy-calculus accounts model disclosure as a tradeoff between anticipated benefits and perceived risks (Dinev and Hart, 2006), and contextual-integrity theory emphasizes that the appropriateness of an information flow depends on the norms of the social sphere in which it occurs (Nissenbaum, 2004), suggesting that the same data practice may be acceptable in one life domain and alarming in another. Empirically, willingness to share information hinges on data-handling practices such as retention and scope of use (Leon et al., 2013), while perceived security risk dampens smart-home adoption indirectly through attitudes and perceived behavioral control, with effects that are stronger among older and more educated consumers (Klobas et al., 2019). Research on LLM-based conversational agents raises similar concerns: users disclose sensitive information to chatbots while holding flawed mental models of how that information is used, resigning themselves to disclosure as a “fair game” for the utility they receive (Zhang et al., 2024), and researchers have begun building user-led data-minimization tools in response (Zhou et al., 2025).Apart from privacy concern, users also care whether the AI agents act in their interests when they delegate tasks to them. An agent may be competent yet optimized toward a platform provider’s engagement or commercial goals rather than the user’s interests, and even well-intentioned optimization can misfire: training language models to be warmer and more empathetic makes them less reliable and more sycophantic, particularly toward vulnerable users (Ibrahim et al., 2025). How laypeople reason about such provider-user misalignment when deciding whether to adopt an agent remains less explored.Economic value may also shape the delegation decision. Classic acceptance models identify perceived usefulness and effort expectancy as principal drivers of technology adoption (Davis, 1989; Venkatesh et al., 2003). Consumer-oriented extensions further incorporate price value, reflecting the tradeoff between perceived benefits and monetary costs (Venkatesh et al., 2012). Yet finding a service useful is not the same as being willing to pay for it, and the value of automating a task plausibly depends on what the task currently costs in time, money, and effort, as well as on whether automation replaces an existing paid service or introduces a new recurring expense. Prior work offers limited evidence on how much economic value people actually assign to automating specific activities, and on how one-time or subscription-style pricing interacts with those valuations.These three considerations, i.e., privacy, provider alignment, and economic value, have often been studied separately, making it difficult to understand how they jointly relate to delegation decisions at the level of individual tasks. Our survey addresses this gap by measuring for each scenario, anticipated savings and added expenses, willingness to pay through a one-time purchase and a monthly subscription, concerns about third-party data sharing and preference profiling, and perceptions of provider-user alignment. These measures allow us to examine how privacy concerns, perceived provider alignment, and anticipated economic costs and benefits relate to people’s willingness to delegate everyday activities to AI agents.

after that, it became a routine.

almost every night, there was something outside my door.

rice, chicken, soup, pastries, sometimes even freshly baked bread.

i wasn't complaining. it was actually thoughtful.

but after a while, i noticed something strange.

linda never seemed to eat the food herself.

whenever i visited her, she would offer me water or biscuits, but she never served any of the meals she supposedly enjoyed preparing.

one evening, i casually asked her why she kept bringing me food.

she smiled and said, "you remind me of someone."

i asked who.

she simply replied, "someone i lost a long time ago."

i didn't push further.

then, one night, i decided to check my security camera because i wanted to know exactly when she dropped the food.

what i saw made my stomach turn.

linda wasn't just dropping food at my doorstep.

she was standing there for several minutes, staring directly at my front door.

then she would quietly whisper something before walking away.

text:
🏆 PREMIER LEAGUE TEAM OF THE SEASON SO FAR | 2026/27

10 games played. This is my team so far, built around a 4-4-2 diamond.

🧤 Raya
🛡️ De Cuyper | Konsa | Gabriel | Calafiori
⚙️ Rice
🎯 Groß | Mac Allister
🎨 Morgan Rogers
⚡ Haaland | João Pedro

👔 Manager: Mikel Arteta

THE TACTICAL BREAKDOWN
🧤 David Raya: The first playmaker
Raya is more than a shot-stopper. His distribution helps initiate possession, attract the opposition press and find defenders or midfielders in positions where they can progress the ball. His positioning also allows the defensive line to hold a higher starting position.

🛡️ Maxim De Cuyper: Width and attacking progression
De Cuyper provides natural width on the left. His overlapping runs stretch opposition defences and create space for the left-sided midfielder to move inside. His ability to deliver from wide areas gives the team another route into the box.

🛡️ Ezri Konsa: Defensive security
Konsa provides recovery pace, positional discipline and the ability to defend space behind an advancing full-back. He is particularly important when the team loses possession and needs to protect against counter-attacks.

🛡️ Gabriel: The aggressive defender
Gabriel brings front-foot defending, aerial dominance and physicality. He can step out to challenge forwards receiving between the lines, while his presence at set pieces adds another attacking weapon.

🛡️ Riccardo Calafiori: The defensive technician
Calafiori offers something different. He can step into midfield, carry the ball through pressure and create numerical superiority in central areas. His movement gives the team flexibility, particularly when De Cuyper advances on the opposite side.

⚙️ Declan Rice: The engine and defensive anchor
Rice is the most important structural player in this diamond. He protects the centre-backs, covers the spaces left by advancing full-backs, wins second balls and drives possession forward.

He also gives Groß and Mac Allister the freedom to operate higher up the pitch without compromising the team's defensive balance.

🎯 Pascal Groß: The tempo controller
Groß brings intelligence to the right-sided midfield position. He understands when to retain possession, when to switch play and when to release runners. His positioning and passing range help move opposition blocks from side to side.

🎯 Alexis Mac Allister: The progressive midfielder
Mac Allister provides verticality. He can receive under pressure, turn into space, break opposition lines and arrive around the edge of the penalty area. His ability to combine in tight spaces makes him particularly useful when the diamond overloads the centre.

🎨 Morgan Rogers: The creative connector
Rogers operates as the number 10. His ability to receive between the opposition midfield and defence, turn on the ball and carry possession at speed makes him difficult to contain.

He can draw defenders out of position, combine with the strikers or attack the space himself. He is the link between the midfield structure and the attacking threat.

⚡ Erling Haaland: The penalty-box reference
Haaland gives this team a permanent threat in behind. His movement pins centre-backs, stretches defensive lines and creates space for Rogers and João Pedro to operate.

He attacks the near post, threatens the space between defenders and turns half-chances into goals. The team does not need to dominate possession to create opportunities for him.

⚡ João Pedro: The intelligent partner
João Pedro complements Haaland because he does not need to occupy the same spaces.

He can drop between the lines, link midfield to attack, drift into wider channels and draw defenders away from Haaland. His movement creates uncertainty for centre-backs who must decide whether to follow him or protect the space behind.

WHY Mikel Arteta?
I seriously considered Fabian Hürzeler. His work at Brighton deserves recognition, but Arteta gets my vote.

His understanding of positional structure, defensive organisation, pressing mechanisms and in-game control gives him the edge.

THE BIGGER TACTICAL PICTURE
This diamond is designed to dominate the centre of the pitch.

Rice provides the security. Groß and Mac Allister control progression. Rogers creates between the lines, while Haaland and João Pedro offer complementary attacking movements.

The full-backs provide the width that the narrow midfield cannot naturally supply.

However, there is a vulnerability: defending wide transitions. If both full-backs advance simultaneously, Rice can be exposed across too much ground. The centre-backs must also be comfortable defending large spaces.

That is the trade-off of playing a diamond. You gain central superiority but must work harder to protect the flanks.

For me, this is a team built on tactical complementarity rather than simply selecting the biggest names.

Who makes your Premier League Team of the Season so far? 👀

text:
In 2015, India pushed 266 crore litres of ethanol through 111 depots.

Today: 1,050 crore litres through 127.

4x the ethanol. Almost the same depots.

Karnataka says its lab found 31% ethanol in petrol. Oil companies say 19.3%.

Someone's test is wrong. Who's checking the 127?

Here's what most people don't know about the E20 in their tank 👇

Ethanol is not mixed at your petrol pump.

Distilleries send it by tanker to oil-company depots. It's blended into petrol at the loading gantry, and that fuel then goes out to every pump in the region.

127 locations. 247 depot points run by IOCL, BPCL, HPCL and MRPL.

That's the entire chokepoint for India's ethanol programme.

Now look at how the load has changed:

2015-16: 111 locations, 266 crore litres. About 2.4 crore litres per location.

2025-26: 127 locations, 1,050 crore litres. About 8.3 crore litres per location.

Each location now handles roughly 3.5x more ethanol than a decade ago. 

The tankage, the moisture control, the gantry calibration and the quality checks all have to keep up with that.

So when the blend goes wrong, it doesn't go wrong at one pump. It goes wrong for an entire region.

Now the fight.

Karnataka says a private lab tested petrol from Bengaluru, Kolar, Tumakuru, Mangaluru and other districts and found 20.6% to 31.2% ethanol.

IOCL, BPCL and HPCL reject this. They say the samples weren't collected under the official procedure, the lab isn't an approved one, and 893 samples across 27 states all came in at 19–21%.

Then BPCL posted a test to prove its fuel was fine, and deleted it within hours after people spotted what looked like ~33% in its own image.

Here's the part nobody is talking about:

The ministry tested at depots and refineries in September.
Karnataka tested at retail pumps in October.

They didn't test the same fuel at the same point. Both sides could be telling the truth, and you'd still have no idea what's in your tank.

Meanwhile, on the supply side:

India has built about 2,000 crore litres of ethanol capacity. E20 needs about 1,100.

Only about 60% of ethanol offered is being bought.

Plants that invested on the promise of long-term offtake lost their preferential allocation this year. That fight is now in the Supreme Court.

Too much ethanol, too few depots, and no independent check in between.

The fix costs almost nothing:

→ Print the blend percentage on every pump
→ Joint state and oil-company testing at the depot and at the pump
→ Publish depot-level quality data, location by location
Until that happens, "E20" is just a sticker you're asked to trust.

As a Side effect Sugar , Maize and Rice prices are up 40% hurting plates of low income population

I was therefore forced to sleep by the door of the NA office at the airport, waiting for the release of the manifest list with my name on it.

I was not alone. There were hundreds of stranded passengers like me there—men, women, young, old, tall, short, thin fat—all sorts of people.
The Murtala Mohamed Airport was different then than what we have now.
There were no security officers. People drifted in and out in their hundreds. It was rowdy. There was no order of any sort. Food hawkers milled among the crowd of the stranded passengers like me, selling hot dogs, sandwiches, puff-puff, moin-moin, gala, meat pie, hamburgers, even rice and dodo.
People hawked sodas such as Cocacola, Fanta, Sprite and malt drinks.

The interior of the airport was packed like the Oyingbo market. There were also pickpockets and other fraudsters pulling fast tricks on unsuspecting victims.
 I was hesitant to buy anything. I had changed all my naira to dollars at the rate of one dollar to three naira. But if I wanted to change my dollar back to naira, I could only collect one naira for my dollar at the airport, which would be a loss.

I was desperate when I got hungry. But someone was willing to give me two naira for a dollar, so I changed two dollars. I bought some moin-moin and coke.

The guys who helped me to change my money said I had no hope of traveling unless I was willing to bribe someone.

I was adamant. I wasn’t going to bribe anybody. It was my right to fly out, after all, I had paid for my ticket.

By day four, I lost hope of traveling out. I used my handbag as my pillow and reclined on the floor, to take a nap.
The young woman who slept a couple of feet away from me was also napping, snoring loudly. I asked her earlier, and she said she had been there for almost a week. She said she was ready at that point to accept the offer of a Nigeria Airways official who wanted sex in exchange for helping her to get on the manifest list.

For how long I had been asleep I couldn’t tell, when I felt a tap on my shoulder. I opened my eyes. It was Segun Odegbami, the famous international soccer star, who played for the Green Eagles. I thought I was dreaming. I had met him through a friend, Tunde Fagbenle, and we had shared drinks at Fagbenle’s house in Lagos a couple of times.

I couldn’t refer to him as my friend, and I didn’t even know he would recognize me or remember my name.
I was a fat nobody next to a big star like him, someone for whom Ebenezer Obey had waxed an album, with the chorus, “It is a gooooal, Odegbami,” a bestselling song throughout Nigeria.
When I opened my eyes and it was him, I wanted to close my eyes back, thinking I was just dreaming.

But he spoke to me. “Moyo, what are you doing on the floor here?”
I quickly sat up, wiped my eyes, and smile at him. I narrated my story.
He shook his head, and said with a sigh, “That’s Nigeria Airways for you. I came to see someone off to London, and as I was leaving I happened to see you.”

text:
This is why I don’t like employing people I know.

A while ago, I posted on my WhatsApp status that I urgently needed a PA. A family friend reached out and said she wanted the job. I told her no—I couldn’t employ someone I know. I wanted a stranger so I could properly hold them accountable, because every PA I’d hired in the past had ended up stealing from me.

She insisted she doesn’t mix pleasure with business and that she really needed the job. I still hesitated, so I spoke to my dad (and she also involved her parents). They basically told me to just do it for her since she’s a family friend and the money would help her. I agreed and offered her ₦150k a month.

She started working. Around that time I wasn’t going out much and was mostly at home. She’d come, and there wasn’t always much for her to do as a PA. I asked if she could cook. She said yes. The rice she made was good, so I told her she could add cooking to her duties sometimes (not every day). It was basically just me, her, and my brother who is usually home. Because of that, I increased her salary to ₦250k.

Most of the time I was in my room, so she barely even saw me. One day I heard her shouting. She said a scorpion had bitten her. I was shocked—I don’t live in the bush; we live in a proper estate that gets fumigated. She claimed it happened when she went to wear my Crocs. I tried to help and even used ChatGPT to figure out what to do. They took her to the hospital. I sent money, but after about five days she still hadn’t properly updated me. When I finally reached her, she said she was fine.

Then she called and said she wanted to see me. Before taking my job, she had been submitting CVs. One company had gotten back to her. She basically told me she was leaving for the other job. I told her okay, just go. I even gave her transport fare because she said she didn’t have any to come to work (despite the ₦250k salary and food).

After she left, she called again saying she didn’t actually get the other job. Her mom then started calling me, asking me to help pay her child’s school fees. At that point I was done.

text:
There's a job in America where $4 an hour would be a raise.

It's waiting tables. In Texas, Georgia, Tennessee, Virginia and about a dozen other states, a restaurant can legally pay a server $2.13 an hour, and that number hasn't changed since 1991.

So what about the AI interviewer in this video offering $4 an hour? It depends on the job. For a fast food crew spot, $4 is illegal everywhere, because the federal minimum is $7.25. For a server job in one of those states, the restaurant is offering almost double the legal base pay. Tips are supposed to make up the rest, and if they don't get you to $7.25, the restaurant has to cover the difference.

The server wage used to go up on its own. Before 1996 it was tied to half the regular minimum, so whenever Congress raised the minimum wage, servers got a raise too. Then the National Restaurant Association, which Herman Cain was running at the time, went to Congress with a deal. They'd stop fighting the minimum wage increase as long as the tipped wage stayed put. Congress went for it and Clinton signed the bill that August.

Nobody in Washington has touched that number since.

The regular minimum wage has gone up five times since 1991, from $4.25 to $7.25, and tipped workers didn't get a penny of any of it. Adjust 1991's $2.13 for inflation and it's worth about $5 today. So the $4 offer in this clip is less than what a server's base pay was worth 35 years ago.

While pay stayed frozen, restaurants went all in on automating hiring. McDonald's hires over a million hourly workers a year in the US, and about 90% of its franchisees screen applicants through an AI chatbot called Olivia. In 2025, two security researchers got into the admin side of that system by typing 123456 as both the username and the password. Behind it were 64 million applicant records.

So we've got AI screening people for jobs where the legal minimum was set the same year the first website went live.

The rest of the story, in one place.

The Harvard → UCLA years
LA Times (2003, citing Rolling Stone): Princeton dropout, master's from Harvard's Kennedy School, researched drug trends in Russia, followed Mark Kleiman to UCLA. UCLA: contract employee Apr 1999 to Sep 2000, deputy director of its Drug Policy Analysis Program. Prosecutors dated the LSD conspiracy Aug 1999 to Nov 2000.

The fentanyl claim, checked
"He predicted fentanyl and RAND cited it." Here's what's real: RAND's 2019 report "The Future of Fentanyl and Other Synthetic Opioids" says it drew on his 1996 Harvard presentation, "Factors Promoting the Spread of Fentanyl Manufacture," then "modified and added to his original list." A real, substantive citation. "Predicted the epidemic" is his bio's framing, not RAND's. https://t.co/z5wncIpWX2

The irony the court named
In 2020 the government called his fentanyl work "praiseworthy," then said it was "ironic" to offer it as grounds for release, given what he was doing at the same time. The judge agreed and set it aside.

The book
"The Rose of Paracelsus: On Secrets & Sacraments": first out in 2015 (Sub Rosa Press), then a 654-page Synergetic Press edition in 2022. The publisher says it was "handwritten over four years from maximum-security federal prison cells" and calls it a "psychedelic biography." It's not a court document, and it doesn't claim to be.

"The Six"
The book centers on a secret circle of LSD chemists with color names (Indigo, Magenta, Crimson among them). Real people? Composites? Allegory? In a 2017 interview, the editor wrote that Pickard "for legal reasons" couldn't comment on the fact/fiction question. I read the Six as literature. Nothing I found in the court record confirms them.

The viral lab-accident story
The one going around: a broken flask, a huge accidental exposure, a night in the New Mexico desert. Source: Pickard himself, in interviews. No police, medical, or court record I could find. The "1998" date mostly comes from retellings. In the book, the spill happens to the character Indigo. I'm not repeating the dose. Nobody measured it.

After prison, by source
• Harvard Law's Petrie-Flom Center listed him as a POPLAR (Project on Psychedelics Law and Regulation) affiliated researcher. Its page now says "Former."
• JLS Fund's team page: "Advisor." His own site: "Science Officer."
• Fireside Project: advisor per his site. I didn't find him on Fireside's team page.

About Fireside itself
It runs a free psychedelic peer-support line (62-FIRESIDE). On Oct 30, 2026, it published a peer-reviewed Science Advances paper on 25,419 support interactions handled by 220 trained peer supporters. https://t.co/1xxeVx0VpZ

My read
Strip out the legend and it's still one of the strangest documented arcs in drug policy: a 1996 fentanyl framework for Harvard fellows, a UCLA drug-policy job held during the same years as the LSD conspiracy a jury convicted him of, 20 years of a life sentence, a book in pencil.

The court record shows what was proven. His own record shows how he wants it read. I keep them apart.

A new framework called carbon at risk (CaR) offers a quantitative way to assess the risk that carbon removal projects fail to deliver their contracted storage over a specified period.

Inspired by financial value-at-risk measures, it estimates potential shortfalls at a given confidence level and time horizon. In proof-of-concept applications, Monte Carlo simulations using satellite fire data show that a single forest carbon project in California has a 95% CaR exceeding 70% over 200 years.

For geological storage, estimates range from 0.15% for well-regulated offshore storage to 17% for poorly regulated onshore sites. The authors also show how combining different removal technologies in portfolios can help manage permanence risks. CaR could provide a common basis for setting buffer requirements, pricing insurance and designing reserve funds across carbon removal pathways.
