text:
$BRSL Q3 2026 earnings: Brightstar Lottery equipment sales jump, but it cuts full-year outlook

Brightstar Lottery, which runs government lotteries and supplies ticket machines, met its third-quarter profit goal thanks to equipment shipments, while ticket buying at stores declined. Reported revenue fell 4% to $607 million because of higher non-cash charges for its Italian Lotto license, though sales excluding those license charges rose 4% by our math as machine and instant-ticket shipments more than doubled. Chief executive Vince Sadusky cut the full-year revenue plan by $80 million at the middle of the range, which by our math leaves fourth-quarter reported sales flat against last year.

• Revenue excluding license amortization: +𝟑.𝟓% (from a year ago (reported revenue $607M, -4%))
• Same-store ticket wagers: -𝟑.𝟗% (from a year ago in constant currency)
• Adjusted EBITDA: $𝟐𝟖𝟗𝐌 (-2% from a year ago (47.5% margin))
• Full-year revenue outlook: 𝐂𝐮𝐭 $𝟖𝟎𝐌 (middle of the range: $2.445B)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because the long-warned risk to the second-half sales plan came true. Management gave up on its target of more than 5% full-year underlying growth, blaming slower store wagers, delayed Italian online launches, and a weaker euro, while everyday scratcher and draw games shrank in both the U. S. and Italy. On the plus side, cost cuts and high-margin equipment sales lifted the Adjusted EBITDA margin to 47.5% and kept the $750 million operating cash flow plan intact.

The question now is whether the drop in store wagers is just a tough comparison against last year's big Powerball jackpots or a wider slowdown in everyday ticket buying and Italian digital rollouts. If it is only jackpot luck and currency, underlying growth should rebound once the Italian license charge stops rising next year; if everyday games stay weak, the company's 2028 targets are at risk. Fourth-quarter instant-ticket wagers and Italian digital sales will settle it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 𝐄𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐨𝐟𝐭𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫
Brightstar runs lotteries for governments and sells them ticket machines, printed instant tickets and software. Finance chief Max Chiara said "Operational growth drivers are contributing at an accelerated pace, reinforcing our medium-term growth outlook." Excluding the accounting charge for its upfront Italian license fee, revenue rose 3.5% from a year ago by our math.

Equipment and instant-ticket sales more than doubled to $60 million from $25 million a year ago. Other service revenue, which comes from software services for new contracts outside the U. S. and Italy, grew 11% to $121 million. Those two lines added $48 million of sales, enough to overcome weaker ticket buying at lottery shops and keep third-quarter revenue at $607 million.

What to watch: fourth-quarter product sales against last year's $57 million result. Because machine deliveries come in lumps, a drop back to normal levels would leave Brightstar leaning on store ticket sales that are currently shrinking.

🟢 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐂𝐮𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐄𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐌𝐢𝐱 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧
Brightstar tracks Adjusted EBITDA — profit before interest, taxes, depreciation, and upfront license amortization — to measure ongoing operations, along with a cost-cutting program called OPtiMa. Even though reported revenue fell 3.5%, Adjusted EBITDA dipped only 1.7% to $289 million, and the Adjusted EBITDA margin rose 0.8 percentage points to 47.5%.

A richer mix of equipment sales and OPtiMa cost cuts protected that margin. The cost of product sales rose from 4.9% to 7.4% of total revenue because machine shipments more than doubled, but fell from 124% to 75% of product revenue by our math. Meanwhile, Reported EBIT margin excluding one-offs fell 8.0 percentage points to 21.4% because Brightstar absorbed an extra $46 million of Italian Lotto license amortization.

What to watch: full-year OPtiMa savings realized at year-end against the $70 million target for 2026. Hitting that mark is necessary to offset the $50 million management is spending on new growth projects.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐁𝐫𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐅𝐮𝐥𝐥-𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧
"Revenue and profit were in line with our expectations," chief executive Vince Sadusky said. Yet on the same day, Brightstar lowered its full-year revenue forecast by $80 million at the middle of the range and dropped its promise of more than 5% underlying sales growth for the full year.

• Full-year revenue outlook: cut to $2.435–2.455 billion from $2.50–2.55 billion
• Operational growth target: reset to mid-single digits for the second half, down from over 5% for the full year
• Implied fourth-quarter revenue: $667 million at the middle of the range, flat against $668 million a year ago by our math

The company blamed the cut on "updated second half same-store sales expectations, timing of certain Italy B2C expansion efforts, and FX impact". For two quarters the old outlook required a big fourth-quarter jump in store wagers and Italian online games, and this cut confirms those projects and ticket sales are running behind schedule.

What to watch: fourth-quarter revenue excluding license fee amortization, which by our math needs to grow about 4% to hit the new midpoint. A miss against that lowered bar would show that core demand is still weakening heading into 2027.

🔴🔴 𝐉𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐩𝐨𝐭 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐩 𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐚 𝐖𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐢𝐜𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧
Same-store sales measure lottery ticket wagers in constant currency at locations Brightstar already served a year ago. Three months ago, the lottery operator expected third-quarter same-store sales to match last year, but instead they fell 3.9%.

Brightstar said wagers fell "primarily due to U. S. multi-state jackpot performance", as big Powerball and Mega Millions games dropped 30.6% against last year's $1.8 billion jackpot run. However, everyday instant scratchers and draw games also shrank 1.0% globally, falling 1.4% in the U. S. and 1.2% in Italy after growing in the first half.

What to watch: fourth-quarter instant ticket and draw same-store sales in the U. S. and Italy. A second straight drop in everyday games would mean the slump reaches beyond bad jackpot luck.

🔴 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐬 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐧 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐀𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬
Brightstar pitches itself as a reliable cash payer and returned $204 million through dividends and share buybacks through November 9. However, the U. K.-based group owns 61.5% of its Italian Lotto joint venture while recording 100% of the venture's operating cash flow on its books, so it must pay out the other 38.5% to its minority partners.

Over the first nine months of 2026, operating cash flow excluding the upfront Italian license payment was $574 million, and capital spending took $313 million. Paying $259 million in dividends and capital returns to joint-venture partners left just $2 million of cash by our math, so the $189 million of shareholder payouts in the first three quarters pushed net debt up to $3.84 billion, or 3.30 times yearly Adjusted EBITDA.

What to watch: fourth-quarter cash distributions to minority partners on the cash flow statement. Further payouts at the nine-month pace would keep Brightstar borrowing to fund its quarterly dividend until capital spending falls after 2028.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐀𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Brightstar's earnings release and presentation left three standing risks without updated numbers, even though one of them contributed to the full-year revenue cut.

• Online lottery (iLottery) wager growth: not in the release after slowing from 30% in Q1 to 22% for the first half; the call transcript or filing will show if growth cooled further.
• Italy direct-to-consumer (B2C) digital metrics: Brightstar cited B2C timing delays in its outlook cut and noted the launch of its OTTO offer, but gave no user or revenue numbers.
• Contract rebids and pricing: no update in the release on the upcoming Italy Scratch & Win license renewal or pricing pressure in U. S. state system tenders.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐖𝐞𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐫 𝐄𝐮𝐫𝐨 𝐀𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐦𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐫-𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠
Brightstar earns over a third of its revenue in Italy, so a weaker euro hurts its U. S. dollar results. The company cut its fourth-quarter euro assumption from $1.17 to $1.12 and said its lower Adjusted EBITDA forecast was "primarily on updated FX". In September, it also issued €500 million of 4.875% notes due 2032 to pay down €342 million of 2.375% notes due 2028 and €155 million of credit lines.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐒𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐬, 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐬, 𝐧𝐞𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟕𝟔𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Contract assets on the balance sheet rose 12.5% from $678 million at the end of 2025, climbing from $707 million in Q1 and $755 million in Q2. This line tracks lottery terminals and central systems Brightstar installs for state and national lotteries during its 2025–2028 contract renewal cycle, which consumes cash now to lock in multi-year service fees.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟏𝟖𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Diluted shares fell 5.6% from 196 million a year ago and edged down from 187 million in Q1 and 186 million in Q2. The lottery group spent $18 million on buybacks in the third quarter and $77 million through November 9, slowing its repurchase pace after borrowing to pay the final Italian Lotto license installment.

𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐬, 𝐧𝐞𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟒𝟔𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Money owed by customers is down 11.0% from $526 million at the end of December 2025 and roughly even with $466 million in the second quarter. Collecting those bills generated $46 million of operating cash over the first nine months, helping offset $80 million of timing outflows across accounts payable and other liabilities.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟐.𝟒𝟑𝟓–𝟐.𝟒𝟓𝟓 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from $2.50–2.55 billion
Cut. The middle of the range dropped by $80 million, pointing to a 2.6% full-year revenue decline after $175 million of extra Italian Lotto license amortization. By our math, that leaves $667 million for Q4, flat against $668 million a year ago and up about 4.1% excluding license amortization. Management cited weaker second-half store wagers, slower Italy digital rollouts, and a lower euro rate.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $𝟏.𝟏𝟒–𝟏.𝟏𝟔 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from $1.16–1.19 billion
Cut. Brightstar lowered the middle of the profit range by $25 million, leaving full-year Adjusted EBITDA up 2.6% from $1.121 billion in 2025. By our math, that implies $289 million for Q4, down 4.9% from $304 million in last year's fourth quarter and an implied margin of 43.3% against 47.5% in Q3. The company attributed the reduction mainly to the lower euro exchange rate assumption.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬: ~$(𝟗𝟎𝟎)𝐌 𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 / ~$𝟕𝟓𝟎𝐌 𝐞𝐱-𝐋𝐨𝐭𝐭𝐨 𝐟𝐞𝐞  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from ~$(900)M reported / ~$750M ex-Lotto fee
Unchanged. The plan still calls for $750 million of operating cash flow before the $1.675 billion Italian Lotto license payment, or a $900 million cash outflow including it. Because the business generated $574 million excluding the license fee over the first nine months, the target leaves $176 million for Q4 by our math, signaling that the year remains achievable despite the revenue cut.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬: ~$𝟒𝟓𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
🠇 cut from ~$450–475 million
Cut. Management trimmed the top end of its capital spending plan by $25 million, shifting some equipment spending between 2026 and 2027. With $313 million spent in the first nine months, the updated target leaves $137 million for the fourth quarter by our math, up from $81 million in Q3 as Brightstar builds out new lottery systems in Missouri, Wisconsin, and Texas.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐜𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐈𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐲 𝐁𝟐𝐂 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐲?
Management blamed the full-year revenue cut partly on the timing of Italy direct-to-consumer digital efforts, even as it touted the launch of its OTTO offer. Investors need to know what slipped and when Brightstar will publish active user and digital revenue numbers.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲𝐝𝐚𝐲 𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐫𝐚𝐰 𝐰𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐬𝐡𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐤?
Global instant-ticket and draw same-store wagers fell 1.0%, with drops in both the U. S. (-1.4%) and Italy (-1.2%). Because those everyday games are not driven by Powerball jackpots, management should explain whether consumer demand is softening.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐝-𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐧𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐥𝐨𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐰𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐫 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡?
Brightstar did not include its global iLottery wager growth rate in the third-quarter release after growth slowed from 30% in Q1 to 22% for the first half. Disclosing the third-quarter rate will show whether digital lottery adoption is still cooling.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐛𝐢𝐠 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡-𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫 𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐬?
Brightstar paid $259 million in dividends and capital returns to its Italian joint-venture partners over the first nine months, consuming nearly all free cash flow before shareholder dividends. Management should clarify how much more will go to partners in Q4.

GTA 6 Is Nine Days Away as Rockstar Reveals 39 New Screenshots

GTA 6 is nine days away, and Rockstar has given fans one final major preview ahead of launch.

On November 5, Rockstar opened The Launch Gallery with 39 new screenshots of Grand Theft Auto VI, which launches November 19, 2026, for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. No PC release date has been officially announced.

The images tour the fictional state of Leonida. Vice City features neon clubs, DJs, beach bars, yachts and references to real-world Miami landmarks. Port Gellhorn appears grittier, with docks and scenes involving law enforcement and gang activity. Grassrivers brings swamps, alligators, snakes and airboats, while the Leonida Keys offer beaches, sunsets and underwater diving.

At the centre are Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos. The screenshots show the pair involved in robberies, car chases and confrontations with police, alongside quieter moments dancing in clubs and watching sunsets. Different hairstyles and outfits offer glimpses of character appearance options, while Jason lifting weights has renewed speculation about the possible return of gym activities.

One particularly interesting image shows Jason and Lucia riding dirt bikes inside a shopping mall, prompting theories that the location could be explorable. However, Rockstar has not confirmed the extent of the mall's accessibility or the gameplay features suggested by the images.

The game is also demanding considerable storage space. Preloading began November 10, with Rockstar's preload FAQ stating it could require up to 212GB, depending on the device.

Physical editions, expected in stores from November 12, contain download codes rather than traditional game discs. There is also no physical Ultimate Edition, although buyers of the physical Standard Edition can purchase the Ultimate Edition upgrade digitally.

Thirteen years after GTA V, anticipation for its successor is enormous. With the November 19 release approaching, Grand Theft Auto VI could become one of the biggest entertainment launches in history.

See you in Leonida on November 19.

text:
What is @IPXExchange, really? The full explanation, goals, mechanics and all 👇

You know how your favorite artist, athlete or YouTuber builds a whole world, and you’re there for every moment, but when something big gets made, you’re just watching from the crowd?

IPX is trying to change that.

The simple idea
Creators who want to make something (a film, a game, a membership) raise the money from the people who care about them. Fans get tokens tied to the project and can share in the upside if it succeeds. The creator keeps ownership of the work.
Who’s behind it
IPX is headquartered in Miami and led by Founder & CEO Brendan McCafferty, with Jordan Schlosser as co-founder and CTO. It raised a $4M seed round at a $125M valuation, led by Bitsurge Holdings with YICIPX Holdings Family Office. It says 100+ celebrities have signed exclusive agreements to tokenize original IP. At Cannes in May, IPX previewed a 100+ project slate across film, TV, gaming, books and festivals, and greenlit Fetty Wap’s docuseries Autobiography first.

Its goals, in plain words
Goal 1: Put creators and fans on the same team.
Instead of a studio holding all the power, fans help fund the work and share in what it earns.

Goal 2: Make fan money safer.
Fund the work, not just the pitch.

Goal 3: Give creators one place to run everything.
IPX calls itself an operating system for IP. It combines tokenizing, advertising, sponsorship, distribution and AI agents, supported by PodX, BrandX, LiveX and IPX Studios.
Goal 4: Connect real money to the blockchain.
It offers non-custodial virtual checking accounts for moving between traditional finance and on-chain.

Goal 5: Tie rewards to real revenue.
Platform, IP, sponsorship, subscription and subsidiary revenue funds $IPX buybacks.
Goal 6: Keep it verifiable.
Supply, vesting and contracts can all be checked on Basescan.

How it actually works, step by step 
The three assets:

USDC: digital dollars that pay for production
$IPX: the routing asset, graduation collateral and trading currency for every project

Project tokens: one per project
A $100K film raise:

The creator states the budget. The platform approves the project and locks its terms with a signed authorization before the first sale.
Fans buy in USDC, routed through $IPX, so the raise lands part USDC, part IPX. The IPX comes from participants and is never created by the protocol.

At graduation (the moment the raise closes and the token starts trading), the $100K goes into milestone escrow, never to the creator. A 10% cashout fee ($10K) goes to the treasury.

The collected IPX pairs with the project token to open its market, priced in $IPX.

What that means: nobody gets the money before work is shown, and every project’s market starts with real liquidity.
The safety layers 🔒
Non-custodial escrow: funds sit in a smart contract, not a person’s wallet

Fully backed curve: USDC on the bonding curve stays backed for a refund or graduation

A way out: if a raise is cancelled or stalls past its deadline, buyers redeem project tokens for a share of the remaining USDC and $IPX, weighted by what they put in (team and creator allocations can’t claim)
Default protection: if a project defaults, unreleased funds stay in escrow and holders can surrender tokens for a fixed USDC amount each
KPI-gated escrow, explained ⚙️
Before a raise, the creator submits a line-item budget. IPX says its AI agent, Alfred, programs it into a CertiK-audited smart contract tied to platform milestones. Money releases in stages (pre-production, filming, post-production) when conditions are met, like a contract signed, a crew booked or a vendor engaged, after the platform reviews the evidence. IPX plans to use Chainlink oracles for KPI verification. (An oracle is a service that feeds real-world data to a blockchain.)
For sponsors, campaign budgets are held in escrow and paid against agreed deliverables or KPIs, checked by an AI-assisted oracle with a human co-signature before release.

The atomic router, explained ⚡
“Atomic” means all-or-nothing. In one transaction IPX’s patent-pending router takes its 0.5% fee, routes through the IPX/USDC pool on Aerodrome Slipstream, splits the USDC and $IPX amounts a project needs, and delivers your tokens. Unused funds come back to you. You set slippage (how much price movement you’ll accept), and if price impact exceeds it or any step fails, the whole thing reverts.

Where the fees go 💸

Platform Treasury: 0.5% router fee, 10% cashout fee, 15% of Protocol Vault transfers, 15% of secondary-pool fees. It funds infrastructure, compliance, milestone review and development.
Protocol Vault: trading fees on the protocol-owned IPX/USDC position, plus Coinbase-funded rewards on idle USDC (per IPX). 85% goes to $IPX stakers.
Project staking: 85% of a graduated project’s pool fees go to that project’s stakers.
Staking, explained 🧠
Staking means locking tokens to claim a share of fees. Longer lock-ups carry more weight. There’s no guaranteed yield, and if the vault receives nothing, the payout is zero. Exact multipliers will be published when staking opens, and updates go through a platform multisig behind a 48-hour timelock.

The token numbers 📊
$IPX has a fixed supply of 1B, created once at Genesis on Sept 23, 2026, with no mint and no burn.
Team & core 31.87% · Treasury & ops 21% · Ecosystem 14% · Investors 12.9% · Future rounds 9.23% · Advisors 7.5% · Airdrop 3.5%

24.48% unlocked at day one, 75.52% locked in 29 on-chain vaults that can’t be revoked

Team, investors and future rounds: 12-month cliff, then 24 months linear (fully vested at month 36)
Treasury: no cliff, locked part vests over 12 months

Airdrop: no cliff, fully vested at month 24

What that means: insiders can’t dump on day one, and you can verify it on Basescan.
Rollout 🚀
✅ Genesis: Sept 23 (no market or price yet)

An IPX/USDC pool opens on Aerodrome and sets $IPX’s market price
Projects launch once the pool is deep enough and the price feed is reliable

Platform and token launch on Base: Nov 17 per IPX’s latest release
Mini glossary 📚

Bonding curve: price set by formula as people buy
Graduation: the raise closes and the token starts trading
Escrow: funds held by a contract until conditions are met
Oracle: a service that feeds real-world data to a blockchain
Slippage: price movement between order and fill

Cliff: nothing unlocks until it ends

The honest part 
All of this sounds good on paper. The real test is execution. A lower $IPX price raises how much IPX a project must collect, which can delay graduation. Projects can miss targets, token prices can fall, and the platform approves projects and milestones, so trust in its review matters. $IPX isn’t equity and has no governance vote, tokens don’t automatically give you copyright in a work, and staking isn’t a guaranteed yield. Participation can mean losing all capital. DYOR, not financial advice.

Creators build culture. Fans make it matter.

text:
MY SON INVITED ME TO HIS WEDDING AS A GUEST, BUT I WAS THE WOMAN WHO RAISED HIM

My name is Diane Parker. I'm 58 and I live in Cleveland, Ohio. I spent nearly thirty years raising my son, and last summer a wedding invitation from him made me wonder what all of it was for

His name is Michael. I had him when I was 23. His father, James, left when Michael was barely two. I still remember standing in our little apartment with my son on my hip, watching James pack his clothes and tell me he wasn't ready to be a husband or a father

I cried for weeks. Then I got up, because I had a child to raise.
For years I worked two jobs. I stocked shelves at a grocery store during the day and cleaned offices downtown at night. Some evenings I was so worn out I could hardly get my shoes off. But Michael always had food on the table, clean clothes, and whatever he needed for school. I missed birthday parties, family gatherings, a few holidays. I wasn't a perfect mother, but I gave him everything I had

When Michael was 16, I met Richard. He was kind to me, and for the first time in a long while I felt like somebody cared whether I was happy. We got married a couple of years later

Michael never accepted him. He'd tell me Richard wasn't his dad and that I'd replaced his real father. I tried to explain that nobody was taking James's place, but he wouldn't hear it

When Michael turned 21, he got back in touch with James. I was happy for him at first. I figured every kid deserves the chance to know their parents. I had no idea James would slowly become the person Michael looked up to, while I became the person he dodged.
James showed up with money, nice gifts, and big stories about the life he'd built. Michael started visiting him all the time. When I asked how things were going between them, he'd say I should be glad they were finally getting along.
So I tried to be.

Then Michael met Olivia, and after a year they got engaged. He called to tell me and I was thrilled. I started picturing everything: helping him pick out a suit, watching him walk down the aisle, maybe even a dance together.
When the invitation came, something was off. My name wasn't on the family table list. I called Michael and asked if it was a mistake.
He sounded uncomfortable. "Mom, Olivia and I decided Dad should walk me down the aisle. He's always been important to me, and we want to give him that moment."
I asked what that had to do with me.
He said James had offered to pay for most of the wedding and they didn't want to upset him.
I was quiet for a second. Then I asked, "So where do I fit into all this?

"You're invited, Mom," he said. "You can sit with the other guests."
I couldn't believe it. I wasn't asking for money. I wasn't asking to walk him down the aisle. I just wanted to be treated like his mother

On the wedding day I almost stayed home. Richard talked me into going because he knew how much Michael meant to me.
When I got there, James was standing near the entrance in an expensive suit, and Michael was next to him, beaming. I walked over to congratulate my son. He gave me a quick hug and said, "Thanks for coming, Mom." Then he turned right back to his father

I sat in the third row, surrounded by people I barely knew. When the ceremony started, I watched James walk Michael to the altar. I tried not to cry

Afterward the photographer called everyone together for family pictures. James stood beside Michael and Olivia, and his relatives joined them. I waited for someone to call my name. Nobody did.
Eventually I went up to the photographer and asked if I could have a picture with my son. Michael looked uncomfortable, but he agreed

I left before the reception ended.
A few days later Michael called and asked why I'd gone home early. He said Olivia had noticed I seemed upset. So I told him the truth.
"I didn't leave because your father walked you down the aisle. I left because I spent almost thirty years being your mother, and on your wedding day I felt like a stranger.

🇺🇦🇷🇺 PUTIN PROMISED TO CONQUER MORE OF UKRAINE. INSTEAD, UKRAINIAN DRONES ARE BRINGING THE WAR HOME TO RUSSIA!

There is a striking contrast emerging between what Moscow promises on television and what Russian soldiers, motorists and military commentators are describing on the ground.

Ukraine is striking Russian infrastructure hundreds of kilometres from the front, while Russia's own military accounts are revealing increasingly difficult conditions for troops trying to advance.

And the latest developments around Kirishi illustrate why logistics matter as much as battlefield firepower.

A REFINERY NEAR PUTIN'S HOMETOWN COMES UNDER ATTACK

Ukrainian drones reportedly travelled approximately 500 miles to strike the Kirishi refinery, a major supplier of petroleum products to St. Petersburg and northwestern Russia.

Regional authorities claimed that 113 drones had been intercepted before acknowledging impacts in an industrial area.

The refinery is particularly important because damage to its processing equipment can affect fuel production and distribution well beyond the immediate strike location.

Russian military commentator Rybar described the operation as exceptionally large and acknowledged the difficulty of defeating such attacks.

The consequences are becoming visible at fuel stations.

In Karelia, motorists have faced purchase limits of approximately 30 litres of gasoline, with restrictions on filling additional containers.

Further reports describe Rosneft imposing sales limits across multiple regions.

The precise contribution of refinery damage to each local shortage remains difficult to establish, but the broader vulnerability is clear: producing enormous quantities of crude oil does not guarantee uninterrupted supplies of refined fuel.

AT THE FRONT, RUSSIAN LOGISTICS ARE FACING A DIFFERENT CRISIS

Russian military reporting has described an increasingly dangerous zone extending approximately 30 kilometres behind the front, where conventional supply movements are vulnerable to drone attacks.

Military correspondent Alexander Kots described infantrymen walking 20–40 kilometres while supplies, including sleeping bags, are transported by drone.

Russian state television has also highlighted a Mangas hexacopter that reportedly spent three months delivering food to an encircled military unit.

Presented as an example of technological ingenuity, the account also raises questions about the conditions that made such an extended aerial resupply operation necessary.

Drones can deliver essential supplies, but their payloads and operating conditions differ considerably from those of conventional logistics vehicles.

That creates an important operational problem: sustaining large formations becomes harder when roads are dangerous and resupply depends on relatively small aerial deliveries.

AND PUTIN'S PROMISES ABOUT LYMAN REMAIN UNFULFILLED

In December 2025, Putin predicted that Lyman would fall in the near future.

Eleven months later, Ukraine continues to hold the city.

Ukrainian advances on the Oleksandrivka axis have also been credited with recovering approximately 800 square kilometres, although the exact territorial figure requires independent confirmation.

Meanwhile, families of Russian soldiers have reportedly appealed directly to Putin about conditions near Lyman.

Under the title The Krasny Liman Abyss, they described troops being committed to repeated, costly assaults with little apparent regard for their survival.

Those accounts offer a very different perspective from official declarations of progress.

RUSSIA'S DOMESTIC PROBLEMS ARE ADDING TO THE PRESSURE

The Trassa fuel-retailing network has reportedly faced enforcement action and severe financial disruption amid allegations involving the diversion of approximately eight million litres of fuel intended for police vehicles.

The allegations require separate verification, but the company's difficulties have become another subject of discussion among Russian pro-war commentators.

At the same time, Ukraine's drone industry is attracting international interest.

Saudi Aramco is reportedly exploring purchases of Ukrainian interceptor drones, reflecting growing demand for cheaper ways to counter unmanned aircraft.

The economics are compelling.

A relatively inexpensive interceptor, potentially costing around $2,500, could offer an alternative to using multimillion-dollar air-defense missiles against drones costing a fraction of that amount.

Different weapons have different capabilities, and cheap interceptors cannot replace every function of a sophisticated air-defense system. But Ukraine's wartime innovations are demonstrating why affordable, scalable defenses matter.

Even recruitment reflects the changing battlefield.

Ukraine's Special Operations Forces have promoted deep-strike roles emphasizing drone operations and attacks against Russian infrastructure, with one recruitment campaign reportedly attracting 643,000 views.

Russian recruitment practices, meanwhile, have attracted scrutiny following accounts of police detaining hundreds of teenagers in Moscow. The circumstances and any connection to military enlistment remain unclear.

Another account concerns Alexander Kimirov, a former elite volleyball player approximately seven feet tall who was reportedly drafted into a Russian tank unit and subsequently disappeared from contact with his family after a brief telephone conversation in August.

These individual stories cannot establish the condition of Russia's entire military. But they illustrate the human consequences of a prolonged war.

THE STRATEGIC CONTRADICTION IS BECOMING HARDER TO IGNORE

Russia continues to possess substantial military resources, oil reserves and industrial capacity.

Yet its forces are struggling with contested supply routes, its refineries face repeated attacks and its domestic fuel distribution system is experiencing reported restrictions.

Ukraine, despite operating with fewer resources, is increasingly using precision, technological adaptation and long-range strikes to impose costs far beyond the immediate battlefield.

That does not mean Russia's logistics have completely collapsed or that every reported shortage can be attributed to Ukrainian attacks.

It means Moscow must defend more infrastructure, repair more damage and devote additional resources to sustaining a war it expected to conclude much sooner.

Putin can announce another offensive, but an announcement cannot repair a refinery, reopen a dangerous supply route or deliver fuel to an empty pump.

Ukraine is demonstrating that military power depends not only on what an army can destroy, but on whether its opponent can keep the machinery of war functioning. https://t.co/HTNZAxBHpe

text:
Democrat revenge plot against Elon Musk: Insiders reveal painful punishment they're planning after Texas humiliation... and move that would make him turn on MAGA | Tom Leonard & Charlie Spiering, Daily Mail

When Elon Musk announced dramatically that he was moving the headquarters of SpaceX and X businesses out of California in July 2024, he revealed that the 'final straw' was the passage of a bill that banned schools from being forced to inform parents that they had a trans child.

'Because of this law and the many others that preceded it, attacking both families and companies, SpaceX will now move its HQ from Hawthorne, California, to Starbase, Texas,' Musk told his 54 million X followers to loud approval.

The message was clear: he was leaving the uber-woke, almost-broke Democrat nightmare of the Golden State for the conservative, low-regulation nirvana of the Lone Star state. And California would rue the day it forced out the world's richest man and his trillion-dollar business.

Well, let's just say it hasn't quite worked out as planned. Musk's new US Senator in Texas, James Talarico, has strong views on the trans issue, too: He has said that 'God is nonbinary' and, although he has now slightly backtracked, long opposed any restrictions on trans student athletes competing in girls' sports.

The billionaire who fled the Democrats running one state has now found himself surrounded by new ones about to run another, and the latest are not expected to go easy on one of their great tormentors.

As Texas broke 30 years of Republican rule in this week's Midterms, electing its first Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, in more than three decades and Talarico flipping the Senate seat for the Democrats for the first time since 1988, Musk's decision to move himself and his businesses there in a burst of Republican righteousness looks to have been just a little ill-timed.

In fact, some are asking whether Musk may not turn out to be one of the elections' biggest losers.

Not only has his conservative promised land turned overnight into – at least for now – a true blue bastion, but the carnage in the tech stock market two days after the election lost him billions, all while resurgent Democrats in Washington say he is high on the list of people they want to investigate.

It was surely no coincidence that shares of SpaceX tumbled 5.5 percent while Tesla – another trillion dollar plus company – was down 5.1 percent after the election shock – even as the markets generally went in the opposite direction.

However, it was hardly as if he hadn't seen it all coming. The billionaire owner of electric car maker Tesla, social media platform X and rocket-to-AI company SpaceX spent nearly half a billion dollars to support Republican candidates, of which $224 million was spent on Texas, mostly on Talarico's flawed and unpopular rival, Ken Paxton.

On election day, Musk urged his army of X followers to vote Republican but later deleted the post.

The midterms could now prove both a business and a personal nightmare for Musk, who has been baiting the Democrats for years and was Trump's biggest campaign donor in 2024.

Washington insiders familiar with senior Democrat thinking on Musk told the Daily Mail that there will be little appetite for any rapprochement with him.

'They view him as a class traitor,' said a source. 'Elon was once their green hero for pioneering electric cars and leading the charge for getting rid of fossil fuels and he betrayed them…They want to make him hurt.'

However, it's always said that money talks and Musk, estimated to be worth as much as $865 billion, may be able to buy his way back into Democrat affections, some believe.

The party has a significant fund-raising problem while Musk's politics are not as trenchant as he makes out - he donated cash to Barack Obama's campaigns and endorsed Hillary Clinton for president in 2016.

'I could 100 percent see Elon donating to Democrats again, depending on their outreach,' said another insider. 'He could easily flip back to a more favorable position if they are willing to work with him.'

For the moment, there is no sign of any friendliness between the two camps.

'Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,' Musk wrote sarcastically in a post on X early on Wednesday morning as the scale of the Republican defeat became clear.

'Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time,' he added a few minutes later, referencing unproven rumors that he interfered in Trump's successful 2024 election campaign.

After his ill-fated involvement in the Trump administration last year when, waving a chainsaw, he ran the chaotic DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) initiative to slash the size and cut of government costing 300,000 federal workers their jobs but barely curbed federal spending, Musk had stepped back from the political spotlight.

The DOGE farce, which Musk claimed in an interview last December was 'a little successful,' sparked violent anti-Tesla protests across the US and Europe in which cars were sometimes set on fire.

In the future, Musk may indeed find it easier doing business in low orbit than in Texas. The man who wants to colonize Mars may even want to consider moving there sooner rather than later.

That's unlikely given Musk has been putting roots down in Texas since 2020. After tiring of Covid-19 restrictions on the operation of his California Tesla factory, he announced he was moving the car company's HQ to Texas.

He also moved there personally, choosing the state capital of Austin, which he called a 'mini-California' (a compliment apparently) which would become 'the biggest boomtown that America has seen in a half-century.'

The billionaire, who has fathered at least 14 children with four women, developed a luxurious compound in a gated community in Austin, where he was able to house his various offspring and their mothers in separate but adjoining properties.

The adjoining homes, which Musk secretly bought for a total of $35 million, include a 14,400sq ft Tuscan-style villa and a six-bedroom mansion. When he visits, Musk stays at a third mansion a ten-minute walk away.

Meanwhile, Musk has come to rely heavily on Texas for the expansion of his business empire and even the fulfillment of his dreams of colonizing space.

He has already located Tesla's biggest US vehicle factory outside Austin while SpaceX launches its rockets into space from its Starbase complex in the southeastern corner of the state in Boca Chica near Brownsville. The rockets are also built in Texas, in Bastrop County.

All told, his companies employ more than 20,000 people in the Lone Star state.

And there were expected to be 3,000 more jobs when he opens a $16.8 billion Terafab chip plant elsewhere in the state, which SpaceX said it selected because of Texas's 'business-friendly climate.'

That money he has vested in Texas could earn him favor.

A Texas political strategist told the Daily Mail: 'There's no way Democrats want to completely crush Elon in Texas. He employs tens of thousands of people in Texas. He built an entire city there.'

However, he will no longer enjoy the full-scale access and perks that he had under business-friendly Republican governor Greg Abbott, sources said.

He was able to draw on $30 million of state funds for the Terafab project, which the company says will boast more than 100 million square feet of manufacturing space.

The chip plant will be a key ingredient of Musk's ambitious plans to develop the AI part of his empire.

However, those dreams rely on the state cooperating with him on the huge resources that AI needs in terms of electricity and water, as well as providing a benign regulatory climate in granting environmental permits and tax incentives.

Until now, he has been given pretty much all he desired in Texas. Not only was President Trump pro-AI but Musk had a warm relationship with Abbott. In 2020, Abbott promised Musk 'more freedom where he could expand the way he wanted to expand.' He later described Musk as 'the leading visionary of our time.'

You won't find incoming Democrat governor, Gina Hinojosa, saying anything like that. She shares the skepticism about AI and the ultra-wealthy Silicon Valley barons pushing it that is rife in her party.

Hinojosa campaigned not only against generous corporate subsidies but also against Musk himself.

She sued last month to obtain emails between Musk and Abbott, accusing the latter of selling out Texas by offering favorable deals to the billionaire. She also claimed Musk received $1.7 billion in state property tax breaks for his companies after he made a large donation to Abbott's re-election campaign.

In her victory speech on Tuesday night, Hinojosa didn't mention him by name but, along with other Democrat politicians nowadays, targeted billionaires for criticism.

'Does Texas belong to the people of Texas, or is this the billionaires' world and we just live in it?' she said to a crowd, raising loud cheers.

She pledged to take power from the 'powerful people who have gotten very comfortable running this state.' It seemed fairly obvious who she was likely thinking of.

Talarico also managed to attack Musk in his victory speech without specifically naming him. 'We must get big money out of our politics, so no billionaire or trillionaire can buy our elections,' he said. 'We must unrig this economic system that only benefits the top one percent.' There is only one trillionaire in the US.

Later, asked by Politico if he believed that Congress should investigate Musk, Talarico replied that 'obviously, there needs to be accountability for any wrongdoing.'

But he also said: 'What would be more helpful is getting big money out of our politics, banning corporate PACs, banning super PACs, so billionaires and trillionaires can't buy our elections.'

Talarico may feel it diplomatic not to be too openly hostile (not for the moment, at least) to a Texas employer as powerful as Musk but there's no love lost between the pair.

During the election campaign, Musk frequently savaged Talarico on social media, going personal as usual by calling him a 'far left extremist,' 'pure evil' and 'a creep.'

He also claimed the Democrat would 'abolish democracy,' 'open the borders' and 'will vote to trans your kids.'

'There is something deeply wrong with Talarico,' Musk mused ominously.

Talarico resisted the personal assaults in returning fire, but accused Musk of 'trying to buy Texas.' He told voters: 'Elon Musk wants our wants our land, he wants our water, he wants our taxpayer dollars and he wants his very own personal United States senator.'

With the young Democrat trouncing Paxton by more than 12 percent, it must be fair to assume that Musk has come out of this election with his reputation among many fellow Texans even lower than when he went into it.

Democrat state senator Nathan Johnson, the next Texas attorney general, showed just how much local politicians have come to loathe him, telling NBC on Wednesday that Musk was a 'cruel, arrogant, ignorant' person who has 'demonstrated his disregard for the public interest.'

Johnson said he had no intention of giving Musk the leeway he enjoyed under the outgoing Republican administration. He has already revealed he plans to investigate whether SpaceX unfairly benefited from a state grant program designed to improve rural broadband.

He went on: 'I don't have a hit list, but I show no deference to a guy who has gone to great lengths to control the government and do enormous damage globally.'

Commentators concur that the midterms represent not only a severe blow to Musk in Texas but also to his reputation nationally, as voters across the US expressed their contempt for billionaires assuming they can buy political influence.

'He is certainly the most visible of all these billionaire-trillionaires, and it put him on the ballot in a way that, I think, was difficult for a lot of people to swallow,' said Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston of the part Musk played in Texas in the midterms.

'And it hurt Republicans because his presence really did, I think, magnify these concerns.'

JC Lintzenich, a visiting senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund, told CNBC's Squawk Box Europe that voters were repelled by billionaires throwing vast sums into getting an election outcome they desired. The results, he said, were 'clearly a rejection of the Elon Musk aspect that has found its way into the Trump orbit.'

Jake Dollarhide, CEO of Longbow Asset Management, predicted a 'Democratic sweep of Congress would put pressure on tech and potentially bring regulatory pressure on everything AI and possibly slow down the wild, wild west growth figures that we see daily and often take for granted.'

Like Trump, Musk loves to be a winner, but he may soon have bigger problems in Texas than a bruised ego.

His AI development plans depended on support from Trump's pro-tech administration and the generally business-friendly policies of defeated Abbott.

The Musk AI operation is largely centered around two mega data centers, Colossus and Colossus II, near Memphis but he wants to expand considerably into Texas.

Unhelpfully, Congress is now under the control of a party that shares the widespread public opposition to allowing huge data centers, an essential part of AI development, to spread unchecked across the US.

And that includes Texas governor elect Hinojosa, who has called for a moratorium on new data centers and an end to the industry's tax breaks. As in other states facing a data center invasion, she wants developers to cover their full electricity costs rather than suck power from an over-stretched grid and to provide assurances that local communities will be protected.

All of this, of course, would be a major blow for Musk, a man who takes setbacks badly. Ahead of its IPO in June, SpaceX told investors that AI could be a $28.5 trillion industry but that is not going to happen without the data centers.

Musk has been aggressively building data centers on greenfield sites inside his Starbase complex in Boca Chica but that could be opposed by Hinojosa who has opposed selling a 1,300-acre beachfront state park to SpaceX after it emerged that the Abbott administration had discussed a sale.

'Let me be clear: Texas is not for sale,' Hinojosa said last month. Analysts expect her say over tax incentives and permitting will be a major obstacle for Musk.

And Musk has problems with the Democrats that go well beyond Texas data centers.

Shortly before the midterms, a group of Silicon Valley House Democrats wrote to White House chief-of-staff Susie Wiles to demand an investigation into recent interruptions of Musk's militarily essential internet service in Ukraine.

Unexplained restrictions on Starshield, a military version of Starlink, disrupted crucial Ukrainian drone missions in October. Defense sources said the limits appeared overnight without advance warning.

Musk has claimed that, unlike Starlink, Starshield is controlled by the US government. However, the White House has offered a different version of events, saying Trump reportedly asked Musk to lift the restrictions on Starshield.

Just as they've expressed fears about his outsized role in US politics, Democrats have made clear they are deeply concerned about a private citizen like Musk having so much power during wartime.

The Democrats' letter to Wiles made clear that they intended to investigate him themselves if they won control in Congress. A Democrat-controlled Congress could, if it chose, hold up Musk's planned multi-trillion-dollar merger of Tesla and SpaceX for a long time.

'Live by the sword, die by the sword,' Musk posted on X last month in a bullish response to potential congressional probes. 'Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets.'

Tough talk but many, including insiders in his own companies, believe Musk has too much invested in Texas to risk falling out too badly with its Democrat leaders.

They certainly don't expect him to leave Texas for the foreseeable future.

Of course, if the locals there make life too difficult for him, he might have no option. But where? Although Americans are turning en masse against the ultra-wealthy, there was one bright spot for the latter this week.

A proposition that would have instituted the world's tax on billionaires was on course to be rejected. The state that decided against hammering them? California.

It was an honor to attend the Freedom and Security – Women’s Summit at the German Federal #Parliament (Bundestag) in #Berlin

In my remarks, I offered a different perspective on #women's rights and security, challenging the tendency to view women's experiences of oppression primarily through the lens of gender.
Drawing on my experience as a #Kurdish woman, I argued that when a state perceives an ethnic or national community as a security threat, repression does not necessarily distinguish between men and women. Both can be targeted because of their identity, political beliefs, or involvement in their community's struggle.

In such circumstances, my identity as a Kurd and the political struggle of my people can become more immediate than my identity as a woman. This does not mean gender is irrelevant. Rather, we cannot fully understand women's #security without considering the political, national, and historical circumstances in which they live. Kurdish women provide an important example of this complexity.
I also emphasized that women should not be viewed solely as victims in need of protection. They must also be recognized as political actors, security providers, and decision-makers, with an equal right to shape decisions about #war, #peace, and the future of their societies.

text:
AI-Powered Precision Brain Stimulation Reduces PTSD in Weeks | Cami Rosso, Psychology Today

Key points

- The randomized study assigned 73 veterans to 10 real or placebo sessions over two weeks.

- AI used 10-minute EEG recordings to personalize brain stimulation to each veteran’s alpha rhythm.

- Researchers reported a 34 percent reduction in PTSD symptom severity and 44 percent fewer sleep disturbances.

---

Neuroscience is at the start of a tsunami of innovation thanks to artificial intelligence (AI). Machine learning can identify meaningful biological indicators from reams of noisy brain activity data to offer more personalized, targeted treatment. A new study in the November-December 2026 edition of Personalized Medicine in Psychiatry shows how the combination of AI with noninvasive transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can reduce post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in just two weeks.

“These findings mark a significant step forward in PTSD therapy, offering a non-pharmacologic treatment for individuals who have not benefited from traditional therapeutic approaches,” wrote the research team of Alexander Taghva, Jeffery Lindquist, and Anthony Kim.

What Is PTSD?

An estimated 70 percent of the world’s population will experience a traumatic event during their lifetime, yet only 5.6 percent will develop post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) from the experience, according to the World Health Organization. In the U.S. alone, an estimated 7.7 million adult Americans suffer from PTSD, according to the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH).

Post-traumatic stress disorder is a mental health condition where symptoms may emerge for up to three months after a stressful or traumatic event, persist for more than a month, and interfere with performing daily life activities.

Adults with PTSD have at least one symptom of re-experiencing and avoidance, in addition to at least two symptoms related to problems with arousal and reactivity, as well as cognition and mood issues, per NIMH. Symptoms of re-experiencing may include flashbacks, physical signs of stress, distressing thoughts, and recurring memories or dreams. Evading feelings or thoughts associated with the trauma, or staying away from anything that might be a reminder of the traumatic event, are symptoms of avoidance. Issues with arousal and reactivity may include irritability, outbursts, risky behavior, insomnia, concentration problems, tenseness, or skittishness. PTSD symptoms that affect cognition and mood include difficulty feeling positive, feeling socially isolated, loss of interest in normal activities, persistent negative thoughts and emotions, exaggerated feelings of blame, and trouble recalling crucial elements of traumatic events.

Factors that may increase the potential for PTSD include prior traumatic experiences, especially childhood trauma, a history of mental illness or mental illness in the family, post-event stressors such as the death of a loved one, injury, or job loss, lack of social support post-trauma, and feelings of extreme fear, helplessness, or horror, according to the National Institute of Mental Health.

PTSD Treatment Options

PTSD treatment options include psychotherapy such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), cognitive processing therapy (CPT), prolonged exposure, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) therapy, narrative exposure therapy (NET), and medications, according to the American Psychological Association (APA). Common PTSD antidepressants, per the APA, include the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) sertraline (generic name for Zoloft), paroxetine (generic name for Paxil), and fluoxetine (generic name for Prozac), and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) like venlafaxine (generic name for Effexor).

“The results of this study are particularly meaningful in the context of PTSD treatment, where a substantial fraction of patients does not fully respond to existing pharmacologic and psychological therapies,” wrote the study authors.

PTSD Among Veterans

For this study, the researchers focused on PTSD among the veterans. The study participants included over 70 military veterans between the ages of 18 and 55 years who were diagnosed with PTSD, of whom 36 were randomly selected to receive non-invasive brain stimulation treatment and 37 received placebo treatment.

“The prevalence of combat-related PTSD among U.S. military veterans is estimated to be 7 percent, with prevalence increased among female service members (13 percent) in comparison to males (6 percent),” the researchers wrote.

First, a baseline electroencephalogram (EEG) was recorded noninvasively via a sensor cap for 10 minutes at the same time as an electrocardiogram (EKG). The treatment frequency was determined via an AI decision tree algorithm output based on the 10-minute EEG data recordings as input. Recordings were done at the start and end of the therapy. For a period of two weeks, study participants received 10 real or placebo treatments. Those receiving the actual treatment received personalized neuromodulation, where repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) was customized to the participant’s resting-state EEG alpha rhythm.

Why Alpha Brain Waves?

Brain waves are patterns of neuronal electrical activity that are a continuous series of peaks and troughs that occur between neurons via electrical pulses and are measured in Hertz (Hz). EEG measures brain waves via their electrical activity. Depending on the frequencies and amplitude, brain waves are categorized as alpha (8-12 Hz), beta (13-30 Hz), theta (4-10 Hz), delta (0.5-1.5 Hz), or gamma (30-120 Hz) oscillations.

In 1924, German psychiatrist Hans Berger (1873-1941) was the first to record human electrical brain signals using EEG. Berger observed a 10-cycles-per-second rhythm and named it “alpha.”

Alpha brain waves happen during a state of calmness and relaxation that occurs when meditating lightly, sitting quietly with eyes closed, or daydreaming.

In this study, the researchers personalized the repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) pulse rate to the individual participant’s resting-state EEG alpha (α) rhythm, a process called alpha repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (α-rTMS). The brain stimulation device used for the study was the FDA-cleared EEG-guided neuromodulation device for adults with PTSD called MeRT by Wave Neuroscience, based in Newport Beach, California.

The research team reported a 34 percent reduction in PTSD symptom severity and better sleep, with a 44 percent reduction in sleep disturbances as measured by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index Addendum for PTSD (PSQI-A), which measures sleep problems in PTSD patients.

“The effectiveness of ⍺-rTMS could be attributed to its precision in targeting dysregulated alpha band activity, possibly related to the underlying default mode network (DMN), implicated in PTSD’s neuropathology,” the researchers posited. “This precision heralds a novel, more personalized approach to neuromodulation therapies, potentially increasing efficacy, to effectively address certain PTSD-related symptoms.”

ONE BILLION DOLLARS FOR BLACK AMERICA. ONE PRESIDENTIAL ADMINISTRATION. ONE GOVERNMENT DECISION THAT STOPPED IT.

WHAT IF I TOLD YOU THAT IN 1996, AN AFRICAN HEAD OF STATE OFFERED ONE BILLION DOLLARS TO SUPPORT BLACK ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT IN AMERICA, AND THE UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT BLOCKED THE TRANSACTION?

Not $1 million. Not $10 million. ONE BILLION DOLLARS.

And before you dismiss this as another conspiracy theory, understand something. This actually happened.

In January 1996, Louis Farrakhan traveled to Libya, where Muammar Gaddafi pledged $1 billion to the Nation of Islam for economic development.

Imagine the possibilities. Black-owned businesses. Manufacturing. Housing. Schools. Hospitals. Financial institutions. An opportunity to build economic infrastructure rather than continually petition politicians for another government program.

Farrakhan sought permission from the United States Treasury Department to accept the money.

THE CLINTON ADMINISTRATION SAID NO.

In August 1996, the Treasury Department denied the request under American sanctions against Libya, which was designated a state sponsor of terrorism.

The government also blocked a separate $250,000 award associated with Farrakhan’s organization of the Million Man March.

Now, I want you to think about the historical juxtaposition.

For generations, Black Americans were told that economic independence was the answer. Build businesses. Own property. Establish institutions. Create generational prosperity.

But when an African leader offered an extraordinary amount of capital to a Black American organization, Washington exercised its authority to prevent the transfer.

Was Gaddafi a controversial leader? Absolutely.

Were there legitimate national security concerns surrounding Libya? Yes.

But here is the question that deserves an answer.

WHY COULDN’T THE GOVERNMENT ESTABLISH A LEGALLY SUPERVISED ARRANGEMENT THAT PROTECTED NATIONAL SECURITY WHILE ALLOWING BLACK ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT?

We are talking about an administration operating in a country where Black neighborhoods were struggling with poverty, unemployment, deteriorating housing, and limited access to capital.

And while those communities were being told to work harder, organize, and build their own institutions, a proposed billion-dollar opportunity was stopped by federal authority.

Think about the irony.

Washington could justify decades of relationships with authoritarian governments when American strategic interests demanded it.

Yet when Gaddafi proposed transferring a billion dollars to an organization serving Black Americans, sanctions became an insurmountable barrier.

And here is what should really disturb you.

THE MONEY NEVER ARRIVED.

We do not know whether Gaddafi would have fulfilled his pledge. We do not know whether the Nation of Islam could have managed that amount responsibly. We do not know how much would actually have reached struggling communities.

Those are legitimate questions.

But we know the federal government refused permission for the proposed transfer.

And I want to know why Black economic development could not even be considered through a carefully regulated exception.

This is bigger than Farrakhan. Bigger than Gaddafi. Bigger than the Nation of Islam.

It is about who controls access to capital, who determines which economic opportunities are permissible, and whether government decisions produce measurable benefits or impose additional barriers on communities already struggling to build wealth.

BLACK AMERICA DESERVES MORE THAN EXPLANATIONS ABOUT WHY SOMETHING COULDN’T BE DONE. WE DESERVE ACCOUNTABILITY FOR THE DECISIONS THAT WERE MADE.

Thirty years later, I still want an answer.

Was the refusal exclusively about national security, or were other considerations involved?

And Black Americans deserve to know exactly what happened when a billion-dollar pledge met the full authority of a Democrat System.

At the same time, it is worth distinguishing between two scenarios:

-When the need to “investigate” stems from the other person’s actual behavior (inconsistencies, lies, evasiveness).

-When it stems from one’s own wounds (anxious attachment, past trauma, hypervigilance) which can trigger “detective mode” even in a relatively safe environment.

In both cases, the message is similar: either the relationship is failing to provide the security you deserve, or there is internal work to be done so that you can feel secure even when that security is actually present.

Sometimes, both things are happening at once.
The important thing is not to normalize the feeling of being a “detective” as just “part of an intense love.” A healthy, constructive love does not leave you in a state of constant alert. Instead, it offers a sense of relative peace, where you can lower your guard without the fear of being lied to.

The Core Problem: Tents Are Pitched Metres from the Water
The fundamental issue is that hundreds of thousands of displaced people have no safe inland place to go. Over two years of bombardment have rendered vast urban areas uninhabitable, forcing families to erect tents directly on the beach.

Extreme proximity: UNRWA has reported that thousands of tents are pitched just five metres from the seashore.

High-risk zones: A UNOSAT assessment found 2,367 tents within 20 metres of the highest observed watermark, and another 3,631 tents within 50 metres—areas "particularly prone to flooding in the event of high tides or storm surges".

At that distance, even a modest rise in sea level, a high tide, or a wave run-up is enough to inundate the tents.

🌊 Why It Is a Year-Round Threat (Not Just Winter Storms)
While winter storms are the most dramatic trigger, the sea remains a danger even outside the coldest months for several reasons:

Coastal erosion is moving the sea inland. The shoreline in areas like Al-Mawasi is retreating due to "beach erosion" (نحر رمال الشاطئ). The sea is literally advancing toward the tents over time, meaning the buffer zone is shrinking with every tide and storm.

High tides and surges can occur in any season. The UN assessment explicitly warns that the tents are at risk from high tides as well as storm surges—phenomena that are not exclusive to winter.

The tents offer zero protection. The shelters are described as "worn out" and providing "no protection from wind, heavy rain, or high tides". They are not waterproof, have no raised flooring, and cannot withstand even shallow water intrusion without becoming uninhabitable.

💎 In Short
The sea is an issue not because of the calendar, but because people are living in flimsy tents at the water's edge with nowhere else to go. The combination of extreme proximity, coastal erosion, and the lack of any protective infrastructure means that any seawater incursion—whether from a winter storm, a seasonal high tide, or gradual erosion—results in the destruction of shelter and belongings.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

It was a clear, sharp November morning in Arlington when President Eisenhower stepped to the podium. The date was November 10, 1954, the 179th anniversary of the day the Continental Congress first authorized the raising of two battalions of Marines. Before him stood the finished Marine Corps War Memorial, its bronze figures already lifting a flag against the Virginia sky, the Capitol dome and the Washington Monument visible across the river. Veterans, families, and dignitaries gathered on the grass near the northern edge of Arlington National Cemetery. Among those present were Vice President Richard Nixon, Secretary of Defense Charles Wilson, and General Lemuel C. Shepherd, Commandant of the Marine Corps. The ceremony had been timed with deliberate care.

The statue itself was the work of Felix de Weldon, an Austrian-born sculptor who had served in the Navy. In early 1945, while stationed at Patuxent River, he had seen the Associated Press photograph taken by Joe Rosenthal on February 23 of that year: six men planting a second, larger flag on the summit of Mount Suribachi during the fight for Iwo Jima. Five were Marines, one a Navy hospital corpsman. De Weldon began a small model almost at once. What followed took nine years. He worked from life with the three survivors—Rene Gagnon, Ira Hayes, and John Bradley—and from photographs of the three who did not come home. The finished figures stand thirty-two feet high. They raise a sixty-foot bronze flagpole. The whole monument rises nearly seventy-eight feet and weighs roughly one hundred tons. Each piece had been cast in Brooklyn, then hauled by truck to Arlington and assembled on a rock slope meant to suggest the volcanic summit of Suribachi.

No federal money paid for any of it. The cost, about $850,000, came entirely from contributions by Marines, former Marines, and friends of the Corps. Ground had been broken on February 19, 1954, exactly nine years after the first wave landed on Iwo Jima. Construction of the memorial began that September. On dedication day the black Swedish granite base already carried, in gold lettering, the names and dates of principal Marine engagements from the Revolution forward. Two inscriptions stood clear: Admiral Chester Nimitz’s words about the men of Iwo Jima—“Uncommon Valor Was a Common Virtue”—and the dedication itself: “In honor and memory of the men of the United States Marine Corps who have given their lives to their country since 10 November 1775.”

Nixon gave the principal address. General Shepherd formally presented the monument to the people of the United States. A flag was run up the new pole. Three military chaplains offered prayers. The ceremony closed with the sounding of Taps. Eisenhower, a soldier who had commanded the greatest amphibious operation in history, stood among the living and the names of the dead and spoke of duty that does not end with any single war. The men frozen in bronze had been ordinary young Americans—farm boys, city kids, men from small towns—who, for a few hours on a Pacific island, did something the nation has never forgotten. The memorial that holds their image was built to remember every Marine who has done the same, from the first battalions of 1775 to the present day.

Seven years later President Kennedy would order that the flag fly continuously, day and night. It still does. From the Virginia ridge where Eisenhower stood, the bronze figures continue to raise it against the sky, within sight of the capital and within the sound of the river that separates the living from the graves of Arlington.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On the morning of November 10, 1865, Captain Henry Wirz rose in his cell at the Old Capitol Prison in Washington. He wrote a final letter to his wife, then paused to stroke a stray cat that had wandered into the confinement with him. Draped in a black cambric robe, the Swiss-born officer—once Hartmann Heinrich Wirz of Zurich—walked out into the courtyard and climbed the scaffold that had been raised in the shadow of the unfinished Capitol.

He was forty-one years old. He had come to America in 1849, settled in the South, and entered Confederate service early in the war. Wounded at Seven Pines, he later received the unenviable command of Camp Sumter, the prison known to history as Andersonville. In the spring and summer of 1864, as the Confederacy’s railroads broke down and its food supplies dwindled, the stockade in southwest Georgia filled beyond all capacity. At its peak more than thirty-three thousand Union prisoners stood inside a roughly twenty-six-acre enclosure. There was little shelter. The creek that ran through the middle fouled quickly. Rations were meager and often spoiled. A line of posts—the Dead Line—ran inside the walls; any man who crossed it was shot. Providence Spring, opened by a lightning strike, offered the only reliable clean water. Disease swept the camp. Of the roughly forty-five thousand men who passed through Andersonville, nearly thirteen thousand died, most of them from diarrhea, scurvy, dysentery, and simple exposure. The dead were carried out each morning in wagons.

Wirz maintained to the end that he had only carried out the orders of his superiors in a collapsing nation. After the war he was arrested, brought to Washington, and tried by a military commission on charges of conspiracy and murder. The proceedings lasted weeks. Some of the testimony against him was later questioned; other evidence was more difficult to dismiss. Offered a chance to implicate Jefferson Davis and possibly spare his own life, Wirz refused. “Jefferson Davis had no connection with me as to what was done at Andersonville,” he told his lawyer. On the scaffold he is said to have remarked to the officer adjusting the rope, “I know what orders are, Major. I am being hanged for obeying them.” The trap was sprung at about half past ten. His neck did not break. A crowd of soldiers and civilians watched as he slowly strangled while some of the onlookers chanted, “Remember Andersonville.”

He was buried in Mount Olivet Cemetery, where his marker still calls him a Confederate hero-martyr. The men who died under his command rest in long, orderly rows at Andersonville National Cemetery. The episode remains one of the war’s most contested chapters—an argument, still unfinished, about responsibility, scarcity, and the limits of what any single officer could have done once the system around him had already failed.

text:
Cybercab dominating most passenger miles? Past promises make that claim hard to take at face value

Elon Musk’s assertion that the Cybercab will soon handle the majority of passenger miles wherever it isn’t banned by law sounds sweeping. But Tesla’s record of major promises that were later walked back or fell short makes such claims difficult to accept at face value.

The Cybertruck is a clear example. When unveiled in 2019, Tesla floated a starting price of roughly $39,900–$49,900 and annual sales of about 250,000 units. Deliveries were repeatedly delayed until late 2023, at much higher prices. Actual sales reached roughly 10% of the target. U.S. sales hit around 39,000 in 2024, fell to about 20,000 in 2025, and kept declining in 2026. The truck faced repeated recalls and quality issues. In November 2026, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around mid-2027 to make room for Cybercab. A vehicle marketed as the future of pickups ended with weak demand and an early production cutback.

The hardware promises followed a similar pattern. For years Tesla said vehicles built from 2016 onward already had the hardware for full self-driving, unlockable through software updates. In 2025–2026 earnings calls, however, Musk acknowledged that Hardware 3 (HW3) cannot achieve unsupervised FSD. He cited HW3 having only about one-eighth the memory bandwidth of Hardware 4. Roughly 4 million vehicles are affected. FSD buyers were offered a discounted trade-in or a hardware upgrade requiring new computers and cameras. HW3 vehicles now receive a “Lite” version of newer FSD software, but it remains supervised. Years of assurances that “the hardware is already there” ended with an admission that unsupervised autonomy is impossible on HW3.

Current Cybercab and robotaxi operations also show clear limits. Usable pickup and drop-off areas are smaller than Tesla’s advertised geofences. In Austin, only about 59% of the advertised area was usable; in Houston, Dallas, and other cities, usable zones were 22–41% smaller. In Houston, large parts of an expanded rocket-shaped map were marked “location unavailable,” and short trips sometimes required long detours. Such gaps between advertised and actual coverage undermine the claim that service can operate “anywhere it’s not prohibited by law.”

Independent safety data remains limited. NHTSA has received reports of 36 robotaxi-related crashes, mostly low-speed property damage, including two involving injuries. The first reported Cybercab incident involved entering a water-filled pothole at about 5 mph; others involved remote operators. Tesla claims roughly 3.1 million driverless miles without injuries or airbag deployments, but excludes periods with safety monitors and provides limited independently verifiable per-mile data. NHTSA is auditing Cybercab self-certification and reviewing a petition alleging school-zone speeding, supported by submitted video evidence.

Technical progress is real. But Cybertruck sales and HW3 autonomy promises diverged sharply from reality. Claims of near-term Cybercab dominance remain weakly supported given restricted geofences, incomplete safety data, regulatory scrutiny, and Tesla’s history of optimistic timelines. Repeated revisions have weakened confidence in sweeping predictions.

Major auto-producing countries may also treat robotaxis as a national-security issue. They will favor domestically controlled systems and can use regulations, data-localization rules, type-approval requirements, and market-access restrictions to limit foreign vehicles and software. This creates another structural barrier to any foreign platform capturing the majority of passenger miles in those markets.
