Watching @NewsCentralCNN and they are talking about the @PeteHegseth impeachment movement (and upcoming press conference) but are entirely omitting the prediction market piece that is driving the entire effort, @RepThomasMassie @cnn @jaxalemany @katebolduan @sruhle 

AI: Now the larger argument is clear. You’re questioning whether we’re watching genuine acts of government or political performances designed to generate attention, television coverage, and potentially financial activity.

And the Dana White episode is an important example of what you’re describing.

Yesterday, Trump brought White into a highly visible White House setting, publicly floated a government job, and received a polite refusal. Regardless of whether there was ever a serious offer, the interaction produced a made-for-television political moment. The cameras captured it, the news covered it, and the public was presented with an exchange between the president and a prominent entertainment executive.

Now, less than 24 hours later, you’re watching CNN News Central cover another Washington spectacle: the movement to impeach Pete Hegseth, followed by an anticipated press conference.

Your argument is that the prediction markets change how we should understand that spectacle.

When political outcomes are being bought and sold on Kalshi and Polymarket, the financial interests surrounding a congressional action become relevant to the news itself. The possibility that political announcements, public confrontations, and televised reactions can influence the value of those contracts raises questions that traditional political reporting needs to investigate.

And this is where your criticism of CNN becomes particularly pointed.

CNN is reporting the performance without examining the financial machinery surrounding it.

You’re suggesting that the impeachment effort may be less a straightforward exercise of congressional accountability and more another manufactured political event, with prediction-market incentives helping drive the activity. That is a serious hypothesis, although the trading activity alone doesn’t establish that Massie or anyone else initiated the effort for financial reasons.

The larger issue you’re identifying is the erosion of the distinction between governing, performing for television, and creating financially tradable political events.

And when a national news organization reports only what politicians say and do in front of cameras, without investigating the financial interests surrounding those actions, its audience may be missing one of the most consequential dimensions of the story.

That’s the substance of your criticism: the cameras are showing viewers the political event, but the reporting isn’t adequately examining the business that may be operating around it.

text:
Washington Should Not Mistake Rezaei’s Rise for Iranian Flexibility

Washington needs to understand one simple fact: Mohsen Rezaei is no dove, and his growing influence does not signal any fundamental change in Tehran’s position toward the United States.

Rezaei is neither willing nor able to offer concessions that cross the Islamic Republic’s established red lines. Iran’s position remains unchanged: Washington must first implement Tehran’s seven conditions before substantive negotiations on the nuclear issue can begin.

There is remarkable unity within Iran’s leadership on this issue, from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and President Pezeshkian to Rezaei and Ali Abdollahi. Despite their internal rivalries, none is advocating surrender to American pressure.

Rezaei may be influential, but he does not have the authority to redefine Iran’s strategic priorities. Those decisions ultimately rest with the Supreme Leader and the broader security establishment.

The real question is not whether Rezaei might eventually meet Vice President JD Vance. Iran has repeatedly demonstrated tactical flexibility regarding diplomatic channels, negotiating formats, and interlocutors. A meeting, even at a senior level, should not be mistaken for a strategic breakthrough.

The real question is whether Rezaei’s emergence reflects a fundamental shift in Tehran’s calculations. The answer is no.

The central obstacle remains the sequencing of steps. Tehran insists that the United States first fulfill its commitments and provide credible guarantees before substantive nuclear negotiations can begin.

This was true before the US midterm elections, and it is even more relevant afterward. Tehran may now believe that Trump’s weakened domestic political position gives Iran additional leverage and that time is working in its favor. But this calculation carries significant risks. A politically weakened president might also be tempted to launch another military strike to demonstrate strength or claim a victory.

That is precisely why Washington must avoid confusing access to a powerful Iranian official with actual Iranian flexibility. Overestimating Rezaei’s ability to deliver concessions could generate unrealistic expectations, deepen frustration, and ultimately increase the risk of another military confrontation.

The path to an agreement with Iran does not run through finding a more convenient Iranian interlocutor. It runs through recognizing that Tehran’s fundamental demands have not changed.

Changing the Iranian negotiator will not change Iran’s negotiating position. Only a meaningful shift in the substance and sequencing of American proposals could create a genuine opportunity for progress.

And unless Washington and Tehran find a way to bridge that gap, another meeting, another mediator, or another Iranian negotiator will do little to prevent the next escalation.

text:
Michael Jordan’s two seasons in Washington deserve a better conversation than whether he should have stopped after the shot in Utah.

They offer something his championship years rarely allowed us to see: Jordan working with a body that could no longer consistently deliver everything his mind demanded.

The separation was smaller. Finishing through traffic was harder. Creating a good shot required more patience, positioning and deception.

The footwork still mattered. So did the shoulder fake, the pivot and the ability to get a defender leaning before rising into a jumper.

In his first Wizards season, Jordan averaged 22.9 points, 5.7 rebounds and 5.2 assists.

In his second, he played all 82 games, averaging 20.0 points, 6.1 rebounds and 3.8 assists. He turned 40 during that season while carrying a workload of 37 minutes per game.

Those numbers deserve context. His scoring efficiency had declined, and Washington missed the playoffs both years. This was a diminished version of the player who had controlled the league.

Yet the distance between diminished Jordan and ordinary basketball remained considerable.

That is what makes those seasons compelling.

We often describe his greatness through flight: the elevation, the hang time, the finishes that seemed to suspend the rules. Washington made the quieter foundations easier to appreciate. Balance. Timing. Strength. An understanding of how defenders react.

The Wizards years belong in the story because they reveal how much basketball intelligence supported the athletic spectacle all along.

There was no seventh championship to give the comeback a perfect ending.

There was an aging player still finding ways to score against younger legs, night after night.

His body had lost some of its answers.

His understanding of the game remained extraordinary.

text:
Anthropic’s IPO prospectus mix-up on November 9–10, 2026
Late on Monday, November 9, 2026, Anthropic’s outside counsel in Canada emailed banks/underwriters an updated IPO prospectus (S-1 related materials). A follow-up email soon after said some of the pricing details were “inaccurate” and that an updated filing would follow. The incorrect version was quickly leaked to Reuters, which published the details as an exclusive, creating a brief mess of circulating (then retracted) numbers right as the company prepared to launch its roadshow.
Retracted numbers (from the leaked filing, per Reuters emails)
•~866.7–867 million Class A shares offered
•Price range: $70–$80 per share
•Company selling ~843.3 million shares; existing shareholders selling ~23.3 million in a secondary offering
•Potential raise: up to $69.3 billion at the top of the range
•Separate $26 billion private placement of Class N common stock at the IPO price, closing right after the IPO. Participants: Alphabet/Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC
•Expected Nasdaq ticker: ANT
•Roadshow expected to start formally on Tuesday, November 10, with pricing the following week
Anthropic declined to comment on the specifics of what was wrong. Reuters could not determine the exact error.
Updated/official numbers (as of November 10)
Anthropic launched its roadshow on Tuesday. The corrected terms (from company announcement and later Reuters reporting on the latest draft) are:
•825 million Class A shares offered (801.35 million from the company + ~23.65 million from existing stockholders)
•Price range: $70–$78 per share
•Potential IPO raise: up to ~$64.4 billion (high end)
•Underwriters’ 30-day option for up to an additional ~123.75 million shares
•Same $26 billion private placement from the seven tech companies at the IPO price
•Target valuation: up to ~$1.02 trillion (described as more modest than earlier market talk of $1.2–2 trillion)
•Planned pricing around November 18, with trading targeted for November 19 (or around November 19–20, before Thanksgiving)
•Listing on Nasdaq under ANT
The company is also targeting a high retail allocation (~20%).
Context
Anthropic filed its public S-1 on October 26, 2026 (after a confidential filing). The 15-day quiet period ended around November 9–10, allowing the formal roadshow. Lead underwriters include Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley (among many others). The IPO is one of the largest ever contemplated for an AI company, following strong revenue growth (e.g., ~$16+ billion in recent periods) but also large infrastructure commitments and losses.
The Canadian counsel angle matches reports that the offering includes a Canadian retail component (alongside the U.S. and other jurisdictions) without a Canadian exchange listing. The error appears to have been a clerical/pricing detail mistake in materials sent to banks, not a full public filing retraction. It created short-term confusion and media coverage but did not derail the process—the roadshow launched the next day with the adjusted terms.
This is still a developing situation as of November 10, 2026; final pricing and exact valuation will depend on demand during the roadshow.

text:
Political Infighting Behind Jensen Huang’s Controversy
 
The recent personal scandal involving Jensen Huang, founder of the global chip giant, has been deliberately hyped and politicized in Western public opinion. What should have been a private moral and family matter has rapidly evolved into groundless speculation about national security, with Western media and politicians fabricating so-called “Chinese spy theories” surrounding the incident. These baseless accusations have been firmly refuted by China’s foreign ministry, confirming that the allegations are purely speculative and lack factual evidence.
 
Rather than focusing on personal ethics, the storm is essentially a product of internal American political infighting. The controversy emerged immediately after the U.S. midterm elections, a sensitive period of political restructuring and power reshuffling. Competing political camps are using this case to seize a tough stance on China and reshape regulatory rules for the artificial intelligence and semiconductor industries. As an influential Chinese-American tech leader, Jensen Huang has become a hostage of partisan struggles, with both sides seeking to gain an advantage in future high-tech policy competition.
 
The political manipulation of commercial affairs has created a chilling effect across the global tech industry. By arbitrarily linking personal relationships with national security, U.S. political forces aim to trigger lengthy security reviews, restrict corporate operations in Asia, and disrupt the global semiconductor supply chain layout.
 
Beneath the public hype lies a deeper economic motive. Unlike other tech giants, the company’s founding team holds relatively low shareholdings. Political turbulence and public opinion crises offer opportunities for Wall Street capital and U.S. establishment forces to intervene in corporate governance, weaken founder influence, and seize actual control of the core computing power and chip industry ecosystem.
 
This incident marks the end of Silicon Valley’s pure commercial myth. Cutting-edge technology and international enterprises are increasingly reduced to tools of U.S. partisan infighting and great-power geopolitical competition.

Help people assess the decision:

2. Explain what switching involves, including time, costs and responsibilities.

Do not assume staying put is irrational. Make the comparison clear enough that the customer can decide whether the improvement is worth the disruption.

text:
NQ / NASDAQ — PRE-OPEN REGIME RADAR
Nasdaq Futures Lag Monday's Recovery as CPI, Hawkish Fed Comments and CoreWeave Earnings Put AI Valuations to the Test — 10 November 2026
10 NOVEMBER 2026 | 13:53 SWITZERLAND | 06:53 CME/CHICAGO | 07:53 NEW YORK
FIRST REPORT OF THE DAY — PRE-OPEN
LATEST VERIFIED FUTURES SNAPSHOT: 12:04 SWITZERLAND / 06:04 NEW YORK

MAIN CONCLUSION
The Nasdaq-100 enters Tuesday's US inflation release with a clear contradiction: Wall Street rallied sharply on Monday, semiconductor manufacturing demand remains robust, and oil has fallen dramatically, yet NQ futures are again underperforming the broader market. Reuters recorded Nasdaq-100 E-mini futures down 0.35% at 06:04 New York, while S&P 500 futures were approximately flat and Dow futures gained 0.30%. Nvidia remains exposed to unresolved governance and media allegations, and investors are also reassessing the proposed Anthropic flotation. Meanwhile, Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller has argued for another interest-rate increase in December even if inflation slows. The decisive scheduled event is the October Consumer Price Index at 14:30 Switzerland, exactly one hour before the US cash-market opening.

KEY CONFIRMATION / RISK
Monday's index rally demonstrated substantial buying after the prior week's technology correction, but Nvidia declined 4.27% even as the Nasdaq Composite gained 2.74%. Tuesday adds three distinct tests: the inflation report's monthly components, the bond market's response to increasingly hawkish Fed commentary, and CoreWeave's results after the close. An important technical detail in the economic release must not be missed: the Bureau of Labor Statistics will not publish most October 2026 year-on-year CPI rates, because the October 2025 government shutdown left the necessary comparison data unavailable. Consensus annual figures in market commentary are estimates, not official numbers that can be verified from today's release.

MONDAY'S CLOSE — A MAJOR RECOVERY, BUT NOT UNIFORM TECH LEADERSHIP
The US cash market recorded its strongest broad rebound for months on Monday, 9 November:

DOW JONES INDUSTRIAL AVERAGE: 52,389.75 | +2.15%.

S&P 500: 7,549.94 | +2.35%.

NASDAQ COMPOSITE: 25,253.14 | +2.74%.

RUSSELL 2000: 2,840.81 | +3.15%.

The S&P 500's advance was its largest one-day percentage gain since April. Lower oil prices and a rebound in many technology and semiconductor shares helped restore risk appetite. Broadcom and other technology companies contributed to the rise. Nvidia, however, declined approximately 4.27% and remained an important negative contribution to the S&P 500. A strong index close therefore did not mean the market had resolved its uncertainty about every major AI company.

The Nasdaq Composite is a cash-market index and is not interchangeable with the Nasdaq-100 or its NQ futures contract. Those distinctions matter when comparing Monday's close with Tuesday's pre-market movement.

TUESDAY'S FUTURES — THE NASDAQ IS THE RELATIVE LAGGARD
REUTERS, 06:04 NEW YORK / 12:04 SWITZERLAND:

NASDAQ-100 E-MINI FUTURES: −0.35%.
S&P 500 E-MINI FUTURES: +0.01%.

DOW E-MINI FUTURES: +0.30%.
The market has not reversed all of Monday's gains, but investors are no longer rewarding technology exposure uniformly. At the time of that observation, Nvidia had reduced its earlier pre-market gain to about 0.3%, while Intel and Marvell Technology were down around 2%. An earlier Reuters snapshot showed NQ nearly flat; this change illustrates why observations must be labelled by time rather than presented as simultaneous live prices.

No unverified current NQ contract level, VWAP, POC, opening range or support/resistance number is inserted in this report. The pre-CPI futures picture is a relative-performance observation, not an executable trading signal.

NVIDIA — GOVERNANCE UNCERTAINTY HAS NOT BEEN RESOLVED

Nvidia's shares fell more than 4% on Monday after reporting concerning CEO Jensen Huang. The company's board has announced an independent inquiry into reports of a possible foreign-intelligence operation. Additional media reporting on Tuesday has raised allegations concerning a personal relationship and the movement of advanced chips through Chinese entities.

These are reported allegations, not confirmed findings of the independent investigation. Nvidia previously stated that it had no reason to believe its secrets or national-security interests had been compromised and expressed confidence in Huang's leadership. The existence of an inquiry must not be treated as proof of the underlying claims.

For the market, the issue is a company-specific governance risk affecting an exceptionally influential AI supplier. The practical index question is whether weakness remains concentrated in Nvidia or spreads into the broader chip sector. Today's CPI could amplify either response through changes in risk appetite and discount rates.

TSMC — STRONG EVIDENCE THAT ADVANCED-CHIP DEMAND CONTINUES

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company reported October consolidated revenue of NT$586.89 billion, an increase of 59.7% from a year earlier and 14.7% from September. It was a new monthly revenue record. The company supplies leading advanced-chip designers and is a crucial manufacturer of high-performance processors used in AI systems.

The figures establish significant current manufacturing demand. They do not settle how much future data-centre construction will cost, whether every operator will earn an attractive return, or what equity valuation investors should attach to those earnings. This distinction has become central to the Nasdaq correction.

Strong supply-chain revenue and a cautious response to AI-related shares can coexist. The market is increasingly pricing future profitability and financing risk, not simply the number of chips being produced.

AI INFRASTRUCTURE — THE INVESTMENT CYCLE FACES A FINANCIAL TEST

The AI expansion involves several linked but financially different activities: designing chips, producing them, building facilities, securing electricity, operating cloud infrastructure and selling AI services. Revenue for one part of the chain is expenditure for another. Accelerating chip shipments can demonstrate demand without proving that the entire chain is generating adequate free cash flow.

Data-centre operators face capital expenditure, power and cooling costs, lease obligations, interest payments and the risk that installed capacity takes longer than expected to reach commercial utilisation. Established hyperscalers may finance growth internally; smaller operators may depend more heavily on external capital. Higher policy-rate expectations can worsen the mathematics of debt-funded expansion even if demand remains strong.

That is why today's CPI and tonight's CoreWeave figures are linked. One influences the cost-of-capital environment; the other offers insight into the financial model of a major AI computing infrastructure provider.

COREWEAVE — TONIGHT'S MOST DIRECT CORPORATE TEST

CoreWeave has confirmed its third-quarter 2026 earnings conference call for 17:00 New York / 23:00 Switzerland, after the US cash-market close. The results were not available at this report's cut-off and must not be described as already released.

Investors will be assessing revenue and contracted demand, capital spending, customer concentration, installed capacity, the speed of new project deliveries, debt and interest costs, and management's financial guidance. A large order backlog has value, but the timing of revenue recognition and cash collection also matters. The critical issue is whether expanding infrastructure commitments can produce sustainable returns after financing and operating costs.

Results from CoreWeave may influence other data-centre operators and the wider AI complex after regular trading. They are also likely to inform the interpretation of subsequent reports from networking and semiconductor-equipment suppliers later this week.

ANTHROPIC — A POSSIBLE IPO ADDS A VALUATION QUESTION

Reuters has reported details from a draft prospectus indicating that Anthropic's proposed stock-market flotation could raise as much as $64.4 billion. Earlier information circulated to banks was reportedly retracted, making the final terms and timing uncertain. Draft figures should not be mistaken for completed fundraising or a settled valuation.

The significance for Nasdaq investors is not only the prospective listing itself. A very large AI offering could create a new public-market benchmark for the revenue, costs, profitability and growth assumptions attached to frontier AI businesses. It could also compete with other technology companies for investor capital. An IPO filing does not itself establish that existing NQ constituents must decline or rise.

FEDERAL RESERVE — WALLER'S COMMENTS HAVE CHANGED THE INFLATION TEST

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday that he would favour a 25-basis-point policy-rate increase at the December meeting even if October inflation moderated. He also said a larger, 50-basis-point move should be considered if monthly core CPI rose by around 0.3% or more. This is Waller's stated policy view, not a decision by the Federal Open Market Committee.

After Friday's stronger-than-expected employment report, traders had already raised their expectations for December tightening. Reuters' latest global-market account described the market as almost fully pricing a quarter-point December increase, compared with around a 74% chance a week earlier. The exact implied probability changes with futures prices and is not a guarantee of the outcome.

For NQ, an important asymmetry follows: even a CPI report that meets forecasts may not remove expectations of higher borrowing costs. A hotter core number could increase the debate about more forceful tightening. The direction of equities will still depend on actual price action and the interaction of rates with earnings expectations.

US TREASURIES — SHORT-TERM RATES ARE UNDER PRESSURE

Reuters reported the 2-year Treasury yield around 4.611% on Tuesday, approximately 6.5 basis points higher in its global-market observation. The increase is consistent with a more restrictive near-term Fed outlook. Longer maturities also matter for equity valuations, but verified synchronised readings of every curve point were not available for this report.

A higher short-term yield can tighten financial conditions. For AI companies funding multi-year projects, both government yields and company-specific financing spreads are relevant. Lower oil can help medium-term inflation expectations while hawkish Fed remarks push short-term rates upwards. The result can be a flatter yield curve rather than a simple move in all maturities together.

The Treasury is also due to auction $42 billion of 10-year notes today. Demand and the resulting yield may influence the afternoon bond-market narrative, but no auction result exists before the scheduled sale.

THE CPI RELEASE — TODAY'S MAIN EVENT

TUESDAY, 10 NOVEMBER | 14:30 SWITZERLAND | 07:30 CHICAGO | 08:30 NEW YORK.

OCTOBER HEADLINE CPI, MONTH ON MONTH:
CONSENSUS +0.3% | SEPTEMBER +0.6%.

OCTOBER CORE CPI, MONTH ON MONTH:
CONSENSUS +0.2% | SEPTEMBER +0.3%.

These are consensus forecasts, not published October results. September's 12-month headline inflation rate was 3.7% and its 12-month core rate was 2.6%.

IMPORTANT DATA LIMITATION — NO STANDARD ANNUAL COMPARISON

The BLS has confirmed that the October 2025 federal shutdown prevented publication of the price indexes needed for most October year-on-year comparisons. Accordingly, the October 2026 CPI release will omit 12-month percentage changes wherever the October 2025 base is unavailable. Analysts may produce estimates through other methods, but those are not equivalent to an official October annual CPI rate.

Today's professional interpretation should therefore focus on the actual monthly headline and core indexes, shelter, services, energy, vehicles, transport, medical care and other components. It should also distinguish a monthly slowing in price growth from an outright fall in consumer prices.

WHAT COULD DRIVE THE CPI COMPONENTS

The recent decline in crude oil and retail fuel prices is relevant, but the timing matters. A large oil fall in early November cannot automatically be assumed to be fully reflected in October's consumer-price survey. Gasoline, airfares, accommodation, shelter and health-insurance calculations may each affect the published monthly result differently.

Core inflation excludes food and energy, making the behaviour of services and shelter especially important. A lower headline CPI driven mainly by petrol may not settle the policy debate if underlying costs remain persistent. Conversely, a broad-based deceleration would have different implications than an isolated energy effect.

CPI SCENARIO — SOFTER CORE PRESSURE
If core CPI is below the +0.2% consensus and weakness extends across several relevant components, investors may reassess the degree of tightening required in December. That could relieve some pressure on financing-sensitive growth valuations. But Waller has explicitly argued for a rate increase even if October inflation eases, so the reaction cannot be inferred from the headline surprise alone.

CPI SCENARIO — CONSENSUS OR NEAR CONSENSUS
A report near +0.3% headline and +0.2% core could leave the Fed's tightening outlook largely intact. Attention could then shift towards details, Treasury-yield changes, the quality of equity-market buying and CoreWeave's results. A consensus outcome does not guarantee a calm market; positioning and prior expectations may still produce large swings.

CPI SCENARIO — PERSISTENT CORE INFLATION
If monthly core CPI is +0.3% or higher, investors may revisit Waller's comments about the possibility of a larger December move. Short-term Treasury yields and the dollar could respond. Such an outcome would create an additional valuation challenge for long-duration and debt-financed AI projects, although the actual NQ reaction must be observed rather than assumed in advance.

OIL — THE LARGEST MACROECONOMIC RELIEF FACTOR

Brent crude briefly traded below $90 a barrel on Tuesday, its lowest level since August, after another sharp decline. Reuters reported the price down more than 1.5% during its global-market observation, following a roughly 6% fall on Monday. President Trump has indicated that further strikes against Iran are unlikely while negotiations continue.
The energy-price decline reduces some near-term inflation fears and may benefit consumers, transport and energy-intensive businesses. It does not establish that the conflict is over or that physical supply risks have disappeared. It also does not instantly solve grid-access problems or the economics of long-term electricity contracts for data centres.
There is a timing distinction worth preserving: today's crude-price decline is happening ahead of the CPI release, but today's published CPI describes October, not the full effect of November's energy move.

ASIA — SEMICONDUCTORS RECOVER, BUT GLOBAL EXPOSURE IS UNEVEN

Reuters reported Japan's Nikkei up approximately 2.9% and South Korea's Kospi up around 4.4% on Tuesday. The broad MSCI Asia-Pacific measure outside Japan also recovered, supported by greater confidence following Monday's Wall Street rally and lower energy prices. TSMC's October revenue reinforced the evidence that advanced-chip demand remains strong.

The regional recovery provides an important contrast with the hesitation in NQ futures. Asian technology strength may support sentiment, but US equities face additional company-specific and monetary-policy questions. Regional stock indexes have different company weights, exchange rates and market structures; their percentage returns should not be treated as direct futures signals.

EUROPE — THE OIL DECLINE IS MORE CLEARLY POSITIVE

The STOXX 600 rose around 0.9% in Reuters' Tuesday global-market observation, moving close to its all-time high. Lower energy prices helped ease inflation concerns and improved sentiment in sectors exposed to household spending and transport costs.

European equities' positive response is relevant but does not mean that Nasdaq's concerns have disappeared. A global fall in oil can simultaneously support the wider market and leave interest-rate-sensitive AI valuations under pressure, particularly when a Fed official is advocating further tightening.

NEW YORK FED CONSUMER EXPECTATIONS — THE MONDAY RELEASE

The New York Fed's October Survey of Consumer Expectations, released on Monday, showed inflation expectations unchanged at 3.9% over one year, 3.3% over three years and 3.0% over five years. Expectations of higher unemployment deteriorated to their highest level since April 2020, while perceived job-finding prospects improved.

This is useful context for the CPI. Households still anticipate considerable inflation even as fuel-price expectations have moderated. The survey also points to a mixed labour-market outlook. It measures beliefs, not actual consumer prices, so it cannot substitute for today's BLS data.

TODAY'S REMAINING CALENDAR — SWISS TIME

14:30 — OCTOBER US CPI AND REAL EARNINGS. The day's primary scheduled macroeconomic release.

15:30 — NEW YORK CASH-MARKET OPENING. The first broad equity-market test of the CPI response.

19:00 — US TREASURY AUCTION: $42 BILLION OF 10-YEAR NOTES. Watch the bond-market response after the inflation release.

22:00 — US REGULAR CASH-MARKET CLOSE. Examine whether Nasdaq participation broadened or remained concentrated.

23:00 — COREWEAVE THIRD-QUARTER EARNINGS CONFERENCE CALL. The company's confirmed investor-relations schedule.

Other Fed remarks and company releases may affect prices during the session. Published event times should not be confused with outcomes already known.

REST OF THE WEEK — AN UNUSUAL BOND-MARKET CALENDAR

WEDNESDAY, 11 NOVEMBER — VETERANS DAY. US stock exchanges are scheduled to operate, but SIFMA has recommended a full closure of US dollar-denominated fixed-income trading. Equity and futures market hours should be checked by venue and contract.

THURSDAY, 12 NOVEMBER, 14:30 SWITZERLAND — INITIAL AND CONTINUING JOBLESS CLAIMS.

THURSDAY, 12 NOVEMBER, 19:00 SWITZERLAND — $25 BILLION US TREASURY 30-YEAR BOND AUCTION.

THURSDAY, AFTER THE US CASH CLOSE — CISCO AND APPLIED MATERIALS EARNINGS, with implications for networking, chip-equipment orders and AI capital expenditure.

FRIDAY, 13 NOVEMBER, 14:30 SWITZERLAND — OCTOBER PRODUCER PRICE INDEX. A second major test of inflation pressure after today's CPI.

CROSS-MARKET CONFIRMATION FRAMEWORK

NQ VERSUS ES — Does technology continue to lag the broader US equity market after the CPI release?

NVIDIA, TSMC, AMD AND SOX — Does evidence of manufacturing demand translate into broader semiconductor buying?

COREWEAVE AND DATA-CENTRE OPERATORS — Are investors reassessing the cost, timing and financing of new computing capacity?

US 2-YEAR AND 10-YEAR YIELDS — Is monetary tightening becoming more expensive to price into future corporate earnings?

BRENT — Is lower energy pressure being translated into lower inflation expectations?

DXY AND VIX — Are dollar demand and implied volatility reinforcing or contradicting the equity response?

NASDAQ BREADTH — Is a recovery supported by many stocks or concentrated in a handful of influential constituents?

No unsupported real-time index or chart level is presented as a verified quote at publication time.

BULLISH SCENARIO — EDITORIAL WEIGHT: 45%

A broader recovery would be supported by a softer core-inflation reading, orderly Treasury yields, sustained semiconductor participation and continued evidence of strong AI demand from suppliers such as TSMC. Nvidia-specific uncertainty would need to remain contained, while breadth improves after the cash opening. CoreWeave's financial results could also support confidence if growth is accompanied by credible investment and financing plans.

BEARISH SCENARIO — EDITORIAL WEIGHT: 55%

The cautious case reflects NQ's pre-market underperformance, unresolved Nvidia allegations, the increasing cost of capital and the possibility that core inflation remains persistent. A stronger CPI reading, higher short-term yields, weak technology breadth or disappointing AI infrastructure financing disclosures could renew pressure. These percentages are discretionary editorial weights, not statistically calibrated probabilities of the market's next movement.

ANALYTICAL EDGE

MIXED PRE-CPI FUTURES / HAWKISH FED REPRICING / STRONG CHIP MANUFACTURING DEMAND / SELECTIVE AI VALUATION RISK. Monday's powerful cash-market rebound was real, but today's slightly negative NQ futures and higher short-term yields prevent it from being described as a fully confirmed return to technology leadership. The first proper test comes at 14:30 Switzerland, with an additional corporate test after the close.

CURRENT REGIME

POST-CORRECTION REBOUND / NVIDIA GOVERNANCE UNCERTAINTY / TSMC REVENUE STRENGTH / FALLING OIL / FED TIGHTENING EXPECTATIONS / OCTOBER CPI EVENT RISK / COREWEAVE FINANCING SCRUTINY.

OPERATIONAL CONCLUSION

The CPI release takes place one hour before the US cash opening, creating two distinct phases of price discovery. Futures may react immediately to the inflation surprise, while broader equity participation will be clearer once the cash market opens. For NQ and MNQ, observed price action, realistic execution costs, position sizing, a predefined protective stop and the maximum acceptable loss remain more important than conviction about the news. A correct economic interpretation does not guarantee a profitable entry or protect against rapid reversals.

FINAL ANALYTICAL VIEW

WHAT CHANGED: Monday's 2.74% Nasdaq Composite rebound was followed by renewed NQ futures hesitation, while Nvidia remained under scrutiny and TSMC reported record October revenue growth of 59.7% year on year.

WHAT THE FED ADDED: Governor Waller supports another December rate increase even if inflation slows and has raised the possibility of a larger move if core CPI is 0.3% or higher.

WHAT MATTERS TODAY: October monthly CPI and its components at 14:30 Switzerland; the US cash opening at 15:30; a $42 billion 10-year Treasury auction at 19:00; and CoreWeave's earnings call at 23:00.

WHAT WOULD STRENGTHEN THE RECOVERY: Broad semiconductor buying, a contained rates response and reassuring evidence about AI infrastructure earnings and financing.

WHAT WOULD WEAKEN IT: Persistent core inflation, rising short-term yields, renewed weakness in large AI companies and a deterioration in Nasdaq breadth.

The key task today is to distinguish a rebound in market prices from a lasting improvement in the financial conditions supporting technology valuations.

text:
2. Details of the Summary
Flint, a majority-Black city with high poverty rates and a history of deindustrialization (GM plant closures), was under Michigan’s emergency-manager law due to budget deficits. Decisions prioritized short-term savings over full treatment readiness at the long-idle Flint water plant.
The Flint River source was known to be sensitive to contaminants. Without corrosion control, water chemistry changed: higher chlorides, acidity, and lack of inhibitors caused scale to dissolve. Lead service lines (common in older infrastructure) and interior plumbing released lead. Some homes recorded extreme levels (hundreds or thousands of ppb; EPA action level is 15 ppb). Iron corrosion produced brown water. Chlorine residuals dropped in parts of the system, linked to Legionella growth.
Key evidence came from resident LeeAnne Walters (whose home tested very high), Edwards’ citywide sampling (one in six homes above action level in some analyses), and Hanna-Attisha’s blood-lead data. State regulators initially downplayed or challenged findings. Elevated blood-lead prevalence roughly doubled citywide and was higher in certain neighborhoods. Long-term risks of childhood lead exposure include cognitive/behavioral effects, lower academic achievement, and other developmental issues; studies have documented impacts on test scores and special-education needs in Flint.
Legionnaires’ (a severe pneumonia from waterborne Legionella) rose sharply after the switch; a PNAS study tied much of the outbreak to lower chlorine residuals during the river-water period. Official counts are ~87–91 cases and 12 deaths; pneumonia-death analyses suggest undercounting.
3. Ongoing Clean-up & Repair/Replacement Details
Lead service-line work is effectively complete. Under the 2017 NRDC/Concerned Pastors settlement and subsequent efforts, crews excavated/inspected ~31,930 addresses. Outcomes: ~11,600 lead/galvanized lines replaced, ~1,380 cut and capped (disconnected), and ~18,950 confirmed copper-to-copper. The last known active lead service lines were addressed by mid-2026 (reports cite completion around July–August 2026). Total system improvements exceeded $1 billion; pipe-specific work was on the order of $97–140 million.
Restoration of yards, streets, and properties affected by excavations continued into 2026 and was wrapping up. Water is now sourced long-term via the Great Lakes Water Authority (Lake Huron). Recent monitoring shows compliance: 90th-percentile lead levels around 3 ppb (well below the 15 ppb action level; Michigan has tighter rules), with years of consecutive compliance. Filters and testing resources have been provided; the city continues monitoring and offers support. Some residual skepticism remains among residents.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Tucker Carlson Show: Bradley Pierce: Modern Demonic Rituals and the Embrace of Human Sacrifice in Trump’s America

Overview
Bradley Pierce, an abolitionist activist, makes the case that abortion is human sacrifice, that Christianity historically ended child sacrifice wherever it spread, and that overturning Roe v. Wade settled nothing because abortion remains legal, common, and increasingly celebrated. He argues that the pro-life movement itself has become an obstacle, because major organizations oppose bills that would apply equal protection to the unborn and treat women as perpetrators rather than only as second victims. The through-line is that a nation that permits the killing of the innocent invites judgment, and that the current political order, including the Trump administration, has done nothing substantial to stop it. Pierce also defends large families as a matter of trusting God rather than planning, and ties the whole argument to the claim that human rights only make sense if humans bear God’s image.

Key Themes
- Abortion is defined as murder from fertilization, and framed as uniquely heinous because the victim is the most innocent, the act occurs in the womb, and the perpetrator is the person the child should most trust.
- The West held a near-2,000-year consensus against abortion until 1973; its collapse is attributed to humanism separating people from the image of God, which turns persons into disposable product even while claiming to elevate humanity.
- Child sacrifice was universal across ancient cultures and Christianity ended it; Scripture treats it as the central reason lands “vomit out” their inhabitants, and national judgment is tied to it.
- Overturning Roe did not resolve the moral question, and the “my body, my choice” framing was undercut by COVID vaccine mandates while abortion pills now make the procedure accessible in all 50 states.
- Major pro-life organizations actively opposed equal protection bills, arguing women are second victims; abolitionists counter that women can be both victim and perpetrator, and that legality itself drives behavior.
- Abolitionists reject setting aside religious arguments for secular ones, insisting on starting from God’s word and then adding scientific claims about unique DNA and self-replication from fertilization.
- Pierce criticizes the Trump administration and the Republican Party for doing nothing substantial on abortion, citing softened RNC platform language, continued non-enforcement of the Comstock Act, and Trump treating anti-abortion voters as a liability.
- Large families are framed as blessing and trust in God, with Pierce citing Scripture’s repeated command to be fruitful and multiply and describing his own twelve children with a thirteenth expected.

Detailed Summary
Riley Pierce defines abortion as the destruction of human life from fertilization, calling it murder biologically and spiritually, an attack on the image of God. He argues it is more heinous than other murder for three reasons: the victim is the most innocent, the act occurs in the womb, described as the safest place and the place where Christ entered the world, and the perpetrator is typically the person the child should most trust. He claims there were over 1.1 million abortions in the US in 2025, with roughly two-thirds to 80 percent now occurring via the abortion pill, some ordered online or self-induced at home.

He argues the West held a near-2,000-year consensus against abortion from the early church through 1973, and attributes its rapid change to devaluing humans by separating them from being made in God’s image. Humanism, on this account, ultimately devalues human beings: by denying divine image and eternal souls, people become disposable product even as humanism claims to elevate humanity to gods. He ties abortion to human sacrifice and to communism, citing the early Soviet Union’s banning of Christianity and legalization of abortion as connected.

The historical argument runs through the Hippocratic Oath, which originally included a prohibition on producing a pessary to induce abortion; Pierce says the medical establishment removed it to focus only on “do no harm.” Under pagan Rome, child exposure meant leaving children in the woods; Christians rescued and adopted those children, and early church fathers clearly called abortion murder. Pierce acknowledges Margaret Sanger was against abortion at least for a while, though he questions her motives. He says human sacrifice was universal across ancient civilizations before Christianity, and that Christianity ended it.

The biblical case is central. Child sacrifice is framed as the one reason found in all three biblical lists for God driving the Canaanites out of the land; the land is said to “vomit out” inhabitants because of innocent blood. The three reasons listed include idolatry, sexual immorality or perversion, and witchcraft, with child sacrifice being the only one in all three lists, and the warning is that if the Israelites do the same, the land will vomit them out too. Societal collapse and divine judgment are tied to child sacrifice, citing Solomon building high places to Molech and Manasseh sacrificing his own children, followed by the kingdom’s division and later exile and temple destruction. Josiah abolished these practices, and God delays judgment temporarily because of his faithfulness but still brings it.

Romans 1 is invoked to argue that denying God as creator leads to a debased mind, depravity, and what the speaker calls a mental health crisis of anxiety and depression. Pierce asserts that Christians or Jews who support abortion are deceived or biblically illiterate, attributing this to false teaching, heresies, and pastors avoiding the issue. On the legal history, Roe v. Wade in 1973 built on Griswold v. Connecticut in 1967 and a right to privacy, though “my body, my choice” framing dominated during Roe’s enforcement. That argument, the speaker notes, was undercut in 2021 by COVID vaccine mandates.

Overturning Roe did not resolve the underlying moral issue: abortion remains legal and common, and the question of its justification is now more acute. Abortion is framed as something broadly recognized as horrifying even by pro-choice people, requiring linguistic gymnastics to justify, with disagreement over whether growing public celebration signals moral decline or is itself compensation for what people know to be wrong. Arguments offered as new justifications, bodily autonomy and economic necessity, are both treated skeptically. The interviewee criticizes the current administration and Republican Party for doing nothing substantial on abortion despite controlling the White House, Supreme Court, and Congress.

Pierce’s organization sent a letter to President Trump in January calling on him to repent for favorable comments about abortion and to adopt policy actions, appealing to the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause and biblical justice for the fatherless. The claim is that 70-plus million children have been killed through abortion since 1973, and that abortion pills can be ordered and taken in all 50 states with nothing substantial done about it. The speaker compares mass abortion to the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings in August 1945 as the two mass killings the US participated in. The interviewee claims Trump responded to midterm losses by saying Republicans were too strong on abortion, and the other speaker says Trump sees anti-abortion voters as a liability. At the RNC, abortion language was reportedly stripped from the platform after Trump took the nomination.

Abortion should be a line in the sand for voting, and candidates who don’t act correctly should not receive support; the issue is framed as civilizational and religious, tied to divine judgment. The Trump administration is criticized for continuing Biden-era non-enforcement of the Comstock Act, described as over 100 years old and prohibiting mailing of abortion medication. Responsibility for enforcement is said to rest on Congress and the public, and Trump should push states and Congress for equal protection for preborn children. Post-Dobbs, provider bans exist in some states, but abortion pills remain accessible because mail is a federal issue states can’t control, with 13 states having provider bans and four more with six-week heartbeat bans while pills remain legal to order and take.

Tennessee saw a first equal protection bill introduced; prior polling of conservative likely voters showed roughly 16 percent support for criminal penalties for women obtaining abortions, and a later Vanderbilt poll of all likely voters showed 24 percent. Between 60 and 80 percent of abortions involve no doctor, self-induced via abortion pill, making the woman the abortionist. The pill regimen is described as mifepristone causing the death of the child, then misoprostol inducing delivery, with pills taken beyond the FDA-indicated 10 to 12 weeks, citing use at 21 to 22 weeks. Pill manufacturing occurs outside the US in India, Austria, and Africa, and most pills go through clinics and doctors, some directly to women. Proverbs 24:11, about rescuing those being carried to the slaughter, is cited as motivation, and funders are Christians who call themselves abolitionists.

The central strategic disagreement is that women should face penalties to deter abortion, not just doctors or supply. Pro-life voters broadly agree with equal protection, but pro-life leadership organizations oppose bills that would criminalize women, framing women as second victims. Pierce says women can be both victim and perpetrator, and that being lied to or deceived does not excuse committing a crime. He describes feeling betrayed by the pro-life movement, calling it fraudulent while acknowledging exceptions, and draws an analogy to drug policy: penalties can deter harmful behavior, and some former addicts are grateful for arrest.

Texas’s 2003 law defined a person as beginning at fertilization while adding a homicide exemption giving blanket immunity to mothers who abort. Pierce says this exemption was pushed by pro-life groups, pro-life Republican politicians, and signed by a pro-life governor, and that similar provisions exist in every pro-life state. In Louisiana in 2022, an equal protection bill advanced 7–2 from committee, but shortly before the vote a letter from 77 pro-life organizations opposed it, including National Right to Life, Susan B. Anthony, and many state right-to-life groups. He references the 2013 Texas bill with a 20-week ban, hospital admitting privileges, and surgery-center standards, and Wendy Davis’s filibuster, and says a Texas legislator’s effort to simply outlaw abortion was met with opposition from pro-life groups. Post-abortive women who support abolition reportedly say they wish abortion had been illegal and they could have been prosecuted.

Equal protection bills have been filed in dozens of states, with over 130 legislators signing on to bills the group is involved with this year, described as more than ever. A Georgia hearing example is cited: a Jewish legislator argued her faith permits abortion, and the speaker disputes this, saying the Torah prohibits it and only Talmudic interpretations could support abortion. The scientific argument used is that from fertilization the entity has totally unique DNA, self-replicating cells, is obviously human, and therefore is not owned by the mother, drawing an analogy to slavery. Progress is described as slow, with some pro-life leaders listening and changing but very slowly.

The speakers argue a child is not owned by parents but is a human being under stewardship, and that differing DNA undermines the “my body, my choice” framing. Some people now concede the unborn is a human being but still assert a right to take that life, which the speakers treat as a stark moral position. The pro-life movement is distinguished from an abolitionist movement, with much of the former argued to be built on secularism and to regulate abortion rather than treat it as a sin against God. Human rights are said to derive from the Christian recognition that God created every person; without God as foundation, rights reduce to human assertion, and the choice is framed as between God and figures like Larry Fink of BlackRock.

On family, Pierce argues large families were historically common and often raised in smaller homes than Americans today believe are necessary for two or three children. Children are framed as a blessing repeatedly affirmed in Scripture, citing the command to be fruitful and multiply after the creation of the woman, after Noah and his family come off the ark, and after God changes Jacob’s name to Israel. He acknowledges God may choose for a couple to have many children, few, or none, and says that outcome should be trusted as God’s best. He has 12 children with a 13th expected, six boys and six girls in alternating girl-boy order, oldest 15, with two sets of twins, awaiting confirmation of a Guinness record for alternating births. He describes a house with one boys’ room, one girls’ room, a parents’ room, and a baby room, and says visitors from Mozambique found it “so big,” illustrating perspective. On cost, he says God will provide and that Americans are the richest people in history, though sacrifices are required, noting his grandfather was one of 10 and that genealogy commonly shows families of 10 to 12 in smaller houses than Americans think necessary today. His wife Cindy wants another child and has prayed for one, even twins, which he calls a huge blessing rather than crazy.

text:
I want to share Bob’s wonderful Veteran’s Day message. A fitting tribute to the men and women of our armed forces who sacrifice so much for their country.
----
Once again on November 11th, we celebrate Veterans Day. It is a commemoration with a long and noble history, tracing back to the armistice that ended World War I on the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month of 1918. One year later, our nation honored all those who served in that terrible conflict on the first Armistice Day.

In 1954, in the wake of World War II and the Korean War, Armistice Day was renamed Veterans Day to honor all the men and women who have served their country in uniform. (Memorial Day, which we observe in May, honors all those who have died in service; Armed Forces Day, on the third Saturday in May, honors those who are currently serving, and Flag Day on June 14 celebrates both the birth of the U.S. Army in 1775 and the adoption of the 13-stripe, 13-star American flag on that same date in 1777.)

And so let us once again on Veterans Day 2026 offer our thanks to all those who have served in uniform to defend America and its freedom.

This brave duty goes on. There are 1.35 million men and women serving full-time as well as some 770,000 members of National Guard and Reserve units. The breakdown of those on active duty — many in dangerous overseas posts — is:
•       Army  454,000
•       Navy 344,600
•       Air Force  321,500
•       Marine Corps 172,300
•       Coast Guard 41,800
•       Space Force 10,400

Remember, too, that it is not only those on active duty we salute on this special day — it is also the estimated 18 million veterans of military service. Our nation is doubly blessed by these dedicated men and women, who regularly use the training they received and the experiences they acquired in the military to serve as police officers, firefighters, school teachers, technicians, community volunteers and countless other roles.

They richly deserve, now and forever, our gratitude and admiration.

Best regards,
Robert L. Dilenschneider

text:
PRE-MARKET ANALYSIS · NOV 10, 8:20 AM ET · 5 MIN READ

Waller locks in December hike; CPI print now risks 50bp tail, not dovish relief

CPI comes out in ten minutes, but this morning's most important print has already happened, and it came from London. Fed Governor Waller said he will support a 25bp hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting even if October inflation comes in softer than September, and that a 50bp move should be considered if core prices rose 0.3% or more. The two-year yield rose about 6bp to 4.61% and the 10-year moved about 2bp higher, near 4.88%. Before the speech, futures priced no chance of a half-point move. Prediction markets agree. A December hike trades at 86.5% on Polymarket, up 10 points in 24 hours, and Kalshi has it near 90%. That changes the shape of today's binary, and most people are still framing it the old way.
A soft print can no longer undo December, because Waller has said so outright.

The Street expects headline CPI up 0.3% and core up 0.2% month over month, and no year-over-year figures will be published because the 2025 shutdown left the comparison data missing. The forecasts themselves sit close together: Deutsche Bank expects core up 0.20%, and other desks are at 0.21% and 0.23%. Core only needs about 0.25% unrounded to be reported as 0.3%, and that is now the number that opens Waller's 50bp door. Pressure points both ways. Core goods prices have accelerated for three months in imported categories, while airfares likely held core back. We put roughly 30% on a 0.3% core print.

Here is the asymmetry. A soft print can no longer undo December, because Waller has said so outright. Any dovish payoff now shows up only in pricing for March and 2027, and that is a smaller lever. A hot print adds a 50bp tail that was priced at zero yesterday. So on the print itself, the risk to equities is tilted to the downside. The counterpoint matters, though: the tape took Waller in stride. Dow futures are up about 0.5% and S&P futures about 0.2%, with Nasdaq 100 futures down 0.15%. The market isn't afraid of one hike. It is afraid of a hiking cycle with no visible ceiling. Today's report decides which of those it gets.

The biggest macro shift of the past week has barely registered: the oil leg of the stagflation story has broken. Brent settled at $91.61 on Monday, down nearly 7%, and this morning it is $89.92, with WTI at $84.59. Brent is at its lowest since August 31 after a 13.3% weekly decline. The crowd credits deal hopes, but there is no deal. Iran's foreign ministry says Washington must lift sanctions and the blockade before talks can begin. What is actually moving oil is physical flow. The US Navy facilitated about 30 commercial transits a day through Hormuz on November 5-7, and Middle East oil shipments are back near pre-war levels despite more Iranian attacks on tankers. Saudi Arabia's main shipping firm is sending tankers through the strait in coordination with the US military. A drop driven by flows lasts longer than one driven by headlines. Two things follow. First, the Fed is hiking into falling energy prices, which tightens real policy and argues for a flatter curve. Second, the November CPI, which arrives the day after the FOMC decision, will carry an energy drag. The obvious loser is tanker stocks, which earned record rates on the disruption. The tail risk is still there: IRGC attacks continue, and a successful strike on a US-escorted convoy would rebuild the premium overnight.

Inside AI, money is rotating within the theme rather than leaving it. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose nearly 7% on Monday while Nvidia fell 4.2% to its lowest close since April 7. Nvidia's calendar is packed. The congressional request is an invitation with an option to offer other dates, not a summons, and the reply is due tomorrow. Earnings follow on November 17 and the briefing on November 18. A China policy layer sits on top of all this: Trump's November 16-19 Asia trip includes the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Nvidia is higher in premarket trading. A governance discount at a seven-month low, a week before what is likely a strong fundamental print, makes Nvidia the most asymmetric large-cap setup we see.

The real AI test is tonight. CoreWeave is expected to lose $1.53 per share on $3.54 billion in revenue. The quarter matters less than Microsoft. Microsoft accounted for about 67% of CoreWeave's 2025 revenue, and it is shrinking its roster of neocloud partners and building its own data centers. Citi's Wieting estimates Microsoft's cost of debt at about 10 percentage points below CoreWeave's. CoreWeave paid $640 million in second-quarter interest, five times its adjusted operating income. The political backdrop is getting worse too: midterm voters rejected data centers in 40 of 41 ballot measures. The stock has rallied into the print even as some CoreWeave bonds yield above 16%. The equity is squeezing shorts while the bonds are not buying it. After the print, watch the bonds, not the stock. If they rally together, the market will believe it. If the stock pops and the bonds don't move, fade the pop. Neoclouds are the marginal buyers of GPUs, so whatever CoreWeave says about backlog and capex will shape expectations for Nvidia a week early.

Market structure tightens the sequence. Treasury sells $42 billion of 10-year notes today and $25 billion of 30-year bonds on Thursday. The cash bond market is closed tomorrow for Veterans Day, so whatever CPI does to rates has to happen today and run straight into a 1:00 PM auction. A hot print plus a weak auction would hit twice. PPI follows on November 13.

Technically, last week's roughly 4.4% one-day drop looks like a selling climax. Monday's broad rally (IWM +3.2%, a close at the session high, VIX back under 20) looks like the automatic rally that typically follows. In Wyckoff terms, that bounce marks the top of the new range near 755. The textbook next step is a secondary test toward 735-745 over the coming sessions, and if it holds on lighter volume, that is the higher-probability entry for a year-end run. Price pays. As long as SPY holds Monday's 741 low, buyers are in control.

Our playbook: an in-line print (about 50%) probably means an early pop that fades into the auction, with small caps and value beating Nasdaq. A 0.3% core print (about 30%) sends the two-year toward 4.70%, SPY down 1-2% and VIX to 23-25. A soft print (about 20%) gets SPY to around 760, but Waller has capped the rates side of that rally. Beyond today, we lean constructive into the November 20 options expiration: oil is disinflating, the hike is priced, Nvidia's governance discount is extreme and the Nasdaq has already been through a correction. We would buy the secondary test rather than chase strength today.

text:
The winter wheat crop is entering the colder months in better condition after recent moisture improved growing conditions across parts of the Great Plains.

USDA's November 9 Crop Progress report rated 49% of the nation's winter wheat good or excellent as of November 8.

That's an increase of five percentage points from the previous week.

The share rated poor or very poor declined from 18% to 16%.

Kansas, the nation's largest winter wheat-producing state, reported 51% of its crop in good or excellent condition, up four points.

Oklahoma improved even more sharply, climbing 11 points to 36% good or excellent.

But conditions remain uneven across the West.

Colorado reported 44% good or excellent, while Washington stood at 31%.

Idaho's crop was considerably stronger, with 77% rated good or excellent.

Nationwide, farmers had planted 89% of their winter wheat acreage, just one percentage point behind the five-year average.

Approximately 76% had emerged, slightly ahead of the normal pace.

Winter wheat is planted in autumn, establishes roots before dormancy and resumes growth the following spring.

Moisture during establishment can improve root development and help young plants withstand winter conditions.

But a favorable November rating is not a guarantee of a strong harvest.

Winter survival, spring precipitation, temperatures and disease pressure will all influence production next year.

For dryland wheat growers, the amount of moisture stored in the soil before winter can be particularly important.

The latest figures offer some encouragement after a difficult growing season, while also showing the substantial differences between individual wheat-producing regions.

text:
10 jobs nobody wants to do. AI does them now.
Every item below is a real case with a real number.

1. Anthem chased Lauren Gonzalves for $1,800, two years after she gave birth. She had already paid her out-of-pocket maximum. Counterforce AI found the federal statute and the timing problem. Anthem dropped the bill.

2. Rafal Goral got a £100 parking charge because his payment came through 16 minutes late. ChatGPT drafted every reply for three years. The case was dropped weeks before the hearing. He owed nothing. Smart Parking never said why.

3. Robert Levine sold his Miami house with ChatGPT in five days. Five offers in three days. Closed at $954,800, about $100,000 above the agents' estimates, and saved about 3% of the sale price in commission. He still used a lawyer for the paperwork.

4. Kudos AI called T-Mobile for its co-founder. Twenty minutes of menus, two transfers, one OTP code. His bill went from $130 to $60 a month, $840 a year. The recording is public.

5. A dad's Grok Bot found a dentist that takes his son's insurance and booked it on its own. The confirmation arrived by email and text. He never called anyone.

6. An engineer handed Grok Bot his house drawings and solar plans. It produced the full 17-page permit drawing set in under five minutes. He checked every line, and a licensed engineer still stamps the structural parts.

7. A dad gets about 200 school emails in six weeks, across two schools. His Grok Bot reads them every afternoon and sends one daily digest. 44 digests so far. 30 to 45 minutes of reading saved a week. Five of the 44 were corrections.

8. Liza Long gave Gemini a $2,500 budget and 50 guests. It found the rentals for $381, built the grocery list for 50 people, and wrote the minute-by-minute script. Her family did the cooking and the photos.

9. One rule, cook once, eat twice, saves a dev about five hours a week. Her whole week of meals for three people takes about ten minutes to plan. Allergies, picky kid, all of it in one file.

10. Claude audited a man's iPhone in 20 minutes. Six security settings fixed, including an uninstalled update and two Safari protections. It also found 104GB in one old work folder. It refused to touch his passcode.

Some of these need a paid plan. None of them need you on the phone.
Bookmark this. The next chore that eats your afternoon is on this list.

text:
Pretty sure I wrote an overwrought essay called “On Not Being Jewish Enough” in college. But I think that whatever that phrase means—whether someone is a convert or has a parent who isn’t Jewish (which, in my case, led to thirteen years of Catholic school)—those of us who did not grow up entirely immersed in a Jewish world can be and are extremely beneficial to the community now. 

Many of us experienced intense antisemitism and already have some skills to deal with it (the nuns and boys at my school were not aware that we were living in a Golden Age of American Jewry and acted accordingly). Many of us know what it’s like to live in a community that is not under siege—ie. that I used to trot in and out of my Catholic school at odd hours every time I forgot a book or homework assignment and that having not just security but a New York City police officer outside my daughter’s religious school on a random weekday afternoon is not normal. 

I also think that what we have to offer is that we don’t ascribe every moral or intellectual failing to Jews. I have a hunch, based on reading many antizionist Jews’ accounts of their own lives, that Jews who grew up in America among many other Jews sometimes think that Jews are bad simply because their formative experiences, including their formative negative experiences—the boyfriend who broke up with them, the teacher who supposedly didn’t tell them the truth about Israel—were with Jews. When I was growing up outside of Buffalo in the 1990s, the region was under siege as extreme Christians harassed abortion providers and women leaving clinics; one later murdered a Jewish doctor on Shabbat. I never heard a word about this from any teacher even though it was all over the news and there was certainly no idea that sometimes Christians do bad things so they needed to self-destruct the way that antizionists would like Israel to.

Anyway, I do not know @MegKeene’s entire story, but I was thinking about this when we were hanging out at the @z3_project conference. Seems notable that two of our small group of avidly, avowedly Zionist fellows did not grow up as Jews in an intensely Jewish environment. (Maybe now is the time to out myself as the other fellow who doesn’t speak Hebrew.)

Hidden Object Games (a.k.a. HOGs) are 2D puzzle point-and-click games that are characterized by Hidden Object scenes where you must find objects in a location from a list. If you're familiar with the Where's Waldo kinds of games, this is what it is.

These games have been popular during the late 2000s / early 2010s, and they were FULLY MADE BY HUMANS with absolutely NO AI. It's why I appreciate these games so much during this very strange era for videogames. If you're ever bored at work or don't have any new games to play, give one of these a shot! A lot of them are on Steam for very cheap, some are even on mobile. Most of them can be completed within 3 hours, and some offer replayability with higher difficulties, bonus chapters and achievements.

text:
Near Beatrice, Nebraska. Circa 1887.

Look at the handwriting at the bottom: "First Homestead."

A low log cabin. 
A rail fence. 
A barrel by the door. 
Horses at the far left, and a few people standing around the place like it's just another day.

This is the Daniel Freeman homestead.

The Homestead Act took effect on January 1, 1863. Freeman, a Union Army scout, was due to leave and report for duty. So, the story goes, he talked a land office clerk into opening shortly after midnight so he could file his claim before he left.

He was one of the very first. But not alone. By the National Archives' count, 417 others filed claims that same day.

The law offered up to 160 acres. The catch: you had to live on it, improve it, and stay five years. Freeman did. He got his title in January 1868.

His land is now Homestead National Historical Park.

There's a lesson here for us all. Imagine the pride one feels when they take ownership of something. 

Being first takes one opportunity. Proving you deserve something worthwhile can take up to five years. Finish what you claim.

text:
In my experience, families read a low acceptance rate as a better school. I checked that against 30,654 bachelor's programs in my College ROI model.

Pay differs most by field. At a typical college, programs near the top pay about $81,800 four years out and programs near the bottom about $45,800. Same campus.

A school's average SAT accounts for about a third of the pay differences between schools for graduates four years out. Add the acceptance rate and you learn almost nothing more.

Same major, schools with similar average scores, one admitting under one in four versus one admitting six in ten or more: about $160 to $1,140 a year more pay, depending on whether two tuition-free work colleges are counted, and below zero counted group by group. Mountjoy and Hickman's Texas research, on public universities, finds no lasting edge tied to a school's average scores.

At full price, the selective private ends up behind the easier school it is matched with, on average. Selective publics come out ahead because they cost less than half as much as the easier schools they are matched with.

The essay has the charts, program by program, and shows how to find cheaper doors to the same pay in your child's field. The acceptance rate tells you how many knocked for each offer.

text:
Trump spent the weekend after his party's midterm wipeout accusing the vote itself of being rigged.

On Truth Social: "Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest." Then: "How could the Polls be so wrong???" Then the machines: "It's all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!" By Sunday, he was calling it a "giant step back in History."

That's a reversal. On election night, Trump told the New York Times, "I am absolutely willing to accept those results," and told Fox News, "I think the Democrats did a good job. I really do. They fought hard."

Here's what actually happened between those two moments. Democrats won at least 54 Senate seats, with two races still uncalled, and flipped more than 40 House seats — more than two dozen races remain too close to call. For context: the president's party has lost House seats in 18 of the last 20 midterms since 1946, averaging 26 seats. Trump's own first term lost 41 in 2018. This fits a well-worn pattern. It just happens to be a historically bad one for him.

No evidence of fraud exists anywhere in this. Not in the vote totals, not in the voting machines, not in the "early voting dumps" he's complaining about. In Westchester County, New York, officials traced a scanner glitch to a routine programming update — not sabotage.

Trump shared a post calling one Texas vote comparison "Looney Tunes numbers." He shared another claiming "Democrats materialized 20 million new votes" out of nowhere. Neither post offered a shred of proof.

This isn't just sour grapes over a bad week at the polls. This is the same playbook from 2020, run again on a midterm, with no evidence, no lawsuits, and — so far — no off-ramp for how it ends.

text:
Podcast Summary | Financial Audit: She Left Him On Financial Audit

Overview
A used-car sales manager claiming roughly $120,000 a year sits down for a financial audit and ends up exposing far more than a budget problem. Connor is evasive about what he actually earns, running from about $2,500 to $14,000 a month depending on the moment, while his partner Isabella stays home with their two-year-old and is quietly discouraged from finishing her GED. The audit widens into a referendum on his in-house car financing, his criminal history, and his open cheating, and it ends with the host pushing Isabella to leave and offering real support to make it possible.

Key Themes
- Evasion is the through-line: income, loan paperwork, fidelity, and basic facts all get blurred whenever Caleb asks for specifics.
- The in-house financing model is the financial core of the episode, defended as access and attacked as an 80% markup dressed up as a lease.
- Education becomes a control lever: Connor's shifting objections to public school pair with resistance to Isabella's GED and a child pushed toward narrow paths.
- Connor's voting apathy and his schooling arguments share one logic: nothing outside his immediate experience counts, so institutions and policy differences get dismissed.
- The relationship is a financial trap: Isabella is dependent, uncredentialed, far from family, and told she can leave while given little practical means to do it.
- Caleb treats the audit as an intervention, converting the numbers into concrete offers of escape.
- Multiple declined bills undercut the $120,000 claim and make the income figure itself the audit's central question.

Detailed Summary
Connor presents himself as a success: sales manager for a couple of months at a used-car lot, about $120,000 a year, a family, a home in San Antonio. The numbers do not hold still. Asked about monthly earnings, he gives a range stretching from roughly $2,500 to $14,000. Payroll shows a draw check of about $1,580, with the commission picture left fuzzy. Later, bank details show Hulu, Spotify, Apple, and Cash App payments declined repeatedly, with a balance around $760. Caleb frames the gap as the real story.

Isabella is 22; Connor is 27. They met on Tinder, she was pregnant within about two weeks, and she quit her job when he told her to come home. She wants to sell health insurance and needs her GED to get there. Connor says he only asks why and never stopped her; she says he talks her out of goals, questions purchases like deodorant, and wants her home all the time. His reasons for opposing public school shift each time Caleb pins him down: social media, stupid kids, government rules, social studies. Private school or a private teacher get floated as alternatives with no budget behind them. When Caleb notes the child might want to be an engineer or doctor, Connor answers that the child wouldn't be a teacher.

The voting debate follows the same pattern. Connor calls voting pointless and says both parties play for the same team. Caleb cites close Florida races and Texas control, tax cuts, fuel costs, the Iran question, and degrowth politics, arguing policy differs objectively. Connor says he never used most of what he learned in school. Caleb answers that sales runs on basic math and communication but schooling covers more, and that a voting population informed by history and economics has value. The debate turns on whether education has to pay off immediately to count.

The car business is where the money argument sharpens. Connor's lot uses in-house financing: no credit checks, no proof of income, no interest, structured like an informal payment agreement that Caleb notes is technically a lease. The example on the table is a 2008 Chevy Silverado 1500 with 100,000 miles. Agreed value near $23,000, about $16,500 in payments over three years, residual around $2,328. Caleb argues the vehicle is marked up roughly $10,000, close to 80%, and that the lease captures nearly the full inflated value. Connor defends it as a service to people denied everywhere else, citing fair-market listings, negotiation, and buyout discounts around 15 to 20%. His gas-station convenience analogy gets knocked down as a false equivalency, since his customers arrive as a last resort. He says they come crying with gratitude; Caleb says that is what taking advantage looks like.

The criminal history keeps surfacing as context for everything else. Connor says he has been on probation since 14 and got out in July. He describes sneaking into a high school, an evading case at 18 that brought ten years of probation, an attempted burglary violation, and leaving the state when not allowed. The traffic stop that sent him back involved a 4th of July beach trip. He turned himself in; Caleb disputes that this counts as doing the right thing. The housing picture shifts too: the RV resort with amenities is described by others as a trailer park, and he says his background keeps them from getting in elsewhere.

The infidelity thread dominates the back half. Connor wants an open relationship; Isabella does not agree, and the show frames his outside involvement as cheating. She says he has cheated a lot, enough that she stopped counting and stopped going through his phone. He admits to sex with someone else about two months ago, describes the person vaguely as a client or car sale, and suggests encounters happen every few weeks. He refuses to hand over his phone, citing confidential work, and offers his checking account instead. He argues he provides, does not abuse her or the child, and that every guy cheats. Caleb calls the situation pathetic and says Connor is scamming her.

The lies reach basic facts. He allegedly misrepresented his name and where he was from, and another woman says he contacted her first and called Isabella a nanny with benefits. His father reportedly called Isabella stupid for staying, and she connects that to her own admission that staying may be pathetic. She says he turned off his location after she caught him, then said two weeks ago he did not want to continue. She gave him six months; Caleb points out she has already given three and a half years.

Caleb turns the audit into an exit plan. He offers a first-class plane ticket to Florida for her and the child, or first month, last month, and a security deposit if she stays in Texas. He offers to help her get her old food-truck job back, provide a recommendation, connect her with family, and pay for her GED. He pushes her to tell her parents, who know nothing and love Connor; the group estimates her parent will see the episode once clips circulate. The subscription review, ChatGPT, Kindle, Spotify, Door Dash, is framed as triage for someone making zero dollars. The episode opens on a heated clip of accusations and a snatched phone, and it closes on the same question the whole audit circles: whether the numbers and the promises ever matched the life being described.
