Evan Spiegel, the CEO of Snap, and his wife, model Miranda Kerr, have made a remarkable donation that will change the lives of hundreds of thousands of people in California. ❤️

Through a multimillion-dollar gift to the nonprofit Undue Medical Debt, they have helped erase $550 million in medical debt for more than 261,000 Californians. This relief is being distributed across the state, with many people receiving letters informing them that their debt has simply disappeared — no application required. 💌

The impact is especially large in certain counties. In San Diego County alone, $99 million in medical debt has been wiped out for over 40,000 residents. 🏥 In Los Angeles County, $26.7 million was erased for more than 17,000 people. Other counties across California are also benefiting from the donation.

Undue Medical Debt uses donated funds to buy medical bills in bulk at a fraction of their original value, then forgives them completely. This model allows relatively modest contributions to create enormous relief for families struggling with healthcare costs.

For many recipients, this means freedom from overwhelming bills that can damage credit, cause stress, and limit opportunities. It offers a real chance to move forward without the constant weight of medical debt hanging over them. 🌱

In a time when healthcare costs continue to burden millions of Americans, this act of generosity stands out as a powerful example of how targeted philanthropy can directly improve lives on a large scale.

Sources: Los Angeles Times, Undue Medical Debt official announcement, Fortune

text:
Crying Out for Mercy
November 11, 2026
Memorial of Saint Martin of Tours, Bishop

As Jesus continued his journey to Jerusalem, he traveled through Samaria and Galilee. As he was entering a village, ten lepers met him. They stood at a distance from him and raised their voice, saying, “Jesus, Master! Have pity on us!” And when he saw them, he said, “Go show yourselves to the priests.” As they were going they were cleansed. Luke 17:11–14

According to the Law of Moses, lepers were declared ritually unclean and required to live apart from the community. They had to wear torn clothing, leave their hair disheveled, cover the lower part of their face, and cry out “Unclean! Unclean!” whenever anyone approached (cf. Leviticus 13:45–46). This separation prevented the spread of disease and maintained ritual purity among the people of Israel. Lepers endured profound social isolation, spiritual alienation, and personal suffering, making their condition one of the most tragic and symbolic representations of sin and its consequences in the Bible.

The lepers in today’s Gospel met Jesus as He was entering a village they were not permitted to enter. They lived on the outskirts, likely with others who shared their condition. Spiritually, they symbolize each of us. If we can humbly recognize ourselves in them, we will more readily embrace the lesson they offer.

In our current state, our souls are spiritually disfigured due to fallen human nature and personal sin. This world is, symbolically, on the outskirts of the Kingdom of God—a place from which we are barred until cleansed by grace. These lepers show us the path to that cleansing. First, they teach us to recognize our need and then to turn to Christ with confident hope in His mercy, that we may be restored to full communion with God and the saints.

Ten cried out from a distance, “Jesus, Master! Have pity on us!” Though Scripture doesn’t say if these were the only lepers near that village, it’s possible others remained silent. If so, these ten who did cry out stand for those who humbly acknowledge their misery, fallenness, isolation from God’s Kingdom, and trust in Christ’s saving power.

Similarly, we must remember that this world is not our true home. With our first parents, we were cast out from Paradise because of Original Sin. Only through the mercy of Christ can we be restored. Recognizing our exile and its cause is the first step toward healing. If we do not acknowledge our spiritual leprosy, we will not cry out for the only cure: Jesus’ mercy.

One beautiful aspect of this story is that it reveals a second, deeper level of spiritual healing. The ten who cried out and were healed represent those who are baptized and remain in a state of grace, either by avoiding mortal sin or by being restored through sacramental confession and absolution. Yet only one, upon realizing he was healed, returned to give thanks to Jesus. The other nine did not.

The fact that only one returned suggests that most of us are best represented by the other nine. Just as an immature child expects his parents to feed and care for him, so we often expect God to forgive and restore us without giving proper thanks. If that is the extent of our spiritual lives, we remain immature. To grow into spiritual maturity, we must also grow in gratitude by continually returning to God in prayer, glorifying Him in a loud voice, and falling at Jesus’ feet in adoration. Only then will we receive a deeper healing and a greater share in God’s mercy.

Reflect today on the lepers’ cry for mercy, and ask yourself whether you recognize your own need for healing. Are you willing to admit your spiritual wounds, to cry out to Jesus, and to persevere in gratitude? If so, are you among the nine who took God’s mercy for granted and failed to express proper gratitude for the gift of spiritual cleansing and restoration? Strive to be like the one who returned to Jesus, humble, grateful, and filled with faith. Fall at the feet of Jesus in adoration, give thanks for all He has done, and hear Him say to you, “Your faith has saved you.”

Most generous Lord, Your mercy is endless and freely given in superabundance. Despite Your goodness, I often take You for granted and fail to offer the gratitude and humble worship You deserve. Please have mercy on me now and always. Remove every sense of self-entitlement, that I may always return to You, fall before You, and express my most humble and sincere thanks to You. Jesus, I trust in You.

Image via Adobe Stock

text:
53/54
Prospective Faith, Prevenient Grace, and Congruence: Bellarmine’s Map of Old Testament Faith Against Retroactive Monergistic Determinism 

The longstanding Patristic, Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic Map and hence Bellarmine’s ontology of Faith in the Old Testament are all prospective and integrated. None are post-hoc retroactive accounting. In the standard Catholic framework—which Bellarmine develops and defends at length in his *Controversies* —the justified of the Old Testament were justified by supernatural faith in the promised Redeemer. That faith looked forward. Its object was Christ (the seed of the woman, the seed of Abraham, the Suffering Servant, the one who would crush the serpent’s head and bless all nations), even when the mode of belief was more implicit or anticipatory according to the stage of revelation and in an earlier economy of Justification. Genesis 15:6, Hebrews 11, Galatians 3:8 (“the Scripture… preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham”), and Romans 4 treat Abraham’s faith as the paradigm precisely because it was faith in the promise whose fulfillment is Christ. The same principle extends to Abel, Enoch, Noah, the patriarchs, Moses, David, the prophets, and the faithful among Israel: they “died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them and greeted them from afar” (Heb 11:13).

To prevent this from collapsing into the High Calvinist model of retroactive application, it is crucial to recognize that the justification of Abraham and those under the Law belonged to a distinct category. Mount Sinai was not pure theater; the grace and justification it mediated were genuine, producing real holiness and friendship with God. Yet, this Old Testament justification was categorically different from the New Covenant regeneration funded post-Ascension, because human justification is never ultimately complete without the historical, incarnate work of Christ. Rather than possessing the exact identical reality of the post-Pentecost new birth and simply having it credited backward, the patriarchs possessed a real but preparatory justification—one that strictly awaited the categorically superior, crowning gifts of the new creation and the opening of heaven that only the finished work of the Cross could unlock. Scripture itself distinguishes the justification of Abraham and of those under the Law from the justification that belongs to the age after the Ascension. The former was anticipatory: it rested on faith in the promised Redeemer, was enabled by prevenient grace, and conferred a genuine standing before God, yet it did not yet include the completed work of Christ, the opening of heaven, or the ordinary instrument of the new birth. The Law, the sacrifices, and the covenant promises were genuine divine economies that prepared for and pointed to Christ. What the Old Testament Justified “had not yet received” (Heb 11:39–40) was not the mere possibility of Faith, but the full funding and consummation that only the finished work of Christ supplies. Their justification was therefore neither provisional in the order of grace nor identical in category to the justification that follows the Ascension. The difference is categorical, not merely quantitative, and proper accounting preserves that distinction without collapsing the earlier economy into a retroactive application of the later economy.

Justification was real and present in their own time—by grace, through prospective faith in the promised Redeemer, with the merits and satisfaction of Christ located in anticipation as the Final Ground. That application does not mean the full post-Ascension regenerative package (the new man, the ordinary instrument of the new birth, or the opened heaven) was already present and merely credited backward. The efficacy is not deferred until after the Cross so that God can then “balance the books”; the standing of the just before God was not provisional or incomplete in the order of grace that belonged to *that* economy. Faith was always ordered to Christ. The difference between the covenants is one of clarity, sacrament, and fullness of revelation, not of a fundamentally different object or formal structure of justification (grace through faith). Yet the Old Testament justification remains categorically preparatory: it conferred genuine holiness and friendship with God, but it did not yet include the completed work of Christ, the opening of heaven, or the crowning regenerative gifts that only the finished historical work unlocks. What the Old Testament just “had not yet received” was that fuller consummation, not the possibility of justifying faith itself. 

Bellarmine’s Congruist soteriology fits this without strain. The same principles he elaborates in Volume IV of Disputations (grace of the first man, original sin and the loss of grace, free choice under grace, the necessity and efficacy of actual grace, justification, good works) apply across the whole history of salvation. God, knowing all counterfactuals, elects and supplies congruous graces suited to each person’s circumstances and the stage of revelation in which they live. Sufficient, resistible grace is truly offered; the elect freely accept the graces congruent to them; the outcome is infallible for those God has decreed to draw. The progressive unveiling of the promise does not require a separate soteriological patch for the Old Testament; it is the same nature/grace and free-will dynamics operating under the light available at the time. The universal salvific will is exercised through the covenant promises and the prophetic hope, not by a narrow post-resurrection forensic transaction that must then be projected backward.

High Calvinist accounts (particularly certain forms of covenant theology or 1689 federalism) often describe the benefits of the New Covenant or the imputation of Christ’s righteousness as applied retroactively once the historical price has been paid. The language of “retroactive application,” “the virtue of the blood extended backward,” or the New Covenant’s benefits reaching the elect only after the cross — leaves the actual faith of the patriarchs under-specified because it literally makes their justification wait on a later mathematical settlement of the debt. For context see: The Narrative Anachronism of the High Calvinist Ordo — Abraham’s Faith 
https://t.co/W58KXyX0uF

Scripture’s own narrative—Hebrews 11’s eulogy of those who “received divine approval” by faith, Paul’s identification of the gospel already preached to Abraham, the reality of their justification and sanctification in their own time—fits more naturally with a prospective faith ordered to the promised Redeemer than with a system that must later credit the finished work backward to make the earlier accounting balance. Bellarmine’s treatment, by contrast, keeps the entire scriptural witness inside one coherent map of nature, grace, free choice, and justifying faith, without forcing a narrow slice of the New Testament’s forensic language to carry the whole Old Testament narrative by retroactive adjustment. The longstanding Partristic, Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic alternative is that justifying faith is possible through prevenient, resistible grace without requiring a prior, absolute monergistic regeneration.

High Calvinism (in its classic TULIP form) holds that fallen man is totally unable to believe, so true faith can arise only after an irresistible regeneration via Exhaustive Monergistic Determinism (effectual calling) that renews the will. Determinism aside, the category of regeneration there is still the category funded exclusively by the finished historical work of Christ applied to the elect — therefore — the system must account for Old Testament saints by some form of retroactive application: the benefits of the cross, or the New Covenant, or the imputation of Christ’s righteousness are extended backward so that the “all or nothing” calculus still holds. The faith of Abraham, Moses, or David is treated as possible only because the later monergistic transaction is credited to them after the fact.

The longstanding Partristic, Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic teaching (Council of Trent, Session VI; Catechism §§1987–1996, 2001–2003; and the ordinary magisterial tradition Bellarmine defends) all reject that premise. Grace is necessary—no one believes or is justified by natural powers alone—but the grace that enables the first movements of faith is prevenient and resistible. It is actual grace that illuminates the intellect and elevates the will so that the person can freely assent. Justification comes *through* acceptance grace (faith working through love), and isn’t the automatic product of a prior irresistible regeneration. The will remains free; the same grace can be refused (Acts 7:51; Trent, canon 4 on justification). Trent (Session VI, chs. 5–8) is explicit: the beginning of justification in adults comes from prevenient grace (God’s vocation that touches the heart by the illumination of the Holy Spirit). Through that grace the person is disposed to convert by freely assenting to and cooperating with it. Faith is “the beginning of human salvation, the foundation, and the root of all Justification.” Nothing that precedes justification—including faith itself—merits the grace of justification. Justification arrives through free reception of grace that both remits sins and renews the inward man (regeneration/sanctification are not a strictly prior monergistic event that funds the possibility of faith; they are concurrent with the free acceptance of the grace that makes faith possible).

Applied to the Old Testament:

The progressive unveiling of the promise does not require a separate soteriological patch for the Old Testament; it is the same nature/grace and free-will dynamics operating under the light available at the time. The universal salvific will is exercised through the covenant promises and the prophetic hope, not by a narrow post-resurrection forensic transaction that must then be projected backward.

High Calvinist accounts (particularly certain forms of covenant theology or 1689 federalism) often describe the benefits of the New Covenant or the imputation of Christ’s righteousness as applied retroactively once the historical price has been paid. The language of “retroactive application,” “the virtue of the blood extended backward,” or the New Covenant’s benefits reaching the elect only after the cross — leaves the actual faith of the patriarchs under-specified because it literally makes their justification wait on a later mathematical settlement of the debt. For context see: The Narrative Anachronism of the High Calvinist Ordo — Abraham’s Faith 
https://t.co/W58KXyX0uF

Scripture’s own narrative—Hebrews 11’s eulogy of those who “received divine approval” by faith, Paul’s identification of the gospel already preached to Abraham, the reality of their justification and sanctification in their own time—fits more naturally with a prospective faith ordered to the promised Redeemer than with a system that must later credit the finished work backward to make the earlier accounting balance. Bellarmine’s treatment, by contrast, keeps the entire scriptural witness inside one coherent map of nature, grace, free choice, and justifying faith, without forcing a narrow slice of the New Testament’s forensic language to carry the whole Old Testament narrative by retroactive adjustment. The longstanding Partristic, Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic alternative is that justifying faith is possible through prevenient, resistible grace without requiring a prior, absolute monergistic regeneration.

High Calvinism (in its classic TULIP form) holds that fallen man is totally unable to believe, so true faith can arise only after an irresistible regeneration via Exhaustive Monergistic Determinism (effectual calling) that renews the will. Determinism aside, the category of regeneration there is still the category funded exclusively by the finished historical work of Christ applied to the elect — therefore — the system must account for Old Testament saints by some form of retroactive application: the benefits of the cross, or the New Covenant, or the imputation of Christ’s righteousness are extended backward so that the “all or nothing” calculus still holds. The faith of Abraham, Moses, or David is treated as possible only because the later monergistic transaction is credited to them after the fact.

The longstanding Partristic, Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic teaching (Council of Trent, Session VI; Catechism §§1987–1996, 2001–2003; and the ordinary magisterial tradition Bellarmine defends) all reject that premise. Grace is necessary—no one believes or is justified by natural powers alone—but the grace that enables the first movements of faith is prevenient and resistible. It is actual grace that illuminates the intellect and elevates the will so that the person can freely assent. Justification comes *through* acceptance grace (faith working through love), and isn’t the automatic product of a prior irresistible regeneration. The will remains free; the same grace can be refused (Acts 7:51; Trent, canon 4 on justification). Trent (Session VI, chs. 5–8) is explicit: the beginning of justification in adults comes from prevenient grace (God’s vocation that touches the heart by the illumination of the Holy Spirit). Through that grace the person is disposed to convert by freely assenting to and cooperating with it. Faith is “the beginning of human salvation, the foundation, and the root of all Justification.” Nothing that precedes justification—including faith itself—merits the grace of justification. Justification arrives through free reception of grace that both remits sins and renews the inward man (regeneration/sanctification are not a strictly prior monergistic event that funds the possibility of faith; they are concurrent with the free acceptance of the grace that makes faith possible).

Applied to the Old Testament:

The patriarchs and prophets received actual graces congruent to both (a) the revelation given and (b) the economies funded in their time. Their faith was genuine faith in the promised Redeemer (the seed, the Messiah to come). It was not a placeholder waiting for a later monergistic event.

Because the longstanding Patristic, Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic accounts don’t make a monergistic regeneration the absolute precondition of faith—a regeneration that could be funded only by the completed cross—there is no need to insert a retroactive “flip” merely to make the earlier faith possible. 

God’s exhaustive foreknowledge includes the Two Economies of Justification as well as the historical work of Christ and the graces supplied at each stage of revelation. The merits of Christ live in Theanthropos and Theanthropos is the ultimate ground of Union regardless of Fall/No-Fall — which is obviously why The Son is the Always-&-Already-Ground of justification. Notice that this doesn’t mean the full post-Ascension regenerative package or its ordinary instruments were already present and simply credited backward. In the causal sequence in the Old Testament Soul the necessary inner work remains actual, prevenient grace that illuminates the intellect and elevates the will, enabling Faith and by Faith the Soul’s cooperation and (ultimately) its assent to the promised Redeemer. That enabling grace is real, interior, and absolutely necessary, yet it is not itself the category of regeneration or “new man” that belongs to the post-Ascension Order or Economy. Faith arises as the free reception of this prevenient assistance, not as the product of an irresistible regeneration that must be back-dated so that bizarre accounting can be balanced. 

What the Old Testament saints “had not yet received” (Heb 11:13, 39–40) was the full enjoyment of the beatific vision and the opening of heaven. They waited in the limbo of the fathers / Abraham’s bosom. Their justification and sanctifying grace were real in their own time; the final consummation of the promise awaited Christ’s descent and the Ascension’s consequences. That is not a delay in the funding of their faith itself.

The longstanding Partristic, Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic Maps don’t need TULIP’s “all else none” funding mechanism or its retroactive adjustments. Prevenient, resistible grace is sufficient to enable real justifying faith in the promised Redeemer wherever and whenever God gives it. The same principles of nature, grace, and free choice that Bellarmine develops at length in Volume IV cover the Old Testament saints without requiring a later balancing of the books.

Regeneration & Prevenient Grace
The question is one of Category, not one of IF.

High Calvinism asks whether any real divine assistance occurs before faith and what it actually achieves. The reply separates two categories: an enabling assistance that makes Abraham’s faith possible, and a later, categorically fuller renewal of the person (“the new man”) that belongs to the post-Ascension order and is not required for the Old Testament just to have justifying faith and to receive “Abraham’s Reward.”

That separation is useful. The longstanding Partristic, Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic alternatives (e.g. Trent Session VI, chs. 5–8; ordinary teaching on prevenient grace; Bellarmine’s development of it) already refuse the High Calvinist premise that true faith is impossible without a prior, absolute monergistic regeneration. Prevenient grace is real assistance: it illuminates the intellect and elevates/strengthens the will so that the person can freely assent. Just as nothing that precedes justification merits the grace itself, so too the free assent is not an empty gesture as it is the cooperative act by which the person is translated into the state of grace.

Catholic teaching does not appeal to merely external aids superadded to nature when it speaks of the grace necessary for Old Testament figures to believe and begin cooperating. Calvinism is correct that the work must be interior; the difference is that it treats the spiritual will as so thoroughly dead that only an absolute, all-or-nothing recreation can restore the capacity for faith. That 100% monergistic requirement is an outlier. 

Across the first fifteen centuries the Fathers and the ordinary teaching of the Church understood the damage as a severe wounding, yet still remediable by an interior, prevenient assistance that repairs and elevates without first requiring a monergistic resurrection of the person. Bellarmine’s account remains inside that established grammar: the assistance is internal, absolutely necessary, and genuinely enabling, yet it is not itself “the salvific” in the technical sense reserved for the distinct category of regeneration proper. That bifurcation—prevenient interior help on one side and the new birth on the other—is the long-standing pattern of the first millennium and a half, not a later invention. The Reformed are historically and patristically thin — isolated — in their rewritting of that expansive swath of Theo-History vis-à-vis the longstanding Partristic, Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic trajectory.

Inside of that same longstanding Partristic, Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic Grammar, regeneration (the new birth, the new man) is not the name given to the prevenient assistance that makes the first act of faith possible. That assistance is actual/prevenient grace. Regeneration proper is the renewal that occurs in justification itself.

Observed Flow

Prevenient grace (enabling, resistible) → 
Abraham/Faith 

—and then— 

If Pre-Christ’s Ascension we get: Faith → free cooperation with grace → Abraham’s Reward (the reward’s full consummation still future; they waited in the limbo of the fathers)

—but— 

If Post-Christ’s Ascension we get: Faith → free cooperation with grace → Regeneration / the new man → the fuller salvific gifts of the New Covenant

Notice: Abraham and a ‘million’ other Old Testament Souls wait to receive what only Christ can Fund vis-à-vis the Post Ascension Promises “Not Yet Received”.

In both eras the first movement is the same: prevenient grace that does not regenerate in the post-Ascension Category but does make free assent possible. What differs is the object of faith (more anticipatory versus explicit) and the fullness of the renewal and gifts that follow the free reception of justifying grace. Old Testament souls did not lack real justifying grace and real faith; they lacked the completed opening of heaven and the ordinary sacramental instrument of the new birth that belongs to the age after the Ascension.

This avoids important the artificial monergistic regeneration-before-faith into the Old Testament as well as collapsing the real difference between the two economies. 

Brief Juxtapositioning of Torrance

If one appropriates Torrance’s vicarious humanity, the math shifts at the starting point. The Son’s assumption of fallen humanity and His perfect faith, obedience, and self-offering already constitute the human response on behalf of all. Inseparable operations as the Mode of enabling assistance then saturates the completed vicarious humanity: people do not begin outside the reality of union and then enter it by a first free assent. Instead they awake already within the objective claim of Christ’s humanity. The “yes” is therefore the Spirit’s subjective realization of a status already achieved in the Incarnate Son—participation rather than a radical conversion from outside—while refusal remains possible as an exit from what has been objectively given. Prevenient grace is not an interior enablement that first restores the capacity for free assent so that faith can then arise; it is the Spirit’s application of the response Christ has already made (the objective) to assist one in realizing it (subjective) and growing into it (Objective/Subjective).

Catholic theology (Trent, Bellarmine, the ordinary teaching on prevenient grace) does not place the completed human response in Christ in that way as the prior ontological condition of every person. Rather, Prevenient grace is real and enabling, but it does not already place the unbaptized or the non-assenting inside the full reality of Christ’s vicarious humanity such that conversion becomes a state of remaining as opposed to refusal/exit. The free assent is still the beginning of the person’s own justification, not merely the recognition of an already-achieved ontic-status.  Bellarmine’s Congruism sits comfortably within the Catholic Catechism’s distinctions there.

Whether it is exhaustive foreknowledge or whether it is middle knowledge makes no difference as in either approach the Map simply describes one of God’s interfaces in supplying the particular graces congruent to free acceptance at whatever stage of revelation the person is located. 

The interface being described is one of ordering which graces (in manner, timing, and circumstances) to be freely received; it is not a calculus for deciding *which *souls receive the offer of prevenient grace itself — there is no [withholding] because there is no Decree of Reprobate. Gnosticism’s Castes of Human Beings is unintelligible within Christocentric Grammar. There is no “all else none” monergistic regeneration that must be funded by the post-Ascension work and then flipped backward for Old Testament Souls.

The same necessary First-Grace, the same resistible prevenient grace, and the same synergy as per the principles of nature and grace cover both sides of the Ascension. What the Old Testament’s Justified still awaited was the many full openings and births of the many rewards yet to be funded, not the Ontic-Possibility of Grace-Funded Faith.

text:
Are Foreign Fighters in Syria Becoming Geopolitical Bargaining Chips?

Recent revelations by Reuters and The Associated Press—citing military sources along with regional and U.S. officials—indicated that Damascus had offered military support to Riyadh, comprising advisors and special forces intended to transfer combat expertise and assist in border security against Houthi threats. Notably, report details from The Associated Press highlighted a strict Saudi prerequisite: the deployed forces must be Syrian nationals, explicitly excluding foreign fighters who had entered Syria during the conflict to join various insurgent factions.

In response, Assad Al-Shaibani, Foreign Minister of the de facto authority, delivered an official denial during a press conference on November 9, 2026, clarifying that military cooperation with Saudi Arabia strictly centers on institutional capacity-building and strategic expertise, denying any agreements for foreign combat deployment.

Yet, the question of military reconstruction cannot be separated from the record of the forces now being incorporated into Syria’s security institutions. UN investigators documented widespread and systematic violations during the March 2025 coastal violence—including extrajudicial executions and torture—as well as grave abuses during the July 2025 Suwayda violence by government forces, tribal fighters, and local armed groups, some of which may amount to war crimes. These findings raise a fundamental question about the authorities’ claims to a unified national military: can armed factions be transformed into state institutions without transparent investigations, accountability, and command scrutiny?

Beyond the immediate optics of regional diplomacy, this friction highlights a deeper strategic dimension: the status of foreign fighters as leveraging tools.

The explicit exclusion of non-Syrian combatants in these reported frameworks exposes how the foreign fighter portfolio is being repurposed. In the absence of a comprehensive structural and legal resolution to the foreign fighter dilemma, the management of this portfolio naturally shifts from a purely institutional security framework toward a functional variable within regional geopolitical calculations. Consequently, the containment and status of these combatants become inherently tied to the broader security arrangements shaping Syria's transitional landscape.

text:
Ever notice how the Liverpool skyline seems to magically "slide" along with you when you walk the Mersey? One minute the cathedrals are to the right of the Three Graces, the next minute they're on the left.⁣
⁣
If you’ve ever walked down Seacombe Promenade or hopped on the Mersey Ferry and watched the background skyscrapers majestically glide behind the historic waterfront buildings, you’ve experienced 𝘮𝘰𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘢𝘹 in action.⁣
⁣
While London’s Thames is OK, the geography of the River Mersey actually makes it the ultimate real world stage for this optical illusion. Here is why it easily wins:⁣
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲: At roughly 1km wide, the Mersey creates the ideal depth gap. It forces the background buildings (like Liverpool Cathedral) to move across your field of view at a grand, slow-motion sweep while the shoreline elements zip right past you.⁣
⁣
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗿𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗦𝗸𝘆𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲: Liverpool’s waterfront is perfectly tiered. Having the historic Three Graces sitting right on the water’s edge with the modern commercial district towers rising directly behind them doubles the sliding effect.⁣
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗶𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗟𝗼𝗻𝗴 𝗩𝗶𝗲𝘄: The Wirral waterfront offers a completely uninterrupted, flat promenade stretching for miles. No bridges, no sudden bends, and no buildings blocking your line of sight - just an hour of pure, shifting cinematic canvas.⁣
⁣
Next time you’re out for a coastal stroll or catching the ferry, keep your eyes on the skyline and watch the architecture 'move' past each other.

text:
Would you trade 20 hours a week for a full-hookup RV site at a desert campground with three natural hot spring pools?

That’s the offer at Agua Caliente in Southern California. We found five volunteer campground host listings for RVers heading south this winter, and the hours and campsites vary quite a bit.

☀️ Agua Caliente County Park, California  
Hosts get a full-hookup site and volunteer at least 20 hours a week. You can start as late as January if you can stay at least four months.

🌴 Bear Island Campground, Florida  
This one is for RVers who like a quiet spot. Bear Island sits at the end of a 20-mile gravel road in Big Cypress National Preserve. The 32-hour-a-week assignment started November 2 and runs through April 18. Check with the preserve about remaining dates and hookups at the host site.

🎣 Magnolia Ridge, Texas  
The Army Corps of Engineers offers a covered 20-by-50-foot concrete pad with full hookups and 50-amp service. Each volunteer puts in 20 hours a week. The posting starts January 1, so ask the lake office about a winter-only stay.

🏜️ Death Valley National Park, California  
The park lists five host openings across three campgrounds for January 12 through April 20. You’ll need to stay the full term and work 32–40 hours a week. Two campgrounds offer full hookups. At Texas Spring, the site has water and sewer, and you’ll need your own solar power.

🦆 Salton Sea State Recreation Area, California  
If you enjoy birding, take a look at this one. Hosts get a full-hookup site at a lakeshore campground and help with the visitor center, camp store, and other park duties. The minimum is three months at 30 hours a week during the October–April season.

Which campground would you pick for the winter?

text:
NASA reveals bold new plan to return astronauts to the Moon in 2028 | NASA, ScienceDaily

NASA has revealed new details about its accelerated effort to return American astronauts to the Moon in 2028. The updated strategy includes testing two competing lunar landers, streamlining rocket preparations, and introducing a lighter spacesuit to help make the first moonwalks possible sooner.

During an October 23 briefing, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other agency leaders outlined the next steps for the Artemis program. The revised approach centers on two major missions: Artemis III, a test flight scheduled for 2027, and Artemis IV, which is intended to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

The announcement builds on priorities introduced earlier this year through NASA's Ignition initiative. Agency officials also highlighted recent progress in spacecraft development, mission preparations, and partnerships with private aerospace companies. These efforts are intended to reduce technical risks, accelerate the schedule, and establish the foundation for a lasting American presence on the Moon.

"This is a very energized NASA, and these updates are only a small part of that story. We are bringing extreme focus to the mission to ensure delivery of world-changing outcomes as quickly, safely, affordably, and successfully as possible," said Isaacman. "NASA is driving outcomes to make Moon missions a reality, and we're not waiting for others to bring their plans to us -- the campaign must move with urgency as strategic competitors pursue a permanent presence beyond Earth."

Artemis III Will Test Two Lunar Landers in Earth Orbit

Before attempting another crewed Moon landing, NASA plans to conduct a major rehearsal in Earth orbit. The Artemis III mission will bring together NASA's Orion spacecraft and experimental lunar landers developed by SpaceX and Blue Origin.

Four astronauts will travel aboard Orion, launching on NASA's powerful SLS (Space Launch System) rocket. During the planned 14-day mission, the crew will practice rendezvous and docking procedures with both companies' lander test vehicles. Rendezvous involves guiding two spacecraft to meet in orbit, while docking allows them to connect so astronauts can move between vehicles.

These demonstrations are designed to verify important spacecraft capabilities before Artemis IV attempts to carry astronauts to the Moon's surface.

The tests will take place in a carefully planned sequence. Blue Origin will first launch a test version of its Blue Moon lander into Earth orbit. NASA will then send Orion and its four astronauts into space aboard the SLS rocket, where Orion will rendezvous and dock with the Blue Moon vehicle.

Next, SpaceX will launch a test version of its Version 3 Starship lunar lander. Orion will separate from Blue Moon and perform another docking maneuver, this time with Starship. By testing both systems during a single crewed mission, NASA aims to gather essential operational experience while reducing uncertainties before the 2028 landing attempt.

NASA Cuts Rocket Preparation Times and Costs

The new mission details follow other recent Artemis progress reports. According to NASA, the hardware needed for Artemis III remains on schedule, and improvements in processing have reduced preparation timelines by approximately 50%.

The agency also reported a significant engineering achievement involving a critical rocket fuel-line component. Rather than relying on an outside supplier, NASA engineers redesigned, manufactured, and tested the component themselves in just five months. The work cost roughly one-tenth of an earlier estimate from an external vendor.

"NASA should be expected to do this kind of work, and we have some of the best technical knowledge in the world on rocket hardware and operations to do it," said Jeremy Parsons, the agency's Artemis program manager. "It's an example of how we are rebuilding our core competencies and developing centers of excellence in technical functions instead of continuing to outsource expertise."

The improvements reflect NASA's broader effort to strengthen its internal engineering capabilities, shorten development schedules, and reduce the cost of preparing missions for launch.

SpaceX and Blue Origin Offer Different Paths to the Moon

For Artemis IV in 2028, NASA intends to launch astronauts aboard Orion using the SLS rocket from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Once in space, the crew will rely on a lunar landing system developed by either SpaceX or Blue Origin to reach the Moon's surface.

Both companies have revised their original mission designs to make operations simpler, more efficient, and more adaptable. Although they share the same objective, their approaches to transporting astronauts to the lunar surface differ considerably.

SpaceX plans to use its Starship spacecraft, which will take on additional propellant while orbiting Earth. After refueling, Starship will meet Orion and carry the spacecraft toward the Moon. Refueling in orbit is an important part of SpaceX's strategy because it allows the vehicle to receive the propellant needed for its journey after leaving the launchpad.

Blue Origin is developing a different approach using its Blue Moon Mark 2 lander. Its plan calls for additional propulsion stages in Earth orbit to send the lander toward the Moon. The lander will then meet Orion in a relatively low lunar orbit before carrying astronauts down to the surface.

Both companies are working toward having their systems ready to support a crewed Moon landing in 2028. Maintaining two potential landing systems gives NASA greater flexibility as development and testing continue.

NASA Explores New Rocket Options for Artemis IV

NASA is also considering two possible upper stages for the SLS rocket used on Artemis IV. An upper stage is the portion of a rocket that provides additional propulsion after the earlier stages have completed their work, helping send a spacecraft toward its destination.

One option is the interim cryogenic propulsion stage already used by SLS. The other is an extended version of United Launch Alliance's Centaur V upper stage, which would hold additional propellant.

By developing both possibilities, NASA hopes to preserve flexibility in its launch plans and avoid becoming dependent on a single technical solution. Having alternatives could help the agency respond to engineering challenges without jeopardizing the broader Moon landing schedule.

A New Lightweight Spacesuit Could Speed Up Moonwalks

Another important change involves the spacesuits astronauts will wear while exploring the lunar surface.

NASA is working with Axiom Space on a second, lighter design known as the "Sortie suit." The new suit is intended specifically for the first Moon surface excursions and weighs approximately half as much as Axiom's larger primary spacesuit.

The lighter design could simplify preparations for the earliest landing missions and help astronauts begin exploring the lunar surface sooner.

However, the Sortie suit is not intended to replace the primary design. Axiom's more capable suit will remain part of NASA's plans for future missions that require longer periods outside the spacecraft and more demanding surface activities.

Building a Permanent Human Presence on the Moon

NASA's ambitions extend well beyond returning astronauts to the lunar surface for a single mission.

As the Artemis program advances, the agency intends to send crews on increasingly challenging expeditions near the Moon's South Pole. This region is an important focus of future lunar exploration, and the missions are designed to expand how much of the Moon humans can investigate directly.

NASA describes the effort as part of a new Golden Age of innovation and exploration. The agency expects its lunar missions to support scientific discoveries, generate economic benefits, and encourage the development of technologies needed for more ambitious space exploration.

Ultimately, the goal is to establish an enduring human presence on the Moon rather than repeat the brief visits of earlier lunar expeditions. The experience gained from operating spacecraft, supporting astronauts, and carrying out increasingly complex missions on the lunar surface will also help NASA prepare for another historic objective: sending the first astronauts to Mars.

Pioneering television personality, chef and author Julia Child once said, "People who love to eat are always the best people." I have to agree. In my career as a journalist, often writing about food, I’m always struck by how good food, from the supremely simple to the over-the-top elegant, can bring people together. With that in mind, we’re closing out 2026 with The Food & Drinks Issue: Under-the-radar foodie finds, chefs’ tables and flavor-forward offerings.

Buckhead and the surrounding neighborhoods are an embarrassment of riches when it comes to culinary offerings, so finding things to fill the pages of our cover story wasn’t the hard part: Narrowing it down was. Nicole Letts writes about over-the-top delicious martinis and secret menu items only available by request; Carly Cooper finds places around town that offer compelling complementary bites and sips to accompany a meal; Lia Picard shares tips for introducing a child to the pleasures of upscale dining and offers recommendations for where to take a pint-sized dinner guest; Managing Editor Giannina S. Bedford leads readers on a tour of chefs’ tables; and Denise K. James profiles a trio of tastemakers doing innovative things.

The rest of our pages are packed with reports from our team of journalists. From articles on a new mahjong studio and the historian behind Preserving Georgia to go-to items for a gift exchange and tips for how to use AI effectively and ethically, this issue has lots to explore.

As we approach the new year, we hope this edition of Simply Buckhead will inspire you to explore some of the local restaurants and drink destinations on our pages. We bet it will have you making plans to celebrate local flavors with some of the best people in your own life.

text:
No cat has ever tried to be funny. That is the entire secret.

Not one. Not the cat that misjudged a distance it was certain about. Not the cat that stared into an empty corner with the focus of a bomb technician. Not the cat that took a corner at full speed and discovered that the floor has opinions. Every cat that has ever made you laugh was, in its own mind, completely and professionally serious.

That gap is where the magic lives. A cat's confidence and the universe's reply almost never arrive at the same moment, and when they miss each other by half a second, millions of people stop scrolling.

I want to tell you why that half second is so powerful, because it is not random and it is not just "cats being cats." Behind every ridiculous moment there is a living machine of astonishing precision that is, once in a while, operating at the edge of its own limits. The funny part is the edge. The impressive part is everything that normally happens before it.

And if you have ever watched a cat do something so absurd that you rewound it three times, this thread is for you. Stay with me, because the real reasons behind these moments are stranger than the moments themselves.

The first thing to understand is that you are not laughing at failure. If you were, a clumsy cat would be funny every time, and it is not. A cat that is genuinely hurt or frightened does not make anyone laugh. What makes you laugh is something much more specific, and psychologists have a name for it.

In 2010, researchers Peter McGraw and Caleb Warren proposed what they called the benign violation theory. The idea is simple and surprisingly powerful: humor appears when something seems wrong, threatening, or out of order, and yet, at the very same moment, it is clearly safe. A violation that is benign. Take away the violation and you get boredom. Take away the safety and you get worry. You need both at once.

Cats are almost perfect delivery systems for this. They carry an ancient, dignified, predatory image. They move like they own the architecture. Then something small and harmless punctures that image, and the brain holds both truths together: the dignity and the collapse of the dignity. That collision is what you feel as a laugh.

The philosopher Henri Bergson saw a version of this over a century ago. In his 1900 essay on laughter, he argued that we laugh when something living suddenly behaves like a machine, rigid, mechanical, unable to adapt. A cat locked into a plan it can no longer change is exactly that. It has committed. The body is going where the body is going. And you, the observer, can see the problem a full second before the cat can.

So the next time you laugh at a cat, notice what you are actually responding to. It is not the mistake. It is the seriousness that came right before the mistake.

Now here is the part most people never think about. The reason cats look so confident is that, most of the time, they have every right to be.

Take the most famous trick in the animal kingdom. A cat dropped upside down will rotate in the air and land on its feet. Everybody knows it. Almost nobody knows how old the scientific puzzle is, or how hard it was to solve.

In 1894, the French scientist Etienne-Jules Marey photographed a falling cat with a technique called chronophotography, capturing a rapid series of images on a single plate. He wanted to understand how an animal with no obvious way to push off the air could still turn itself around. His images were published that year and they stunned people, because they showed the cat twisting its body in stages rather than spinning like a top.

The modern explanation is that the cat bends in the middle. Its spine is unusually flexible, and it can rotate the front half of its body and the back half in different directions, pulling in the legs of one half to make it easier to turn while extending the legs of the other. Then it switches. Two small counter-rotations, and the cat ends up facing the right way without ever violating the laws of physics. Reported measurements put the whole maneuver at a fraction of a second.

It is not magic. It is a reflex so refined that it develops in kittens at only a few weeks old and is typically fully tuned within the first couple of months of life.

This matters for the story, because it means that when a cat gets something wrong, you are looking at an animal whose normal level of performance is extraordinary. The failures are funny precisely because they are rare. We have all been trained, by years of watching cats do the impossible with total calm, to expect perfection. When it does not arrive, the brain does a double take.

Then there is the question of the body itself, which seems to follow rules that other bodies do not.

Cats do not have a rigid collarbone like ours. Their collarbone is small and floats free in the muscle, not locked to the rest of the skeleton. That is one reason the shoulders can compress so dramatically, and why a cat can squeeze through any opening its head can fit through. The whiskers help it judge the width, which we will get to in a moment.

The spine is another story. Cats have a long, flexible backbone with a large number of vertebrae, and the connections between them are loose and cushioned in ways that allow extreme bending. The result is an animal that can turn almost in place, stretch to reach a surprising distance, and fold itself into a space that looks too small by half.

This is serious enough that a physicist once wrote a paper about it. In 2014, the French researcher Marc-Antoine Fardin published a study called "On the Rheology of Cats," exploring whether a cat should be classified as a liquid or a solid, because it so readily takes the shape of its container. The work later earned him an Ig Nobel Prize in physics, the award given to research that makes you laugh first and then makes you think. The conclusion was playful, but the question was real: how can a mammal flow like that?

Hold that thought. A body that flexible, that fast, that confident, is also operating with a few built-in blind spots, and the blind spots are where the best moments come from.

Here is one almost nobody expects. A cat is not good at seeing things that are very close to its face.

Cats are superb at distance and motion. They detect the slightest flicker at a range. They see in dim light using roughly a fraction of the light humans need, helped by a reflective layer behind the retina that bounces light back for a second pass, the same layer that makes their eyes glow in a flashlight beam. They have a wide field of view, and the vertical slit shape of the pupil, which studies on ambush predators link to depth judgment, lets them control light and focus with great speed.

But up close, things get blurry. The object right under a cat's nose is often harder for it to resolve than the object across the room. That is why a cat will sometimes seem to lose a treat that is sitting right in front of it, then locate it by smell or touch instead.

So how does a cat manage the final few inches of a pounce, or the last step of a narrow ledge? Mostly with its whiskers.

A cat's whiskers are not just stiff hairs. They are touch organs. The follicles are set deeper than ordinary fur and are densely supplied with nerve endings, and they are often described as being about as wide as the cat's body, which makes them a built-in measuring device for tight spaces. Whiskers also sense the tiniest movement of air, so a cat can detect the presence of an object in the dark by the way the air bends around it.

Put these facts together and you can see how a cat can be breathtakingly accurate one moment and a little off the next. It is running a hybrid system: sharp eyes for far away, delicate touch for near, and a gap in the middle that it normally covers with experience. Experience is excellent. It is not infallible.

Before a big jump, many cats do something that looks almost comical in itself. They stare at the target and bob or sway the head, back and forth, sometimes up and down. This is widely thought to be a way of calculating distance through motion parallax: when you move your viewpoint slightly, near objects shift more than far ones, and the shift tells you how far away something is. In other words, the cat is taking a measurement.

Then it commits. A healthy adult cat can leap roughly five times its own height from a standing start, driven by the immense power of its hind legs and a body built like a loaded spring. No run-up needed. That is the equivalent of a person jumping from the ground onto the roof of a single-story house.

When you know all this, a cat's occasional miscalculation looks different. This is a creature that is running a complicated estimate, in real time, on a surface it may never have tested, with a body that is made for speed rather than caution. Of course the estimate will occasionally be wrong. The surprising thing is how rarely it is.

Now think about ears, because something else cats do causes more confusion, and more laughter, than almost anything.

You have seen it. A cat suddenly freezes and fixes its gaze on a spot where nothing appears to be. Ears swivel. The whole body tightens. You look. You see nothing. The cat sees something, or rather hears it.

Cats hear far higher frequencies than humans do. People top out at around 20 kilohertz, and cats can hear well above 60. That range happens to cover the ultrasonic squeaks of small rodents, which is the whole point. Each ear is controlled by dozens of tiny muscles, commonly cited as thirty-two per ear, and the ears can rotate independently like small radar dishes. A cat can pinpoint the source of a faint sound to a very small area, and it does so without even moving its head.

So when a cat stares at the wall, it is probably not seeing a ghost. It is probably tracking something in a world of sound that you are shut out of. Insects in the wall. A tiny creak in a pipe. The scrape of a distant wing. You are standing in the same room, and the cat is living in a different one.

That is the funny and slightly eerie truth about cats. They share your home, but not your reality.

Which leads to the other thing that makes people laugh: the sudden explosion of energy for no apparent reason.

Cat people call it the zoomies. Animal behaviorists sometimes use the clumsier name frenetic random activity periods, and it is a real, recognized pattern. A cat that has been lounging for hours suddenly sprints from one end of the home to the other, with eyes wide, tail puffed, and a total absence of any visible cause.

Why does it happen? Part of the answer is simple arithmetic. Cats sleep a lot, often twelve to sixteen hours a day, because they are built as ambush hunters who conserve energy for short, intense bursts. Ancestral cats did not trot across a field for hours. They waited, and then they exploded. A well-fed house cat has all of the explosive design and none of the hunting outlet. The energy accumulates, and at some point it has to go somewhere.

Add the fact that cats are most naturally active around dawn and dusk, and you start to understand the 3 a.m. stampede. It is not a malfunction. It is an ancient schedule colliding with a modern living room.

Researchers who study play in cats describe a sequence of stalk, chase, pounce, and bite, a loop that mirrors the stages of a real hunt. In a home, that loop often has nothing to land on. So it lands on a sock, on a curtain, on your ankle, or on the air itself. The cat is not being silly. It is completing a program that was written long before sofas existed.

Once you see the program, the chaos stops looking random. It looks like a very serious instinct trying to find a target in a very comfortable world.

One more piece of the puzzle hides in the tail. A tail held straight up is, for most cats, a friendly greeting, a signal kittens use toward their mothers and adult cats use toward companions they trust. A puffed tail with raised fur is the opposite, an attempt to look larger in a hurry. The tail also works as a counterweight, shifting in tiny adjustments to keep the body balanced on narrow edges. So when a cat's tail suddenly swings wide in mid-air, that is not decoration. It is a rudder. Cats do this without thinking. Of everything a cat wears on its body, the tail is probably the hardest part to keep a secret.

Now for the questions that every cat owner has asked at some point.

Why do cats seem so fascinated by running water? Nobody has a single definitive answer, but there are a few leading ideas. Moving water in the wild tends to be fresher and safer than still water that might be stagnant, so an instinct to pay attention to it would make sense. Water also gives a cat an endlessly changing, touchable, sound-making toy. And some veterinary behaviorists point out that cats may simply prefer to drink from a source that feels different from a bowl, which is part of why many cat fountains exist.

Why do cats knock things off tables? Again, the honest answer is that it is not fully proven. One widely discussed explanation is that a cat is testing the world with its paws the way a hunter would test whether something is alive. A tap that produces movement is interesting. A tap that makes something fall and make a noise is more interesting still. And if the human reacts, the cat learns that this action gets results. Whatever the cause, it is a fine example of an animal running experiments on its environment.

Why do cats sit in boxes, and even in squares drawn on the floor? In 2021, a team of researchers published a study showing that cats will sit inside an illusory square made of nothing but four corner marks, a pattern called a Kanizsa square, as if the shape were real. It suggests that their sense of an enclosed space is not just about walls, but about the perception of an outline. Add the possibility that confined spaces feel safer, warmer, and more hidden, and the preference makes sense.

None of these are silly questions. They are windows into a mind that works on different rules, and every one of them ends with the same discovery: the weird behavior is usually the result of logic that makes perfect sense in a different context.

Here is where the story gets bigger than a single funny moment.

Why do these animals live with us at all?

The oldest widely known evidence of a close relationship between people and cats comes from Cyprus. In 2004, archaeologists reported a grave on the island, around nine and a half thousand years old, in which a human had been buried with a cat placed close by. Cats are not native to Cyprus, which means that people must have carried them there by boat. Think about that for a second. Thousands of years before the pyramids, someone was transporting cats across the sea and honoring them in death.

The prevailing view among researchers is that cats were not so much tamed as they drifted into human life. As people began farming and storing grain, rodents arrived to eat it, and the wildcats of the Near East arrived to eat the rodents. Humans noticed that these animals solved a problem for free. They tolerated each other, and over a very long time, that arrangement became something closer to friendship.

Genetic work over the past decade points to the Near Eastern wildcat as the main ancestor of the cats in our homes. And unlike dogs, which were bred over thousands of years into countless forms of labor, cats were never given a job description. They kept most of their independent wildcat instincts. The result is an animal that lives with people but never fully became their servant.

That is the deeper reason the funny moments hit so hard. We are watching a small, fully equipped hunter, a creature with the reflexes of a wild predator, operating inside our kitchens and living rooms, wearing the manners of a pet. Every now and then the two layers do not match perfectly. That mismatch is not a flaw. It is the visible seam between a wild animal and a domestic one.

There is another part of this relationship that most people have never considered: the meow.

Adult cats rarely meow at each other. Researchers who have studied feline communication, including work reviewed by the animal behavior scholar Nicholas Nicastro, have noted that the meow appears to be a sound developed largely for communicating with humans. Kittens meow to their mothers, but once they grow up, they tend to switch to scent, posture, tail position, and other signals when talking to other cats. With us, they keep the meow, and many cats tune it carefully.

Different cats seem to develop their own particular sounds for their own particular people, and studies on owners have found that humans can often tell the emotional context of a cat's vocalization, such as a request for food versus a greeting, with better-than-chance accuracy. Some researchers have also reported that cats can mix a purr with a higher-pitched cry to create a sound that humans find especially urgent and hard to ignore.

Which means every cat that has ever yelled at you from across the room is using a language it invented for you. Think about that the next time it seems like nonsense. It is not talking to the cat next door. It is talking to you.

The same goes for something much quieter.

In 2020, researchers at the Universities of Sussex and Portsmouth published a study in the journal Scientific Reports on what many owners call the slow blink. In experiments, cats were more likely to approach an unfamiliar person who narrowed their eyes and slow blinked at them, and cats were also more likely to slow blink back to their owners after the owners did it first. A slow blink from a cat is widely interpreted as a sign of comfort and trust, and the study offered the first experimental evidence that this signal works in both directions.

So the next time a cat stares at you, you have a tool. Soften your eyes, blink slowly, and wait. It is a conversation, and it is not even in a spoken language.

Why does any of this matter? Because it means that the comedy and the relationship are the same thing. The reason you can laugh at a cat so freely, without cruelty, is that you are looking at an animal you understand, at least a little. You know its dignity. You know its code. You are in on the joke without anyone being its victim.

And that brings us to the question of why millions of people watch cats at all.

There is actual research on this. In 2015, Jessica Gall Myrick, a media researcher at Indiana University, surveyed nearly seven thousand people about their cat video habits and published the findings in the journal Computers in Human Behavior. The participants reported feeling more energetic and more positive after watching cat videos, and they reported fewer negative feelings such as anxiety, annoyance, and sadness. Many described the viewing as a kind of guilty pleasure, but the data suggested it did something real. The researchers framed it as a form of emotional regulation, a short reset button.

That is a strange thing to say about an animal that, a few thousand years ago, was mostly a rodent control employee. And yet it is accurate. In a world that is loud, fast, and full of news that makes our stomachs tighten, a few seconds of a creature doing something absurd and entirely harmless can drop the shoulders by an inch.

Cat images were part of the culture long before the internet. Photographers in the nineteenth century, including the Brighton photographer Harry Pointer, were already making a name with staged cat portraits, so humans have been sharing funny cats for a very long time. The platform changed. The impulse did not.

Notice what is different about this kind of laughter. It is not mocking. Nobody is being humiliated. The cat does not lose anything. It simply recomposes itself and walks away as if nothing happened, which is itself half the joke. And that recovery, that magnificent pretending that nothing occurred, is something the human audience recognizes all too well. We have all stumbled in public. We have all straightened up and tried to look like it was intentional.

The cat just does it better.

One more twist, and it is a good one, because it reveals the biggest difference between us and the creature we are watching.

You laugh. The cat does not.

The neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp discovered in the late 1990s that rats emit high-pitched ultrasonic chirps when they play and when they are tickled, which he described as a form of laughter. The finding was controversial, but it shook up the assumption that humor and joy are exclusively human. Play, it turns out, is deeply ancient, and the sounds of play may be shared across many species.

Cats play hard, and they have clear play signals of their own: the soft bite, the play crouch, the chase. But whatever delight they feel, they do not do the thing we do. When something goes wrong for a cat in a moment of pride, the most common response is not laughter. It is an instant act of grooming. A cat that has had an embarrassing moment will often begin licking a paw or a shoulder with enormous concentration, a behavior that ethologists call displacement activity, a way of dealing with tension or conflict by switching to something familiar and calming.

We may read this as the cat saying, "That did not happen." It might be nothing of the sort. But the interpretation is so perfect, and so human, that we can never un-see it. That is the real art of the cat video. We pour our own feelings into a being that will never confirm or deny them.

There is also a gentle responsibility inside all this, and it is worth saying out loud, because the best content about animals respects the animal.

A funny cat moment is a moment in the life of a creature with real needs. The explosive energy that looks so comical is a sign of a hunter without a hunt, and cats are healthier and happier when they get what the experts call enrichment: short play sessions that imitate the stalk and pounce sequence, places to climb, spots to hide, and surfaces to scratch. A cat that stares at the window is a cat that is hungry for stimulation. A cat that knocks things over is a cat that is asking for an interesting life.

The best owners treat these moments as information. They notice that the cat has too much energy at night and schedule a play session before bed. They notice that a cat is fixated on a window and add a perch with a view. They notice that a cat's jumps are getting shorter and take it to the vet, because a cat that stops leaping is often a cat that is in pain.

That last point is the one worth remembering. The extraordinary athleticism that makes cats so entertaining is also one of the most reliable indicators of their health. When it fades, something is wrong. When it is strong, they are thriving. A cat that can launch itself onto the highest shelf in the house is telling you its body is in good shape.

So when you laugh at a cat doing something ridiculous, you are also, without knowing it, checking in on its wellbeing. A healthy cat is a cat willing to take risks. A healthy cat is an animal that still believes it can make that jump.

That is also why the best clips are not about cats being foolish. They are about cats being committed. And commitment is a universal language.

Think about what that means. We watch a creature that does not know it is being watched, that never rehearses, that has no social media account, no fear of embarrassment, and no concept of the audience. It goes about the day with total belief in its own plan. Sometimes the plan works spectacularly. Sometimes the world pushes back. In both cases, the cat moves on within seconds, unbothered.

Most of us do not live like that. We replay the awkward moment for years. We rehearse conversations that never happen. We read the room and edit ourselves before we have spoken. A cat has none of that machinery. It has an enormous capacity to be fully in the moment and then fully out of it.

Maybe that is the real secret behind the laugh. Maybe it is not only the benign violation, or the dignity of an animal punctured, or the physics of a leap that went a few centimeters wrong. Maybe it is envy, a tiny, warm, harmless envy of a creature that can fail in front of the world and simply walk away, tail up, like a head of state leaving a press conference.

Which brings us back to where we started.

No cat has ever tried to be funny. They are just entirely, wonderfully, unreasonably certain. And the world, which owes them nothing, keeps turning around them just a little too fast.

If you want to see what that looks like, watch the video. Watch how many different animals, in how many different rooms, arrive at exactly the same expression of absolute composure at exactly the wrong moment.

Then ask yourself the question this whole post has been circling.

Who was really being serious, the cat, or the one watching it?

text:
Let's clear up something that confuses almost every first-time buyer: earnest money.

Earnest money is not a fee. It's not extra money on top of your down payment, it's part of it. When you make an offer, you put down a deposit, often 1-2% of the price, to show the seller you're serious. That money sits in escrow, and at closing it gets credited toward what you owe.

Here's the misconception that trips people up. "Is it refundable if I back out?" The honest answer: it depends on your contract. If you have contingencies in place (inspection, financing, appraisal) and you exercise them properly within the deadlines, you typically get it back. If you waive those contingencies or walk away outside the terms, the seller may be able to keep it.

That's exactly why reading your purchase agreement line by line matters before you sign anything with a deadline attached.

Questions about how this works in Indiana or Kentucky? Happy to walk you through it. (502) 379-2365

text:
To the Fremen, water is more precious than gold. Every drop represents survival on a planet where water is almost impossible to find.

In Frank Herbert’s Dune, Stilgar spits on Duke Leto’s table because he is offering something incredibly valuable: his own bodily moisture. What would be considered disgusting elsewhere is a genuine sacrifice in Fremen culture.

Leto understands the gesture and orders his servant not to wipe it away. This shows that he recognises the importance of Fremen customs rather than treating them as primitive.

Villeneuve’s Dune (2021) preserves this moment almost exactly, showing how something that looks like an insult to outsiders is actually an expression of respect.

On Arrakis, spitting isn’t disrespect. Giving away your water is one of the greatest honours you can offer someone.
