text:
The Landmark Julius Caesar: The Complete Works: Gallic War, Civil War, Alexandrian War, African War, and Spanish War - Review - 3 of 4

Without using the Greek terms, Caesar recognizes Hubris and Nemesis before Pharsalus:
"In short, everyone was debating about offices or monetary gains or the persecution of their personal enemies. They were thinking not about how they could win the war but how they could exploit their victory."

Civil Wars

Rome’s successful and sturdy Republic under the blended government of their constitution had begun wobbling soon after they succeeded in conquering all the lands around the Mediterranean with the destruction of Carthage and Corinth in 146. Polybius and other thoughtful historians such as Appian and Cassius Dio viewed the loss of external enemies as fatally weakening the Roman people’ political virtue and resolve.
In Book 1 of the Civil Wars, Caesar devotes the first seven chapters to explaining the internal factions and turmoil that now deny him his dignitas and the respect he deserves for his accomplishments in pursuing the greater glory of Rome. While Caesar himself doesn’t put it this way, other historians position him as the leader of the populares, the common people of the Republic of Rome. His former ally Pompey the Great, to whom he gave his beloved daughter Julia as a wife, is now favored by the optimate, the better people who are mostly rich patricians who control the power of the Senate. In January, 49 Caesar desires to stand for the high office of Consul without having to return to Rome, as the people had earlier decreed. His enemies order him to surrender his armies and return as a common citizen, where he would be vulnerable to trial and condemnation for accused crimes of his first consulship, ten years earlier. He offers to surrender his armies if Pompey surrenders his. Always a great rhetorician, Caesar invariably paints his own position as fair and reasonable.
Since the rise of the Gracchi brothers as Tribunes of the People in 135, and their subsequent murders as the rich faction in the Senate opposed them, domestic peace has been broken often and civil violence has become more frequent in the Republic. The catastrophic conflict of the civil wars erupted when two great generals, Marius on the side of the populares, the common people, faced another great general, Sulla, about 40 years earlier. Rome recovered from the horrors of that period, but by 49, the major Civil Wars started. Later writers point out the irony that Julius Caesar was related to Marius, and Pompey was a successful general under Sulla, and now they re-enact this earlier conflict. Unable to find any compromise, Caesar decides to do the unthinkable, and march on Rome with his army.
“Crossing the Rubicon” has come to mean the act of taking an action from which there is no turning back, but Caesar never mentions the Rubicon, that’s an invention of more dramatic or romantic writers like Plutarch. In 9.7 and 9.8 he describes this famous event, the forbidden act of bringing an army into Italy, without declaring that this is the start of the Civil Wars.

"He urged his troops to defend his reputation and dignitas against his enemies; after all, it was under his command and leadership that for nine years they had achieved the greatest deeds for the state, fighting a great many successful battles and pacifying all of Gaul and Germany. The soldiers of the 13th Legion – present because he had called them up just as the conflict was becoming acute, the others not having arrived yet – shouted their agreement: they were ready to defend their general and the tribunes of the plebs from the outrage they had suffered."

Now that he knew the soldiers’ attitude, he marched to Ariminum with that legion, and there he met the tribunes of the plebs who had fled to him. He called the remaining legions out of their camps and ordered them to follow him.
Pompey sends messengers to negotiate, but their terms are never acceptable. As Caesar makes his way south down the east coast of Italy along the Adriatic Sea, many towns welcome him as the famous Roman leader he is, and many troops defect from Pompey’s side to Caesar’s growing army. Proceeding farther, even in skirmishes, Caesar seeks to minimize bloodshed and allows opposing leaders to go home rather than imprisoning or punishing them. Then, a bitter foe named Domitius Ahenobarbus decides to engage in a large battle in the town of Corfinium, against the orders of Pompey who is still trying to avoid a larger civil war. After making short work of these opponents and capturing the town, Caesar again allows all the elite Romans and Italians he captures to go free. Even before this, on January 18, 49, rumors had reached Rome that Caesar was marching on the city. This caused such panic that Pompey’s allies, including the consuls, magistrates and most senators fled Rome for Capua. Upon the easy defeat of the opposition at Corfinium, the elite refugees decided to flee Italy entirely and approach the port of Brundusium (modern Brindisi) to escape across the Adriatic to western Greece.
Caesar presents his position as always seeking peace, and in pursuit of this goal, he attempts to blockade the waterway off Brundusium to stop Pompey from getting to Greece where he will be able to join large armies of Roman legions who are positioned there. At this point, there has been little bloodshed, and in the week of March 9-16, 49, Caesar’s troops have captured some of Pompey’s officers, so he chooses to send a message through them to avoid war, as he tells us at 9.25.

"Caesar sent him back to deliver a message: because up to this time there had not been any opportunity for a meeting and because Caesar was headed for Brundusium, it was in the interest of the state and the common welfare that Caesar could speak with Pompey."

Pompey refuses to meet, and through his own military ingenuity converts merchant ships to fighting ships with towers three stories high and “equipped them with many catapults and every kind of missile and drove them against Caesar’s works.” Pompey escapes to Greece, joining his armies, thus ensuring a much larger civil war to come. Caesar goes to Rome and addresses the Senate where he expresses his grievances and justification for his actions, and once again proposes negotiations, explaining at 9.32.

"Caesar spoke of the willingness to compromise that he had shown in taking the initiative and proposing that both his and Pompey’s armies be disbanded, even though this meant that he himself was going to suffer a loss of dignitas and prestige. … He urged them and demanded, in consideration of these and all other matters, to come to the rescue of the state and manage it together with himself. But if they let fear deter them from doing so, he would not want to impose on them but would manage the state on his own. Caesar concluded … he himself, in contrast, was eager to be better than others in justice and fairness – just as he had made every effort to set a model through his achievements."

While Caesar presented his position as seeking peace, his armies had rapidly seized Roman provinces in Africa, Sicily, and Sardinia. His strategy led him to march on Spain where his army handily defeated the Pompeian forces in Ilerda. The ancient town of Massilia (Marseille) was heavily fortified and required use of their “innate cleverness” for innovative siege engineering to overcome the defenses.
In the early Spring of 48, major battles are being fought between Pompey’s and Caesar’s forces, both land and naval, across Greece, Thessaly, and Macedonia. After losing most of his fleet, Caesar uses deceptive tactics to feign retreat and manages to capture Dyrrachium on the coast to cut Pompey off from his supplies, not just food, but arms, missiles, and catapults. Reading chapters 11.41 through 11.74, we realize that we are seeing of two of Rome’s greatest geniuses in combat for over three months, a combination of both siege warfare and massed cavalry and infantry battles. In July 48, Caesar launches a surprise attack on a single legion, but Pompey unexpectedly responds with five nearby legions. What makes this a disastrous rout is that Caesar’s troops are unfamiliar with the terrain and become trapped. At 11.68, Caesar begins to describe the consequences.

"But Fortune exercises an overwhelming power in all our affairs and most strikingly in warfare; out of small contingencies, she creates huge differences in the way things turn out. That was the case here."

After becoming trapped between walls, with enemies both inside and outside, Caesar continues the terrible consequences at 11.69.

"Everywhere there was chaos, panic, and rout. It was so bad that when Caesar seized with his own hand the standards of those who were fleeing and ordered the bearers to stand their ground, some of these men turned their horses loose and continued to run for it in the same direction on foot. Others, in their terror, actually let go of the standards. There was not a single man who stopped and took a stand."

At 11.71, Caesar provides the tally.

"In these two battles on a single day, Caesar lost 960 soldiers, several well-known Roman equestrians (second richest class of Romans) … military tribunes, and thirty-two centurions."

At this point, Caesar’s great hero general of the Gallic Wars Labienus, has changed his allegiance and is leading Pompeian troops, and he has taken charge of a number of captives.

"He marched them all out, made a big show – apparently to gain more credibility, being himself a defector – by saluting them as “comrades” and asking them in extremely insolent words whether it was typical of veteran fighters to run away, and then killed them in front of the assembled army."

In 11.72, Caesar does not use the terms of classic Greek drama, hubris, and nemesis, but his message comes through in his description of the currently victorious troops.

"These accomplishments increased the spirit and confidence of the Pompeians to such an extent that they were no longer thinking of how to win the war but instead were presuming they had won already. … Nor did they bear in mind the dynamics that often affect warfare: how tiny causes such as an error of assumptions, sudden fear, or religious concern have often resulted in major disasters, or how often as well, when a failure occurred in an army, the cause was a mistake by the commander or the fault of a tribune. The Pompeians, on the contrary, behaved as if virtue had gained them this victory and no reversal could possibly happen…."

Caesar retreats with his army south through Epirus, Greece and east through Thessaly, fighting and taking cities along the way, resupplying his troops, and readying for another major battle that cannot be avoided with Pompey. The culmination is approaching by August, 48. Caesar again recounts the hubris of his opponents in their internal discussions at Larissa at 11.83.

"Now that Pompey’s forces had been increased and two large armies joined together, everyone’s already ardent optimism was intensified and the expectation of victory strengthened to an extraordinary degree… Already some were openly fighting among themselves for prizes and priesthoods and allotting consulships for years to come; others were angling for the houses and the other property of those in Caesar’s camp."

He comes to his conclusion at the end of 11.83.

"In short, everyone was debating about offices or monetary gains or the persecution of their personal enemies. They were thinking not about how they could win the war but how they could exploit their victory."

text:
In September 1916, Britain introduced a machine that would fundamentally change warfare. 

The tank.

Built to cross trenches, survive machine gun fire and break through fortified positions, it gave armies something they desperately needed, protected mobility.

For the next 110 years, increasingly sophisticated weapons would be developed specifically to destroy it.

And repeatedly, the tank's future would be questioned. Yet the machine kept returning, transformed by the very weapons designed to eliminate it.

> The first British Mark I tanks could barely reach 6 km/h.
> They frequently broke down, became stuck and struggled across difficult terrain.
> Yet they brought armoured firepower into positions infantry could scarcely cross.
> By 1917, hundreds were being deployed in major offensives.
> Germany responded with armor piercing ammunition and dedicated anti tank rifles.
> The century-long contest between armor and the weapons designed to defeat it had begun.

Then came World War II, and the weapons hunting tanks became considerably more dangerous.

> High-velocity anti-tank guns could penetrate thick armor.
> Minefields could immobilize entire armored formations.
> Germany introduced the Panzerfaust, giving infantry a cheap, portable weapon capable of threatening tanks.
> America developed the bazooka, using shaped charges to penetrate armor.
> A soldier carrying a relatively inexpensive launcher could now threaten a machine costing vastly more.
> Yet tanks evolved with sloped armor, stronger guns, better engines and improved mobility.
> They remained central to mechanized warfare.

But the greatest crisis of confidence was still to come.

> In October 1973, Israeli tanks advanced against Egyptian defenses during the Yom Kippur War.
> Egyptian infantry carried Soviet Sagger guided missiles, RPGs and other anti-tank weapons.
> During one disastrous counterattack, Israel's 162nd Armored Division lost 83 of its 183 tanks.
> Relatively small weapons, operating within prepared defenses, had devastated a formidable armored force.
> Military commentators began questioning whether guided missiles had made tanks obsolete.
> In 1977, The Washington Post published an article titled Army Leaders Betting Billions That Tanks Aren't Obsolete.
> Yet armies were already investing heavily in a new generation of armored vehicles.

And what followed was an extraordinary transformation in tank engineering.

> Conventional steel gave way to increasingly sophisticated composite armor.
> Explosive reactive armor offered additional protection against shaped-charge weapons.
> Powerful engines allowed some tanks weighing over 60 tonnes to approach 70 km/h on roads.
> Stabilised guns, laser rangefinders and computerised fire control transformed their accuracy.
> Thermal imagers made night fighting far more effective.
> The Abrams, Leopard 2 and Challenger emerged as formidable modern combat systems.
> In 1991, coalition tanks demonstrated their effectiveness during the Gulf War
> Less than two decades after the missile shock of 1973, armored warfare remained extraordinarily relevant.

But anti-tank weapons were evolving too.

> Guided missiles became more accurate, portable and capable of attacking vulnerable areas.
> The American Javelin introduced fire and forget guidance and top-attack capability.
> During the 2006 Lebanon War, Hezbollah's missiles penetrated several Israeli Merkava tanks.
> Even advanced armor remained vulnerable.
> Israel subsequently fielded Trophy, an active protection system capable of intercepting incoming threats.
> Tanks could now attempt to destroy approaching weapons before impact, rather than relying entirely on armor.

And then came Ukraine.

> Since February 2022, more than 4,400 Russian tank losses have been visually documented.
> Mines, artillery, missiles and drones have all contributed to the destruction and attrition.
> But inexpensive FPV drones have fundamentally changed the threat facing armored vehicles.
> Some costing only hundreds or a few thousand dollars can threaten tanks worth millions.
> A tank surviving one strike may face another, and another, before it can escape or be recovered.
> Persistent aerial surveillance has made armored movement increasingly dangerous.
> And once again, the familiar argument has returned: the era of tanks is finally over.

But armies are already preparing for what comes next.

> Poland is investing billions in new tanks, while European armies continue ordering advanced Leopard 2 variants.
> America is developing the M1E3 Abrams, prioritizing lower weight, improved survivability and reduced logistical demands.
> Engineers are exploring integrated sensors, automated defenses and new ways to counter drones.
> The battlefield has changed, but the military requirement for protected mobility and heavy firepower has not disappeared.

There is a remarkable historical irony here.

The tank was invented because the weapons of its time had made movement across the battlefield extraordinarily dangerous. 

Over the following 110 years, mines, rockets, guided missiles and increasingly sophisticated ammunition repeatedly challenged its survival. Each time, armies adapted the machine and the way it fought.

Now drones have brought the tank to another crossroads. 

The advantage may currently lie with the inexpensive drones hunting it, but history offers a compelling reason to expect another reinvention.

Perhaps the tank isn't obsolete. Perhaps it's the tank designed for yesterday's battlefield that is. https://t.co/q3p9MAuoF2

Former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo has recounted the circumstances of his arrest and imprisonment under the late military Head of State, General Sani Abacha, stating that he declined an offer of political asylum from the United States despite being warned that he would be detained upon returning to Nigeria.

Speaking in an interview with BBC News Pidgin, the 89-year-old former leader said that after handing over power to civilian President Shehu Shagari in 1979, he retired from the Nigerian Army at the age of 42 as a four-star general. With no further ranks available in the military, he turned to farming, which he described as progressing successfully until his detention.

Obasanjo alleged that Abacha had determined he “must be liquidated” because the military ruler would otherwise be unable to “have his way.” While traveling abroad, he said the American ambassador contacted him to convey that the United States government had offered political asylum, as authorities expected his arrest if he returned home.“This was difficult for me. I don’t — I haven’t done anything. What do they want to arrest me for? Um, I don’t want political asylum,” Obasanjo stated.

Upon his return, his passport was seized. At his farm, a security detail informed him that the premises had been surrounded. Shortly afterward, a policeman in civilian clothing arrived with an invitation from an Assistant Inspector-General of Police. Obasanjo said he rejected the summons as improper, insisting the senior officer should come to him if assistance was genuinely required. He then drove himself to the police station, where the AIG informed him that he had been instructed to carry out the arrest.

Obasanjo said he was initially held at an undisclosed location. He credited former U.S. President Jimmy Carter with intervening on his behalf, after which he was placed under house arrest. Security operatives later removed him from his residence around 1 a.m. while he was playing squash and transferred him to prison.

Obasanjo was released following Abacha’s death. He subsequently entered partisan politics, won the 1999 presidential election on the platform of the Peoples Democratic Party, and was inaugurated on May 29, 1999, as the first democratically elected president of Nigeria’s Fourth Republic. He served two terms, leaving office in 2007.

Nine years ago, on the eve of Veterans Day, I wrote a commentary for the Los Angeles Business Journal about an overlooked source of executive talent: America's military veterans.

What follows is the commentary exactly as it appeared in 2017, a perspective on veteran leadership that remains just as relevant in today's conversations about executive talent, workforce development, and organizational success.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
𝗗𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗩𝗲𝘁 𝗶𝗻 𝗦𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗧𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁
By David Farrow
Los Angeles Business Journal | November 5, 2017
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
The war for talent has never been more intense than it is today.

Corporations compete for senior- and mid-level executives who can succeed under pressure, gain the respect of subordinates, and convey a selfless and loyal attitude focused on getting the job done.

Yet many corporations ignore an extraordinary pool of available talent: separating and retiring members of our military. Many companies are reluctant to consider veterans for executive or management positions because some don't fit the specifications of published job descriptions.

Sometimes there's no way around these published requirements, but where there's a bit of latitude, veterans usually come to the civilian workforce with track records of responsibility and authority that exceed civilian peers.

At the age of 58, Gen. Tony Thomas, the commanding general of the U.S. Special Operations Command (SOCOM), oversees nearly 80,000 employees worldwide. He has authority over a budget exceeding $10 billion.

Young officers and senior enlisted leaders in their late 20s and early 30s have responsibility, today, for hundreds of employees and authority over budgets in the millions of dollars. Comparable experience in the civilian world at similar ages is rare, indeed.

This isn't to say that all veterans are qualified for any open position. Nor does it suggest that veterans should be offered jobs out of gratitude for service. It argues, instead, that veterans often have greater management experience than their civilian peers and almost certainly have far better leadership training, both formal and informal.

Let's take a look at leadership:

• Veterans have demonstrated leadership under challenging circumstances during times of both war and peace.
• They have a military "mindset" that focuses on specific objectives and on the steps required to meet objectives.
• Veterans view themselves as "servants," never putting their own needs ahead of those they lead or ahead of the larger organization. Notions of "self-enrichment" and "self-aggrandizement" are anathema.
• Veterans are known for focus, tenacity, and persistence.
• They understand accountability, never blaming others for their failures.
• The finest veterans give "lawful" orders. This means that officers and non-commissioned officers would never ask subordinates to do something they wouldn't do themselves.
• Veterans understand that leadership by example and by persuasion is far more effective than leadership by authoritarian threat.
Veterans bring strong interpersonal skills to the civilian workforce. The skills have been honed inside a large management hierarchy of extremely diverse individuals. In order to survive in this meritocracy, many veterans are quick learners who get up to speed on assignments on their own and complete those assignments with little or no supervision.

Veterans are capable of this because they assume different and more challenging positions every two or three years. They must master new skills and manage new sets of superiors and subordinates on a regular basis.

Indeed, the U.S. military might be the purest meritocracy in American life. It doesn't matter where you grew up or who your parents were or where you went to school.

It's true that Thomas graduated from West Point, but Colin Powell graduated from City College of New York.

What does this meritocracy mean to you as a hiring manager? It means that a military track record of advancement speaks volumes and that the responsibility and authority that came with each of those promotions weren't granted lightly or granted for any reason other than demonstrated competence and excellence.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

I remember the first time I walked into the Oval Office to brief President Biden. I'd just been appointed as the White House Special Advisor for AI. The President sat behind the Resolute desk and began with a single question: "What is the worst harm that AI could enable?"

I had no shortage of worries. We talked about the pace of technological progress — how, thanks to better chips and algorithms, what was cutting-edge that day would be commonplace within a couple of years. We talked about how high the ceiling on intelligence was, and about the dangers that AI would likely bring in areas like cybersecurity and bioweapons. We talked about how technology was fast and government was slow. 

Then he asked about the benefits. He cared about ending cancer as much as anything in the world, and AI — managed well — offers more hope for that than anything else. 

Most of all, we talked about what became the argument of the book my White House colleague @TantumSCollins and I have written: that democracies must lead in inventing this technology, turn that lead into a lasting advantage, and do it all without betraying their own values. Achieving all three at once will be a bitter struggle. Every choice pits security against liberty, speed against caution, power against principle.

Today THE BITTER STRUGGLE is out from Crown, in hardcover, ebook, and audio. It’s our account of what happened, what’s coming, and what’s at stake. We don’t pretend the answers are easy — in some ways we’re more worried than when we started. But these questions are too important to be debated only behind closed doors, including the door to the Oval Office. We hope you will join the debate.

A bipartisan group of US lawmakers comprising 91 members of the congress have sent a letter to Republican and Democratic leadership in the House of Representatives asking them to formally invite Pope Leo XIV to address a joint session of Congress next year. Addressed to House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana, and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-New York, the letter was signed by 91 Republican and Democratic members of Congress.

“The election of Pope Leo XIV serves as a sign of great pride for millions of Americans. As the first ever American-born Pope, his unique perspective, and ties to our country, would serve as a unifying force for members of Congress,” the bipartisan members wrote in the letter.

“Following a divisive election, Pope Leo’s unifying message of service, compassion for fellow mankind, and the importance of human dignity would be especially timely,” the letter added. The Congress representatives also said that a visit from the Holy Father “would offer a much-needed outlook as we navigate complex foreign and domestic issues.”

Citing the “undeniable historical significance and cultural impact of Pope Francis’s address to Congress in 2015”, the lawmakers urged the leaders to work to schedule a joint address as soon as possible in the beginning of the 120th Congress with the first American-born Pope.

text:
Financial models and the people who use them are worth studying together. 

These six books offer complementary perspectives on investment practice, market theory and hedge fund history.

Investment practice and theory

“10½ Lessons from Experience” by Paul Marshall draws on decades of investment experience to examine the practical demands of managing money.

“The Myth of the Rational Market” by Justin Fox traces the development of efficient-market theory and the debates surrounding it.

“The Physics of Wall Street” by James Owen Weatherall explores how physicists brought mathematical methods into finance.

“The (Mis)Behavior of Markets” by Benoit Mandelbrot challenges conventional risk models, examining how fractals and fat-tailed distributions can better describe extreme market moves.

Hedge fund history and “investainment”

“More Money Than God” by Sebastian Mallaby follows the development of the hedge fund industry through its managers, strategies and crises.

“The Man Who Solved the Market” by Gregory Zuckerman tells the story of Jim Simons and Renaissance Technologies, exploring the research and organization behind an exceptional quantitative investment business.

Limited education, rough backgrounds, constant drama, accusations, and a history of fighting seem to be the common denominator. They learned to survive by fighting because that’s the environment they were accustomed to.

And while they may have managed to turn that lifestyle into some level of success, that doesn’t automatically make them respectable, professional, or marketable.

This is exactly why I call it a panel of shame. There’s a reason major brands haven’t lined up to offer them legitimate endorsement deals. Being loud, controversial, and known for fighting isn’t the same as being a credible representative of a company. Brands look for professionalism, reputation, presentation, and standards.

Everybody who gets attention isn’t somebody who deserves a platform, and everybody who makes money isn’t somebody who meets the standard. There’s a difference between being popular and being respected. This panel proves it.

BHAI DOOJ 2026: A SACRED CELEBRATION OF SIBLING LOVE – WHERE TILAK SYMBOLISES PROTECTION AND PRAYERS!
—————————————————
11 NOVEMBER 2026 | WEDNESDAY
#BhaiDooj, also known as BHAIYA DOOJ, YAMA DWITIYA, BHAU BEEJ and BHAI PHONTA, is one of India’s most cherished festivals celebrating the beautiful relationship between brothers and sisters. Observed on KARTIK SHUKLA DWITIYA, it traditionally marks the conclusion of the five-day Diwali festivities.
—————————————————-
🌺 THE TWO LEGENDARY STORIES BEHIND BHAI DOOJ
1. THE STORY OF YAMRAJ AND YAMUNA
According to Hindu mythology, Yamuna, the daughter of Surya Dev, repeatedly invited her brother Yamraj, the God of Death, to visit her.
Finally, on Kartik Shukla Dwitiya, Yamraj visited his sister. Overjoyed, Yamuna welcomed him with a traditional tilak, performed aarti and prepared a delicious feast.
Touched by her affection, Yamraj offered her a boon. Yamuna wished that brothers receiving their sisters’ blessings on this auspicious day should enjoy long lives, happiness and protection.
Yamraj granted her wish. Thus, the festival became known as YAMA DWITIYA.
—————————————————-
2. LORD KRISHNA AND SUBHADRA
Another popular legend associates Bhai Dooj with Lord Krishna. After defeating the demon Narakasura, Krishna visited his sister Subhadra. She welcomed him with flowers, sweets, aarti and a ceremonial tilak.
Her affectionate welcome is traditionally remembered as another origin of this beautiful festival.
————————————————-
🌼 HOW IS BHAI DOOJ CELEBRATED?
• Sisters apply a sacred tilak of roli and rice on their brothers’ foreheads.
• Aarti is performed, accompanied by prayers for their long life and prosperity.
• Traditional sweets and festive meals are shared.
• Brothers reciprocate with gifts, affection and promises of lifelong support.
🇮🇳 REGIONAL NAMES
• North India – Bhai Dooj
• Maharashtra and Goa – Bhau Beej
• West Bengal – Bhai Phonta
• Nepal – Bhai Tika
———————————————
❤️ THE DEEPER SIGNIFICANCE
Bhai Dooj is not merely a religious ritual; it celebrates LOVE, TRUST, PROTECTION, GRATITUDE AND LIFELONG FAMILY BONDS.
Unlike relationships built by circumstances, the bond between siblings carries childhood memories, shared laughter, occasional disagreements and unconditional affection.
———————————————
A SISTER’S TILAK IS A PRAYER, A BROTHER’S PROMISE IS A COMMITMENT, AND THEIR BOND IS A BLESSING THAT LASTS A LIFETIME!
Wishing everyone a very Happy and Blessed

text:
What if he had said yes?

The counterfactual is irresistible. Had Obasanjo accepted asylum, would he have become a permanent political exile, issuing measured statements from Washington or Virginia? Would the 1999 presidential election have produced a different candidate and a different Fourth Republic? We cannot know. What is certain is that accepting the American offer would almost certainly have altered the trajectory of his public life — and Nigeria’s.

Instead, Abacha died in June 1998. Obasanjo was released. Less than a year later he won the presidential election and was inaugurated on 29 May 1999 as the first president of the Fourth Republic. From prison cell to Aso Rock in under twelve months. If this were a Nollywood script, producers might reject it for excessive drama.

A complicated love affair

The episode remains revealing. A country can be the place where a man has served at the highest level and still become the place that threatens his freedom. Obasanjo’s experience is a reminder of how swiftly authoritarian power can turn on those who once wielded it.

Today Nigerians continue to argue about Obasanjo’s presidency, his interventions and his public pronouncements. This particular chapter, however, stands apart. America offered him asylum. Nigeria offered him prison. History, with its characteristic sense of timing, eventually offered him another chance at the presidency.

Baba rejected Washington, encountered Abacha, and still found his way back to Aso Rock. In Nigeria, sometimes the journey from the farm to the Presidential Villa passes through the prison gate and apparently requires no American visa.

authorBio: Communicator | Community & health advocate | Turning complex ideas into clear human stories | Storytelling, engagement & campaigns that drive real impact.

text:
Baba Balks at American Asylum, Braves Abacha’s Bars, Then Bags Aso Rock - part 1

If Chief Olusegun Obasanjo had taken Washington’s offer, he might today be a comfortable political exile granting the occasional interview from a quiet American suburb. Instead, he came home, walked into Abacha’s net, survived prison, and later returned to the Presidential Villa. In Nigeria, it seems, the road to power sometimes runs straight through a prison gate.

There are many ways to display patriotism. Obasanjo appears to have selected one of the more theatrical options: rejecting political asylum from the United States, flying back into danger, and eventually finding himself behind bars.

In a recent recollection that has sent Nigerians diving back into the archives of the Abacha years, the former president described how the American ambassador approached him with an offer of asylum. Intelligence, he was told, indicated he would be arrested if he returned to Nigeria. 

The message was clear enough: things were about to become unpleasant, and Washington was prepared to provide a safe alternative.

Obasanjo’s reply was equally clear. He did not want political asylum.

And so, a man who had once ruled Nigeria as military Head of State discovered that the country he had commanded could also revoke his freedom.

Irony only deepens when one recalls 1979. After the assassination of General Murtala Muhammed in 1976, Obasanjo had become Head of State at 38. By 42 he had reached the summit of both military rank and political power. Many in his position would have searched for ways to remain relevant. Obasanjo chose farming.

After issuing orders to generals, he turned his attention to soil, livestock, and harvests. By his own account, the agricultural venture was going reasonably well — until General Sani Abacha decided otherwise.

America saw the storm. Baba went home anyway.

The Abacha years remain among the darkest chapters in Nigeria’s political history. After seizing power in November 1993, Abacha’s regime became notorious for repression, intimidation, and the systematic neutralisation of perceived threats. Obasanjo has said Abacha concluded he needed to be eliminated, politically if not physically.

While travelling abroad, Obasanjo received the American offer. One can almost reconstruct the exchange:

America: Chief, we have information you may be arrested if you return.   Obasanjo: Arrested for what? I have done nothing.   

America: Precisely why we are offering protection.   Obasanjo: I don’t want political asylum.

While many Nigerians would move mountains for a temporary American visa, Obasanjo declined a permanent political escape route. He wanted to go home. Nigeria, unfortunately, had prepared a rather different reception.

The farm becomes a police operation
Upon his return, his passport was seized. He proceeded to his farm, only for his security detail to report that government operatives had surrounded the property. A policeman in civilian clothes soon arrived with a message: an Assistant Inspector-General of Police wanted to see him.

Obasanjo was unimpressed. If the AIG needed his assistance, he replied, the AIG should come to him. The invitation, of course, was not social. When Obasanjo eventually drove himself to the meeting, he was informed that orders had been given for his arrest.

A former Commander-in-Chief, four-star general and Head of State was now being summoned by the police. Power, Nigerian history repeatedly demonstrates, can change hands faster than a siren.

Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter intervened and appealed to Abacha. Obasanjo was briefly moved to house arrest. The relief was temporary. One night around 1 a.m., while he was playing squash, security operatives arrived and took him away. From there, the road led to prison.

He had rejected a comfortable life in America, returned to Nigeria, gone to his farm — and ended up in a cell. Even finishing a game of squash was not guaranteed under Abacha.

text:
I am an attorney-adviser at the Civilian Protection Center of Excellence, which is a real office with a real door in Virginia.

I would like to congratulate Congressman Thomas Massie on the most thorough evaluation ever written about my chain of command. It runs 34 pages and has eight sections. He spent an hour and twenty minutes reading every word on the House floor, which is longer than any supervisor has ever spent on my file, and I include the one who was let go.

The Congressman believes he has drafted articles of impeachment. I understand the confusion, because the forms look alike. Both list a man’s accomplishments in numbered order, both are signed by someone on his way out of the organization, and both close with a recommendation about future employment. But I have nineteen years in government, and I know a glowing review when one is read into the Congressional Record.

Consider the author’s own summary. Asked why colleagues who admire the Secretary should still vote yes, Mr. Massie explained, “we’re not impeaching him for being bad at his job.” Counsel thanks the gentleman from Kentucky. In my profession we call that a stipulation. The prosecution has opened by conceding effectiveness, and effectiveness is the only metric this building still collects.

Allow me to describe how we became so efficient, since I played a small part. Small is the operative word.

When this administration began, forty people worked at the Center. We trained targeteers. We kept data. We wrote the long, sad memoranda that tell a commander what is standing next to the thing he wishes to remove. A defense official later told a reporter the Center had been just “hitting its stride.” Stride, I have since learned, is a form of drag.

By the end of 2025 we were nine. Across the wider enterprise, a little under two hundred people became roughly two dozen, some of them part-time, which is the correct number of hours to devote to a question nobody is asking. The Secretary did not act rashly. He polled his commanders first and offered three choices: lose 65 percent, keep a small office in Washington, or disappear. Nine picked the gentlest cut. Two refused the menu and asked to keep everything. Central Command wrote that our people “enhanced our precision and accuracy, making us more lethal.” They used his favorite word and lost anyway. I have kept that memo. It is the kindest thing anyone in uniform has ever said about a lawyer.

Our annual budget was seven million dollars. I mention it only because I have seen what we pay for things that work.

Senators wrote to remind the Secretary that Congress created the Center and that “the law requires you to operate it.” And he does. That is the elegance. The law requires that the office exist. It is silent on whether anyone inside should be able to reach a telephone. We exist magnificently. I have a badge, a chair, and a statutory mandate. By published account, more of the assessing now falls to artificial intelligence, which has never once asked a follow-up question, requested a site visit, or wept in the parking garage.

A lesser organization would have abolished us and taken the headline. We kept the nameplate and removed the friction. In the old days a strike package had to pass people like me, and we were slow. We asked what the building was at nine in the morning as well as at midnight. We asked who lived upstairs. Every question cost minutes, and in minutes a target moves, and then a perfectly good morning is wasted. The process is frictionless now. Nothing rubs against anything.

Which brings me to Article IV, the section about my office, and the only one I am professionally qualified to grade. Its centerpiece is a strike on a girls’ school in Minab, Iran, where the resolution counts at least 156 civilians dead, at least 120 of them schoolchildren. I have been asked whether my office reviewed that target. I can say with complete confidence and a clear conscience that we did not. We did not review it before. We did not assess it after. No memorandum bears my initials. In nineteen years I have never had a cleaner file.

That is what efficiency feels like from the inside. A quiet inbox.

The other seven sections sit outside my lane, but I read them with collegial admiration. Three concern Iran and the War Powers Resolution, including the charge, in the Congressman’s own summary, that the Secretary “treated mandatory statutory deadlines as discretionary.” Every lawyer in this building has that sentence embroidered on something. Article V tallies at least 243 dead in strikes on suspected drug traffickers, a caseload that maritime law enforcement, with its warrants and its Coast Guard cutters and its tedious habit of arrests, would have needed decades to clear. Article VI concerns a senator who told troops they could refuse illegal orders. Article VII concerns a head of state collected from his own country. Article VIII is Yemen, for anyone who had forgotten Yemen, which was rather the idea.

Did he do the things described? “And the answer is yes, eight times,” says the reviewer. Eight for eight. I have never seen a federal employee meet every objective in a rating period. Most of us receive “meets expectations” and a lanyard.

The Secretary answered this morning from our own briefing room, as a confident man does. The document, he said, is “a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.” “It’s a farce and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it.” A week earlier he had gone with “sham articles of impeachment.” Mr. Massie had invited him to explain, article by article, why he was not guilty. The coverage I have seen records adjectives. This is sound practice. One never answers an interrogatory one can characterize.

Moments later the President filed his own evaluation: “A+++.” Three pluses. I have sat on promotion boards, and a grade is normally supported by a narrative. This one arrived with 34 pages of it.

House leaders must hold the vote by Wednesday, November 11, which is Veterans Day. Members who had hoped to end the year without their names beside this war will now sign something, and they resent the paperwork. I sympathize. Nobody hates a mandatory deadline like a body that has just learned they are discretionary. Should it pass, he would be the third Cabinet secretary in history to be impeached, which this building will log as a top-three finish.

Whatever they decide, my office is safe. It cannot be cut further without offending the statute, and it cannot be consulted without offending the culture. I will be at my desk Thursday, one of nine, guardian of a function Congress ordered and nobody ordered used. The phone works. I tested it. I called my own extension and it rang, and for a moment it was like the old days: someone, somewhere, wanted to know what was next to the target.

I let it go to voicemail. We are very lean now.

text:
Congress weighs tighter chip curbs. Can NVIDIA keep Washington at bay?👇
⠀
The board at NVIDIA ($NVDA) launched an investigation on Sunday to clarify media reports that CEO Jensen Huang became the target of a foreign intelligence operation.
⠀
In the same statement, the board said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security were harmed and expressed confidence in Huang's leadership.
⠀
The chip designer's market cap hit $4.5 trillion on Nov. 6, 2026.
⠀
Huang held 3.6% as of late March 2026, worth more than $150 billion at recent prices.
⠀
Whether he stays or leaves also raises the risk of a leadership disruption; Seeking Alpha noted that's one of the issues the board probe has put on investors' radar.
⠀
-----
⠀
🔴 Follow me on X: @rich_compass
⠀
U.S. stock, crypto, and technical analysis
⠀
-----

▋ The board faces scrutiny for defending Jensen Huang on day one
⠀
The statement didn't name the person involved or describe the nature of Huang's relationship with that person.
⠀
A committee of independent directors oversees how the probe is run, with help from outside independent lawyers.
⠀
The board said the investigation will review 'all available information'; Huang fully supports it and has promised to cooperate.
⠀
The board also called U.S. national and economic security a priority and critical to NVIDIA and shareholder interests.
⠀
It also said it would provide updates in due course, but didn't announce a deadline for finishing the probe.
⠀
That creates some timing tension.
⠀
The board says it wants to get to the bottom of this, yet before the probe even started it said it had no reason to believe secrets or national security were harmed.
⠀
Harry Kraemer Jr., a former Baxter International CEO and management scholar now teaching at Northwestern's business school, called that stance 'inappropriate' and said, 'That's how you lose credibility.'
⠀
Some public company directors at The Wall Street Journal's board council meeting on Monday questioned whether NVIDIA's board was too quick to protect Huang or accepted his assurances about the relationship from the start, the paper reported.
⠀
The importance of succession planning also came up in the directors' discussion of the matter.
⠀
Heidrick & Struggles CEO Tom Monahan said every company should think about management depth, succession, and risk management.

▋ The intelligence probe into Alice Huang and Megaspeed chip sales
⠀
Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen, also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang.
⠀
She was a senior executive at Singapore data center company Megaspeed International at the time.
⠀
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier that U.S. officials concluded last year she shared information with the Chinese government while working with NVIDIA to build data centers in Asia.
⠀
Reuters, citing a New York Times report last month, said Huang and Alice Huang had a close relationship and that she was suspected of providing information directly to Beijing.
⠀
Reuters said it couldn't independently verify those allegations or Alice Huang's current role at Megaspeed, and couldn't determine her whereabouts.
⠀
Seeking Alpha, citing The New York Times and people familiar with the matter, reported that a highly classified memo warning senior officials about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang was drafted under Secretary of State Rubio's supervision.
⠀
Seeking Alpha's account said electronic surveillance was the basis for that warning, and U.S. officials concluded from it that Alice Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security.
⠀
ShareCast also reported that U.S. officials concluded Alice Huang was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, an intelligence agency.
⠀
When authorities began surveilling her in late 2024, she disappeared in China for a while, the Wall Street Journal reported.
⠀
Her current whereabouts are unknown, as is whether she still holds a senior position at Megaspeed.
⠀
The company was spun off from a Chinese company in 2023, is based in Singapore, and builds data centers across Southeast Asia.
⠀
It's one of several companies that partnered with NVIDIA and promised to use its chips in data centers.
⠀
It rents out computing power to customers, a business under scrutiny for potentially moving chips to China and letting Chinese customers use the compute.
⠀
Reuters, citing Megaspeed's website, said the company is NVIDIA's cloud partner in Asia Pacific and offers GB200 NVL72 and HGX H100 chips.
⠀
In early 2025, Alice Huang and business partner Kang Wei pitched investors on a Southeast Asia data center project worth hundreds of millions of dollars, using access to NVIDIA chips as a selling point.
⠀
One investor told the Financial Times they assured backers there was 'no problem' getting chips and described Alibaba as a customer for the project.
⠀
Alibaba was a major customer of Megaspeed's Southeast Asia cloud services from the start and has remained its biggest customer.
⠀
Company documents say Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed in June 2024 through Singapore subsidiary Apex Enterprise Solutions.
⠀
The loan was arranged through Malaysian company Speedmatrix, which used the entire business as collateral.
⠀
Megaspeed's balance sheet ballooned from $33 million to $3 billion in 2024.
⠀
This is Live Mint's account of the Financial Times report, not a court finding that she illegally moved chips to China.
⠀
Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion of chips from NVIDIA over two years, Seeking Alpha reported, citing The New York Times.
⠀
Business Today put it differently: the company acquired at least $4.8 billion of AI equipment containing NVIDIA chips between June 2024 and February 2026; in November 2025 it also imported at least 17,544 GB300 chips worth about $787 million.
⠀
Seeking Alpha's account said that even after The New York Times disclosed the Commerce Department was investigating whether Megaspeed helped move restricted AI chips into China, NVIDIA kept selling to the company.
⠀
Opening an investigation is not itself a finding of wrongdoing, Seeking Alpha noted in its report.
⠀
The probe into Megaspeed and its potential ties to the Chinese government has lasted more than a year, with U.S. agencies including the Commerce Department and the Justice Department involved, people familiar with the matter told the Wall Street Journal.
⠀
Those people said Megaspeed came up in recent discussions about whether to add dozens of companies to the U.S. entity list, a debate that includes companies based in China or tied to Chinese firms.
⠀
For now, Megaspeed and other companies haven't been added, and agency officials have left the decision to senior officials involved in U.S. and China trade talks.
⠀
In August 2025, NVIDIA general counsel Tim Teter wrote to a Commerce Department Bureau of Industry and Security staffer, saying senior Commerce official Jeff Kessler had agreed they could reach out about the Megaspeed case.
⠀
The staffer declined to meet and forwarded the letter to Kessler.
⠀
Kessler replied that the case had to be handled strictly by the book.
⠀
The Justice Department later asked Commerce to pause, Commerce complied, and the probe shifted to a criminal investigation by Justice.
⠀
The Next Web reported that follow-up, citing The New York Times, and said it hadn't independently verified it.
⠀
Megaspeed couldn't immediately be reached for comment at the time, the Wall Street Journal reported.
⠀
The company had previously described itself as 'a company that follows the law and is legitimate.'
⠀
On Alice Huang's alleged ties to a Chinese intelligence agency, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said it 'did not conduct any investigation.'
⠀
A Singapore Police Force representative said the investigation into Megaspeed is ongoing and didn't provide details.
⠀
China's embassy in Washington has previously denied the espionage allegations, saying China opposes hyping the narrative and that its technological development is based on 'independent innovation.'

▋ Jensen Huang apologizes for an affair but NVIDIA says business will not slow down
⠀
Jensen Huang sent an internal message to employees on Sunday apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife.
⠀
He said, 'I owe my family and all of you an apology,' and added that his actions hurt his wife and children, with 'no excuse.'
⠀
NVIDIA had first denied the relationship, and Huang later admitted it himself, the Wall Street Journal noted.
⠀
An NVIDIA spokesperson said 'today's news won't slow NVIDIA down' and added that Huang is committed to continuing as CEO without interruption.
⠀
He will stay CEO while the investigation proceeds, according to Seeking Alpha, citing The New York Times.
⠀
NVIDIA previously said that given business dealings, Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were 'not unusual or unexpected.'
⠀
On the operations front, Ryu Jemyung, vice minister of South Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT, told a National Assembly budget committee on Monday that the controversy affecting NVIDIA won't affect South Korea's already contracted GPU supply, and that previously contracted NVIDIA GPU deliveries are still on schedule.

▋ Shares fall over 4% and prediction markets price in leadership risk
⠀
After the board announced the investigation, NVIDIA shares fell 4% in Monday premarket trading.
⠀
Another Wall Street Journal report the same day put the latest premarket drop at 5.4%.
⠀
Yahoo Finance market data shows NVDA closed at $178.67 on Nov. 9, 2026, down 4.27% from the prior trading day's close of $186.64, a drop of $7.97.
⠀
That same day, a shareholder filed a civil class action.
⠀
TechCrunch wrote that New York law firm Rosen, representing investor Mark Kistenmacher, sued NVIDIA and Huang in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California.
⠀
The case docket page lists case number 5:26-cv-13448, filed Nov. 9, under securities law, as a class action.
⠀
TechCrunch wrote the proposed class period is Oct. 9, 2025 to Nov. 8, 2026; Kistenmacher made seven purchases this year totaling about $20,500.
⠀
The complaint points to three public statements: spokesperson John Rizzo said in late October that Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were 'not unusual or unexpected'; the company earlier said it found no evidence chips were transshipped; and Huang told Bloomberg on Oct. 30 that dealings with Megaspeed were 'normal and not unusual.'
⠀
The complaint claims those three statements were false or misleading because Huang and Alice Huang had a private relationship.
⠀
These are the complaint's allegations, and a court hasn't decided who is right or wrong.
⠀
TechCrunch wrote that the closing drop gives plaintiffs' lawyers a lot to work with.
⠀
TechCrunch also cautioned that a law firm's investigation notice, or this new lawsuit, doesn't mean the case has merit.
⠀
NVIDIA stock is roughly flat this year and about 22% below its October high, according to data in the Wall Street Journal's Monday premarket report.
⠀
Semiconductor stocks sold off last week, and Democratic midterm election wins intensified market anxiety about the AI trade that had been building for weeks, the Wall Street Journal reported.
⠀
Prediction markets also put odds on it.
⠀
Benzinga reported Polymarket priced a 35% chance Huang resigns or is removed by year end, and Kalshi priced a 35% chance he is removed before July 1, 2027.
⠀
Those prices reflect how market participants see the probability of an event.
⠀
NVIDIA's market cap rose from about $420 billion at the end of 2022 to $4.5 trillion on Nov. 6, 2026, according to data cited by Reuters.

▋ Analysts warn innovation could slow without a clear successor to Jensen Huang
⠀
Analysts cited by The Wall Street Journal said the investigation will at least trigger a congressional probe and pressure the stock.
⠀
Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives and others wrote that Huang will likely stay CEO near term without interruption, but the board probe's outcome creates a possibility he's removed.
⠀
They think this will add stock risk because Huang is so central to NVIDIA's global story and strategy, and it will increase U.S. scrutiny of chip sales to China.
⠀
Citrini Research's Jukan Choe thinks Huang's influence over NVIDIA is too large, and the company lacks an obvious successor.
⠀
Choe noted the company has kept a culture similar to a startup even as it scaled, largely driven by the cofounder; if Huang's leadership is weakened, there are concerns innovation could slow.
⠀
Bernstein analysts said there's no immediate clear successor if Huang is unwilling or unable to keep leading; they put it this way: 'NVIDIA is not a normal company, and Jensen is not a normal CEO; he is NVIDIA.'
⠀
Seeking Alpha noted that for investors, the probe raises questions about protecting NVIDIA's confidential information, oversight of customer relationships, and possible leadership disruption; those issues are especially important for a company whose chips power AI systems.

▋ Over sixty direct reports and no succession plan expose governance concerns
⠀
NVIDIA has no chairman and no succession plan, the Wall Street Journal noted.
⠀
Other famous tech founders often keep control through huge stakes or shares with super voting rights, the paper noted.
⠀
The board agenda is set jointly by Huang and lead independent director Stephen Neal, former Cooley CEO, and the two decide what information directors get and run meetings.
⠀
Only about 1% of Russell 3000 public companies have no chairman.
⠀
The Wall Street Journal reported that as of spring 2026, 3 of NVIDIA's 10 independent directors had served 25 years or more, and 2 more had served over 10 years.
⠀
The company's 2026 annual meeting proxy gives different numbers: the board had 10 people, 9 were nominated as independent directors, and Huang was the one company executive who wasn't independent.
⠀
On the proxy, Tench Coxe and Harvey C. Jones had served since 1993, A. Brooke Seawell since 1997, making all three over 25 years by spring 2026; Dawn Hudson had served since 2013 and Mark A. Stevens' current term dated to 2008, making both over 10 years.
⠀
John O. Dabiri, Melissa B. Lora, Stephen C. Neal, and Aarti Shah had served less than 10 years.
⠀
Those 3 and 2 counts still stand, except the independent directors are 9, not 10.
⠀
The Wall Street Journal also cited a comparison: directors at large U.S. companies serve less than 8 years on average, and only about 10% serve more than 10 years.
⠀
The proxy and NVIDIA's May 8 press release both say Suzanne Nora Johnson joined on July 13, 2026, taking the board from 10 to 11 members.
⠀
The spring count didn't include her.
⠀
Proxy adviser ISS gave NVIDIA's board structure its highest risk rating in spring 2026, citing multiple long serving directors, no chairman, and no board refreshment mechanism.
⠀
Over the past five years, NVIDIA added only two directors: former Taco Bell international president Melissa Lora in 2023 and former Goldman Sachs vice chairman Suzanne Nora Johnson this summer.
⠀
Some corporate governance experts say a lead independent director is usually enough.
⠀
In earlier years, boards often met rarely, or never without the CEO present; that's the Wall Street Journal's description of companies generally, not NVIDIA specifically.
⠀
A lead independent director can also act as a check on a CEO who is also chairman.
⠀
The paper also wrote that Stephen Neal schedules quarterly private meetings without Huang.
⠀
The company proxy says independent directors hold closed sessions with only independent directors present, and also meet with the CEO present; in fiscal 2026, both types met at four regular board meetings.
⠀
David Astorino, a senior partner at leadership advisory firm RHR International, said this kind of overlapping roles and a respectful, accommodating dynamic toward a founder is fairly common at companies of a certain size that are led by founders.
⠀
Doug Chia, former Johnson & Johnson corporate secretary and president of advisory firm Soundboard Governance, said that when you see Huang setting the agenda with the lead independent director, deciding what directors get and running meetings, 'it's pretty clear Jensen Huang is the chairman.'
⠀
There's no obvious No. 2 at the company.
⠀
More than 60 people report directly to Huang; he has said he runs the company with a fairly flat structure.
⠀
On NVIDIA's most recent earnings call, Huang answered analysts' questions almost entirely by himself, leaving only routine opening remarks to others, the Wall Street Journal reported.
⠀
The paper said that's normal for NVIDIA but unusual at other companies.
⠀
Huang is 63, cofounded NVIDIA in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, and has led it ever since, making him one of the longest serving founder CEOs in Silicon Valley.
⠀
He was born in Taiwan, grew up in the U.S., and transformed NVIDIA from a gaming graphics chip maker into a leading supplier of AI processors.

▋ Trump backs Jensen Huang despite an FBI probe and mounting Congressional pressure
⠀
Trump told reporters at the White House Monday that he asked Huang earlier that day whether he knew the other person was a spy, and Huang answered 'absolutely not.'
⠀
Trump said 'I really believe him' and called him 'an amazing person' and 'a respected person.'
⠀
The FBI is investigating the matter, Trump also told reporters that day; he didn't give details.
⠀
Asked whether he had read the classified memo drafted under Secretary of State Rubio's supervision warning about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, Trump said the memo 'didn't have much of an impact on me.'
⠀
He also said he didn't know the relevant intelligence existed when Huang traveled with him to China in May.
⠀
Asked Sunday whether Huang should remain CEO, Trump said 'I think so, of course,' and said he 'has done amazing things for our country.'
⠀
On his trip to China later this month, Trump doesn't plan to raise Huang with Xi Jinping on his own, but expects Xi will ask about him, he said.
⠀
In Congress, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, and Intelligence Committee Chairman Rick Crawford have sent a letter asking Huang for a closed joint briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang and how NVIDIA guards against foreign espionage.
⠀
A Foreign Affairs Committee press release says they asked him to brief on Nov. 18, 2026, and to accept that date by Nov. 11, or propose another meeting day.
⠀
The Verge wrote the letter was sent Nov. 4.
⠀
The press release is a request and doesn't say he has agreed to appear.
⠀
Texas Republican Senator John Cornyn wrote on X Sunday that Congress needs to investigate.
⠀
These pressures come as Huang lobbies the U.S. government and world leaders to let chips flow freely and tries to push back on concerns that doing so could endanger national security.
⠀
His role leading the world's largest chip design company has made him a global tech superstar and drawn criticism from opponents of NVIDIA's agenda inside and outside government.
⠀
NVIDIA sells hundreds of billions of dollars' worth of advanced AI processors and other hardware and provides financial support and guarantees across a wide swath of the AI industry.
⠀
Washington has restricted advanced AI chip exports to China since 2022, effectively shutting NVIDIA out of a lucrative China market, while Huang has long argued for more U.S. and China dialogue on AI development.
⠀
NVIDIA has won Trump's approval to export some older chips to China, and Trump has taken an approach friendly to the AI industry.
⠀
That policy has split the Trump administration, with officials who favor stricter export limits and more oversight frustrated by the influence of industry executives like Huang.
⠀
Seeking Alpha, citing The New York Times, reported that Huang's position is to allow exports of advanced AI chips a generation behind while keeping the newest technology in the U.S.
⠀
Whether export rules get tighter is now in Congress's hands.
⠀
CHOSUNBIZ wrote that Reuters, citing lawmakers and people involved, said this controversy makes bills tightening AI chip exports to China more likely to pass.
⠀
Three bills are being considered for the fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, but none has become law.
⠀
All three passed the House Foreign Affairs Committee earlier this year and are now candidates to be included in the NDAA in the Senate.
⠀
The AI Overwatch Act would give Congress more oversight of advanced chip exports.
⠀
The Chip Security Act would include measures like location tracking to prevent chip smuggling.
⠀
The MATCH Act would push allies to restrict exports of chipmaking equipment to China.
⠀
A joint statement from Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren and Republican Senator Jim Banks argued that Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative makes national security concerns more urgent, and called for provisions like the AI Overwatch Act to be put in the NDAA.
⠀
Democratic Representative Bill Foster also backed moving forward on X and pressed for the Chip Security Act to become law; he introduced it with Republican Representative Bill Huizenga, and it passed the Foreign Affairs Committee unanimously.
⠀
Reuters, citing a former congressional staffer who dealt directly with NVIDIA for months, said NVIDIA is seen as the main opponent of the Chip Security Act and AI Overwatch Act, CHOSUNBIZ reported.
⠀
The Information Technology Industry Council, which counts NVIDIA as a member, opposes the bills, saying they could weaken U.S. companies' competitiveness and make export controls more complicated.
⠀
The White House hasn't separately weighed in on the provisions.
⠀
CHOSUNBIZ wrote that whether they pass still depends on where the White House stands.
⠀
An NVIDIA press release on Oct. 28 said the company will hold its fiscal 2027 third quarter earnings call on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at 2 p.m.
⠀
Pacific time and 5 p.m.
⠀
Eastern time.
⠀
The quarter ended Oct. 25.
⠀
Earnings will be released around 1:20 p.m.
⠀
Pacific time.
⠀
5 p.m.
⠀
Eastern on Nov. 17 is 6 a.m.
⠀
Taiwan time on Nov. 18.

▋ Dan Ives sees Jensen Huang staying near term pending final probe results
⠀
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun denied reports Monday that China planned to surveil Huang; he said the so-called Chinese spy narrative is 'completely based on unfounded speculation' and is 'slander and smearing.'
⠀
Bernstein gave NVIDIA an upbeat 'outperform' rating and a $400 price target, the Wall Street Journal reported; the paper also noted the stock closed at $186.64 on Nov. 6.
⠀
The $4.5 trillion market cap figure is from Nov. 6, before the board announced its investigation on Sunday.

text:
Some amazing facts and definitely worth sharing…

On Jeopardy the other night, the final question asked: “How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb of the Unknown?”

All three contestants missed it.

Tomb of the Unknown Soldier

1. How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb and why?

He takes 21 steps — symbolizing the 21-gun salute, the highest military and foreign tribute.

2. How long does he pause before turning to walk back and why?

He waits 21 seconds, again in honor of the same tradition.

3. Why are his gloves damp?

They are lightly moistened to ensure he never loses his grip on his rifle.

4. Does he keep his rifle on the same shoulder, and if not, why?

He always carries it on the shoulder farthest from the Tomb. After each crossing, he performs an about-face and moves it to the outside shoulder.

5. How often are the guards changed?

Every 30 minutes, 24/7, 365 days a year.

6. What are the physical requirements for a Tomb Guard?

Applicants must be between 5'10" and 6'2" and have a waist no larger than 30".

Other expectations of the Guard:

They devote two years to the Tomb, live in the barracks beneath it, and must refrain from drinking alcohol on or off duty for the rest of their lives.

They can never swear in public or dishonor the uniform or the Tomb.

After two years, they earn a wreath pin signifying their service — fewer than 400 are currently worn.

If they violate the code, they must relinquish the pin.

Their shoes have thick soles to protect against extreme temperatures and metal heel plates that create the crisp click when they halt.

Uniforms must have zero wrinkles or lint and are inspected in a full-length mirror.

For the first six months, guards do not speak to anyone and do not watch television.

Their off-duty time is spent studying the 175 notable individuals buried at Arlington National Cemetery, memorizing who they are and where they rest.

Among them: President Taft, Joe E. Lewis, and Audie Murphy, the most decorated WWII soldier.

Every guard spends five hours daily preparing their uniform.

ETERNAL REST GRANT THEM, O LORD, AND LET PERPETUAL LIGHT SHINE UPON THEM.

When Hurricane Isabel approached Washington, D.C. in 2003, Congress shut down for two days. The guards were offered permission to suspend duty due to danger.

They replied: “No way, Sir!”

Drenched and marching through the storm, they insisted that guarding the Tomb is the highest honor, not just a task.

The Tomb has been continuously guarded — day and night — since 1930.

God Bless and Keep Them Safe

Jennifer Welch is still playing the victim after sponsors dropped her over comments she made about Charlie Kirk. On her show Tuesday she said, “Sadly, some of the advertisers have caved. But we still have other advertisers, and we’re still standing.” She then read a message from a Wisconsin brewery that called Kirk “an awful human being” and offered to step in as a sponsor. Welch called it “so sweet” and gave the company a free shout-out.

That’s not a recovery. That’s her signaling that companies willing to attack a murdered man are welcome. Reports put the number of sponsors that have cut ties or said they will not advertise with the show at around two dozen, including Cash App, Chewy, Boll & Branch, Casper, and others. They didn’t leave because they were “harassed,” as Welch claimed on Tuesday. They left because of what she and her co-host said.

Welch’s claim that she still has plenty of advertisers and isn’t going anywhere is the same line she has used since her insincere and political apology. The apology came after the money started leaving, and she has since said it wasn’t meant for Kirk’s allies. Take her statements about new sponsors the same way. She hasn’t shown remorse for the original segment. She has shown that she’ll keep the bit and look for smaller partners who share her contempt for a deceased husband and father of two.

Any company that steps in now to support Welch is choosing to associate with that record. Consumers can decide whether that is the kind of brand they want to support. Welch’s problem was never outside pressure. It was her own words.

text:
Markets are shifting from chasing AI growth to questioning its cost, governance and valuations. A hawkish Fed, approaching U.S. fiscal deadlines, Nvidia uncertainty and a potentially enormous Anthropic IPO are testing risk appetite, even as investors look for opportunities elsewhere.

Ray Dalio is warning about another round of Washington fiscal brinkmanship. Temporary government funding expires December 11, with debt-ceiling pressure building in 2027. The danger isn't just political theater. Repeated standoffs can raise Treasury funding costs and undermine confidence in the collateral underpinning global financial markets.

Monetary policy offers little relief.

Christopher Waller reportedly favors another December rate hike, potentially 50 basis points if core inflation remains stubborn. With October CPI due, the market faces an uncomfortable possibility: restrictive rates lasting longer just as highly valued technology companies need enormous amounts of capital.

Nvidia illustrates how quickly sentiment can change. Shares fell 4.3% to $178.67 even as the semiconductor index surged 6.9%. Reports of an internal investigation and chip-diversion scrutiny are weighing on confidence, although the underlying allegations remain unresolved.

Meanwhile, Anthropic is reportedly preparing one of history's largest IPOs. Revised offering discussions suggest proceeds of up to $64B, with valuations around $1.1T–$1.3T. Terms remain unconfirmed.

The offering could become a major test of whether public investors still have the appetite to finance frontier AI at trillion-dollar valuations.

Capital is also looking beyond U.S. technology.

Citi raised its December 2027 Nifty target to 28,000, while HSBC upgraded India and downgraded China. The shift highlights growing differentiation across Asian markets as investors reassess growth prospects and policy risks.

Geopolitics remains the wildcard.

Trump's meeting with Qatar's prime minister produced no reported breakthrough on Iran. Military warnings persist, and conflicting accounts of Gulf support for the blockade keep Hormuz shipping and oil supply exposed to renewed disruption.

The common thread is becoming difficult to ignore.

Investors are being asked to finance extraordinary AI ambitions while navigating expensive money, fiscal uncertainty and geopolitical instability.

The next market winners won't necessarily be the companies promising the most growth. They'll be the ones capable of financing it without sacrificing returns.

Abu Dhabi Talks Put Europe’s Security at Stake—American, Ukrainian, and Russian negotiators have gathered in Abu Dhabi for renewed peace talks, with Washington exploring an Article 5-style security guarantee for Ukraine. A US official said Moscow had been asked whether it would object to such protection from Washington and NATO. Russia continues demanding Ukrainian withdrawal from territory it has failed to conquer and rejects direct talks with European representatives there.

Europeans will instead coordinate separately with Kyiv and Washington. Any American guarantee would require Trump’s approval. Previous negotiations produced limited results: February’s Abu Dhabi round secured a prisoner exchange, but subsequent talks in Geneva ended without a breakthrough before the Iran war diverted Washington’s attention. The diplomatic danger is giving Russia an effective veto over the protection offered to the country it invaded. Consulting Moscow about an agreement is part of negotiation, but making Ukrainian security dependent on Russian approval would undermine the guarantee’s purpose. Equally, European participation through side meetings provides coordination without ensuring influence over the central bargain.

📌 NEGOTIATIONS IN THE UAE WILL NOT CHANGE THE REALITIES ON THE BATTLEFIELD

The three-way talks in Abu Dhabi are unlikely to produce a lasting settlement unless the military and economic realities on the ground change. The central issue is not diplomatic demands, but each side's ability to sustain the war and achieve its objectives.

Russia's position is that neither side's capabilities are growing, making a temporary ceasefire or frozen conflict increasingly realistic. Expectations that Washington will offer Moscow major concessions, including Ukraine, to pull Russia away from China are described as unrealistic.

The longer-term question is whether the underlying causes of the conflict will be addressed. Without changes to European policy and Washington's approach to supporting and positioning Ukraine, any agreement risks becoming a temporary pause rather than a lasting peace.

Territorial questions, European security arrangements and the future of Ukraine therefore remain central obstacles, regardless of the outcome of the UAE meetings.

Meanwhile, Rybar argues that Russia should continue its strategy of targeting Ukrainian cities and economic infrastructure, claiming that sustained pressure will weaken Ukraine's economic and demographic potential over time.

The negotiations are taking place alongside an ongoing war of attrition. A ceasefire may become possible without resolving the underlying confrontation. That would postpone rather than settle the conflict, leaving the conditions for renewed hostilities in place.

text:
As Washington and Beijing continue to fight over access to advanced technology, a US courtroom is examining an episode from Huawei's past that deserves more attention.

A former Huawei manager has testified about a 2013 internal initiative that offered employees cash rewards for gathering intelligence on competitors, including product roadmaps and pricing.

The striking detail is that the initiative reportedly continued through revisions even after legal concerns were raised. A revised draft added instructions to comply with local laws, but retained the reward rankings and encrypted submission process.

Why does this matter now?

Huawei has spent years at the centre of the US-China technology dispute, facing restrictions over national security and concerns about its relationship with the Chinese state. Its access to advanced chips and Western markets has become a major issue in the wider contest over technological power.

This courtroom testimony does not, by itself, prove the allegations behind those restrictions. But it brings another dimension of Huawei's corporate conduct into public view.

The battle over technology is usually discussed in terms of chips, patents, supply chains and national security. The less visible contest is over information: who can obtain it, how they obtain it, and where companies draw the legal line.
