text:
Every generation of Americans says the same three words about the next one.

"Kids these days."

So for one month, I collected stories from Japanese people who have spent real time around American teenagers. Host mothers. Teachers. A tour bus driver. A grandmother who got stuck at a train station.

I got sixty-three. Here's what they said about your kids.

"A high school group from Ohio found out it was my birthday. They practiced 'Happy Birthday' in Japanese on my bus for an hour. It was the worst singing I have heard in 30 years of driving. I had to pull over." (Tour bus driver, 61)

"Twelve football players from Texas ate at my restaurant. When they left, the table was clean, the plates were stacked, and the biggest one offered to carry them to the kitchen. He was the size of my refrigerator." (Restaurant owner, 70)

"I could not work the ticket machine in Atlanta. A girl, maybe sixteen, purple hair, took out one earbud, fixed it, and walked me to the right train. She never mentioned it. She just put the earbud back in." (Grandmother, 79)

"My car slid into a ditch outside Des Moines. Four boys in a pickup pulled me out with a strap. I tried to pay them. The smallest one said, 'Nah. Have a good one, sir.' He was fifteen." (Engineer, 48)

"Our American exchange student carried my 84-year-old mother's groceries up our stairs every day, all year. Nobody asked him to. On his last day, my mother bowed to him. He hugged her. She stood there like a startled cat. She talks about it every week." (Host mother, 52)

Then my wife's friend Hiroko answered. For nine years, she taught Japanese to high schoolers in Utah.

"My husband died in my third year. I didn't tell my students. I just came back on Monday.

When I walked in, all thirty-one of them were already in their seats. Nobody on a phone. Nobody talking. Teenagers.

On the board, in Japanese, in the worst handwriting I have ever seen, someone had written:

'We are here, sensei.'

They had found out. Nobody said anything. They just did the whole lesson so quietly that I didn't have to raise my voice once.

I left it on the board for a week."

America, you keep saying "kids these days."

We've met your kids.

They're fine.

You raised them.

text:
TRUTH MATTERS PERSPECTIVE

OIL PRICES FALL AFTER TRUMP SIGNALS AN END TO THE IRAN WAR. BUT WHAT DOES THAT ACTUALLY MEAN FOR AMERICAN FAMILIES?

Oil prices fell sharply on November 10 after President Donald Trump signaled that further military action against Iran may not be necessary and suggested the conflict could end soon.

Gunther Eaglemann credits Trump for the decline, arguing that cheaper oil is exactly what American families have been waiting for.

The price decline is real. But the economic picture deserves a closer look.

WHAT THE DATA SHOWS

• Brent crude briefly dropped below $90 per barrel, its lowest level since late August.

• U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude traded near $84–$85 per barrel.

• Brent had already fallen approximately 5.9% during Monday’s trading session.

• Markets reacted favorably to reduced expectations of additional military strikes and prolonged disruptions to Middle Eastern oil supplies.

Those are meaningful developments.

But falling prices do not establish that the war has formally ended or that a lasting agreement has been reached.

WHAT THE HEADLINE LEAVES OUT

Oil markets respond to multiple forces simultaneously: geopolitical risk, global supply, demand expectations, production decisions, and economic conditions.

Trump’s statements appear to have helped reduce the market’s perceived risk of escalation.

That is a legitimate development to acknowledge.

But the broader decline also reflects expectations about supply and demand. Attributing every dollar of the decrease to one individual oversimplifies the market.

AND HERE’S WHAT MATTERS TO HOUSEHOLDS

A lower crude-oil price does not mean gasoline immediately becomes cheaper by the same percentage.

Pump prices also depend on refining costs, distribution, taxes, regional supply, and how quickly wholesale price changes reach retailers.

And families buy more than gasoline.

Transportation, groceries, heating, electricity, and other household expenses can be affected by energy costs—but those effects vary and often arrive with delays.

THE QUESTION ISN’T SIMPLY WHETHER OIL FELL.

It’s whether families experience sustained relief.

A temporary market decline may offer some breathing room. Lasting affordability requires prices to remain manageable relative to household incomes.

KEY PERSPECTIVES

Supporters can reasonably argue that Trump’s signals of military restraint helped calm markets and reduce immediate energy-price pressure.

Critics can reasonably question whether the conflict’s costs, ongoing risks, and uncertainty outweigh the benefits of a short-term price decline.

Both arguments should be judged against actual outcomes.

THE BOTTOM LINE

If the administration’s actions contribute to a durable reduction in hostilities and sustained energy-price relief, that deserves recognition.

But a single day’s market movement is not proof of lasting peace or lasting affordability.

The measures worth watching are straightforward:

Are hostilities actually ending? Are oil shipments becoming more secure? Are gasoline prices falling? And are American households keeping more of their earnings after essential expenses?

The market measures expectations. Families measure what they can afford.

Not Right. Not Left. Straight Ahead.

We don’t inflame. We inform.

I appreciate the reply. The Bastrop environmental concern was addressed in 2024, and the terminology of "billionaire tax incentives" is not correct.

On wastewater: Bastrop residents raised real concerns in 2023, and Musk's companies worked with the community to resolve them. In 2024 SpaceX and The Boring Company both withdrew their permits to discharge into the Colorado River. 

SpaceX signed an agreement with the City of Bastrop and Corix Utilities to send its wastewater to the city's new treatment plant, and the Musk sites are being connected to it. 

The city says having SpaceX as a customer helps pay for the plant and keeps rates low for residents. The environmental issue was resolved without denying people jobs or hurting the economy.

On "billionaire tax breaks": Texas has no income tax (for now), so no way to provide "billionaire" tax breaks. Further, @elonmusk isn't a billionaire in cash. His wealth is almost all tied up in his companies, like Tesla and SpaceX. 

The incentives aren't tax breaks for him personally. They're business incentives that go to the companies for building facilities and hiring workers here, the same kind TX offers any company that brings jobs. The incentives pay off in jobs, paychecks, & funding for schools and infrastructure.

And on cost of living: Austin-area home prices are down about 24% from the 2022 peak, & rents have fallen too, while these companies kept growing.

Run Musk out of TX and the jobs and the income go w/him. That means fewer customers for small businesses, falling home values for homeowners, & a smaller tax base for our schools. 

Also the environmental footprint doesn't leave with Musk. The buildings are already built. Bastrop would just be left with empty factories and warehouses.

text:
I Got a Line on You may be Spirit’s biggest single. Released off the band’s second album, The Family That Plays Together, the 1968 song hit 25 in the US and 28 in Canada the following year. The story of Spirit is almost as interesting as the band’s music. Randy Wolfe was playing in a band called Jimmy James & the Blue Flames at Caffe Wha?! in the Village in 1966. The frontman was a singer/guitarist from Seattle named Jimi Hendrix. There were two musicians in the band named Randy and Jimi kept getting them mixed up at he gave Wolfe the name Randy California (the other guy was Randy Palmer nicknamed Randy Texas). Chas Chandler of the Animals saw a performance and offered Jimi the chance to move to the UK to record music. He wanted to bring Randy California along but his mom refused to give him permission. As a consolation, she got her boyfriend, jazz drummer Ed Cassidy, to form a band with him which they named Spirit. Randy was the principal songwriter, lead guitarist and co-lead singer with Jay Ferguson (who had a hit in the 70s with Thunder Island). Mark Andes played bass and John Locke was on keyboards. The band took the name from a book by Khalil Gibran. Spirit played together on and off through 1997. That year tragedy struck when Randy California drowned saving his 12 year old son from a deadly rip current in Molokai, Hawaii. He was only 45.

text:
Is Jensen Huang the world’s best CEO? Tough call. There are lots of brilliant execs. But today at least, the math says the CEO and co-founder of Nvidia is the most valuable person on Earth. 
 
The news that Jensen Huang admitted having an affair with Alice Huang, a woman the U.S. government believes was providing information to China’s intelligence services, is a stunner. Nvidia is arguably one of the world’s most important companies, designing and selling GPUs, or graphics processing units, chips that play a crucial role in the AI food chain.  How they allocate chips to customers picks winners and losers in key sectors.  
 
No overnight success story, Nvidia was once an obscure producer of PC graphics cards. Huang’s (Jensen, not Alice, as best I know) intuition that graphics chips were perfect for AI workloads has transformed Nvidia, and the world. The first company to ever reach a $5 trillion market cap, Nvidia is still worth north of $4 trillion, more than every company other than Apple. Huang (still Jensen) co-founded Nvidia in 1993, kicking things off in a Denny’s in San Jose, California. Talk about a Grand Slam breakfast. 
 
For now, Jensen remains in charge. But he faces not just an Nvidia board investigation, but also Congressional hearings and other probes. This is less a sex scandal than a tale of international espionage. Whether he survives as CEO we’ll see, but his reputation seems permanently tarnished. Investors spy opportunity: On Monday, AMD rallied 13%, Qualcomm 4%, ARM, 12%. 
 
Nvidia shares by contrast fell 4.3%, trimming the company’s market value by about $193 billion. 
 
Best I can tell, that’s the single-largest one-day market cap evaporation tied to an executive crisis or departure ever, and by a wide margin. UnitedHealth Group lost about $60 billion in value, falling 18% when CEO Andrew Witty resigned for “personal reasons” in May 2025. When Mark Hurd got the boot at HP for sexual improprieties in August 2010, the stock dropped 8%, trimming its value by $9 billion. Wynn Resorts shares took a 9% hit, or $3.5 billion, when founder Steve Wynn resigned over sexual misconduct allegations in 2018. Chipotle shares fell 7% one day in 2024, when its CEO defected to run Starbucks. Renault shares dropped 8% on the day CEO Carlos Ghosn was arrested in Japan.  
 
What makes today’s slide all the more remarkable is that the NASDAQ Composite rallied more than 2.7% on Monday, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied more than 1,100 points, even though Nvidia shares docked the index more than 50 points. text:
Eli Gillman carried the ball eight times on Saturday and ran for 196 yards and four touchdowns.

That is 24 and a half yards every time they gave it to him. The touchdowns went 45 yards, then 15, then 43, then 84.

He touched the ball nine times in all, counting a catch, and finished with 244 yards of offense.

The fourth one was the 78th of his career, and it moved him past Cooper Kupp for the most touchdowns anybody has scored in the history of the Big Sky Conference.

Kupp played at Eastern Washington from 2013 to 2016.

Gillman knew exactly whose number he was chasing. He said so to Colter Nuanez of Skyline Sports afterward, without any of the pretending that usually goes with it.

"I'm very aware of Cooper Kupp."

"I didn't even think that was a reachable goal when the season started."

"I still think Cooper's a stud."

"It'll be crazy to me probably forever."

Gillman is from Cokato, Minnesota and went to Dassel-Cokato Senior High. As a senior he scored 43 touchdowns and ran for more than 1,900 yards and the school won its first state championship.

His mother is Dawn Gillman and she sits in the Minnesota House of Representatives.

He had offers from Central Michigan and Northern Iowa and North Dakota, and from Georgetown and Dartmouth, and he went to Montana.

He ran for 968 yards as a freshman, which no freshman at Montana had ever done. They gave him the Jerry Rice Award that year for the best freshman in the country.

Then 1,104 yards. Then 1,261 and Big Sky Offensive Player of the Year. He owns the longest touchdown run in the history of the program, and he made second team All Big Sky in each of his first two years.

Every January since then he could have left. A running back with those numbers can walk into an FBS building and get paid.

He is still in Missoula.

"I didn't regret it for a second."

"It's made it more known that I made the right decision every single week."

His head coach is Bobby Kennedy.

"He made the conscious decision to stay at Montana and do some special things."

"How many times in my career, other people's careers, do they get to be around one of the all-time greats?"

The coach on the other sideline Saturday was Chris Fisk of Portland State, who watched four of those touchdowns go past him.

"The guy is unflappable. He's never too high. He's never too low. He's got ice in his veins."

Fisk has watched a lot of them.

"I think he's got about nine or 10 of those touchdowns on me."

Gillman has 5,034 rushing yards now, which is fourth in the history of the conference. His 25 touchdowns this season tied Marcus Knight's Montana record.

Montana won 57 to 24.

"Touchdowns, I can't score by myself, really."

Marketing ordered 2,000 business cards with our new company email domain.

Small problem.

Nobody told IT we were changing domains.

Bigger problem.

They hadn't purchased the domain.

I checked.

Already registered.

By a dentist in Ohio.

I explained that approving a logo doesn't transfer ownership of the internet.

They asked me to contact the dentist.

I did.

He wanted $15,000.

Marketing called it extortion.

Then they asked if we could sue him.

I explained he'd owned the domain since 2013.

Our company was founded in 2021.

Legal confirmed that being older than our branding strategy was not a crime.

Meanwhile, the CEO had already handed out 60 business cards at a conference.

Three potential clients emailed him.

All three emails went to the dentist.

The dentist replied to one.

Apparently he'd been getting our sales inquiries all week.

He was extremely nice about it.

Offered to forward the emails if we paid his asking price.

Finance refused to approve $15,000 for a domain.

Marketing refused to reprint $800 worth of business cards.

The CEO refused to admit he'd been giving people the wrong email address.

We're now negotiating a commercial agreement with a dentist who accidentally became our head of business development.

Yesterday he forwarded us a $400,000 sales inquiry.

Finance approved the domain purchase immediately.

The dentist increased his asking price to $25,000.

I respect him.

He's the only person in this entire situation who understands how business works.

“JESUS IS IN HEAVEN. AND SO IS RYAN.” OHIO SAYS GOODBYE TO A FALLEN FIREFIGHTER

Hundreds gathered to honor North Royalton firefighter Ryan Milligan.

He was 36, a husband and a father of two young children. He died in the line of duty last week while fighting a house fire in Broadview Heights, Ohio.

His older brother, John, told mourners that Ryan would always be his hero.

“We are so proud of you Ryan,” he said. “We love you with all our hearts.”

Pastor John Zahrte, the North Royalton safety forces chaplain, offered these words of comfort.

“Jesus is in heaven,” he said. “And so is Ryan.”

After the funeral, dispatch honored Ryan with one last radio call.

“Ryan, your duty is complete. You have answered your last call. We’ll take it from here.”

And in a quiet act of kindness, his wife’s coworkers at Cleveland Metropolitan School District have been donating leave so she can spend more time with her children.

Please pray for Ryan’s wife, their two children, his brother John, and the firefighters who served alongside him. May Jesus give them comfort in the days ahead. 🙏

text:
Four hikers murdered in three national forests. One was 24-year-old Meredith Emerson, a martial artist who fought back. He held her for three days before he killed her. Gary Hilton traded the location of her body to escape the death penalty. Years later, in his first TV interview, he grinned: "I think I prefer the Beast of Blood Mountain." Then: "I'm the oldest serial killer in American history. Isn't that amazing?"

October 2007. John and Irene Bryant, 79 and 84, married for 58 years, set out on a hike in North Carolina's Pisgah National Forest. They never came back.

December 2007. Cheryl Dunlap, a 46-year-old nurse and mother of two, was killed in Florida's Apalachicola National Forest.

On New Year's Day 2008, Meredith Emerson went hiking on Blood Mountain in Georgia with her black Lab mix, Ella. She was an experienced hiker and a blue belt in aikido. On the trail she met a grizzled drifter in his sixties with a dog of his own.

That night, someone tried to use Meredith's bank card at an ATM. Three days later, Ella was found wandering in a grocery store parking lot, 50 miles away. Hilton later said he couldn't bring himself to kill the dog.

He had no such feelings about Meredith. She was killed on January 4.

Police arrested Hilton the next day. He offered a deal: he would lead investigators to her body if prosecutors took the death penalty off the table and found a new home for his dog, Dandy. They agreed. On January 7, he took them to her.

He also told investigators he would have kept killing if they hadn't caught him.

In Georgia he got life with the possibility of parole. In Florida, a jury convicted him of murdering Cheryl Dunlap and unanimously recommended death. "May God have mercy on your soul," the judge told him. He later pleaded guilty to killing the Bryants.

In the video below, Hilton gives his first-ever TV interview. He corrects the reporter's name for him: he prefers "the Beast of Blood Mountain." He brags about being "the oldest serial killer in American history." "I'm your worst nightmare," he says. And then, smiling: "I'm gonna give you a new scoop. I did it. I'm confessing to a murder. On camera."

He is still on death row in Florida.

Should prosecutors ever make a deal with a killer to find a body?

text:
A TALE OF TWO ECONOMIES, THE ULTRA-WEALTHY ARE PLAYING BY DIFFERENT RULES

We’re witnessing two very different economies in America right now. While everyday Americans are struggling with affordability, rising housing costs, and the American dream becoming increasingly out of reach, the ultra-wealthy are operating in an entirely different market.

And nowhere is that more evident than in South Florida.

I’m seeing a surge in aggressive, off-market real estate activity, particularly in Miami Beach, the Venetian Islands, Miami Shores, and other highly desirable Florida enclaves. We’re talking about extraordinary numbers, unsolicited offers, buyers competing against one another, and bidding activity reminiscent of what we experienced during COVID.

What’s particularly interesting is that this activity was already accelerating ahead of the midterm elections.

My take is that political uncertainty played a significant role. Many wealthy buyers were concerned about potential Democratic victories and what those outcomes could mean for taxes, regulation, and the long-term business environment. Florida’s continued Republican leadership, favorable tax structure, and pro-business reputation make it an attractive destination for high-net-worth individuals looking to protect and grow their wealth.

And these buyers aren’t waiting for properties to hit the market. They’re proactively pursuing properties that aren’t even listed, sometimes offering extraordinary premiums to convince owners to sell.

The bigger story is the growing divide between two Americas.

For the average American, the question is, “Can I afford to buy a home?”

For the ultra-wealthy, the question is, “How much do I have to offer to get the property I want?”

We’re seeing two completely different realities playing out in the same housing market.

text:
Gogo estimates that its Eutelsat OneWeb satellite-powered Galileo inflight connectivity product has achieved a remarkable 35% to 40% share of the Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satcom market in business aviation.

As of November 6, 2026, “cumulative shipments have surpassed 760 units, which we believe gives us between 35% to 40% market share of the LEO business aviation connectivity less than 12 months after introduction — making Galileo the most successful LEO product launch in business aviation,” CEO Chris Moore revealed during Gogo’s third quarter earnings conference call. Gogo achieved 690 Galileo shipments by the end of Q3.

That’s no small feat, given that the Broomfield, Colorado-based firm is competing on the LEO front with SpaceX’s popular Starlink IFC service.

An electronically steerable antenna-based IFC system, Galileo is based on Hughes Network Systems’ ESA technology, and offered in two flavors: a half-duplex (HDX) solution for smaller aircraft, which currently provides download speeds of 60 Mbps and upload speeds of 10 Mbps; and a full-duplex (FDX) configuration, supporting speeds of 195 Mbps down and 32 Mbps up.

Shipments of Galileo are pacing “well above our expectations,” Moore noted, with the company achieving “a record quarter of shipments for Galileo of 172 units” for the three months ended September 30, 2026, representing a 59% increase from the second quarter and a 95% increase year over year.

Gogo ended the third quarter with 297 Galileo aircraft online, up 61% from the prior quarter, demonstrating its ability “to convert shipments into aircraft online quickly,” Moore said. Each aircraft that activates “represents a seven to 10-year recurring revenue relationship,” he added.

With Eutelsat in the process of replenishing its OneWeb LEO network with higher-capacity satellites, Gogo recently outlined a long-term Galileo technology roadmap that calls for performance enhancements to be implemented roughly every 24 months over six years. 

The company’s continued investment in hardware and satcom will see Galileo HDX pivot to a 300 Mbps down/100 Mbps up service by 2032, while FDX is earmarked for 1.5 gig down and 350 Mbps up over the same period. 

It  remains to be seen if Gogo will ultimately tap into Europe’s future IRIS² multi-orbit network, but the company appears well positioned to avail of opportunities given that Eutelsat OneWeb is the LEO lead on the project.

text:
The Novocherkassk massacre occurred on June 2, 1962, in Novocherkassk, Russian SFSR (Soviet Union), when Soviet military forces and internal security troops fired on a peaceful crowd of striking factory workers...

Workers stopped production and blocked the nearby railway lines. Local authorities panicked, and Moscow dispatched top party officials (including Frol Kozlov and Anastas Mikoyan) alongside military units and tanks to the city. An estimated 5,000 to 12,000 unarmed demonstrators—many carrying red banners and portraits of Vladimir Lenin—marched peacefully toward the city's party headquarters (the city council building) to demand better living conditions and lower prices.

The Soviet regime immediately imposed a strict curfew, washed away the blood in the square, and secretly buried the victims in unmarked graves to prevent them from becoming martyrs. All mentions of the event were classified. Authorities arrested hundreds of participants. A closed-door trial resulted in 105 to 114 people receiving heavy prison sentences (10 to 15 years), and 7 alleged "ringleaders" were sentenced to death and executed.

The massacre remained a state secret for nearly 30 years. Details leaked abroad during the Cold War via sources like Radio Liberty and Alexander Solzhenitsyn, and the full story was finally investigated and exposed in the late 1980s and 1991 during Glasnost and the collapse of the Soviet Union. A memorial now stands in Novocherkassk to honor the victims.
. . . 

At 7:30 AM on the sweltering morning of Friday, June 1, 1962, inside the steel-casting shop of the Budyonny Electric Locomotive Works (NEVZ) in Novocherkassk, the shift workers refused to pick up their tools. Just an hour earlier, state radio had broadcast a decree that hit Soviet households like a thunderclap: to combat chronic agricultural shortages, Nikita Khrushchev’s government was hiking nationwide consumer prices overnight—butter by 25 percent and meat by 30 percent. For the foundry workers of NEVZ, the timing was unbearable. Just weeks prior, factory management had arbitrarily hiked production output quotas by nearly a third, effectively cutting their take-home pay. When a crowd of soot-covered laborers confronted factory director Boris Kurochkin in the yard, complaining that their families could no longer afford basic staples, Kurochkin offered a sneering, Marie-Antoinette retort that sealed his fate: "If you don't have enough money for meat and sausage, eat liver pies instead."

The insult lit a fuse across the industrial city. Within minutes, workers pulled the switch on the factory’s steam siren, its deafening wail rolling across the steppe to summon machinists, welders, and neighbors from nearby settlements. 

By midday, thousands had seized the Moscow-to-Rostov railway line running past the depot, halting the *Saratov-Rostov* passenger train. Workers painted a desperate slogan across the locomotive’s steel flanks in white chalk: "Khrushchev, give us meat and butter!" 

Inside the Kremlin, the news triggered blind panic. Khrushchev, terrified that the unrest would spread through the Donbas coalfields and ignite a nationwide uprising, dispatched a high-powered crisis delegation to the region: Politburo heavyweights Anastas Mikoyan and Frol Kozlov, backed by KGB chief Vladimir Semichastny.

On the morning of Saturday, June 2, a column of more than ten thousand workers, housewives, and schoolchildren began a five-mile march from the industrial outskirts toward the city center. To make it indisputably clear that they were not counter-revolutionaries or foreign agents, the marchers carried red banners, portraits of Vladimir Lenin, and carnations, singing revolutionary anthems as they crossed the bridge over the Tuzlov River.

text:
Hegseth Said Iran Started the War 47 Years Ago. The File Starts 26 Years Before That, With a CIA Officer Named Kermit Roosevelt.

Pete Hegseth, Secretary of War: "History will judge the Iran war quite differently than conventional wisdom right now. We didn't start this war. Iran did 47 years ago."

Forty-seven years. 2026 minus 47 is 1979. Hegseth is dating the war to the Islamic Revolution. He is picking the year the Iranians acted.

The file he skipped is dated 19 August 1953.

The Coup

On that date, the CIA and MI6 overthrew Mohammad Mossadegh, the democratically elected prime minister of Iran. The operation was coded TPAJAX. The CIA officer who ran it on the ground was Kermit Roosevelt Jr., the grandson of Theodore Roosevelt. He carried a budget that has been reported at roughly $1 million in today's terms, distributed to street gangs, newspaper editors, and bribed officers.

Mossadegh's offence was the nationalisation of the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, the predecessor of BP. The company's revenues were British. The oil was Iranian. He wanted the money to stay in Iran.

The CIA's own internal history, The Battle for Iran, was first released in 2013 after decades of redaction. It confirms the agency planned, funded, and executed the coup. The document is on the agency's own website.

The coup restored Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the Shah. He ruled for 26 years with SAVAK, the secret police created with CIA and Mossad assistance in 1957. SAVAK ran the torture chambers. It ran the prisons. It ran the censorship.

That is the war's actual starting point. Not 1979. 1953.

What the Shah Did With American Backing

1964. The Capitulations law, the judicial immunity bill that gave American military advisers and their contractors immunity from Iranian courts for crimes committed on Iranian soil. The law placed American personnel above Iranian law.

Imam Ruhollah Khomeini spoke against it on 26 October 1964. He was arrested and exiled. The speech is the founding grievance of the revolution.

1971. The Shah's regime celebrated 2,500 years of the Persian monarchy at Persepolis while the country's oil revenue was being paid to a Western consortium. The opulence and the poverty coexisted.

1978. The Cinema Rex fire in Abadan. Hundreds died. The regime's response was to blame the opposition.

1979. The revolution. The Shah fled. The embassy seizure followed, and the students took the embassy's own files, the documents that proved the CIA had used the diplomatic mission as the base for the 1953 operation and for subsequent subversion.

That is the Iranian action Hegseth dates the war to. It was a response to 26 years of the government the CIA had installed.

The War the US Actually Fought

1980-1988. Iraq invaded Iran. Washington backed Iraq.

1982: the Reagan administration removed Iraq from the state sponsors of terrorism list, clearing the way for arms and credits.
1983: Donald Rumsfeld shook hands with Saddam Hussein in Baghdad as the US special envoy. The photograph exists.
1983-1988: Operation Staunch, the US diplomatic campaign to block arms sales to Iran worldwide. Washington was blockading Iranian arms purchases while Saddam was buying Western equipment.
The US provided agricultural credits, dual-use technology, and battlefield intelligence to Iraq during the war.

The war killed an estimated one million Iranians.

The Direct US Attacks

18 April 1988: Operation Praying Mantis. The largest US naval engagement since World War II. The US struck Iranian oil platforms and sank the frigate Sahand after the USS Samuel B. Roberts struck a mine in the Gulf. The operation targeted Sirri and Sassan platforms.

3 July 1988: The USS Vincennes, under Captain Will Rogers III, shot down Iran Air Flight 655, a civilian Airbus A300 flying a scheduled passenger route from Bandar Abbas to Dubai. 290 people were killed, including 66 children. The US government expressed regret and described it as a tragic accident. The captain received the Legion of Merit. The US never formally apologised.

That is a war the United States fought against Iran. It happened before 1979 was 47 years old. It happened when Hegseth was in college.

The Sanctions That Followed

15 March 1995: Executive Order 12957, signed by Bill Clinton, declared a national emergency with respect to Iran and prohibited US investment in the petroleum sector. It has been renewed every year since — by Clinton, Bush, Obama, Trump, Biden, and Trump again. Thirty-one years.

5 August 1996: Iran and Libya Sanctions Act. Passed the House 415–0, the Senate 96–0. Signed by Clinton. Secondary sanctions on any company investing more than $40 million in Iranian petroleum.

29 January 2002: George W. Bush named Iran part of the "Axis of Evil" in the State of the Union. The name was invented four months after Iran had cooperated with the US in Afghanistan, facilitated the Bonn Conference, and offered a comprehensive dialogue.

2010-2012: The Stuxnet cyberweapon attacked the Natanz centrifuges. The assassinations of Iranian scientists began Alimohammadi (2010), Shahriari (2010), Rezaeinejad (2011), Ahmadi Roshan (2012), Fakhrizadeh (2020).

8 May 2018: Donald Trump withdrew from the JCPOA, the deal that had removed 11.5 tonnes of enriched uranium from Iran and placed the programme under the most intrusive inspections in history.

3 January 2020: The US assassinated Qasem Soleimani at Baghdad International Airport while he was on a diplomatic mediation mission, travelling under a diplomatic protocol, meeting Iraqi and Saudi intermediaries. The strike was ordered by Trump.

The 2026 War

The war Hegseth is describing did not begin with an Iranian attack. The US and Israel bombed Natanz, Fordow, and Isfahan while the IAEA was inspecting them. They assassinated Imam Ali Khamenei. They struck the Minab school and killed 160 schoolchildren and teachers. They destroyed 87 hospitals and struck 25 pharmaceutical plants.

Iran's IAEA file was clean. Rafael Grossi stated: "Until the last time we inspected Kuh-e Kolang, there was no nuclear activity or equipment inside it." And: "We should not confuse the audience; Tehran does not have nuclear weapons."

The war was launched against a state the IAEA said did not have the weapon, over a programme the IAEA had certified, after the US had destroyed the deal that was working.

Who Writes History

Hegseth says "history will judge." History is written by the institutions with the archives. The CIA's archive confirmed the 1953 coup. The Senate Intelligence Committee confirmed the fabricated WMD intelligence for Iraq. The declassified documents exist.

But the archives are also redacted. The CIA fought for decades to keep The Battle for Iran sealed. The British government withheld the 1953 documents until 2009. The US has never formally acknowledged the Iran Air 655 shootdown as anything but an accident.

The record Hegseth is counting on is the published record. The record that survives is the declassified one, plus the testimony of the people who were there.

Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei was arrested and exiled for opposing the Capitulations. The 1979 revolution was the answer to 1953. The 2026 war was the answer to 2018.

Hegseth's 47 years is a selected window. The file is 73 years old.

The Wrath

Hegseth is the Secretary of War who presided over a war that lost his party both chambers of Congress. His own Vice President, JD Vance, published a post-mortem admitting it. Donald Trump Jr. endorsed the post-mortem. Marco Rubio is reportedly preparing to resign. Admiral Brad Cooper is mocked as a podcast host by the IRGC spokesman and the Foreign Ministry.

Rezaei used the word "surrender." Baghaei compressed the deadline from seven days to two. Araghchi called the negotiation reports "media fabrications."

The enemy killed the Leader. The state answered with 80 handwritten directives, a missile city, a gamma cell, and trade delegations to Hanoi and Montevideo. The enemy bombed the universities. Research output rose 2 per cent.

Hegseth says history will judge differently. The ledger is already being written, and the pen is not in his hand.

The Bill

text:
4,000 Spanish Tercios refused 50,000 Ottomans. "Let them come whenever they want." 🏰⚔️ Castelnuovo, 1539.

In the summer of 1539, 4,000 veteran soldiers of the Tercio Viejo de Nápoles under Captain Francisco de Sarmiento were left completely isolated in the coastal fortress of Castelnuovo (modern Montenegro).

Trapped without naval support, they awoke to find Hayreddin Barbarossa’s Ottoman armada of 200 ships and 50,000 troops surrounding the city.

Knowing the garrison was cut off, Barbarossa offered generous surrender terms: keep their weapons, retain their gold, and receive safe passage to Italy.

Sarmiento put the choice to his officers and veteran soldiers. Their response was unanimous: they would hold the fortress to their last breath.

For three brutal weeks, the Spanish defenders held the breach. They launched desperate nighttime counter-attacks (encamisadas) into the Ottoman lines, forcing the besiegers to pay for every foot of shattered stone.

When heavy artillery finally demolished the upper walls, a bloodied Sarmiento—shot in the face with arrows—gathered his remaining 600 men for a final stand in the lower plaza. When Barbarossa sent one last herald to demand their yield, the Spanish captains gave their legendary reply:

"Que vengan cuando quieran"—"Let them come whenever they want."

Though the garrison was ultimately wiped out, they inflicted over 15,000 casualties on Barbarossa’s elite force, breaking the momentum of the Ottoman fleet in the Adriatic.

Is a soldier’s highest duty owed to personal survival so he may fight another day, or to an uncompromising standard of military honor? Tell us what you think below! 👇

Question: Can U.S. defeat Iran by moving in through Iraq?
"No. A large-scale U.S. ground invasion of Iran through Iraq is widely assessed by military analysts as extraordinarily risky, logistically nightmarish, and unlikely to produce a decisive “defeat” of the Iranian regime or lasting control. Limited raids or operations on the periphery (e.g., coastal areas or islands) are more plausible; a full invasion and occupation is not. Air and naval power, combined with economic pressure and blockade efforts, can impose serious costs and constrain Iranian options (as in the 2026 campaign focused on maritime interdiction and stand-off strikes). A ground invasion through Iraq does not offer a realistic path to decisive military or political defeat. It would more likely produce a protracted, high-cost war of attrition that favors the defender’s geography, manpower depth, and asymmetric tools. Military planners treat large-scale ground operations against mainland Iran as a low-probability, high-risk contingency rather than a viable strategy."

text:
Let’s talk about the EDGE defenders Cincinnati could have realistically explored if it was effectively willing to sacrifice a third-round compensatory pick AND a sixth-round selection to acquire Arnold Ebiketie.

Because the more you examine the alternatives, the more questionable this decision becomes.

1. WILL McDONALD IV — NEW YORK JETS

This would have been one of my first phone calls.

McDonald reportedly requested a trade, has 18.5 sacks across the previous two seasons, and is a former first-round selection with legitimate pass-rushing upside.

He’s younger, more explosive, and offers significantly more potential as a long-term contributor than Ebiketie.

Why would the Jets consider it? They’re rebuilding, and acquiring additional draft capital for a player reportedly seeking a change of scenery would at least warrant a conversation.

A third and sixth would be a reasonable opening offer, although New York reportedly wasn’t interested in moving him.

2. KHALIL MACK — LOS ANGELES CHARGERS

Perhaps the most compelling comparison from a pure value standpoint.

Mack remains an effective pass rusher, with three sacks through six appearances this season, and offers the kind of veteran presence Cincinnati desperately needs.

ESPN previously suggested his potential acquisition cost could be as low as a quality Day 3 selection.

That is LESS than the effective draft capital Cincinnati may have sacrificed for Ebiketie.

Why would Los Angeles consider it? Mack is 35, approaching free agency, and could theoretically return draft capital to a team evaluating its future.

The Chargers reportedly prefer to retain him, but he absolutely warranted a call.

3. YAYA DIABY — TAMPA BAY BUCCANEERS

One of the more intriguing potential acquisitions.

Diaby is a younger EDGE defender with explosiveness, athleticism, and the ability to generate pressure beyond simply cleaning up sacks.

Unlike an aging rental, he offers the possibility of becoming a meaningful contributor beyond the current season.

Why would Tampa Bay consider it? If the Buccaneers were willing to sell, a third-round selection plus additional compensation would provide useful draft capital.

The asking price is unconfirmed, but this is exactly the type of player Cincinnati should have explored.

4. JOSH SWEAT — ARIZONA CARDINALS

A more ambitious target, but one worth investigating.

Sweat is an established starting-caliber pass rusher coming off a 12-sack season in 2025.

He would provide a legitimate upgrade to Cincinnati’s defensive front rather than simply another rotational body.

Why would Arizona consider it? With the Cardinals struggling, moving a veteran for meaningful draft compensation could accelerate a roster reset.

Reports suggest Arizona would want a high Day 2 pick, meaning a third and sixth might not have been sufficient.

But if you’re already sacrificing third-round value, why wouldn’t you explore the possibility of acquiring a substantially better player?

5. DORANCE ARMSTRONG JR. — WASHINGTON COMMANDERS

This is where the alternative approach becomes interesting.

Armstrong is an experienced EDGE defender capable of contributing as part of a rotation.

He’s not a superstar, but Cincinnati wasn’t necessarily shopping for one when it acquired Ebiketie.

Why would Washington consider it? The Commanders have struggled, and Armstrong has been mentioned as a potential trade candidate.

His estimated acquisition cost has been in the fifth- or sixth-round range.

If Cincinnati simply wanted defensive line depth, why not explore a comparable low-cost option that wouldn’t create the same compensatory-pick concern?

6. JOSH UCHE — MIAMI DOLPHINS

Another alternative if the objective was inexpensive pass-rush depth.

Uche has demonstrated situational pass-rushing ability and could contribute in obvious passing situations.

Why would Miami consider it? The Dolphins have struggled, and moving a rotational veteran for draft compensation would make sense if they were looking toward the future.

He likely wouldn’t require anything approaching a third-round selection.

Again, the point isn’t that Uche is some transformational defender. It’s that Cincinnati could have investigated cheaper ways to address the same roster need.

⸻

And that’s the entire issue with this Ebiketie transaction.

There were two logical approaches available to Cincinnati:

OPTION A: If you’re willing to sacrifice the equivalent value of a third and sixth, aggressively pursue a legitimate starting-caliber EDGE defender with substantially more upside or production.

OPTION B: If you simply need rotational depth, acquire a lower-cost veteran without potentially destroying the value of a premium compensatory selection.

Instead, Cincinnati appears to have found the worst possible middle ground.

They acquired a rotational defender with zero sacks this season while potentially sacrificing the draft capital that could have been used to pursue a much more impactful player.

None of these alternatives were guaranteed to be available at the proposed prices. Contracts, salary-cap considerations, and the willingness of other teams to negotiate all matter.

But that’s what makes the decision-making process so frustrating.

The Bengals didn’t need to land every player on this list. They needed to understand the true cost of the player they were acquiring and evaluate that cost against the alternatives.

And if the compensatory-pick projection holds, they failed spectacularly at maximizing their assets.

This is bigger than Arnold Ebiketie.

It’s about roster construction, opportunity cost, and understanding how to maximize a championship window with Joe Burrow.

Whether Cincinnati knowingly accepted this cost or simply failed to account for the compensatory formula, neither explanation is remotely encouraging.

Good organizations understand the value of their assets before making decisions. Bad organizations consistently find ways to squander them.

And this is exactly how bad organizations stay bad.

text:
🇮🇷 Iran says two more tankers are burning in Hormuz and tells Trump to "fold your hand"

A day after President Trump spoke of "positive momentum" toward ending the Iran war, Tehran answered with fire claims and an ultimatum. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Tuesday that two "violating" oil tankers on an "unauthorised route" through the Strait of Hormuz had been halted "following massive explosions and are left burning." 

Per the IRGC Navy statement carried by Tasnim, one, a supertanker, struck a naval mine. The second, which the Guards claim was under US fighter jet escort, "also had an incident." The IRGC said both had switched off their tracking systems. It did not name the ships, their flags or any casualties, and there has been no independent confirmation of either fire. There was no immediate US comment, Anadolu reported. Tehran has made several similar claims in recent weeks, and CENTCOM said last month that all mines had been cleared from the waterway, AFP noted.

The diplomacy is just as hard-edged. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told IRNA the war "will not be resolved through military means, nor by intensifying sanctions," and urged Washington to accept Iran's standing offer: reopen Hormuz within two days in exchange for ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US counter-blockade of Iranian ports. Supreme National Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei was blunter on X: "FOLD YOUR HAND. STOP manufacturing FAKE NEWS about imaginary talks."

That contrasts with Trump, who after meeting Qatar's prime minister on Monday said further strikes were "quite unlikely" while the US stays "locked and loaded." Analysts quoted by Iran International describe the core deadlock as sequencing: Tehran wants sanctions, blockade and oil relief before nuclear talks, while Washington wants nuclear movement first.

Why it matters: Hormuz normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil. For Americans, that is gasoline prices. For Europeans, it is energy costs heading into winter.

What to watch: whether CENTCOM or shipping authorities confirm or deny Tuesday's fires.

text:
In case you missed today's MLB hot stove news and rumors, here's everything you need to know:

🚨 BIGGEST NEWS

▸ Agents are already FURIOUS with this market. Some say teams aren't making good offers, or any offers at all, before the Dec. 1 lockout. One agent's verdict: "It's ugly." What's out there are one-year deals clubs can get out of if no games get played, and one exec said it makes no sense to barrel ahead without knowing the new rules (via @JonHeyman) (free agency is cooked)

⚾️ YANKEES

▸ Rest in peace to Bob Boone, Aaron Boone's father, who passed away at 78. Seven Gold Gloves, four All-Star nods, a 1980 World Series ring with the Phillies and 2,225 games caught over 19 seasons. The Yankees released a statement mourning him this morning. Our thoughts are with Aaron and the whole Boone family.

▸ The Padres are coming for Teruaki Sato. San Diego's free agent wish list includes multiple Japanese-born players, with Shota Imanaga, Seiya Suzuki and Sato ranking HIGH on it (via @dennistlin). Sato just won the Central League Triple Crown at .306 with 39 HR and 106 RBI, and our third base situation needs a real bat (we can't watch another Japanese star go somewhere else)

⚾️ METS

▸ Kodai Senga is drawing trade interest from MULTIPLE teams (via @Ken_Rosenthal). He fared better as a late-inning reliever after the Mets moved him to the bullpen, but he has long preferred to start. He's owed $14M in 2027, the final guaranteed year, with a club option for 2028 and limited no-trade power (the ghost fork era in Queens might be done)

▸ New Mets co-hitting coach Johnny Washington has history with posted KBO slugger Si-hwan Roh. Washington made a big impact on Roh during the 2021 season with the Hanwha Eagles, and the 25-year-old is now posted for MLB teams (via @jonmorosi)

⚾️ RED SOX

▸ Craig Breslow wouldn't guarantee Trevor Story as Boston's starting shortstop in 2027. Last year at these same meetings he went out of his way to commit to Story as the everyday guy.

▸ Triston Casas is a candidate for winter ball, and new hire Shelley Duncan will coach a base (rough week to be Trevor Story)

⚾️ ANGELS

▸ The Angels' sale to Stan Kroenke's group is STILL not on the docket for a vote at next week's owners' meetings in New York (via @JeffFletcherOCR). Kroenke's people are holding informal meetings with GM candidates in Vegas, but interim GM John Mozeliak doesn't expect a hire until the ownership transfer goes through.

▸ Mozeliak also said they have to be "open-minded to our entire roster," and Zach Neto and Reid Detmers are the most intriguing names on it (Anaheim is stuck in limbo)

⚾️ FREE AGENTS

▸ Adrian Morejon is drawing interest from teams that want to make him a starter, and he'd rather stay in the bullpen (via @Ken_Rosenthal). The lefty posted a 2.83 ERA with a 30.4% strikeout rate over a career-high 86 innings with 28 holds in 2026.

⚾️ WHITE SOX

▸ Grant Taylor is moving into the rotation, Chris Getz said on MLB Network Radio. Taylor posted a 2.25 ERA, a 31.5% K rate and 10 saves over 84 innings out of the pen, and Getz called adding more starting pitching their "top priority" (the White Sox are spending more energy on pitching than some teams in New York)

Agents are mad, the Angels are frozen and the Padres are circling the one bat we actually want. Cashman, PICK UP THE PHONE.

text:
TFI VIEW | CONFLICT MONITOR

The Pause Is Not Peace: America Shifts from Military Strikes to Economic Pressure

November 10, 2026

The United States is signaling a shift in how it intends to confront Iran.

Speaking after meetings with G7 foreign ministers in Paris, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington does not need major military operations against Iran at this stage. Sanctions and the naval blockade, he argued, are already imposing severe economic costs on Tehran.

This follows President Donald Trump's decision to hold off on further strikes after appeals from regional partners, including Qatar. But the military pressure has not disappeared. The US blockade of Iranian ports remains in place, and Washington continues to keep its military options open.

What Changed

The immediate priority appears to be maintaining pressure without reopening a large-scale bombing campaign.

For Washington, controlling access to energy markets, restricting maritime trade and limiting Iran's ability to generate revenue may offer an alternative to continuous military escalation.

Tehran faces a different calculation. Accepting negotiations while the blockade remains in place could weaken its bargaining position. Rejecting negotiations, however, risks prolonging economic isolation.

TFI View

The pause in military strikes does not necessarily represent a reduction in strategic pressure.

Power is also exercised through access: access to markets, shipping routes, financial resources and critical infrastructure.

Washington is attempting to turn military leverage into economic and political leverage. Whether that pressure can produce concessions without triggering another round of conflict remains uncertain.

Watch Next

1. Whether Qatar can bridge the gap between Washington and Tehran.

2. Whether the US maintains its naval blockade without expanding military operations.

3. Whether Iran responds through maritime pressure or regional partners.

4. Whether the Strait of Hormuz moves toward normal commercial traffic.

The question is no longer simply when the next strike might happen. It is whether economic pressure can achieve what military force has not yet secured.

Iran vows to ‘rain down hell’ if US escalates war
Tehran’s proposal remains on the table, but Washington must meet its conditions, the Iranian foreign minister has warned
Published 9 Nov, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/sMOPVzwd7L
The US risks “dire consequences” if it escalates the war, Iran’s Foreign Ministry has warned, urging Washington to accept its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and pave the way for further negotiations.
The warning followed American strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island near the strait on Sunday night, according to local officials. Air defense and radar installations on Qeshm were also targeted last week.
Tehran’s proposal remains on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday, urging the White House to choose diplomacy.
”Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell,” he wrote on X.
Tehran’s conditions include lifting the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, easing sanctions, releasing frozen assets, and ending hostilities on all fronts. Under the proposal, Washington would implement the initial measures on the first day, followed by the reopening of the waterway on the second. Before the war, about a fifth of the world’s oil passed through the strait.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio dismissed some of those demands as “outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.” Tehran’s spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei described the offer as “the most logical plan on the table,” saying it could restore security in the strait and the Persian Gulf.
Iran insists on retaining what it describes as sovereignty over the strait, including requiring vessels to coordinate passage with its authorities, a demand Washington opposes.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Tehran’s lead negotiator, accused Israel on Monday of drawing the US into an endless war. “Unless Washington drops the ‘Israel First’ mindset, America and its allies are headed straight for a dark age,” he said.
Israel has left open the prospect of further military action, with Defense Minister Israel Katz saying on Sunday that the mission against Iran was “still not complete” and accusing Tehran of renewing efforts to obtain nuclear weapons. The Islamic Republic maintains its nuclear program is peaceful.
 Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House on Monday for talks on Doha’s mediation between Washington and Tehran.
Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin reportedly said US Vice President J.D. Vance would meet Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Doha next week. However, Tasnim news agency cited a senior Iranian security official as denying any such plans until Washington meets Tehran’s conditions.
Russia has also backed a diplomatic settlement. President Vladimir Putin met Rezaei in Moscow on Thursday to discuss the conflict and regional security.
The US and Israel launched their military campaign against Iran on February 28, triggering months of fighting that have disrupted global energy supplies and shipping.

author: sbauerap
authorBio: Politics. Wisconsin. Music. Not always in that order. Associated Press Statehouse correspondent based in Madison.

text:
My thoughts for today:

For the first time in 44 years, I started my morning without having to think about work. No calls to make. No sources to check in on. No deadlines to meet.

And I’m OK with that. At least for now.

Day-to-day journalism is hard. It can be demanding, unpredictable and occasionally exhausting. But I loved doing it.

It was never simply a job for me. It was a passion, and I had the incredible good fortune to make that passion my life’s work. Along the way, I worked alongside an extraordinary group of colleagues. They are truly awesome, and I’m grateful to so many of them.

My career began in 1982 as a young reporter in Peoria, Illinois. My first stop in Wisconsin was WBAY in Green Bay, a very good place to land. It’s also where I met my wife, Sharon. In 1986, I arrived in Milwaukee and spent 15 years at WITI-TV. After a three-year detour to Madison at WKOW, I came back to Milwaukee in 2004 and spent the next 22 years at TMJ4.

There were plenty of big stories along the way. Thank you, Packers, Bucks and Brewers, for giving me some championship seasons to cover. When I arrived in Wisconsin 40 years ago, I had no idea I would stay this long. But there were always stories to tell, places to go and, of course, politics in battleground Wisconsin to keep me busy.

What an incredible journey it has been.

I leave this chapter filled with gratitude. Most of all, I’m thankful to the people of the Milwaukee area who trusted me to tell their stories and help make sense of a complicated and ever-changing world. That trust has meant more to me than I can adequately express.

As for what’s next, I honestly don’t know. “Retiring” doesn’t seem to fit my DNA, so I’ll still be around. I hope there’s more to do but I’ll keep you posted. 

I’ll definitely be on the bicycle more. Wisconsin has some great bike trails. And I expect to spend a little more time hanging out in coffee shops.

So if you see me, say hello. I love a good conversation.

My final farewell at TMJ4 will be on Wednesday during the 4p News.

I too am a refugee from academia.  I know the truth of Kissinger's dictum "Academic disputes are so violent, only because the stakes are so small".

When I was an undergrad, at one time I was bringing in more money than the entire EE and ME department combined in contracts.

That made me no friends.

I was once explicitly threatened by a department chair for winning a contract that he was going for and lost to my group.  I was very fortunate to have the VP of Research in my corner along with working for the Research Institute at my school.

I was offered a grad position at Stanford, but after ten years I just said no, and left for the real world.

Thomas Mallon (b. 02 November 1951) is an American novelist, essayist, literary critic, and openly gay writer celebrated for his meticulously researched historical fiction, sharp wit, and fascination with the private lives concealed beneath America's public history.

Born in Glen Cove, New York, Mallon graduated from Brown University and earned a doctorate from Harvard. He taught at Vassar College and George Washington University, served as literary editor of GQ, and contributed frequently to The New Yorker, The New York Times Book Review, The Atlantic Monthly, and other periodicals. His acclaimed novels include Henry and Clara (1994), Watergate (2012), Landfall (2019), and Up With the Sun (2023).

Perhaps his most personally resonant novel, Fellow Travelers (2007), explores a clandestine homosexual romance between two Washington men during the McCarthy-era Lavender Scare, when careers could be destroyed and lives ruined by the mere suspicion of homosexuality. Its mixture of political intrigue, forbidden desire, and institutional hypocrisy proved irresistible to television, inspiring an acclaimed 2023 Showtime miniseries starring Matt Bomer and Jonathan Bailey.

Mallon has never shied away from examining homosexuality, secrecy, and the compromises demanded by respectable society. His 2025 memoir, The Very Heart of It: New York Diaries, 1983–1994, offers an intimate portrait of his literary and personal life against the backdrop of the AIDS epidemic, when gay New York was simultaneously enjoying a cultural flowering and enduring devastating losses.

A recipient of Guggenheim and Rockefeller fellowships and numerous literary honors, Mallon remains a distinctive chronicler of American ambition, political duplicity, and sexual discretion—a writer particularly adept at exposing what respectable people were doing behind closed doors, and why they desperately wanted those doors kept shut. 🏳️‍🌈

text:
Russia appears to be using the Trump team’s initiatives to win an important round in the negotiations. The discussion about how to stop its aggression is turning into a bargaining process over how Europe should defend itself. The Russian delegation explicitly describes the Ukraine issue as part of a broader agreement covering the entire continent. By agreeing to link these issues, Kushner is legitimising the Kremlin’s demands.

Until now, Washington has mainly pressured Kyiv to make concessions for the sake of a quick deal. Kushner is now bringing the Europeans into this bargaining process too. He has not yet published a specific list of concessions, but he is already proposing negotiations with Russia over their security. Europeans are having to defend their own military capabilities in talks that should be aimed at making Moscow end its aggression. According to the FT, the broader American proposal was not agreed with European capitals in advance.

**Meanwhile, Moscow wants the war to continue.** On 10 November, Lavrov explicitly stated that Russia would not agree to an immediate ceasefire. He insists on the following sequence: first define the parameters of the future security system, then address a settlement of the war. He also rejected the deployment of European stabilisation forces after a ceasefire. Russia’s demand is clear: the West must first accept new rules, and only then will Moscow consider ending hostilities—with no certainty that it will agree to do so.

For the Kremlin, negotiations and continued warfare complement each other. Russian strikes are intended to convince Ukraine and its partners that rejecting Moscow’s demands will become increasingly costly. Moscow demands concessions in exchange for the prospect of stopping those attacks. FT sources involved in back-channel contacts reported that Putin expects to weaken Ukraine through winter bombardments, while broadening the negotiations to encompass European security allows Moscow to drag out the process. According to those sources, he regards even Ukraine’s withdrawal from the remaining parts of Donbas merely as a precondition for a ceasefire. Further demands may follow.

Russia’s objectives have long extended beyond Ukraine. As early as 14 June 2024, Putin called for the gradual withdrawal of the military presence of “external powers” from Eurasia and described dependence on the US as Europe’s main threat. Ryabkov now says that a future European security system can exist only as part of a Eurasian one, while Lavrov refers to a Russian position paper, mentioning the CSTO, CIS and SCO. Europe is being offered a place in an order in which Moscow will have a decisive say.

Russia laid out its maximalist demands long ago. In December 2021, Moscow demanded that force and weapons deployments return to their May 1997 configuration, that NATO stop expanding, and that military activities in Ukraine and other countries in the region be restricted. Separate demands included returning American nuclear weapons to the US, dismantling the infrastructure used to deploy them abroad, and restricting military deployments, missiles, bomber flights and naval operations.

A new structure modelled on the NATO–Russia Council could become a permanent forum for such pressure. The old council did not give Moscow the right to block Alliance decisions: Russia’s consent was required for joint activities, while NATO remained free to act independently. In any future arrangement, everything will depend on the new obligations. If strengthening defences requires every participant’s approval, or if Russia can demand that such measures be suspended as a threat to its own security, consultations will become a means of obstruction. In its 2021 draft, Moscow already proposed allowing exceptional deployments beyond the established limits only with the consent of all parties. Such a rule would effectively give it the power to decide whether allies can reinforce their defences.

Washington has its own reasons to accept some of these demands. The 2026 US National Defense Strategy describes Russia as a persistent but manageable threat to NATO’s eastern members and assumes that Moscow cannot establish dominance over Europe. Europeans are expected to take primary responsibility for conventional defence, while the US concentrates on defending its own territory and deterring China. This creates a temptation to strike a deal with Moscow to reduce American involvement.

Kushner has political backing to advance this approach. Trump himself announced a broad agreement concerning Europe, while Rubio supports the negotiating team and discussions about the post-war order. There is no confirmation that a specific package of concessions has been agreed within the administration. There is also bipartisan opposition in Congress to easing pressure on Russia. But presidential support is enough to conduct negotiations, propose options and gradually get allies used to the idea that their defence, too, is negotiable.

The most dangerous scenario is taking shape: weak guarantees for Ukraine are being negotiated alongside restrictions on European defence. Rubio is already saying that these guarantees must be acceptable to Russia; meanwhile, American officials are discussing shifting the financial burden onto Europe and gradually easing sanctions, with the option of reimposing them. In this arrangement, the West pays with concrete concessions in exchange for a promise to end the aggression, while Moscow strengthens its position and gains the ability to bargain over how its opponents defend themselves. The Trump administration’s effort to save money on its military presence weakens alliances—one of the main sources of American power. Declining trust in the US pushes European governments towards separate deals and undermines a common policy towards Russia. The Russian threat remains, while Washington loses the ability to confront it together with its allies.

text:
It's a small matter of trivia, but notice the fit of the kepis on the troopers.   The civil war kepi had a taller crown and fit lower on the head. It  was actually less common than the forage cap, or "bummer", because it was a private purchase item.  By the Indian Wars, the US Army had ditched the forage cap in favor of the kepi.  It had been somewhat redesigned with a lower crown height so it sat higher on the head.  This gave the wearer the constant sensation that the cap was going to fall off.   

Troops hated it in comparison to the brimmed slouch hat not only for this reason, but also the fact that it offered very little protection from the sun. Below is a pic of the civil war forage cap for comparison.  The crown was very tall and flopped down over the forehead.  It was intended to be issued with a stiffener that caused it to stand straight up like a shako cap, but these stiffeners were never issued.

(This is my authentic forage cap from Dirty Billy's in Gettysburg, PA).

Russian opposition economist Vyacheslav Shiryaev argues that Ukraine’s ability to strike deep inside Russia is changing the strategic calculations of the war.

His assessment goes beyond the damage caused by individual attacks.

Shiryaev believes Ukraine is demonstrating something far more consequential: the potential to disrupt the functioning of the Russian state itself.

That distinction matters.

Destroying military equipment imposes costs on an army. Disrupting refineries, logistics networks and critical infrastructure can place pressure on the economic systems that sustain military operations.

In Shiryaev’s view, this growing vulnerability offers a possible route toward ending the war by making continued aggression increasingly difficult for Moscow to sustain.

It is an assessment, not proof that Russia is already facing paralysis. But it highlights how Ukraine’s long-range capabilities have expanded the battlefield far beyond the front lines.

The question is no longer simply how much damage Ukraine can inflict. It is how much disruption Russia’s war economy can absorb while continuing the invasion. https://t.co/Hbv2QJeNQ5

text:
copying another brand's Black Friday discount might be the worst thing you can do

because not every brand is trying to achieve the same thing

look at these 3 DTC strategies:

1. THE ARMY PAINTER — EARLY ACCESS

they started promoting their Black Week deals back in October

the strategy?

build anticipation weeks before the sale starts

early access gives people a reason to pay attention now, even if they're not ready to buy yet

and gives the brand more time to build interest before the Black Friday rush

the real test is how much of that interest turns into purchases once the deals go live

2. EVERYDAY DOSE — OFFER STACKING

75% off + 10 free gifts

they're going BIG on the offer

→ the discount makes trying it cheaper
→ the gifts add perceived value
→ the whole package feels like a bigger deal

especially interesting for a product people might be curious about but haven't tried yet

and since coffee is a repeat-purchase product, there's potential to earn more from those customers over time

which could help justify a stronger first-order incentive

3. INGLEWOOD COFFEE — DIRECT DISCOUNT

a straight 50% off

no bundles or extra incentives

just a strong offer that's immediately clear

for shoppers already looking for Black Friday deals, that simplicity can work really well

and when the goal is to turn existing interest into purchases, a straightforward offer can be enough

THE BIGGER PICTURE:

here's where copying gets risky

you can see the offer a competitor is running

but you don't see:

→ how much demand they've already built
→ how familiar shoppers are with the brand
→ whether that offer is actually working

a discount that gets one brand thousands of orders could get another very little

text:
Battle of Bosworth, 22 August 1485. 

Richard III’s Yorkist army occupies the high ground of Ambion Hill as Henry Tudor’s Lancastrian forces approach, with the Earl of Oxford commanding the vanguard.

Richard’s elevated position offered tactical advantages for his archers and artillery, while marshy ground complicated the Lancastrian advance. Royal guns opened fire as Oxford’s troops approached, followed by exchanges of arrows and infantry engagements.

The battle’s outcome turned on the intervention of Lord Stanley and Sir William Stanley, whose forces eventually joined Henry’s side. Richard III launched a cavalry charge aimed directly at Henry Tudor but became isolated and was killed in the fighting. His death ended the Plantagenet dynasty and secured Henry VII’s claim to the English throne. #WarsoftheRoses

text:
“I WILL NOT BE EXCHANGED FOR 20 RUSSIAN SOLDIERS.”

Volodymyr Mykolayenko spent nearly three and a half years in Russian captivity. He endured interrogations, beatings, threats, and relentless pressure to betray his country. But the Russians never managed to break him.

On February 24, 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Mykolayenko woke to the sound of explosions. He turned to his wife and said, “That's it. I'm going to defend the city.” The former mayor of Kherson joined the volunteers preparing to resist the advancing Russian army. They were taken to a school with broken windows and missing doors, given weapons, and told to wait for orders. Then came the fighting near the Antonivskyi Bridge, mortar fire, the first wounded men, and Russian military columns pushing into the city. When Kherson fell under occupation, Mykolayenko did not disappear or accept the new authorities. He marched at the front of a demonstration carrying a huge Ukrainian flag. Thousands of residents openly confronted the occupiers, shouting at Russian soldiers and demanding that they leave Ukrainian territory. The Russians eventually responded with gunfire, stun grenades, arrests, and beatings.

Mykolayenko was captured after being lured into a meeting arranged as a trap. He managed to call his wife before his captors took control of his phone, preventing the Russians from using it to lure other Ukrainians into similar traps. He was taken to the basement of the regional police headquarters, where interrogations and beatings began. From the first day, his captors offered him freedom in exchange for cooperation. Recognize the occupation authorities, join their administration, and neither you nor your family will be harmed. He refused. When the Russians decided he must be directing the underground resistance in Kherson, they demanded information about hidden weapons depots. He gave them nothing. At one point, they brought him before Russian propagandists and asked whether he considered Roman Shukhevych a Ukrainian hero. He answered that Shukhevych was a hero to Ukraine. His captors told him he would never leave prison.

His imprisonment continued through Russian detention facilities, including Sevastopol. He witnessed the treatment of young Ukrainian prisoners whose psychological suffering, he fears, may follow them for the rest of their lives. He also had an opportunity to be released earlier, but the Russians demanded 20 of their soldiers in exchange for him. Mykolayenko refused. “How could I look into the eyes of the mothers of those Ukrainian soldiers who would remain in prison while I walked free in exchange for 20 Russians?” Even after his release, he admitted that he sometimes woke up feeling guilty because he was free while so many younger Ukrainian prisoners remained behind bars. When he finally returned to Ukraine, people lined the road from the Belarusian border toward Chernihiv, waving Ukrainian flags and welcoming the returning prisoners. He had not expected such a reception. “Ukrainian air heals, and Ukrainian people inspire,” he said.

And when asked about Russia's future, Mykolayenko offered a remarkably simple answer. He believes this war will eventually destroy the Russian Federation itself. Then he added a sentence worth remembering:

“I personally intend to outlive the Russian Federation.”

Some Thoroughbreds take a little more time to find their footing in a second career. For Savel, it took finding someone who understood her.

When the five-year-old gray mare arrived at Sandia Creek Ranch Auxiliary Foundation (SCRAF), she was spirited, sensitive, and not particularly interested in keeping all four feet on the ground. Kiersti Wylie recognized that beneath Savel's tough exterior was a talented horse who needed consistency and a little patience.

Through thoughtful training and the introduction of liberty work, their relationship began to change. The mare who once kept her guard up now eagerly meets Kiersti at the pasture gate, loves exploring the hills, and rarely lets her out of sight. And apparently, there isn't a cookie she doesn't like!

As a CARMA Placement Program graduate, Savel was one of the Thoroughbreds representing California at the 2026 Retired Racehorse Project Thoroughbred Makeover. With support from CARMA's Messineo Makeover Scholarship, Kiersti and Savel made the journey to Kentucky, earning:

26th Place, Competitive Trail Preliminary Competition
32nd Place, Freestyle Preliminary Competition

Kiersti's work with Savel is also part of a larger effort at SCRAF to introduce young riders to the skills and responsibilities of retraining off-track Thoroughbreds. Her experience with this spirited mare offers a firsthand example of how much the right approach can change a horse's future.

Savel may not have found success on the racetrack, but she's discovering something just as valuable in her second career: confidence and a partner who believes in her.

Congratulations to Kiersti and Savel on their Thoroughbred Makeover journey!

text:
A bipartisan group of lawmakers sent a letter to Republican and Democratic leadership in the House of Representatives encouraging them to formally invite Pope Leo XIV to address a joint session of Congress next year.

The letter — addressed to House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana, and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-New York — was signed by 91 Republican and Democratic members of Congress.

“The election of Pope Leo XIV serves as a sign of great pride for millions of Americans,” the letter said. “As the first ever American-born Pope, his unique perspective, and ties to our country, would serve as a unifying force for members of Congress.”

“Following a divisive election, Pope Leo’s unifying message of service, compassion for fellow mankind, and the importance of human dignity would be especially timely,” the letter added.

The lawmakers wrote that a visit from the Holy Father “would offer a much-needed outlook as we navigate complex foreign and domestic issues.”

“Given the undeniable historical significance and cultural impact of Pope Francis’s address to Congress in 2015, we urge you to work to schedule a joint address as soon as possible in the beginning of the 120th Congress with the first American-born Pope,” the letter added.

Neither Johnson’s nor Jeffries’ offices immediately responded to EWTN News’ request for comment.

A decision to invite a pope to address Congress has come from congressional leadership in the past, often together with the executive branch, according to the Congressional Research Service (CRS). “No formal procedure on when or how to issue invitations is codified in law or in House or Senate rules,” according to CRS.

The Chicago-born pontiff does not have a visit to the United States on his schedule yet but did say in June that he intends to travel to the country soon: “We were looking at the calendar for the next couple of years. Nothing is set in stone yet, but I certainly hope to be there soon.”

In July, Leo honored the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence by penning a letter that said that moment “gave enduring voice to the ideals of liberty, equality, the pursuit of happiness, justice, and democratic self-government.” He also accepted the National Constitution Center’s 2026 Liberty Medal.

text:
No, those are biases from magical thinking.

If executives can grab all they want, why doesn't every executive get paid a billion dollars a year? Surely, they would all want that. Yet, they don't get it, so no, an executive can't "grab all he wants."

It's foolish to call working slavery because people voluntarily choose to take a position offered at a certain wage. Enslaved people don't get wages, and their employment is not voluntary.

It's also naive to think that lower-level people are "doing the work," implying the executive does no work. Everyone is working, providing the business with the value they are paid to deliver.

An executive gets paid what the company is willing to pay for the value they deliver.

A janitor gets paid what the company is willing to pay for the value they deliver.

A person who delivers more value will be more sought after and can charge more for it.

Anybody can be a janitor, so that skill is worth less. Few people have the skills of a CEO, so that skill is worth more... usually a lot more.

Why don't janitors get paid $500 an hour? Because the value they provide is not worth $500 an hour.

How do we know this? Because someone else who can provide the same value will do it for $8 an hour. That is how much that janitor skill is worth. It's not to be cruel or greedy.

When you go to the grocery store and choose the $1.75 generic brand of soup and not the $2.75 name-brand soup, you are not being cruel to the people who make the name-brand soup. Nor are you being greedy, wanting to keep more of your money. The value you seek is worth $1.75 to you, but not $2.75. Someone else may value the name brand more and be willing to pay the $2.75. That's all: no greed or avarice, and certainly no cruelty.

So rather than live in a fantasy world where your feelings determine wages, abandon your magical thinking and embrace reality. You'll be happier, and the world will seem a less mysterious place.
