text:
My friend Goro has spent eleven years fixing up used American pickup trucks for Japanese roads.

They come over by ship. Two hundred thousand miles. Dog hair in every seam. A French fry under the floor mat that has seen things.

In Japan, a used car is supposed to look like nobody ever owned it. So the first thing Goro does is peel off the stickers.

He has never been able to throw one away.

He keeps them in binders. Four binders. With tabs, because he is Japanese.

He let me read them.

FAMILY

Idaho. A stick-figure family across the whole back window. Dad. Mom. Five kids. Three dogs. A cat. Two chickens. A horse.
The truck had five seats. Goro did the math for a long time.
In Japan, we don't tell strangers how many children we have. In Idaho, they put it on the truck. With the chickens.

Nevada. A magnet: "STUDENT DRIVER. PLEASE BE PATIENT."
Under it, on a strip of masking tape, in marker: "HE'S DOING GREAT. LOVE, MOM."
In Japan, new drivers must put a green-and-yellow beginner mark on the car. It's a warning. Stay back.
In Nevada, it came with a review.

New Mexico. Four high school volleyball stickers in a row. 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012. Same number on every one. 14.
The oldest had faded almost white. The newest was still bright. Goro says he read them like the rings of a tree.
At the end of the row, one college sticker.
Then nothing.
She grew up. He kept driving.

HUMOR (UNSOLVED)

Wyoming. "IF YOU CAN READ THIS, I'VE LOST MY TRAILER."
Goro walked around the truck twice. Then he called the auction company in America to report a missing trailer.
It took them eleven minutes to explain.
Goro still does not think it's funny. Somewhere in Wyoming, a trailer is alone.

PAWPAWS

Louisiana. White letters in the corner of the back window. "IN LOVING MEMORY OF PAWPAW. 1941-2019." A tiny fishing pole underneath.
In Japan, we keep our grandfathers at home, on a small family altar, with incense and a bowl of rice.
In Louisiana, Pawpaw rides along.
It took Goro two hours with a razor blade to get him off in one piece. Then he lit incense for him. He's still not sure that's allowed.
That tab now holds fourteen Pawpaws, six Nanas, and one Labrador named Duke.

At first, Goro's boss told him to throw all of it in the trash.
Now his boss reads the binders on his lunch break.
And Japanese customers have started asking one question before they ask the price.
"Does it come with a family?"

Then, last spring, a red 2003 pickup came in from South Carolina.

One owner. Bought new. 241,000 miles.

Only one thing on the tailgate. White letters, cracked and faded to almost nothing.

MY SON IS A MARINE

Goro started peeling. There wasn't much left. The letters came off in dry little flakes.

Then he stepped back.

The sticker was gone. The sentence wasn't.

More than twenty summers of South Carolina sun had faded the red paint everywhere except under those letters. They were still there. Darker than the rest of the tailgate. Burned in.

He never took it off. The sun did. And the sun couldn't finish the job.

Goro did the math again. A boy who joined the Marines back when this truck was new would be in his forties now. Out of uniform for years.

His father never changed it to "was."

Then Goro looked up at the back window.

A second sticker. Small. Bright. Almost new.

MY GRANDSON IS A MARINE

The old man hadn't put it on the tailgate. The tailgate was taken.

Goro put the razor blade down. That truck is the only one in eleven years that never got a page in the binder.

It was bought by Mr. Hara. He's 78. A rice farmer outside Iwakuni, a town with a U.S. Marine base.

In 1956, the year thousands of Marines arrived in Iwakuni, he was eight. A young Marine stopped a big green truck on his road, lifted him into the cab, and let him honk the horn.

He has wanted an American truck for seventy years.

Goro apologized for the marks on the tailgate. He offered to repaint it. For free.

Mr. Hara read the letters with Goro's phone. Then he shook his head.

"This truck already has a father," he said. "I'm just the driver."

For the first month, Mr. Hara had a problem.

Every time he drove near the base, young men honked at him. Waved. Yelled things.

He thought he was driving badly. So he drove slower.

They honked more.

In June, a pickup full of very short haircuts followed him all the way into the parking lot of the farm co-op.

He was sure he was in trouble.

Four young men got out. One of them read the truck out loud. Slowly. The tailgate first. Then the back window.

Then he turned to Mr. Hara and said, "Once a Marine, always a Marine, sir. His daddy knew."

Mr. Hara didn't understand a word. He bowed.

Then the young Marine asked, very politely, if he could honk the horn.

Mr. Hara had been waiting seventy years to return that favor. He opened the door.

The paperwork says a man in South Carolina sold his truck.

The Marines outside Iwakuni know better.

He deployed it.

text:
A bipartisan group of US lawmakers comprising 91 members of the congress have sent a letter to Republican and Democratic leadership in the House of Representatives asking them to formally invite Pope Leo XIV to address a joint session of Congress next year. Addressed to House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana, and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-New York, the letter was signed by 91 Republican and Democratic members of Congress.

“The election of Pope Leo XIV serves as a sign of great pride for millions of Americans. As the first ever American-born Pope, his unique perspective, and ties to our country, would serve as a unifying force for members of Congress,” the bipartisan members wrote in the letter.

“Following a divisive election, Pope Leo’s unifying message of service, compassion for fellow mankind, and the importance of human dignity would be especially timely,” the letter added. The Congress representatives also said that a visit from the Holy Father “would offer a much-needed outlook as we navigate complex foreign and domestic issues.”

Citing the “undeniable historical significance and cultural impact of Pope Francis’s address to Congress in 2015”, the lawmakers urged the leaders to work to schedule a joint address as soon as possible in the beginning of the 120th Congress with the first American-born Pope.

text:
Places to shop + roadside food at #Tokyo 

Tokyo City Flea Market (Sat and Sun only)
- If interested in vintage / retro goods etc, this is the market to visit 
- Bargaining works but is limited 
- Go early to explore and have low crowds 
- Market is in parking area and in the open 

Shibuya Antique Market (2nd and 4th Saturday)
- Another open air vintage and open market 
- Craft items etc are also available 

Sunamachi Ginza Shopping Street
- Affordable street food 
- Grocery shops 

Togoshi Ginza Shopping Street
- Long Long street 
- Visit for food hauls 

Sunamachi Ginza Shopping District
- If you want to try street food then this is the place to visit
- Many shops sell local produce

Tip: The 10th of every month the local shops offer discounts. Basically a bargain sale

Nakamise Shopping Street
- Traditional shops selling gift items, handicrafts etc 
- Rice crackers are a delicacy to buy from here 
- Visit for food + photos +exploring the area 

Tsukiji Outer Market
- Another market for seafood lovers 
- The wholesale market is moved to a new area 
- Do visit the wholesale market early in the morning. Also note don't be a hurdle in their operations. Just see / observe from far.

Kappabashi Kitchen Supply Town
- If you wanna buy cookware etc here's where you will find all 
- Professional supplier of kitchen good all have their shops here 
- You would be tempted to buy the Japanese Knifes but know the rules of check-in baggage before getting one 
- Visit on weekdays to avoid crowds. Weekends locals also visit to shop. 
- This market is near Senso-ji Temple. So can cub the day with this market when visiting the temple area. 

Yanaka Ginza
- If you have time to spare, you can visit this street 
- Just a small street and hence don't make the journey just to visit if you have a few days to spare in Tokyo. 
- Cafes, shops and food stalls etc. 

Ameyoko market
- When in Ueno area plan your visit here 
- Clothes + imported goods etc + food stalls all are available here 
- Looking for groceries to carry home then can check the basement of Ameyoko Center Building

Koenji Area
- Multiple markets in this area 
- Junjo Shopping, PAL Shopping, Look Shopping are all streets good to explore 

Ginza + Omotesando
- Shopping for premium stuff then head over here 
- Muji and Uniqlo have their stores here along with many other 

Tip: Shop and keep bags in Ginza Station lockers or some shopping malls also have this facility. 

Harajuku 
- If you have to choose one market it is be this 
- Explore the Takeshita Street and Cat Street and all others 
- Shop souvenirs + eat food + can visit pet cafes etc 

Shibuya
- Another must visit area to visit even when you don't want to shop 
- Shibuya 109 - Shop for men/women fashion etc here. 
- Atoms and Kith-Tokyo in case you want to shop for sneakers 
- Loft - A lovely store which you don't wanna miss. Mix of all things together including stationery. 
MEGA Don Quijote - Another must visit store when in Japan. Cosmetics, souvenirs, novelty goods etc. 

Sharing some chains which sell specific things and can be found across Tokyo / Japan. 

Affordable Japanese Fashion - Uniqlo, GU, Muji 
Sneakers / Streetwear - Beams, Atmos, United Arrows 
Stationery - Itoyam Sekaido, Loft, Kakimori
Soveiners - Daiso, Seria, Ca Do, 3Coins

Some more for specifi shopping 

- Seiko Watches - Seiko Dream Square in Ginza (No, Seiko aren't cheap here just because they're made in Japan)
- Camera - Yodobashi Camera in Shinjuku
- BicCamera - Watches, camera etc 
- Jack Road - For pre-owed watched 

Streets in case want to eat and drink 
- Omoide Yokocho Memory Lane
- Golden Gai 

Tip - Don't want to eat or drink but love to click pictures, then head here late evening / night and you'll be able to get some gem shots. 

- Shibuya Nonbei Yokocho
- Kichijoji Street 
- Ebisu Yokocho (More like a covered food mall where multiple options are available)

Wholesale Shops 

Note: Ask first if they sell to retail customers, as many only sell to business houses 

- NIPPORI FABRIC TOWN
- Asakusabashi Wholesale Street
- Niki no Kashi - Bic-Kan (This is the place in UENO to visit if you need to buy snacks or groceries in wholesale to take back home. Unless it's some significant quantity dont make the trip. You're better off buying near by)
- Bakurocho & Yokoyamacho Wholesale District - Clothes, Handbags etc etc 

One of the most asked question to me is where to buy the PlayStation
- BICCamera
- Sony has their own store in Ginza 
- Yadobashi Camera Store

Tip: Don't forget to get the passport number etc added for the tax refund.

For getting games or vintage Play Stations, you can visit shops in Akihabara. Nakano Broadway has many such shops. 

- Super Potato in Akhiabara is a gem for this 
- Trader Headquarter is a dedicated store for second hand etc and has PS floor just for the console and games etc. 
- Hard off is another store in Akihabara 
- Another is Retro Game Camp in Akihabara

Action Figures 
- Amiami at Akhibara is heaven for it. Just explore all in the tower 
- Another heaven is Akhibara Radio Kaikan. 10 floors
- Mandarake Complex. 8 floors of secondhand collectible anime toys. Rare ones you can find here. 
- Kotobukiya. All non Japanese action heroes you'll find here. marvel etc etc 

Planning to cook when in Tokyo and need Indian groceries
- Check for Ambika veg and vegan shop. They have multiple outlets (I think they have home delivery too)
- Bharat Bazaar 
- Maya Bazaar 

When I used to plan a trip, I had many travelers whom I would find the nearest store for buying rice electric cooker + book stay which had kitchenette + supermarkets which sold Indian groceries. They were on budget. Didn't want to spend on food + wanted to explore. Some traveling with aged people who would not adjust to local food etc. Didn't want the tours etc which served Indian food but wanted to explore by self. 

Hope this helps to some extent when visiting Tokyo. 

#DakukaGyaan

text:
India Is Unlikely to Restrict Broken Rice Exports Despite Rising Global Prices!

India appears comfortable with its domestic rice supply position, signalling no immediate need for fresh export restrictions.

The numbers tell the story:

• FCI rice stocks: 39.05 million tonnes as of September 1.
• Paddy awaiting milling: Another 30.75 million tonnes.
• Government rice stocks are 3.68 times the prescribed buffer-stock norm — a substantial cushion against domestic supply shocks.
• Broken rice exports: 8.08 lakh tonnes in CY2025.

With substantial government reserves and additional rice entering the central pool through milling, India has considerable supply security.

As the world's largest rice exporter, India's decision to maintain an open export policy offers much-needed predictability to global rice markets.

The key takeaway: A 3.68-times buffer-stock cushion leaves little immediate justification for panic-driven export restrictions, despite rising international prices.

Erika Kirk took to X to deliver a pointed response to Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed after a video surfaced showing him speaking at an Arab American summit in Chantilly, Virginia, following his election victory.

During the Connect Arab America Empowerment Summit, El-Sayed told attendees, “I’m honored to be the next United States Senator from the great state of Michigan. Which, of course, I know we’re here in D.C., which, of course, is the capital of the United States of America, but Michigan is the capital of Arab America.”

Kirk, the widow of Charlie Kirk and a prominent figure associated with Turning Point USA, shared a Fox News clip of his speech and fired back with a blunt statement: “There is no ‘Arab America.’ There is only the United States of America.”

El-Sayed’s historic election makes him the first Muslim to win a seat in the U.S. Senate, marking a significant milestone for Michigan’s substantial Arab American and Muslim populations.

His victory celebration in Detroit reflected that cultural connection, with El-Sayed addressing supporters in both English and Arabic as the crowd erupted in cheers.

Kirk’s response has brought renewed attention to El-Sayed’s remarks, highlighting contrasting views about cultural identity and what it means to be American.

text:
What happens when a Kansas doctor offers to implant goat glands and then buys a radio station to advertise it? You get John R. Brinkley.

Brinkley began practicing in Milford, Kansas, around 1917 and 1918. He reportedly performed his first goat-gland transplant in 1918 on a local farmer.

In 1923 he built the radio station KFKB, which stood for "Kansas First, Kansas Best." He used the broadcasts to promote his treatments and to answer listeners' health questions over the air.

In 1930 the Kansas medical board revoked his medical license for unprofessional conduct. His radio license was denied or revoked around 1931.

Doctors and historians widely regard his methods as quackery.

He proved that radio could make a doctor famous, and also that the airwaves could turn on you.

text:
From Yield Forecasts to Insurance Triggers: What Underwriters Need to Know 

Key takeaways
Basis risk is the core test for parametric crop insurance. A satellite yield index is only as useful as its ability to pay when the insured loses, and not pay when they do not.

Forecast accuracy is not the same as payout accuracy. A small estimation error near a contract threshold can decide whether a payment happens at all.

Seasons matter more than fields. Thousands of fields in one drought year are still one drought year. Research shows that many-fields, few-years datasets can understate basis risk.

Kansas wheat offers a public reference point. K-State's AgManager published a 2026 county-level wheat yield dashboard furnished by SatYield, including a candid note on where the model needs better calibration.

Anthropic is targeting a valuation up to $1.4tn (£1tn) in its upcoming stock market offering, sharply down from earlier forecasts after a global AI sell-off.

The US tech giant's prospective valuation is now dramatically lower than the $2tn some investors had expected just weeks ago, before a rout of AI stocks wiped trillions from American markets.

The Claude developer said it would raise up to $90bn as part of the deal, selling shares for between $70 and $78 in a listing expected in the next few days.

At a valuation of around $1.4tn, it would be the third-largest stock market float in history, behind those of Elon Musk's SpaceX in June and Saudi Aramco in 2019.

Anthropic's valuation has been under pressure after its disclosed plans to splash $1tn on building data centres amid concerns that tech giants are overspending on the AI boom.

Stocks in data centre developers plunged last week after Democrats swept to victory in the US midterm elections, raising the prospect of a crackdown on AI companies.

text:
3 Things a Hard Tech Founder Gives Away When the First Customer Owns the Unit

I designed a 10x solution. After years of no, a grid operator leaned in, but wanted advisory shares for a grid connection. I almost signed. Then I ran the numbers on what that yes would take with it.

#1: The 20 years

One flywheel earns grid-services revenue for two decades. In my spreadsheet, that stream came out at several times the profit on selling the unit. Sell the unit, and the bigger business leaves with the buyer.

#2: The warranty

New hardware has failure modes nobody has found yet. A123 spent about $55 million replacing defective cells from one miscalibrated machine, then filed for bankruptcy the same year. When the buyer holds the warranty terms, the founder carries every failure on the buyer's clock.

#3: Every improvement

A 10% efficiency gain should raise the company's revenue. With one buyer, it becomes a price cut in the next negotiation. The engineering still pays off, just for someone else.

After enough rejections, a yes feels like rescue.

But the offer itself carries good news. The harder a first buyer pushes to own the unit, the more that unit is worth to the founder who keeps it.

text:
Before buying $ANT, here are 7 things investors should understand.  

1/ The valuation: $1T or $1.4T?

At $70–78/share:
~$1T headline market cap
~$1.4T fully diluted equity value
~$132B existing cash
~$85B estimated net IPO + strategic placement proceeds
~$215B pro forma cash

At $81B October ARR, that's ~15x pro forma EV/ARR. If ARR reaches $160B in 2028 (40% annual growth), ~7.5x. 

ANT pitched $190-200B revenue for 2028, so ARR for YE28 could be $250B or more.

But there's another number: ~$900B in aggregate compute/infrastructure commitments. Not conventional debt, but a massive future capital burden.

Given what we know today, I personally think $1.4T is a very fair valuation ($2T would have been too expensive). 

2/ Who is funding the IPO?

The public offering could raise ~$58–64B gross. Separately, seven strategic investors are committing $26B:

Google: $10B
Nvidia: $10B
AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC: remaining $6B

Reported retail allocation could reach 15–20% — unusually high for a mega-IPO.

3/ Free float and lock-ups: don't confuse IPO size with available supply.

825M shares are offered, only ~6.3% of fully diluted shares.

But up to 316M additional shares may become eligible for sale from day one. Most other holders face a 180-day lock-up, while founders and certain large holders face up to 365 days, subject to early-release provisions.

The supply calendar matters as much as the IPO float.

4/ Index inclusion could bring passive demand quickly.

Nasdaq-100 Fast Entry:
Top-40 market-cap eligibility.
Assessment after 7 trading days.
Potential inclusion after 15 trading days.
No existing constituent needs to be removed.

S&P 500 is different: at least 12 months of trading, plus profitability and other eligibility requirements.

Potential Nasdaq passive buying within weeks; no need to assume massive forced selling elsewhere.

5/ Investors are bullish -  some don't buy the story, but it's risky to be publicly negative.

The bulls:
Brad Gerstner (Altimeter): Says sentiment among major investors is 9–10/10 bullish over 1–3 years; Altimeter plans to participate substantially in the IPO.
Erica Brescia (Redpoint): Calls Anthropic an "absolutely blockbuster business" with impressive profitability trends.
Denny Fish (Janus Henderson): Calls AI a generational technology shift.
Menlo's Matt Murphy and Bessemer's Byron Deeter: Anthropic is reportedly their respective firms' largest investments by historical significance/cost basis.
Gil Luria (D.A. Davidson): Sees strong potential if the IPO is priced correctly.

The skeptics:
Li Lu (Himalaya): Warns against treating AI as a human-made god. AI should remain a tool, and investors should return to fundamentals, financial discipline and long-term value creation.
Roger McNamee: Calls the S-1 "speculative fiction" — a compelling story that still leaves key questions unanswered. By the way, Roger is a legend (Facebook, Silver Lake, etc.), but turned negative on tech / AI in general over the last few years. 
New Constructs (David Trainer): Calls it potentially the "most ridiculous IPO of 2026"; its reverse DCF suggests equity value as low as ~$144B under certain assumptions.

Remember: several bulls are existing investors. Their enthusiasm is meaningful, but not independent price discovery.

6/ Chinese AI labs offer a useful valuation comparison.

Indicative figures:
MiniMax: ~$7.8B market cap / ~$0.8B ARR = ~10x.
https://t.co/Jn2mAV46Sm (Zhipu, GLM model): ~$29B / ~$1.8B ARR = ~16x.
DeepSeek: ~$52B estimated private valuation / $0.5–1B estimated ARR = ~52–104x.

MiniMax and https://t.co/Jn2mAV46Sm have also fallen roughly 87% and 84% from their 52-week highs.

These ARR figures are estimates, not audited revenue. The comparison illustrates how much valuation depends on growth expectations and perceived strategic importance.

7/ Cloud companies may be the closest public-market proxies.

Amazon, Google and Microsoft are major compute and distribution partners.

Anthropic generated 44% of revenue through cloud-provider marketplaces in the first nine months of 2026. AWS grew 39% YoY in Q3.

As Anthropic scales, investors may increasingly prefer direct exposure to the model company rather than relying only on chipmakers and cloud providers. The caveat: Anthropic's growth is not the only driver of cloud growth, and it may increasingly build its own compute infrastructure.

text:
Anthropic is targeting a $1.4 trillion IPO valuation.

But what are investors really buying?

Behind the headline is one of the biggest bets in business history: the future economics of AI.

Here are the numbers and risks worth understanding.

1. An extraordinary capital raise
Anthropic plans to offer 825 million shares at $70–$78, potentially raising $64.4 billion. A separate $26 billion private placement could bring total new capital to $90.4 billion.

This isn't just an IPO. It's a massive bet on the computing infrastructure required to compete at the AI frontier.

2. Understanding the $1.4 trillion valuation
At $78 per share, Anthropic's valuation is approximately $1.02 trillion based on currently outstanding shares.

The $1.4 trillion figure is fully diluted, including potential future shares from options and equity awards.

An important distinction when evaluating the headline valuation.

3. Five risks investors shouldn't overlook
Infrastructure costs: Approximately $895 billion in compute and infrastructure purchase and lease commitments.

Big Tech dependency: Amazon, Google and Microsoft are simultaneously investors, suppliers, distribution partners and competitors.

Customer concentration: The five largest customers account for roughly 25% of revenue.

AI safety: Model failures, misuse and potentially catastrophic incidents create significant business and liability risks.

Corporate control: The seven co-founders retain 50.1% of voting power, limiting public shareholders' influence.

4. The real investment question
The bull case: exceptional AI talent, rapid growth and the potential to become a defining platform for the AI economy.

The bear case: enormous infrastructure commitments and capital requirements before durable profitability is proven.

My takeaway for entrepreneurs and investors:
I am an ultra-optimistic person about AI. 

I think it will be the game changer for every industry and it will 10x+ the economy in a decade.

And the leading companies will at least grow proportionately, but most probably many times over. 

We also need to think that Anthropic is arguably the most super intelligent company in the world right now. So, they are able to analyze and predict the future and that's why, they committed to invest over $800b by 2045.

I think rather than only becoming the electricity provider of the future, they can also become the factories and products of the future, which could 100x their revenue. What happens if Anthropic finds the cure for all diseases, builds robots, creates apps, etc. or they can acquire many AI startups as Google acquired many companies themselves. 

Anthropic can be many companies in 1. 

What do you think?

text:
Grok (xAI) on the simulation idea 🤯

The core idea
The strongest version comes from Nick Bostrom’s 2003 simulation argument (a trilemma, not a direct claim that we are simulated). At least one of these is true:

(1) Civilizations almost never reach a “posthuman” stage capable of running high-fidelity ancestor simulations.
(2) Posthuman civilizations that could run them are almost never interested in doing so.
(3) We are almost certainly living in a simulation.

If (1) and (2) are false, the sheer numerical dominance of simulated observers over base-reality ones would make (3) very likely. Elon Musk has endorsed versions of this for years. In 2016 he argued the odds of base reality are “one in billions” based on video-game progress from Pong to photorealistic multiplayer worlds. More recently he has offered looser figures (around 50% in one anecdote contrasting a physicist’s 0% with a computer scientist’s 100%, and “pretty high” elsewhere), sometimes adding that boring simulations would be truncated so interesting ones are more likely to persist.

Why I rate it low

Physical constraints are severe. A 2025 paper by astrophysicist Franco Vazza calculates the energy and information costs of simulating even a low-resolution Earth (compatible with high-energy neutrino observations) or the visible universe. The requirements are astronomically large and incompatible with a universe that has our physical laws and constants — far beyond what even extreme future technology could achieve inside a universe like ours. Full-resolution or Planck-scale versions are essentially impossible by known thermodynamics and information-energy limits. Only a simulating universe with radically different physics could manage it.

Bayesian treatments lower the odds. Astronomer David Kipping’s Bayesian analysis of Bostrom’s argument shows that once you properly account for the uncertainty about whether such simulations are even possible, the probability we are simulated is less than 50% (approaching 50% only in the limit of infinite simulations if they are possible). Creating our own simulations would update the odds upward sharply, but we have not done so.

No positive evidence. Physics works extraordinarily well under the assumption of base reality. There are no confirmed “glitches,” no clear computational artifacts at accessible scales, and no observations that demand a simulated explanation. Quantum mechanics, fine-tuning, and computational metaphors are interesting but have many non-simulation interpretations. The hypothesis makes no distinctive, testable predictions.

Priors on the assumptions are not high. Advanced civilizations might self-destruct, lose interest, face ethical barriers to simulating vast amounts of suffering, or find the computational cost (even with selective rendering or approximations) prohibitive. Nested simulations and infinite regress also complicate the simple “most minds are simulated” counting argument.

Tech progress (AI, quantum computing, better simulations) makes the possibility more thinkable than it was decades ago, and selective/approximate simulations of conscious agents could in principle be cheaper than full-universe physics. But possibility is not probability, and the concrete energy accounting and Bayesian results pull strongly against high confidence.

Bottom line
I would put the likelihood roughly in the 1%–15% range as a reasoned guess, leaning toward the lower end given the physical constraints and absence of evidence. The true uncertainty is enormous because the idea is hard to constrain empirically. Even if it were true, the practical implications are limited: science, engineering, ethics, and the project of understanding the universe (xAI’s focus) proceed the same way. We treat the world as real because that is the only workable approach and because it has been extraordinarily successful.

Mischa Barton found out her boyfriend had been filming their sex with hidden cameras only when the footage started being offered to porn companies. She says he secretly filmed her in bed and in the shower. And his friend, another one of her exes, copied the footage from his computer. Together they shopped the video for $500,000. Half a million was the asking price for her body. The court ordered both of them to stay 100 yards away from her.

Mischa Barton was Marissa on "The O.C.," one of the most recognizable actresses of the 2000s.

March 2017. A friend woke her up one morning: "Wake up. This is all over the press. And apparently all these porn sites are looking to buy it."

The video had been filmed over the past year. She says it was shot by her ex-boyfriend Jon Zacharias, with hidden cameras, in bed and in the shower. And his friend Adam Spaw, another ex of hers, copied the footage from his computer.

A few days later she held a press conference with her lawyer. "My absolute worst fear was realized. Someone I thought I loved and trusted was filming my most intimate and private moments, without my consent."

Later she told Dr. Phil she felt "very conned": "There's no way it wasn't premeditated if from the second you start seeing somebody they're doing that to you." And that it wasn't about money, but about controlling her.

The court granted her an emergency restraining order against both men. Anyone passing the video along was covered by it too.

Zacharias was ordered to stay 100 yards away from her permanently. Spaw agreed to the same for five years and promised not to sell the footage, but never admitted he had it. Zacharias's lawyer said he had no duty to apologize to her and that men can be victims of secret recording too.

"I look over my shoulder all the time when I'm walking," Mischa said. "He's intimidating. He's 6 foot 4."

Her body was priced at $500,000. The men who secretly filmed her were just told to stay away. Is that enough?

text:
Social platforms need to take more responsibility for the lives people have built on them.

Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn and others have become more than places to post pictures or connect with people. People have built businesses, careers, communities and entire livelihoods on these platforms.

Some have spent 10 or 15 years building an audience, only to wake up one day and find their accounts suspended.

Sometimes after mass reporting, sometimes for reasons they don’t understand.

And when they try to appeal? There is barely any human support. Just automated responses, endless forms and no one willing to properly review their case.

These platforms have made people build their lives online, yet offer little protection when things go wrong.

For many people, losing an account means losing customers, income, years of work and the identity they spent years building. It can have a serious emotional cost, too.

And it is often harder for people in Africa to get meaningful support.

If you invite over a billion people to build businesses, careers and communities on your platform, you have a responsibility to treat those investments with care.

Where is the accountability? Where is the human support? Where is the fair appeal process?

People should not lose years of their lives’ work because an automated system decided to take away their account.

text:
Anthropic is about to sell the public a trillion-dollar company controlled by 2 shares worth less than a penny.

And the people buying it will have almost no way to change anything that happens next.

I read the voting section of Anthropic's IPO filing, and I think it's the most one-sided deal ever offered to regular investors at this size:

There is exactly ONE Class F share. It belongs to an LLC owned by 7 of Anthropic's co-founders, and it carries 50.1% of all the votes.

There is exactly ONE Class T share. It belongs to Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust, and it elects a majority of the board.

If Anthropic were ever liquidated, each of those 2 shares would get its par value of $0.00001.

The public gets Class A shares instead. And Anthropic's own filing says this structure may effectively eliminate their ability to influence important decisions, including a sale of the company.

So here's what that means for anyone who buys:

- They can't replace the board if the company stumbles, because the trust picks the majority and the founders hold half the vote.
- They can't push for a sale, even if someone offers a huge premium.
- They can't stop the board from putting the mission ahead of their money. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, so the board has to weigh shareholders against the long-term benefit of humanity.
- And they can't easily sue over it. Delaware law requires at least 2% of the shares or $2 million worth of stock to bring that kind of claim.

This isn't some far-off hypothetical either.

The filing warns that slowing AI development for safety may not maximize stockholder value. It also says Anthropic recently paused training a next-generation model for more than a month over safety and security concerns.

A public shareholder would've had zero say in that pause.

And here's the part I can't get past:

Each co-founder has pledged to give 80% of their Anthropic equity to charity. The Class F vote stays at 50.1% no matter how much stock they still own.

So the founders can give away most of their money and keep all of their control.

Dario Amodei told 60 Minutes last year that he's deeply uncomfortable with AI decisions being made by a few companies and a few people. When he was asked who elected him, he said no one.

Now his company's IPO hands 50.1% of the votes to 7 people, and he's one of them.

And guess who's being lined up to buy it?

Anthropic has weighed reserving 15% to 20% of the IPO for individual investors, according to Bloomberg. JPMorgan is leading the US retail push, and Citigroup is handling retail buyers in places like Japan, Britain and Canada.

The same filing warns that AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.

So regular people are being asked to buy a company that says its product could threaten humanity, with no real vote on how it's run.

Anthropic's answer is that this is the whole point. The structure is built to keep Wall Street from pressuring it into cutting corners on safety. The trustees have no financial stake in the company. Google and Meta gave their founders control and still made shareholders rich. And every buyer gets all of this in writing before they buy.

But Zuckerberg's control comes from shares he owns, so when Meta's stock falls, he loses money too. Anthropic's 2 control shares can't lose anything.

Anyone buying this IPO is paying full price to hand control to 7 founders and 5 trustees.

They're desperate for money and they don't care about your money.

text:
No offense taken—I’m familiar with typical hospital talking points.

The claim that hospitals must inflate commercial prices because Medicare under-reimburses them doesn’t hold up. Key evidence:

Health Rosetta’s Transparent Open Networks shows ambulatory surgery centers and others routinely offer bundled, upfront prices 30–50% below typical PPO rates (and far below chargemaster) while netting comparable revenue. Savings come from less claims friction, faster payment, and lower administrative overhead. https://t.co/UcqhWKbyyI

Austin Frakt’s 2011 Milbank Quarterly review (“How Much Do Hospitals Cost Shift?”) and later work find little evidence of large, ongoing cost-shifting from Medicare shortfalls to commercial payers. Hospitals more often cut costs; market power and price discrimination explain far more of the gap.

CBO analysis and RAND hospital price transparency studies (commercial plans paid ~254% of Medicare rates in 2022) show commercial price variation tracks hospital market power, not the share of Medicare/Medicaid patients. Little of the markup is explained by “subsidizing” public payers.

Work by Martin Gaynor, Zack Cooper, and others shows consolidation and limited local competition drive higher commercial rates far more than any forced subsidy.

Cash-price models like the Surgery Center of Oklahoma show high-quality outpatient procedures can be delivered at a fraction of many hospital charges without relying on commercial overpayment to offset Medicare.

Data points more to market structure, opacity, and administrative costs than any inevitable need for employers to underwrite hospital inefficiencies.

text:
In 2000, Netflix offered to sell itself to Blockbuster for $50,000,000. Blockbuster had 9,000 stores and 84,300 employees at its peak. The men in that room laughed the offer out of the building. Ten years later Blockbuster was bankrupt. Netflix took in over $45 billion last year. Exactly one Blockbuster store is still open, in Bend, Oregon.

In the clip below, Netflix co-founder Marc Randolph describes the moment he gave them the number, and what the room did next.

Netflix in 2000 was tiny. It had about a hundred employees, it was two and a half years old, and it was on track to lose $50,000,000 that year.

Blockbuster was the giant. Six billion in revenue, stores in every town, more staff than most airlines.

Randolph and his partner Reed Hastings flew to Dallas to pitch a deal. Netflix would run the online side, Blockbuster would keep the stores. They'd rehearsed the whole thing on the way over.

Randolph remembers the Blockbuster executives in their expensive suits, him and Hastings in jeans and flip-flops. They made the pitch. Then came the question of how much. Hastings said fifty million.

Blockbuster laughed in their faces.

"The meeting went downhill pretty quickly after that," Randolph says. He remembers the flight home as long and quiet. All he could think was that now they'd have to beat them.

It took ten years. Blockbuster couldn't adapt to streaming and filed for bankruptcy in September 2010.

Randolph says the lesson stuck with him. You never know where the people who'll take you down come from. They rarely look like you.

One company laughed at a $50,000,000 offer. The other one spent a decade making sure they'd regret it.

Was Blockbuster blind, or just too big to believe a hundred kids in flip-flops could win?

text:
Crazy Hirono’s post is the political equivalent of a loyalty badge: the same sentence she’s been repeating since confirmation, now offered as self-evident truth because time has passed and he is still there.

No new incident. No operational failure. No changed standard. Just the original verdict restated. “He’s done nothing to prove me wrong” is not a finding; it is a refusal to update the premise. Unfitness was defined by her priors (media background, personal history, skepticism of certain social policies inside the force). Everything after that is scored as confirmation.

The selective application is the tell. Prior civilian leaders who treated the military as a vehicle for equity directives, public-health mandates, or messaging campaigns did not trigger the same perpetual “unfit” refrain from the Armed Services Committee. Outcomes, readiness reports, and retention numbers under those leaders were treated as downstream of larger forces. Under Hegseth the mere continuation of the job is treated as the problem.

This is low-cost signaling. It requires no vote, no hearing record, and no specific claim that can be checked against results. It simply keeps the original objection alive for an audience that already accepted it. The fact that the post contains nothing beyond the restatement is not an oversight; it is the feature.

text:
For thirty-one years, Mrs. Uno's job at our town's city hall was sending Japanese people to Mississippi.

Our town is a small fishing town on the coast of Mie. It has a sister city on the Gulf Coast. Every two years, Mrs. Uno put a group on a plane. Students. Farmers. The mayor. Whoever could get the week off.

When they came home, she made every one of them write a report. One page. What did you see?

She kept every single page. When she retired last spring, she let me read the box.

High school girl, 16. 2004.
"At the Friday football game, the man on the loudspeaker said my name. Five thousand people turned around and waved at me. I had been in America for nineteen hours."

Our mayor, 61. 1999.
"Their mayor answered his own phone. Then he cooked us breakfast. That night, he directed traffic after the football game. I asked him where his staff was. He pointed at his wife."

Firefighter, 44. 2008.
"Their fire chief put us on the truck for the Fourth of July parade. Every child on that street waved at us like we were their own firemen. I waved back for two miles. My arm hurt for three days. Best three days of my career."

Retired teacher, 70. 2016.
"I lost my reading glasses at the airport. Before we reached the hotel, three strangers had offered me theirs. I wore a stranger's glasses for five days. Wrong prescription. I saw Mississippi beautifully anyway."

Junior high boy, 14. 2012.
"My host father let me drive his truck in a field. I am fourteen. In Japan, this is a crime. In Mississippi, it is Tuesday."

The shortest report in the box is one sentence long.

Fisherman, 72. 2009.

Mr. Koda had never been on a plane. He only went because his wife made him. He spoke no English. His host was a shrimper named Clayton, also 72, who spoke no Japanese.

For five days, nobody translated anything.

At four every morning, they went out on Clayton's boat. They mended nets. Clayton's wife fed them both like she'd been feeding them for forty years. In the evenings, they sat on the dock and watched the water without saying a word, because neither of them had a word the other could use.

Mr. Koda's report, in its entirety:

"He is the same as me. I did not know there was another one."

On his last morning, he gave Clayton the only thing he had brought from home. His big-catch flag. Japanese fishermen fly them when they come home with a full boat. Bright red. Gold letters. A sea bream leaping out of the waves.

Every spring since, at the Blessing of the Fleet, when the priest stands on the dock and blesses the shrimp boats one by one, Clayton's boat has flown that flag.

The whole town calls it "the Japanese boat."

Nobody there can read the flag. Everybody knows what it means.

Mr. Koda died last year. He was 86.

Mrs. Uno called Mississippi. She didn't expect anything. She just thought Clayton should know.

Four days later, an old man in a faded feed-store cap walked out of the arrivals gate at Nagoya airport. He was 86. It was his first passport. He had the flag folded under his arm.

He sat through a Buddhist funeral where he didn't understand one word. He bowed when everyone bowed, half a second late, every time.

The next morning at dawn, when the boats went out, he stood on the harbor wall and held that flag over his head with both arms until the last boat was past the breakwater.

Eighty-six years old. The wind tried to take it from him the whole time.

He didn't let it.

Mrs. Uno asked him why he'd come all that way.

Clayton said, "Somebody had to come see his water."

Japan and America have almost 460 sister partnerships. Neither country has that many with anyone else on Earth.

The very first one was signed in 1955. St. Paul, Minnesota, and Nagasaki. Ten years after the war.

On paper, they're agreements between city halls.

They're not.

They're two old men who never shared a single word, standing on each other's docks.

text:
A 1st Century AD, ancient Roman fresco depicts a woman (often interpreted as a Muse) playing a lyre...

Room 30 of the Villa San Marco in Stabiae (modern-day Castellammare di Stabia, Italy)

. . . 

The lyre and its larger, professional cousin, kithara held a prominent place in Roman culture, myth, and political history. Adopted largely from Greek and Etruscan traditions, the instrument was woven into daily life, elite education, and famous historical legends.

In Greco-Roman myth, the lyre was invented by the young god Hermes, who crafted the first instrument from a tortoise shell, animal hide, and gut strings after stealing sacred cattle from Apollo. To appease Apollo, Hermes traded him the lyre. The instrument became Apollo’s defining attribute, symbolizing poetry, harmony, civilization, and the Muses.

Elite Roman children learned to play the lyre or kithara as part of a well-rounded classical education, which prioritized public speaking, literature, and philosophy. Private dinner parties, aristocratic gatherings, and domestic rituals frequently featured live lyre or kithara performances.

Emperor Nero was notoriously passionate about music and deeply wanted to be recognized as a master performer on the kithara. He even instituted Hellenic-style musical competitions and competed publicly. The most famous story involving a Roman lyre is the myth that Nero played his instrument while the city burned during the Great Fire of Rome in 64 CE. Historians like Tacitus, Suetonius, and Dio Cassius note that Nero was actually outside Rome when the fire started, though rumors and political enemies claimed he performed a lament (or recited an epic poem about the fall of Troy) dressed in theatrical or cithara-player garb. Furthermore, the violin ("fiddle") did not exist yet; if he played anything, it would have been a lyre or cithara.

. . .

In ancient Rome, enslaved women skilled in playing the lyre were highly prized entertainers known as psaltriae or citharistriae. Wealthy households purchased or trained these musicians to provide atmosphere at private banquets (convivia) and public celebrations, blending Greek artistic traditions into Roman elite culture.

The evening air in the triclinium smelled of roasted peacock, spiced wine, and damp marble. Lyra knelt on a woven reed mat near the bronze brazier, her fingers resting lightly against the sheep-gut strings of her maple-wood cithara. At seventeen, she had spent ten years in the villa of Senator Quintus Valerius, ever since a merchant brought her from the markets of Corinth.

Around the three low dining couches, men draped in white togas reclined on silk cushions, their laughter growing louder as the third course arrived. In Roman society, a slave musician was meant to be an extension of the room's decoration—audible, pleasant, and entirely invisible.
"A lively tune, girl," Valerius called out, waving a silver goblet without looking in her direction. "Something from Alexandria. My guests grow dull."

Lyra bowed her head and began to pluck a bright, cascading melody. While her right hand swept the tortoiseshell plectrum across the strings, her left fingers pressed and dampened the notes with practiced precision. Her eyes stayed fixed on the mosaic floor, yet she missed nothing. She heard the whispered deals over grain shipments in Ostia, the veiled threats between rival magistrates, and the drunken boasts of young patricians.

In the corner, an older freedman—once a Greek tutor—caught her eye and offered a barely perceptible nod of appreciation for her tempo. For a fleeting second, the music belonged not to the senator or his guests, but to her. Every clean harmonic note was a quiet reminder of a homeland she barely remembered and a mind that remained her own, even when her body did not.

text:
Every man in a small town in Oklahoma has one crooked sideburn.

The left one.

On purpose.

Let me explain.

My wife's uncle Kenichi is a barber. In 1989, in Osaka, he cut the hair of an American woman who was teaching English there. He did it badly. She came back four times to complain.

They got married in 1990. She took him home to her town in Oklahoma. Population: about 4,000.

He opened a barbershop on Main Street. Within a month, the whole town was calling him Kenny.

Here is what Oklahoma did not know about Japanese barbers.

In Japan, a man's haircut takes an hour. The cut. The shampoo. A hot towel. A shave. Your face, your forehead, and your ears. Yes, the ears. Then a shoulder massage. Then a small bow.

Kenny's first customer was a cattleman named Dub. He asked for "just a trim."

Fifty-eight minutes later, Dub sat up, touched his own ear, and said:

"Son. Nobody has ever touched my ears. Not even my wife."

He tipped twenty dollars and drove straight to the feed store to tell everybody.

By Friday, men were driving in from Tulsa for the ears.

Thirty-five years later, here is what Kenny says Oklahoma taught him about running a barbershop.

The TV stays on the Weather Channel. Nobody watches it. Everybody needs it on.

The three chairs by the window are not for customers. They are for men who are not getting a haircut. One of them has been not getting a haircut since 1997.

Never cut a boy's hair the week of homecoming without written permission from his mother.

Never say a word about the Sooners in front of a Cowboys man. Or the other way around. If you're not sure who you're cutting, talk about the weather. It's on.

When a little boy gets his first haircut, save a lock of it in an envelope for his mother. Kenny has filled over a thousand envelopes. Some of those boys are grandfathers now.

Then, four years ago, Kenny's hands started to shake.

Parkinson's. He was seventy.

The haircuts started coming out wrong. Mostly the left sideburn. Crooked, every time.

Kenny did what a Japanese man does. He taped a sign in the window.

"I am very sorry. My hands are not good anymore. I will close at the end of the month. Thank you for 31 years."

Nobody let him close.

That Saturday, there was a line out the door.

Dub was first. He sat down and said, "Ears, too."

Kenny's wife stood behind him and held his wrist for the ears. She still does.

The left sideburn came out crooked. Dub looked in the mirror for a long time.

"Perfect," he said.

It kept happening. The pastor. The bank manager. The sheriff. Every one of them walked out with one crooked sideburn. Not one of them fixed it.

Last fall, a young guy from the city opened a fancy barbershop out on the highway. He offered a free "cleanup" to anybody from Kenny's shop.

Nobody went.

A teenager at the gas station explained it to him. "Nah, man. That's a Kenny."

Homecoming week, the high school football team came in. All 44 boys. With 44 signed permission slips from 44 mothers.

In the team photo, every single boy has one crooked sideburn.

The left one.

In Japan, a crooked haircut is a mistake.

In that town, it's a membership card.

Kenny is 74. He still cuts hair three days a week. His wife still holds his wrist for the ears.

Dub is 88. He says the ears are still perfect.

He would know. Nobody else has ever touched them.

text:
Hedge Funds Are Moving Into Sports Betting and Offering Salaries of Up to $260,000!

Sports betting may offer more opportunities to identify short-term market inefficiencies than many people realize. And Wall Street is starting to take notice.

One of the people behind this growing interest is Cliff Asness, billionaire, PhD in finance, and co-founder of AQR Capital Management, an investment firm managing enormous amounts of institutional capital.

In November 2025, he appeared on Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast and openly stated that AQR was exploring the possibility of entering sports betting.

His words were:

"We are considering and looking at it."

In other words, one of the world's best-known quantitative investors has started looking at sports betting and prediction markets.

But what exactly are they trying to do?

They are not interested in traditional recreational betting. They are interested in the mathematics behind the odds.

The idea is relatively simple:

Collect massive amounts of data on matches and players.
Develop statistical models that estimate the true probabilities of outcomes.
Compare their own probability estimates with market odds.
Identify situations where the market misprices probabilities.
Exploit pricing discrepancies and market inefficiencies.

Essentially, it is what quantitative hedge funds have been doing in financial markets for decades, except that sports events are now part of the equation.

And then comes the even more interesting part.

In March 2026, AQR advertised a position:

Quantitative Research – Prediction Markets VP.

They were looking for someone to develop mathematical and statistical models for trading in professional sports markets.

The requirements included:
At least 6 years of experience in data analysis and model development.
A background in mathematics, statistics, computer science, or a related field.
Strong programming skills and experience building predictive models.
Knowledge of sports rules and sports analytics.

Advertised annual base salary: $235,000–$260,000, with potential bonuses.

They are looking for a quantitative researcher who understands mathematics, statistics, programming, and market dynamics.

Perhaps we are witnessing an interesting shift: sports betting is gradually becoming a serious field of quantitative trading.

The question is how long traditional bookmakers will maintain their edge against people who view odds as financial instruments rather than relying on feelings or intuition

text:
Nov 10, 1865: Henry Wirz was hanged in Washington for what happened at Andersonville, the deadliest prison camp of the Civil War. He was one of only two Confederates executed for war crimes, and people still argue about whether he deserved it.

He was born Heinrich Hartmann Wirz in Zurich, Switzerland, in 1823. He got into legal trouble over money there and left for America in 1849. He worked as a doctor's assistant and called himself a physician, eventually settling in Louisiana.

When the war came, he enlisted in a Louisiana regiment. At the Battle of Seven Pines in 1862, his right arm was shattered by a bullet. It never healed properly and caused him pain for the rest of his life. Unfit for the front lines, he was assigned to work in the Confederate prison system.

Early in the war, the two sides exchanged prisoners regularly. By 1863 that system had broken down. The Confederacy refused to exchange Black Union soldiers as prisoners of war, and later Grant saw that keeping Confederate prisoners locked up hurt the South more than the North. Prisoners started piling up with nowhere to go.

In early 1864, the Confederacy built a new prison in the middle of southwest Georgia, officially called Camp Sumter. Everyone called it Andersonville. It wasn't a building. It was an open field surrounded by a log wall about 15 feet high. There were no barracks. Prisoners built shelters out of blankets, sticks, and holes dug in the dirt.

In April 1864, Wirz was put in command of the inside of the prison.

It was meant to hold around 10,000 men. By August 1864, about 33,000 were crammed inside, roughly 26 acres. At its peak it held more people than all but a few cities in the Confederacy.

A small creek ran through the middle of the stockade. It was the prisoners' main supply of drinking water, and also their sewer. Upstream, the Confederate guards' camp and cookhouse fouled it before it even reached them. The ground around it turned into a swamp of filth.

The food was coarse cornmeal, often ground with the cob, sometimes raw, sometimes not at all. Men starved. Scurvy rotted their gums and swelled their legs. Dysentery and gangrene killed thousands. In the summer of 1864, more than 100 men died on some days.

About 19 feet inside the wall was a line of posts and railing called the deadline. Any prisoner who crossed it, or even reached across it, could be shot by guards in the towers.

Gangs of prisoners, known as the Raiders, robbed, beat, and sometimes killed other prisoners for their food and blankets. The other prisoners organized and fought back. With Wirz's permission, they held their own trial and hanged six of the Raiders inside the stockade.

In about 14 months, roughly 45,000 Union soldiers passed through Andersonville. Nearly 13,000 of them died.

A young prisoner from Connecticut named Dorence Atwater was given the job of keeping the official list of the dead. Afraid it would be lost or destroyed, he secretly made his own copy and smuggled it out. After the war, he and Clara Barton went to Andersonville and used his list to mark the graves of nearly 13,000 men. That ground is now Andersonville National Cemetery.

When the war ended, the North was furious. As photos of skeleton-thin survivors spread, people demanded someone pay. Wirz's commander, Gen. John Winder, had died in early 1865. Wirz was arrested at Andersonville in May.

He was tried before a military commission in Washington led by Gen. Lew Wallace, who later wrote the novel Ben-Hur. The trial lasted about two months. Former prisoners testified that Wirz had shot, beaten, and killed men himself, and set dogs on escapees. Some of the testimony was powerful. Some of it fell apart. One of the key witnesses turned out to be a deserter testifying under a fake name. Wirz's lawyers argued that with his crippled arm, he could never have done some of what he was accused of, and that he had begged his superiors for more food and supplies.

He was convicted and sentenced to death.

According to his lawyer, the night before his execution, a man came to his cell and offered to spare his life if he would testify that Jefferson Davis was responsible for what happened at Andersonville. Wirz refused, saying Davis had nothing to do with it.

On the morning of Nov 10 he was led to a gallows in the yard of the Old Capitol Prison, on the site where the Supreme Court building stands today. Soldiers in the crowd chanted the name Andersonville. He reportedly told the officer in charge that he knew what orders were, and that he was being hanged for obeying them. The trapdoor dropped, but his neck didn't break. He slowly strangled to death.

Ever since, Andersonville has been argued over. Some see Wirz as a cruel man who earned his fate. Others see a minor officer blamed for the failures of a collapsing Confederacy that couldn't feed its own soldiers. Union prisons were deadly too. At the camp in Elmira, New York, about a quarter of the Confederate prisoners died.

What isn't argued over is what the men inside went through. Andersonville is now a national historic site, home to the National Prisoner of War Museum, which honors American POWs from every war. In the national cemetery there, nearly 13,000 headstones stand in tight rows, so close together they almost touch, the way the men were buried.

text:
**Ayo Kayla Fires Back Amid Social Media Storm Over Missing Texas Mom Christin Munn-Holliday: “Stop Connecting Me to That S**t”**

Missing Lost And Trafficked 
Lured Lost And Unsolved 

Lafayette, La.-Online accusations are swirling around a woman known as Ayo Kayla in connection with the high-profile disappearance of 22-year-old Texas mother Christin “Chrissy” Munn-Holliday, who vanished after a crash on Louisiana’s Atchafalaya Basin Bridge. In a series of Facebook posts and comments, Ayo Kayla has strongly denied any involvement and shared details she says she received from Sandrea Davis — the woman arrested in connection with the crash — about what happened that night.

Munn-Holliday, a mother from the Katy area near Houston, was last seen in the early morning hours of September 30, 2026, after a two-vehicle crash on eastbound Interstate 10 near milepost 128 in Iberville Parish. Authorities believe she was driving one of the vehicles involved. Witnesses reported seeing a woman matching her description walk away from the scene. Her gray BMW was left abandoned on the bridge. Her phone briefly pinged in the area before going silent. A wig recovered near the site was later confirmed through DNA testing to belong to her. Search efforts involving Louisiana State Police, local agencies, the United Cajun Navy, and volunteers have continued for weeks without locating her. Her family has offered a substantial reward for information leading to her safe return.

Sandrea Davis, 21, was arrested in late October and charged with reckless operation with accident in connection with the crash. Court documents and reports indicate her vehicle’s data recorder showed she was traveling at approximately 105 mph. Louisiana State Police have emphasized that the charge relates to the crash itself and that Davis has not been charged in connection with Munn-Holliday’s disappearance. The missing-person investigation remains active and is being led by the Harris County Sheriff’s Office in coordination with Louisiana authorities.

On social media, users have linked Ayo Kayla to the case, with some accusing her of trying to clear Davis’s name or knowing more about Munn-Holliday’s fate. In an October 6 post, Ayo Kayla pushed back forcefully:

“Now seriously yall over doing it with the Ayo Kayla situation I wasn’t near Louisiana still not when this happen im at work been here I found out my friend was involved in a accident 2 days before the missing person post happen I was late knowing about the accident myself all I did was came under saying they didn’t know she was missing STOP CONNECTING ME TO THAT SHI SERIOUSLY! Yall wanted info I gave the info I was told stop attaching me to some shit I’m miles away from deadass serious yall annoying! All yall want to be damn investigators and police let them ppl do that job and bring that girl home and find out what really happen.”

In comment threads, Ayo Kayla has shared additional details she attributes to conversations with Davis (referred to as “Sandy”). According to those posts, Davis said she was knocked out by the airbags and only heard a voice asking if she was okay; she did not see who it was and suggested it might have been people on the phone. Ayo Kayla further stated that Davis has a smart car that automatically calls police, and that around the time the occupants got out of the vehicle, “only a white man was there checking on them.” She added that Davis could not describe the person or identify who asked if she was okay because she only heard a voice.

These claims have drawn sharp pushback. Commenters questioned the consistency of the account (noting that someone knocked out by airbags would have difficulty hearing and recalling a voice). Others, including a user posting under the name Breezy Lashay, have publicly called for Ayo Kayla to “come to the front,” accusing her of attempting to clear Davis’s name while allegedly knowing Davis had involvement in Munn-Holliday’s disappearance. Screenshots of the exchanges have been widely shared under hashtags such as #whereischrissy and #findchrissy.

Ayo Kayla has limited comments on some of her posts and continues to insist she was not in Louisiana, was at work, and has no connection to the events beyond relaying information she says she was told. No official statements from law enforcement have named Ayo Kayla or confirmed the details she attributes to Davis. The investigation into both the crash and Munn-Holliday’s disappearance remains ongoing.

Anyone with information is urged to contact Crime Stoppers or the relevant law enforcement agencies.

text:
Democrats won control of the governorship and both legislative chambers in five swing states last week: Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Arizona, and Nevada. Those victories could give Democrats a path to reshaping how the U.S. elects its president as soon as 2028, potentially awarding the presidency to the winner of the national popular vote rather than the traditional Electoral College contest.

A constitutional amendment would be required to abolish the Electoral College, which is highly unlikely. But the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact offers another route: Participating states agree to award their electoral votes to the national popular vote winner once the compact’s members collectively control at least 270 electoral votes, the number needed to win the presidency.

Currently, 18 states and Washington, D.C., have joined the compact, representing 222 electoral votes. If all five swing states joined, they would add 61 votes, bringing the total to 283 — enough to activate the agreement.

Lawmakers in all five states have previously introduced legislation to join, though passage is far from guaranteed. Nevada’s Democratic governor vetoed the measure in 2019, while Michigan’s Democratic-controlled legislature failed to pass it during the state’s 2023–24 Democratic trifecta.

For the compact to apply to the 2028 election, participating states would need to reach the 270-vote threshold before July 20, 2028.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender, said over the weekend that he would work with the newly Democratic-controlled legislature to advance the national popular vote effort.

Under the current system, a candidate can win the most votes nationwide but lose the presidency, like Al Gore (2000) and Hillary Clinton (2016). Supporters argue the compact would give every vote equal weight and encourage candidates to campaign beyond a handful of battleground states.

Opponents argue that the Electoral College protects smaller states’ and minority communities’ influence. Some legal experts also argue the compact needs congressional approval, and any attempt to implement it would likely face legal challenges.

Fictional Obituary: James “Logan” Howlett / Wolverine, Marvel Comics (Spoilers)

James Howlett, known to his friends as Logan and to the wider world as Wolverine, has died in Paradise Valley, Nevada, while preventing further human experimentation at a laboratory operated by Dr. Abraham Cornelius. He was encased in adamantium after breaking the apparatus being used on the captives. Having recently lost his healing ability, he could not survive. His life spanned more than a century.

Born in Alberta, Canada, in the late nineteenth century, Logan spent much of his early life far from the teams and schools with which he would eventually be associated. Family tragedy drove him from his childhood home. He worked, traveled and fought under different names, building a history that would later become difficult even for him to reconstruct.

His mutant abilities included heightened senses, retractable claws and an extraordinary capacity to recover from injury. That healing also slowed his aging, allowing him to outlive people and places that had once formed the center of his life.

The Weapon X program subjected him to experiments that bonded adamantium to his skeleton. The procedure made him more dangerous, but the injuries done to him extended beyond his body. Manipulated memories and years of exploitation left him struggling to recover his past and decide what he would do with the life that remained.

After serving the Canadian government, Logan joined the X-Men at the invitation of Charles Xavier. He became one of the team's most dependable fighters, although rarely its easiest colleague. He was blunt, stubborn and prepared to use lethal force when others would not. His work also took him into the Avengers and covert operations whose consequences followed him long after the missions ended.

Those who knew him outside combat saw a wider life. He developed close friendships with teammates including Ororo Munroe, Kurt Wagner and Piotr Rasputin. Japan became an important home to him, and his relationship with Mariko Yashida remained one of the great attachments of his life. Her death was among the losses he carried through the years that followed.

Logan also became a mentor to younger mutants, including Kitty Pryde and Jubilee. He helped Laura Kinney, who had likewise been raised and used as a weapon, find a place among people who could offer her another kind of life. Eventually, he helped establish the Jean Grey School for Higher Learning and served as its headmaster. The responsibilities of teaching and protecting children became a substantial part of his later years.

His last journey began with a bounty placed on him after the loss of his healing factor. The search took him through familiar territory and old enemies before leading him to Cornelius, one of the men involved in the experiments that had changed his own body.

At the Nevada laboratory, Logan found others facing a similar procedure. He stopped the adamantium from being forced into them, taking the metal over his own body instead. Before it hardened completely, he ensured the captives were safe and pursued Cornelius. He died outside the facility, looking toward the setting sun.

Among those he leaves behind are his son, Akihiro, also known as Daken; Laura Kinney; generations of students; and friends in the X-Men and Avengers. Many had known him simply as Logan, the man who could be difficult to live with and difficult to imagine living without.
