(Photo by Milo Mitchell) November 9, 2026 By Denise Heady, MA 7 min read When Jamil Newirth was just 32 years old, doctors told him he had terminal brain cancer and had about 17 months to live.  That was 14 years ago.  Today, at 46, the Hawaii native is a practicing attorney in Maui, a future he once feared he would never have. He credits his remarkable survival in part to a novel cancer vaccine developed at UCLA that uses the body's own immune system to recognize and attack brain tumors.  Newirth is among a group of patients who have experienced long-term survival after receiving the personalized vaccine through clinical trials led by UCLA neurosurgeon Linda Liau, MD, PhD and tumor immunologist Robert Prins, PhD.  For more than two decades, Dr. Liau and her team at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have been working to develop new treatments for glioblastoma, the most aggressive and deadly form of brain cancer. Their work is now helping shape the next generation of cancer vaccines and combination immunotherapies that could offer new hope for patients facing this devastating disease.  "Patients like Jamil are such an inspiration to me and my team," said Dr. Liau, chair of neurosurgery at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. "He and other patients like him are what inspires me to go to work each day and to maintain hope that immunotherapy could potentially lead to a cure for brain cancer someday."  A devastating diagnosis In 2012, Newirth had just graduated from the University of Hawaii William S. Richardson School of Law and was preparing for the bar exam when he began experiencing severe headaches.  After multiple emergency room visits, where his symptoms were initially attributed to stress, he developed nausea, vomiting and numbness on the left side of his body. An MRI eventually revealed a large brain tumor. He was diagnosed with glioblastoma.  Glioblastoma grows and spreads quickly.  Even after standard treatments such as surgery, chemotherapy and radiation, the disease almost always returns.  "I wasn't really given any hope when I was diagnosed," Newirth recalled.  📷 Jamil Newirth found Dr. Linda Liau when he was searching for neurosurgeons investigating new treatments for glioblastoma. (Photo by Milo Mitchell) Determined to find another option, he began searching for a neurosurgeon who could offer something beyond standard treatment. That search led him to Dr. Liau, who was enrolling patients in a clinical trial testing the first personalized brain cancer vaccine.  "Dr. Liau is confident, caring and does everything with a personal touch," Newirth said. "She even flew back early from her vacation to do my surgery and start my treatment. You can tell she just really cares."  Teaching the immune system to fight brain cancer One of the biggest challenges in treating glioblastoma and other malignant brain tumors is that the tumors are particularly effective at evading the immune system. Unlike some other cancers, these tumors often contain relatively few of the immune cells (also known as killer T cells) needed to recognize and attack cancer.  Dr. Liau and Dr. Prins have spent years investigating whether a personalized vaccine could help overcome that barrier.  The vaccine, an autologous tumor lysate-pulsed dendritic cell vaccination (ATL-DC) known as DCVax-L, was developed to help overcome this challenge by teaching the body to recognize proteins found in a patient's tumor.  To create the vaccine, initially developed at UCLA, researchers collect tumor tissue removed during surgery and isolate immune cells called dendritic cells generated from the patient's own blood. These cells act as messengers for the immune system, helping it identify threats.  In the laboratory, the dendritic cells are exposed to proteins from the patient's tumor, essentially training them to recognize and attack the cancer. When the cells are injected back into the patient, they help activate an immune response directed against the tumor.  Unlike traditional vaccines, which are typically given to prevent disease, this therapeutic vaccine is designed to help the immune system fight an existing cancer.  The approach is especially promising because each vaccine is tailored to the individual patient's tumor.  “This is a personalized vaccine that we developed and have spearheaded all the way from the initial preclinical studies to the original first-in-human clinical trial, to newer work testing novel formulations of the vaccine combined with adjuvants and immune checkpoint blockade,” said Dr. Prins.  For Newirth, the experimental treatment offered a possibility that conventional therapies alone could not guarantee.  While undergoing treatment, Newirth continued studying for the bar exam and ultimately passed. He credits the innovative research from Dr. Liau and her team for saving his life.  And he is not alone.  So far, approximately two dozen patients who received the vaccine through clinical trials have become long-term survivors. Their experiences are particularly meaningful for a disease where survival beyond five years remains uncommon.  However, the vaccine does not benefit everyone, and researchers are still working to understand why some patients respond more favorably than others.  “There is a significant subgroup of patients who have lived more than five years,” Dr. Liau says. “But the challenge is trying to determine which patients it may work for and for which patients it doesn’t. Each new discovery gets us closer to improving survival and quality of life for patients facing this devastating disease.”  Building on the promise of cancer vaccines The encouraging responses seen in some patients have helped shape the next phase of Dr. Liau's research.  Rather than relying on the vaccine alone, her team is now investigating whether combining it with other immunotherapies could produce stronger and more lasting responses.  One approach involves pairing the vaccine with immune checkpoint inhibitors, a class of drugs that helps immune cells overcome signals that prevent them from attacking cancer.  Although checkpoint inhibitors have transformed treatment for several cancers, they have shown limited success against glioblastoma when used alone. One reason may be that brain tumors often lack sufficient numbers of cancer-fighting T cells for these drugs to activate.  The vaccine could help address that problem by first teaching the immune system to recognize the tumor and drawing cancer-fighting T cells into it. Checkpoint inhibitors could then enhance the function of those T cells within the tumor and help them remain active. How personalized vaccines are changing the fight against brain cancer
UCLA researchers are advancing cancer vaccines that train the immune system to recognize and attack brain tumors, offering new possibilities for patients diagnosed with one of the deadliest forms of cancer
📷
Dr. Linda Liau examines clinical trial patient Jamil Newirth. (Photo by Milo Mitchell)
November 9, 2026
By Denise Heady, MA
7 min read
When Jamil Newirth was just 32 years old, doctors told him he had terminal brain cancer and had about 17 months to live.

That was 14 years ago.

Today, at 46, the Hawaii native is a practicing attorney in Maui, a future he once feared he would never have. He credits his remarkable survival in part to a novel cancer vaccine developed at UCLA that uses the body's own immune system to recognize and attack brain tumors.

Newirth is among a group of patients who have experienced long-term survival after receiving the personalized vaccine through clinical trials led by UCLA neurosurgeon Linda Liau, MD, PhD and tumor immunologist Robert Prins, PhD.

For more than two decades, Dr. Liau and her team at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have been working to develop new treatments for glioblastoma, the most aggressive and deadly form of brain cancer. Their work is now helping shape the next generation of cancer vaccines and combination immunotherapies that could offer new hope for patients facing this devastating disease.

"Patients like Jamil are such an inspiration to me and my team," said Dr. Liau, chair of neurosurgery at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. "He and other patients like him are what inspires me to go to work each day and to maintain hope that immunotherapy could potentially lead to a cure for brain cancer someday."

A devastating diagnosis
In 2012, Newirth had just graduated from the University of Hawaii William S. Richardson School of Law and was preparing for the bar exam when he began experiencing severe headaches.

After multiple emergency room visits, where his symptoms were initially attributed to stress, he developed nausea, vomiting and numbness on the left side of his body. An MRI eventually revealed a large brain tumor. He was diagnosed with glioblastoma.

Glioblastoma grows and spreads quickly.  Even after standard treatments such as surgery, chemotherapy and radiation, the disease almost always returns.

"I wasn't really given any hope when I was diagnosed," Newirth recalled.

📷
Jamil Newirth found Dr. Linda Liau when he was searching for neurosurgeons investigating new treatments for glioblastoma. (Photo by Milo Mitchell)
Determined to find another option, he began searching for a neurosurgeon who could offer something beyond standard treatment. That search led him to Dr. Liau, who was enrolling patients in a clinical trial testing the first personalized brain cancer vaccine.

"Dr. Liau is confident, caring and does everything with a personal touch," Newirth said. "She even flew back early from her vacation to do my surgery and start my treatment. You can tell she just really cares."

Teaching the immune system to fight brain cancer
One of the biggest challenges in treating glioblastoma and other malignant brain tumors is that the tumors are particularly effective at evading the immune system. Unlike some other cancers, these tumors often contain relatively few of the immune cells (also known as killer T cells) needed to recognize and attack cancer.

Dr. Liau and Dr. Prins have spent years investigating whether a personalized vaccine could help overcome that barrier.

The vaccine, an autologous tumor lysate-pulsed dendritic cell vaccination (ATL-DC) known as DCVax-L, was developed to help overcome this challenge by teaching the body to recognize proteins found in a patient's tumor.

To create the vaccine, initially developed at UCLA, researchers collect tumor tissue removed during surgery and isolate immune cells called dendritic cells generated from the patient's own blood. These cells act as messengers for the immune system, helping it identify threats.

In the laboratory, the dendritic cells are exposed to proteins from the patient's tumor, essentially training them to recognize and attack the cancer. When the cells are injected back into the patient, they help activate an immune response directed against the tumor.

Unlike traditional vaccines, which are typically given to prevent disease, this therapeutic vaccine is designed to help the immune system fight an existing cancer.

The approach is especially promising because each vaccine is tailored to the individual patient's tumor.

“This is a personalized vaccine that we developed and have spearheaded all the way from the initial preclinical studies to the original first-in-human clinical trial, to newer work testing novel formulations of the vaccine combined with adjuvants and immune checkpoint blockade,” said Dr. Prins.

For Newirth, the experimental treatment offered a possibility that conventional therapies alone could not guarantee.

While undergoing treatment, Newirth continued studying for the bar exam and ultimately passed. He credits the innovative research from Dr. Liau and her team for saving his life.

And he is not alone.

So far, approximately two dozen patients who received the vaccine through clinical trials have become long-term survivors. Their experiences are particularly meaningful for a disease where survival beyond five years remains uncommon.

However, the vaccine does not benefit everyone, and researchers are still working to understand why some patients respond more favorably than others.

“There is a significant subgroup of patients who have lived more than five years,” Dr. Liau says. “But the challenge is trying to determine which patients it may work for and for which patients it doesn’t. Each new discovery gets us closer to improving survival and quality of life for patients facing this devastating disease.”

Building on the promise of cancer vaccines
The encouraging responses seen in some patients have helped shape the next phase of Dr. Liau's research.

Rather than relying on the vaccine alone, her team is now investigating whether combining it with other immunotherapies could produce stronger and more lasting responses.

One approach involves pairing the vaccine with immune checkpoint inhibitors, a class of drugs that helps immune cells overcome signals that prevent them from attacking cancer.

Although checkpoint inhibitors have transformed treatment for several cancers, they have shown limited success against glioblastoma when used alone. One reason may be that brain tumors often lack sufficient numbers of cancer-fighting T cells for these drugs to activate.

The vaccine could help address that problem by first teaching the immune system to recognize the tumor and drawing cancer-fighting T cells into it. Checkpoint inhibitors could then enhance the function of those T cells within the tumor and help them remain active.

Dr. Liau’s team is also investigating which treatments work best together, and the order in which they should be given. Researchers hope that understanding how to sequence these treatments could make them more effective against tumors that have historically resisted immunotherapy.

“Because of the heterogeneity of glioblastoma, I don’t think there is going to be one drug or one treatment that is going to be effective for all patients. The future of glioblastoma treatments is going to be these combination approaches,” said Dr. Liau.

Scientists are also exploring other types of cancer vaccines, including vaccines designed to target specific genetic mutations found in brain tumors.

Some newer vaccines are designed to target molecular features shared by patients with the same type of cancer. This approach could help researchers develop treatments for specific groups of patients without needing to identify unique targets from each person's tumor.

Building on this research, UCLA neurosurgeon Anthony Wang, MD, director of the Pediatric Brain Tumor Program at UCLA Health, is leading a clinical trial testing a new vaccine for a rare and aggressive type of brain cancer called H3 G34-mutant diffuse hemispheric glioma, which primarily affects adolescents and young adults. The vaccine targets abnormal proteins produced by changes in how tumor cells process genetic information, with the goal of helping the immune system recognize and attack the cancer.

Developed in collaboration with Dr. Liau and Dr. Prins, the vaccine uses patients' own dendritic cells to activate an immune response against these tumor-specific targets. The first-in-human trial is designed to evaluate the vaccine's safety and explore whether it can generate a lasting immune response against the cancer.

More time, more possibilities
For Dr. Liau, the long-term survivors who have emerged from these clinical trials offer an important reason to keep pushing forward. Each patient provides valuable insight into how the immune system responds to brain cancer and how future treatments might be improved.

Her goal is to build on those discoveries so that more patients can benefit from treatments that once seemed out of reach.

For Newirth, the opportunity to participate in a clinical trial changed the course of his life. Fourteen years after being told he had little time left, he has built a life and career that once seemed impossible.

“The hope is that stories like Newirth's will one day become less of an exception and more of a reality for patients facing brain cancer,” said Dr. Liau.

text:
Cops offered Brian Laundrie a night in a hotel. He joked about getting a ride to Delicate Arch instead. About 2 weeks later, Gabby Petito was dead.

In the video below, Brian Laundrie stands next to his white van on a roadside outside Moab, Utah, on August 12, 2021, and talks to the officers who just pulled him and Gabby over.

They were 4 or 5 months into a cross-country van trip that Gabby was filming for her travel channel. A 911 caller had reported a man hitting a woman in the van. Officers saw scratches on Brian's face, decided that 22-year-old Gabby was the "primary aggressor," and told 23-year-old Brian that he was legally the victim.

When an officer asks whether he wants to press charges, Brian says, "I'm not going to pursue anything. I love her. It's just a little squabble." When they talk about splitting the couple up for the night, he jokes, "You want to drive me to Delicate Arch?" A minute later he adds that now he "can't go camping."

Nobody was charged. Gabby kept the van, Brian got a hotel room, and the trip went on.

In September Gabby's family reported her missing. Her body was found on September 19 at a campsite near Grand Teton National Park. The coroner ruled she died from blunt-force injuries to the head and neck, with manual strangulation. Brian had already driven her van back to his parents' home in Florida, then disappeared. His remains were found on October 20 in a Florida nature reserve, next to a notebook in which, according to the FBI, he wrote that he was responsible for her death. He was never tried.

1 traffic stop. 38 days until her body was found. 69 days until his. 0 trials.

Should the Moab police have arrested someone that day, or was there no way to know where this was heading?

text:
It's hard to imagine that just over a year ago Laura & I departed Lighthouse Baptist Church of Oakdale, where in the role of interim pastor I helped them secure a pastor after serving them for 10 months. We relocated to Frankfort, Kentucky, where we had been invited to stay in the home of dear friends. We visited relatives and friends along the way. Just after arriving in Frankfort, I was invited to preach at Latham Baptist Church of Latham, Illinois, which was without a pastor; the people promptly invited me to remain as interim pastor.

The church provided us a lovely parsonage. After 8 months, God gave them a permanent pastor (Noah Gibson, son of Pastor Maury Gibson of Arkansas).

I then got to preach in Michgan at the end of May and in Maine at the beginning of June. West Sumner Baptist Church of Sumner, Maine, invited me to remain as interim pastor. They provided us a beautiful parsonage. After 4 months, we left them in the hands of a permanent pastor, Trey Dillon.

God used another friend to offer us residence at a gorgeous, furnished house he owns in Branson, Missouri.

As we traveled from Maine to Missouri, Pastor Noah Gibson invited me to return to Latham Baptist Church and preach for them again (Sunday, October 11). That was a joy!

We arrived in Branson on Tuesday, October 13.  

We visited Calvary Baptist Church of Branson on Wednesday the 14th. I preached at Lighthouse Baptist Church of Fayetteville, Arkansas, on Sunday the 18th. We returned to Calvary on the 21st. We visited Talking Rocks Road Baptist Church (Pastor Delbert Davis) and Branson Baptist Church (Pastor David Wagner) on Sunday the 25th.

On Friday, October 30, Laura & I departed Branson, Missouri, in a rental vehicle, headed for California. 

On Sunday, November 1, we visited Solid Rock Baptist Church of Grand Island, Nebraska (Pastor Jeremy Reagan), which we thoroughly enjoyed!

Last Thursday (November 5) we arrived in Lodi, California, located between Stockton and Sacramento. On Friday we returned our rental vehicle and retrieved our 2008 Lincoln Town Car from Pastor Dave Packard (Big Valley Baptist Church of Lodi), who has been kindly holding it for us for the past year.

This past Sunday (November 8), I preached at the truly outstanding Central Valley Baptist Church of Manteca, California (Pastor Chris Asprelli), which is between Stockton and Modesto. It proved to be a great Lord’s Day!

The plan forthcoming is for me to preach this Sunday for my very good friend, Dr. Joe Carson, who is serving as interim pastor at Heritage Baptist Church of Anderson, just south of Redding. On the 22nd I will preach for my son, Pastor William Maricle, at New Hope Baptist Church of Santa Rosa (where I served as pastor from 2003-2022). Laura & I will remain for New Hope's Thanksgiving Eve Service. We will then experience the joy of celebrating Thanksgiving with William's family plus the family of our youngest child, Julia, and other loved ones.

On Sunday the 29th I will preach at the fabulous Lighthouse Baptist Church of La Verne, Los Angeles County, in the room of Pastor Brian Dunlop, who will be leading a group on a tour of Israel.

After that, if no further preaching opportunities materialize, we will begin the return journey to Branson.

We are extremely grateful to the pastors and churches who have opened their pulpits to me, and are providing us with nice accommodations. We are also humbled by friends who have donated to help my humble ministry. Others have inquired about assisting us. If you are so led of the Lord, you may use Zelle (Arthur Maricle: 707-338-4328) and PayPal (@DrMaricle).

With your prayer and support, we remain...
In the glad service of our glorious King, 
Dr. Arthur & Mrs. Laura Maricle

text:
The Steelers offered Le'Veon Bell a five-year, $70 million contract, with only about $17 million truly guaranteed. He sat out a $14.5 million franchise-tag season rather than sign it.

In the video below, Le'Veon Bell says, "Give me 45 million guaranteed. Even though it was a 60 million dollar deal, give me something. They like, no."

He had already played the 2017 season on a $12.12 million tag. Pittsburgh then came back with a long-term offer that looked huge on paper. Bell wanted the first three years guaranteed, or $18 million a year if they would not lock the money in. The Steelers said no.

He left $14.5 million on the table, about $855,000 a game, and sat out all of 2018 rather than take another heavy workload with no real guarantee behind it.

In March 2019 he signed with the New York Jets for four years and $52.5 million, with $35 million guaranteed, more than double what Pittsburgh had truly locked in.

The Jets deal did not last. He ran for 789 yards and averaged 3.2 yards a carry in year one, then was waived two games into year two.

So did Le'Veon get shorted on that guarantee, or did sitting out cost him the prime he was trying to protect?

text:
The right just lost Congress, and part of the right is cheering. That is the guaranteed way to hell. Pay attention.

Last Tuesday the Democrats took the House and the Senate. Seven Republican Senate seats flipped, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina among them. And a loud part of the right wanted it. They said so for months: let the Republicans lose. Let the Democrats burn it down. Let them hang themselves doing crazy things for two years, and the country runs to a far-right candidate in 2028 and beyond.

That is not strategy. That is volunteering to be the match the other side already wanted.

The election is over. This is now about moving forward. Here is the lesson.

Evil has two sides: the psychotic and the despot.

1. The left is the psychotic, the demonic enemy. It smashes, burns, and murders, and the Democrats drive to hell at 1,000 mph. Nobody here is letting them off. But left against right is only one war. It is the war against the obvious evil. It is the war the ultimate evil uses to keep us distracted while it conquers the world, as it has from the beginning (Ephesians 6:12). None of the "burn it down" men are taking that into account.

2. The deep state is the despot, the ultimate enslavement. It is the orderly devil. Not smash and burn. Absolute control. It is not stupid. It is patient, competent evil that knows no bounds. It uses controlled opposition on the left and on the right. It gets a vote in 2028 and beyond, and it always has. Any plan that leaves it out is either naive or compromised already.

3. The despot wants the fringes raging. It has always used the psychotic to create demand for itself. The psychotic burns. The despot offers to put out the fire. A far left and a far right screaming at each other, which has led to murder and will lead to mass murder, is what it is building. Then it presents a milquetoast Mitt Romney and lets the country flee to him. A far-right candidate to counter a far-left candidate is the matchup it is hoping for. The left already wants its despots to rid the world of the right. The right will offer to do the same with despots of its own: the smash-and-burn rage machine and the total-control despot or king. Either way the despot wins. We must avoid becoming the demonic and our own devil despot.

4. It wants us to discredit ourselves. Nazi salutes. Ridiculous talk. It wants the undisciplined, selfish, feel-good dunks where we shoot ourselves in the foot. Every man who does it on camera works for the other side for free, and we have made that far too easy. Matthew 10:16 was written for men surrounded by wolves. We must be loud, but disciplined. No unforced errors.

5. It kills or arrests those it cannot control. It always has. It strangled and burned William Tyndale in 1536. His crime: putting the Bible in English. Most of the King James New Testament is still his work. It jailed John Bunyan for twelve years. His crime: preaching without the crown's license. He began The Pilgrim's Progress in that cell. Look at Charlie Kirk. Look at JFK.

What wins in 2028 and beyond:

Not a mirror of the far left. A conservative Obama. A palatable, smash-mouth incrementalist who can say the hardest truths like honey, and the female palate will not gag on them. He says things in a way that does not offend, even though it is offensive. That is what Obama did. He won twice, and he was one of the most powerful forces for evil we have ever seen. Imagine that skill in the hands of a righteous man. He speaks to the future young men have to live in: a house they can afford, children they can raise, a country that does not treat them as the enemy.

It is too early to say who the candidate will be. But there are men already showing us what it takes.

James Fishback is 31, the son of a Colombian immigrant, a guy who could be any race. He left Georgetown, built an investment firm, and ran for governor of Florida on what young families cannot afford: a house, the taxes on it, a future. He lost. But he took the college precincts, and his crowds were young men. He showed that young men will show up for a man who speaks to their future.

Joe Kent has integrity and a sympathetic story. Twenty years in the Army, Ranger and Green Beret. Eleven combat deployments. Six Bronze Stars. In 2019 an ISIS suicide bomber in Syria killed his wife Shannon, a Navy cryptologist, and left him with two young sons. He went on to run the National Counterterrorism Center, and in March he resigned it rather than back a war he could not support. He was the highest-ranking official to walk away over it. That is a man who has paid for what he believes.

The standard is integrity plus competence plus the ability to say the hard thing without handing the other side the clip.

What we do here:

Stop amplifying the men who make us easy to dismiss. Every share is a vote for the matchup it wants.

Reward the man who says the hard thing well. Follow him, fund him, and send him to your people.

Stop minimizing the grievances of the young. A man who cannot afford a house or a family is not whining. Hear him and help him. He needs a father, not a dictator.

Look to what Luther got right. He wrote his Small Catechism for fathers to teach at their own tables. We win this around our own kitchen tables, catechizing and discipling our families and neighbors, so that a Christian population creates a Christian nation worth having. This is the way forward for Christian Nationalism.

"A soft tongue will break a bone." Proverbs 25:15. Evil has been patient from the beginning. Now we have to be.

text:
Al-Hijri’s National Guard shuts three SDF-linked offices in Suwayda

Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri’s National Guard sealed three offices in Suwayda city on Monday that had operated under the supervision of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) and with its support, Suwayda 24 reports. The closures point to a rift between al-Hijri’s camp and the Kurdish-led alliance, which reportedly once helped channel Israeli funds to a militia affiliated with the Druze cleric.

Suwayda 24 identified the shuttered premises as the Women’s Political Office, the Women’s Association Office and the military office of the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ). Verify Syria separately documented the closures and reported that staff were referred for questioning by the National Guard’s own military judiciary. The National Guard operates outside Syria’s state military and security institutions and strongly opposes the post-Assad government.

The Women’s Political Office was associated with the Syrian Women’s Council, a civilian organisation that advocates for women’s rights and has coordinated with the Syrian Democratic Council, the SDF’s political counterpart. The YPJ is a military formation within the SDF alliance, which is an affiliate of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK). The Kurdish People’s Protection Units (YPG) have formed the backbone of that alliance, which also includes Arab and other factions.

Local sources told Suwayda 24 that the closures followed a halt in SDF support for the National Guard. Sources who spoke to Verify Syria offered a different explanation, linking the closures to alleged efforts to promote integration with Damascus in Suwayda as the SDF moved towards integration with the Syrian state. Verify Syria said it could not independently substantiate allegations of recruitment and intelligence gathering and had received no response from the YPJ by publication.

Israel has publicly presented itself as a defender of both Syrian Kurds and Druze. In 2019, after US troops pulled back from Kurdish-held areas and Türkiye launched a cross-border offensive, then-Israeli deputy foreign minister Tzipi Hotovely confirmed that Israel had provided aid to Syrian Kurds without identifying the recipients or specifying what was supplied. She claimed that Israeli support for the SDF in northern Syria was a check on Iranian influence, although the SDF routinely worked with the Assad-allied Iranian forces. In January 2026, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar called for international action to protect Syrian Kurds during fighting between government forces and the SDF in Aleppo.

Israel has similarly invoked the protection of Syrian Druze to justify military intervention, depicting itself implausibly as a defender of Syrian minorities. The Washington Post confirmed previously that Israel began supplying weapons to Druze fighters within days of Assad’s fall in December 2024 and that Israeli funds reached the Suwayda Military Council, a militia close to al-Hijri, through the SDF. This week, it was al-Hijri’s National Guard that shut the three SDF-linked offices. The closures show how sharply the priorities of these Syrian groups can diverge, even as Israel presents itself as the protector of both communities.

text:
The Other War Trump Can't End

Ukraine is another war President Trump has been unable to bring to an end.

Despite renewed diplomatic efforts, the fighting continues, and the obstacles to peace extend well beyond Moscow.

American, Russian, and Ukrainian negotiators are scheduled to meet in Abu Dhabi this week, with European representatives also attending.

Trump is also discussing a possible meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping later this month.

But even if these three leaders reach an understanding, that does not mean Ukraine, European governments, or influential elements within Washington will accept it.

Each has its own political objectives and conditions for peace. Russia also continues to demand concessions that Ukraine rejects.

As I argued in my earlier Project Authentic essay, history offers an important warning.

Napoleon, Abraham Lincoln and Jefferson Davis during the American Civil War, and leaders during World War I faced difficult choices between continuing their wars and compromising on fundamental political objectives. In several cases, continued fighting brought increasingly destructive consequences.

Ukraine risks facing a similar dilemma.

Understanding Russia's security concerns does not justify its invasion of Ukraine. But neither does understanding Ukraine's historical fears mean every demand made by Kyiv and its Western supporters is realistic.

The longer the war continues, the greater the risk that Ukraine will face an even worse settlement.

A ceasefire may stop the fighting. But a lasting peace requires addressing the political and security disagreements that helped produce the conflict.

Until then, Ukraine will continue paying the price.

Read my full Project Authentic essay:

The Other War Trump Can't End

The West Won't Look Towards the Future, and Ukraine Is Paying the Cost

text:
The phenomenon in which remarks by Iranian officials are essentially discarded by price action on markets is worth studying tbh.

The juvenile, reflex answer is "markets don't listen to terrorists" (read that as you wish)

But is that the whole story? Ofc people make more nuanced versions of essentially this arg, as Gareth notes.

"It's just posturing for domestic audience." But Gareth is right here. This is not that. This is an incredibly specific, pointed, denial and indictment. It echoes the same vibe from his post yesterday:

"The war on Iran has already wrecked the US government. But Washington flails like a desperate gambler. FOLD YOUR HAND. STOP manufacturing FAKE NEWS about imaginary talks. Stop denying the West Asian NEW ORDER. Time to SURRENDER to the seven conditions Iran has repeatedly set out."

This is not domestic posturing. This is crystal clear, public, rejection of the fundamental approach of the US and mediators to brokering a deal. The Iranians have said no. They have rejected it. They are SHOUTING that they have rejected it. But no one wants to listen.

These are not modest tweets. "Stop denying the West Asian NEW ORDER." Is not a sign that a begrudging compromise is right around the corner.

Lastly, its worth noting that the perpetuation of these rumors will now start costing the mediators their credibility with the Iranian party. This already happened to Pakistan, which is why Islamabad has drifted off the face of the diplomatic earth.

Qatar is likely framing its approach like this:

To the Iranians, they say: "we are the last chance for peace. We think your claims are justified. We have even sought to not really transit Hormuz, not work with CENTCOM, like the UAE and Saudi have. And this is costing us. Please give us a chance. We will make the Americans come to reason."

To the US they say: "Look, we know you can fight a war. But no one wants that. All the Iranians need is a little lip service, and then we can break the ice and get to dealing. Just a little something up front. Just anything. Give them some of their own money back. And I bet if you do, we can get them to say something about nuclear stuff to make it look like its even steven."

But the US won't budge. They won't make the up front offer. Rubio has made that dead certain as of this morning. He called the whole situation detached from reality and the Iranian leadership "lunatics." The Qatari trip to DC I think was the last leg of their marathon in mediation.

Now we wait and see what happens next. Will the US escalate? Will Iran escalate? If Iran escalates, where?

People expect Hormuz, and that will definitely be part of any strategy.

But I have my eyes on Iraq...

That’s a pretty significant career reset.

text:
THE END AND

An ending, to end, a state of having no hereafter…

It is the desire we all share in these lands—

When will it end? When will the end finally arrive?

I watch the birds from my window; my cat has taken cover.

I look toward my window, having taken cover from my own fears—is this the end?

My corpse reeks before it has even grown cold; I can still smell it—disgusting!

The decay within me began the moment I surrendered—disgusting!

The glint upon the blade of my fears—the blade that pierced me through while I slept—

The moment it claimed me,

That was when my decay began…

I offered no reaction—I could not.

Fear—my fears—were bound to me with a profound, deep-seated love.

And

The very moment I sought to betray that fear,

That night,

While I lay asleep,

It stabbed me, over and over again.

To die would have been a great honor—but my honor, too, had died—or perhaps, it had committed the killing.

I awoke that morning, fully aware that I had become a corpse.

I longed to be an animal—a noble, reptilian creature—

But instead, I found refuge in the utter hopelessness of being a walking corpse.

That morning,

I rose; the day had long since broken. I felt no hunger.

Then, the first scents reached me—the fresh, pungent odor of my own corpse.

My soul—I know it well—will carry me upon its back,

And with every passing moment,

My burden will grow heavier,

And so will the stench…

The end.

Each day, I yearn for the end—to reach the finish, or to be brought to one.

But my soul is stubborn; it bears my body—my putrefying body—

Tossing it, aimlessly, from one place to another…

Hakan Karaduman

text:
🇫🇷|They Simulated the Cyber Pandemic in 2020. They Wrote the Law in 2022. They Ran the Exercise in October. They Blamed Iran in November. You Are Supposed to Believe This Is a Coincidence.

In July 2020, the World Economic Forum ran a live simulation called Cyber Polygon. The scenario involved a supply-chain cyberattack that would cascade through the financial system. Participants included Interpol, the Russian government, and major banks. The WEF's own material described it as preparation for a "cyber pandemic."

In 2021, they ran the exercise again. This time, the scenario involved a global internet outage affecting banks.

Also in 2020, the WEF and the Carnegie Endowment published a joint report on cyber risk in the financial system. Its advisers included representatives from the Federal Reserve, the Bank of England, the IMF, JPMorgan Chase, and Amazon. The report described a systemic cyber collapse as "the final yet necessary step" towards digital currency and global governance of the economy.

Now, consider the French statement.

11-12 October 2026: The refrigeration systems of 700 retail sites were attacked. Fires broke out, food spoiled, and the damage reportedly reached tens of millions.

9 November 2026: France attributed the attack to SHAHID KAVEH, an IRGC unit. It summoned the Iranian ambassador and proposed EU sanctions.

The exercise was the rehearsal. The attack became the scene, while the attribution became the script. Meanwhile, the legislation had already been written before any of it happened.

The Legislation That Was Waiting

NIS2: The EU's Network and Information Security Directive was adopted in 2022 and came into force in October 2024. It expands mandatory cybersecurity obligations across critical sectors and requires member states to adopt national cyber crisis management plans.

DORA: The Digital Operational Resilience Act has applied since January 2025. It requires financial entities to report cyber incidents, work with vetted third-party providers, and submit their ICT supply chains to supervisory oversight.

The Cyber Resilience Act: Adopted in 2024, it mandates security requirements for digital products and establishes a vulnerability reporting regime through ENISA.

eIDAS 2.0: Adopted in May 2024, it requires every member state to offer a digital identity wallet to its citizens by 2026. This wallet provides the infrastructure for digital identity, connecting it to banking, healthcare, and government services.

The digital euro: The ECB moved from the investigation phase to the preparation phase in 2023. Its legislative proposal was tabled in June 2023. The Governing Council has stated that the objective is to establish a digital currency issued by the central bank, with programmable functionality also under discussion.

The Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive: As amended by Directive (EU) 2026/806 and the CMDI package published in April 2026, it establishes the bail-in order. Shareholders come first, followed by subordinate creditors, senior creditors, and finally uninsured depositors holding more than €100,000.

Every one of these instruments was drafted, negotiated, and adopted before the October attack.

The Sequence

First, simulate the crisis: Cyber Polygon in 2020 and again in 2021.

Next, publish the threat assessment: The WEF-Carnegie report in 2020, followed by IMF warnings and ECB letters.

Then, set the deadline: The ECB's letter dated 7 July 2026 required AI cyber defence plans by 31 October 2026.

After that, run the drill: G7 tabletop exercises on AI cyberattacks were agreed upon on 15-16 October 2026 in Bangkok.

Then, the attack happens: On 11-12 October 2026.

Finally, issue the attribution: On 9 November 2026, after the ECB deadline had passed and the G7 drills were already on the calendar.

The response follows: Sanctions, further integration, additional reporting obligations, expanded supervisory authority, and greater reliance on digital identity.

The attack did not produce the policy. Instead, the policy had already established the conditions under which the attack could become the justification for the next phase.

The Attribution Is the Tell

France published a conclusion. However, it did not publish:

· The malware samples.

· The command-and-control infrastructure.

· The attribution methodology.

· The signals intelligence.

· The forensic timeline.

· The human sources.

A state that has evidence can publish that evidence because it serves as a deterrent. A state that publishes only a conclusion, however, turns that conclusion into a political instrument.

Furthermore, the conclusion points to the one state that is already sanctioned, designated, embargoed, at war, subject to a UN resolution architecture, and already the target of a military campaign that has cost $47 billion and 56 MQ-9 Reapers.

Iran is the only country on earth for which an attribution appears to require no proof, because the pre-existing designation itself is treated as proof.

The Precedent They Are Counting On You Not Knowing

Stuxnet: The cyberweapon that destroyed roughly 1,000 centrifuges at Natanz in 2010. It was a joint US-Israeli operation, authorised by George W. Bush and continued by Barack Obama. The operation was confirmed through reporting by The New York Times, Dutch intelligence reporting, and the Equation Group leaks.

Did France summon the American ambassador?

WannaCry: The ransomware was built on EternalBlue, an NSA exploit leaked by the Shadow Brokers in 2017. It struck the NHS, cancelled 19,000 appointments, and cost the NHS £92 million. It also spread to 150 countries.

Did France propose sanctions against the United States?

Operation Socialist: In 2010, GCHQ penetrated Belgacom, Belgium's largest telecommunications operator. In other words, a NATO ally was hacked by another NATO ally.

Did France summon the British ambassador?

PRISM: The NSA accessed the servers of Google, Microsoft, Apple, Yahoo, Facebook, YouTube, Skype, AOL, and PalTalk. Edward Snowden revealed the programme in June 2013, and the US government confirmed that the documents were authentic.

Did France propose EU sanctions against the United States?

The countries that built the internet, own the cables, control the root servers, operate the cloud, design the chips, write the protocols, and conducted some of the largest cyberattacks in history are now summoning the ambassador of a country that did none of those things.

The Real Target Is You

The French statement is not aimed at Tehran because Tehran already knows what France thinks. Instead, the statement is aimed at the French public, the European public, and ultimately, you.

The message is clear: the threat is external, the threat is real, and the threat requires more surveillance, more reporting, greater data sharing, more identity verification, greater central bank authority, and further supervisory integration.

This is the problem-reaction-solution structure, and it has been repeated so many times that the public has stopped noticing it.

Covid: A real virus was used to build the digital health certificate infrastructure. That infrastructure became the EU Digital COVID Certificate, which subsequently provided a template for eIDAS 2.0 and the digital identity wallet.

Ukraine: A real war was used to build the frozen asset architecture, the bail-in directive, and the reconstruction fund.

The cyberattack: A real attack was used to justify the incident reporting regime, expanded supervisory authority, and the digital resilience framework.

The pattern is not a conspiracy theory. It is the legislative calendar. Every crisis produces a law that was already being drafted. That law consistently expands control, identity systems, and centralised authority, while the crisis provides the justification.

The Word They Use to Silence You

If you ask for the evidence, you are called a conspiracy theorist.

If you point out that the attribution came without a technical dossier, you are labelled a Russian asset.

If you notice that the legislation predates the attack, you are accused of undermining the security services.

If you ask why Stuxnet was never sanctioned, you are dismissed as a whataboutist.

These words serve as instruments of containment. They are deployed to stop the question before it reaches the legislative calendar.

The Bill

Cyber Polygon 2020 and 2021. The WEF's simulation of a cyber pandemic and a global internet outage affecting banks.

The WEF-Carnegie report in 2020. Advisers from the Federal Reserve, Bank of England, IMF, JPMorgan, and Amazon. The report described systemic cyber collapse as "the final yet necessary step" towards digital currency and global governance of the economy.

NIS2, adopted in 2022. DORA, applied in 2025. The Cyber Resilience Act, adopted in 2024. eIDAS 2.0, adopted in 2024. Digital euro preparation, beginning in 2023. BRRD and the CMDI package, published in April 2026.

The ECB letter, dated 7 July 2026, required AI cyber defence plans by 31 October 2026.

The G7 tabletop exercises were agreed upon on 15-16 October 2026.

The attack took place on 11-12 October 2026, affecting 700 retail sites and causing tens of millions in damage.

The attribution followed on 9 November 2026, naming SHAHID KAVEH without publishing a technical dossier.

Stuxnet destroyed roughly 1,000 centrifuges in 2010 through a US-Israeli operation. It was never sanctioned.

WannaCry caused £92 million in damage to the NHS in 2017. It was never sanctioned.

Belgacom was penetrated by GCHQ in 2010. It was never sanctioned.

PRISM exposed NSA access to major technology companies in 2013. It was never sanctioned.

They simulated the crisis. They drafted the law. They ran the drill. They set the deadline. Then the attack happened, the attribution was issued, and the legislation was already waiting.

You are not supposed to notice the order of the paragraphs. Instead, you are supposed to read the headline, believe the attribution, and accept the next law.

Open your eyes. The attack is real, but the attribution is the instrument. That instrument is aimed at your rights, your privacy, your cash, and your identity. And the name they are using to advance this agenda is Iran, because Iran is the one name they believe requires no proof.

A private family battle in Arkansas just exposed something the public was never supposed to see. Michael Austin Kennedy served as an Arkansas State Police trooper. In April 2026 his wife, Alana Delaney Kennedy, filed for divorce and asked for joint custody of their two young children. Weeks later she amended the filing. She told the court she believed her husband was a white supremacist whose views could poison the minds of their children. She asked for sole custody and said any time he spent with the kids should only happen after he completed a course meant to confront hatred and prejudice.

With the amended papers she submitted roughly thirty screenshots of messages the couple had exchanged. The texts contained slurs aimed at Black people, Hispanic people, Muslims, and LGBTQ individuals. In some messages Black people were compared to gorillas and monkeys. One exchange called for Ramadan to be banned in Arkansas. Other messages included photos of Kennedy posing with people he had arrested while referring to them with racist terms, including one that treated the image like a trophy.

The messages entered the public record through the divorce case in Saline County, not through any police investigation. Once they surfaced, Kennedy resigned from the Arkansas State Police on May 15, 2026. Through his attorney he later told the court he offered no excuse for the language. He called the statements entirely improper, said he was profoundly ashamed of them, and claimed they did not reflect his values at the time of the filing. He denied the white-supremacist label itself. The state police reviewed his stops, citations, and warnings from the day he was hired until the day he left and stated there was no sign the views in the messages had shaped his official work.

What began as a custody dispute ended a trooper’s career in a matter of days. The divorce and custody case continues.

Fly into Victor Attah International Airport near Uyo, then travel by road through Eket to Ibeno Beach. The journey from Uyo takes approximately 90 minutes, depending on conditions. Arrange a trusted driver in advance.

🗺️ What to Explore
Prioritize a walk along the expansive Atlantic shoreline, coastal photography, and observing the local fishing landscape. Freshly grilled fish may be available from beachside vendors. Facilities vary across the coastline.

⏱️ Time & Stay
Allow several hours at the beach, or plan a full-day excursion from Uyo. Eket offers a convenient nearby base, while Uyo is better suited to a broader Akwa Ibom itinerary.

🌤️ When to Visit
November to March is generally drier. April to October brings heavier rainfall, which may affect outdoor plans.

📋 Access & Planning
Confirm local access, transport arrangements, facilities, and any applicable charges before departure. Check current security advisories: UK guidance warns against travel to boat-only riverine areas of Akwa Ibom. Road-accessible destinations require their own security assessment.

text:
The Racist and Antigentile Plot | Leo Frank's Black Scapegoat: Newt Lee at the Coroner's Inquest

The Atlanta Constitution | Friday, May 9, 1913 | Atlanta, Georgia

The Night Watchman Who Became a Prime Murder Suspect

On Friday, May 9, 1913, The Atlanta Constitution reported the final proceedings of the Fulton County coroner's inquest into the murder of 13-year-old Mary Phagan. 

The old Negro was intended to die for Leo Frank's crime. 

Newton Jasper Lee, the Black night watchman who discovered her body in the National Pencil Company basement early Sunday, April 27, was still being held alongside factory superintendent Leo Max Frank.

Lee had called the police to report the murder. Yet investigators soon treated him as a suspect, questioning his time-clock punches, confronting him with two handwritten murder notes, and examining a heavily bloodstained shirt discovered in a trash barrel at his home. In the racially charged atmosphere of 1913 Atlanta, these three pieces of evidence could easily have been enough to send a Black man to the gallows to swing. But there was one serious problem: all three raised suspicions of having been contrived to make Lee appear guilty, and investigators had reason to question their authenticity.

The three items could work together against him. The notes pointed toward a Black night watchman. The clock appeared to give him time away from the factory. The bloody shirt suggested he had changed clothing after a violent crime. Prosecutors later argued that Frank was attempting to direct suspicion toward Lee. The May 9, 1913, Constitution provides testimony central to evaluating that accusation (AC, 1–2).

The Thursday, May 8, 1913, Hearing and Its Verdict

Fulton County Coroner Paul V. Donehoo, an attorney who had been blind since childhood, conducted the inquest. The jury had first assembled Monday, April 28, at P. J. Bloomfield's undertaking establishment on South Pryor Street, where members examined the victim's remains. They also inspected the pencil factory at 37–41 South Forsyth Street.

On Thursday, May 8, testimony resumed around 9:30 a.m. at Atlanta police headquarters. Newt Lee, Leo Frank, detectives, factory employees, and other witnesses were questioned. Foreman Homer C. Ashford headed the six-man coroner's jury.

The hearing ended at 6:28 p.m. Within about twenty minutes, the jurors decided that both Lee and Frank should be held on murder charges for further investigation by the Fulton County grand jury. County physician Dr. John W. Hurt signed the verdict with Ashford. Both men remained in the Fulton County Tower. The recommendation was neither an indictment nor a conviction (AC, 1).

Lee's Account of Saturday, April 26

Lee had worked as night watchman for about three weeks and lived at the rear of 40 Henry Street. He patrolled the factory and punched a mechanical clock at roughly half-hour intervals. Those punches were supposed to establish when he made his rounds.

On Friday, April 25, Frank instructed him to report at 4 p.m. Saturday, rather than his usual 6 p.m. starting time. Saturday was Confederate Memorial Day, a Georgia state holiday. When Lee arrived early, he found the inner doors locked, an unusual condition in his experience. Frank emerged from his private office, rubbing his hands, apologized for summoning him, and sent him downtown until 6 p.m.

Lee walked through central Atlanta, watched street performers and a medicine seller, and returned as directed. Frank told him to wait before punching the clock while he changed the paper slip. Lee testified that Frank took unusually long to fit it. Frank later explained that fewer employees had worked because of the holiday.

Shortly afterward, former bookkeeper James Milton Gantt arrived to retrieve shoes left in the building. Lee thought Frank appeared frightened when Gantt arrived. Frank permitted the visit and instructed Lee to accompany Gantt. Later that evening Frank telephoned to ask whether everything was all right, a call Lee said Frank had never made during his shift before (AC, 2; AJ, 1).

None of these events alone established a crime. Together, they raised questions about Frank's dealings with a watchman who would shortly become a suspect.

Lee Discovers the Body and Calls Police

During his patrol early Sunday, April 27, Lee entered the basement with a lantern, visited the toilet area, and noticed a form beyond a partition. When he recognized a body, he hurried upstairs and called the police shortly after 3 a.m. He stayed at the factory and led the responding officers downstairs.

Lee's description of the body's position differed from the officers' recollection. He insisted that he had not turned it over. Sergeant Levi Sanford Dobbs also questioned how well Lee could have seen the body by lantern light and discussed the difficulty of carrying a body through the narrow scuttle opening and down the basement ladder. The elevator offered another possible route (AJ, 1).

These discrepancies justified inquiry. They did not prove the watchman had committed the murder. He was the employee who had summoned the authorities in the first place.

First Piece of Evidence: Frank Says the Time Slip Was All Right Sunday

The clock was the most serious problem for Frank's account. On Sunday morning, April 27, after police brought him to the factory, Frank unlocked the patrol clock and removed Lee's recording slip. Former county policeman W. W. “Boots” Rogers testified that Frank examined it and declared the punches correct. Factory foreman N. V. Darley also understood the record to be satisfactory. Lee later testified that Frank's words meant he had missed no punches (AC, 2; AJ, 1).

That initial approval mattered. If Lee had registered every half hour, he had little unaccounted-for time in which to leave the factory, travel home, change clothes, and return. The time slip initially supported his account of remaining on duty.

Frank had also handled the clock paper before Lee's Saturday night shift. On Sunday he controlled the mechanism again and removed the completed slip in front of officers. The custody of that paper should have been carefully documented, especially once it became evidence against the watchman.

Monday, April 28: A Different Story About Missing Punches

By Monday, the clock record had become a source of suspicion. Detective John R. Black later testified that Frank had drawn attention to irregular punches, and Black thought Frank had raised the missing time on Monday. Another detective, however, recalled speaking with Frank on Monday afternoon without hearing him mention errors. The testimony therefore conflicts about exactly when Frank first identified every discrepancy.

What is not in dispute is the change between Sunday morning's assurance and the irregularities reported by Tuesday, April 29. The Atlanta Constitution of Wednesday, April 30, described three irregular periods: a gap after approximately 9:32 p.m. until 10:29 p.m., another missing adjustment after about 11:04 p.m. before midnight, and a further gap between 2 and 3 a.m. (AC, 1). The time slip had remained in Frank's control when he said it was alright and then said it wasn't alright between Sunday and Monday. Sunday it was alright. Monday it wasn't all right. 

These were substantial periods for a watchman expected to register at half-hour intervals. But a missed punch did not by itself prove that Lee had left the factory. The clock might have malfunctioned, a punch might have failed to register, or the slip might have been mishandled. The issue for Frank was why he had first pronounced the same record satisfactory. And why did four miss-punches appear a day later?

Frank Says Lee Had Time to Go Home and Return

This is the connection the prosecution later emphasized. During the July murder trial, Detective Black was asked whether Frank had said that the gaps gave Lee time to travel to his house and back. Black testified that Frank had made that remark after examining the tape again. He also placed the search of Lee's home after Frank called attention to the discrepancies, although his recollection of the exact order was challenged during cross-examination (AJ, 1).

In the trial's Brief of Evidence, Black recalled Frank saying that the missing hour would have given Lee time to go home and return. That claim turned an irregular clock slip into a reason to suspect the watchman had left his post.

The prosecution's criticism was straightforward: on Sunday, Frank's inspection apparently cleared Lee's clock record; afterward, Frank identified missing time and suggested it was enough for Lee to travel home. If the slip had changed, who changed it? If it had not, why did Frank first describe it as correct?

Frank denied manipulating the evidence. He later explained that he and Darley initially looked for skipped numbered lines, not unequal intervals between the recorded times. That explanation deserved consideration, but it did not erase the contradiction or the danger it created for Lee.

Second Piece of Evidence: The Bloodstained Shirt

Detective John R. Black testified at the inquest that he and Detective Fred Bullard found a bloody linen shirt at the bottom of a trash barrel behind Lee's residence at 40 Henry Street. The barrel contained refuse. The shirt Lee had been wearing when arrested was woolen, unlike the linen garment found in the barrel (AC, 2).

Pinkerton detective Harry Scott described the discovered shirt as bloody, apparently recently washed, and carrying a strong odor. Lee said it resembled a shirt he once owned but had not worn for approximately two years. He explained that Mrs. Bowen had made shirts for him and insisted that, if the bloody shirt was store-bought, it was not his (AC, 2).

The shirt looked damaging only when connected to the missing punches. If Lee had been away from the factory long enough to go home and back, detectives might suppose he had changed out of bloodied clothing. The timing of Frank's changed interpretation of the clock therefore became crucial.

But a garment found among discarded clothing is not proof that its owner wore it during a murder. Police had to establish whose blood it contained, when it was stained, and how it reached the barrel.

The Bacteriologist's Findings and the Planted-Shirt Theory

On Thursday, May 8, The Atlanta Constitution reported city bacteriologist Dr. Claude A. Smith's examination of the shirt. He regarded the stains as relatively recent and identified human blood, but he had not compared them with blood from Mary Phagan's clothing. More strikingly, he believed the shirt was not being worn when the stains were made and suggested it had been used to wipe up blood (AC, 1).

This weakened the claim that Lee had worn the garment while struggling with the victim. It also strengthened the possibility that blood had been put on an unused shirt to create incriminating evidence.

During the July trial, Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey openly argued that the shirt had been planted and that Frank's conduct had encouraged detectives to search Lee's home. That was the prosecution's accusation, not a proven finding about who placed the shirt in the barrel (AJ, 1).

The prosecution's theory connected the two items: the time slip created a supposed opportunity to go home; the bloodstained shirt made that trip appear sinister.

Third Piece of Evidence: Murder Notes Pointing Toward the Watchman

Two handwritten notes discovered near Mary Phagan's body contained peculiar spelling and language apparently identifying a Black night watchman. Lee fit that description. The notes could be read as an accusation by the victim, even though their authorship was unknown and their wording was suspicious from the start.

The early investigation made matters worse for Lee. Three handwriting examiners, Frank M. Berry, Andrew M. Bergstrom, and Pope C. Driver, initially concluded that samples of Lee's handwriting resembled the notes. Their opinion added to the suspicion already created by the time slip and shirt (AJ, 1).

Later in May, factory employee Jim Conley admitted writing the notes. He alleged that Frank instructed him to do so; Frank denied it and maintained that Conley committed the murder. Conley's admission established that the original identification of Lee as the writer was mistaken. Whether Frank directed the notes remained contested.

The notes nevertheless carried the same apparent message as the other disputed evidence: look at the night watchman. During his later trial testimony, Lee recalled reacting to the notes by saying, “Boss, it looks like they are trying to lay it on me.” His fear was understandable (Trial testimony).

Lee's Account of Frank's Warning at Police Headquarters

One of the most damaging episodes in the May 9 Constitution was Lee's account of a private conversation with Frank at police headquarters. Lee testified that he had been handcuffed to a chair and complained that it was hard to be held for something he had not done.

According to Lee, Frank insisted that he knew something about the crime, then warned him: “if you keep up that same story we're both going to hell” (AC, 2).

Lee said he tried to explain that he had passed through the second-floor machine department every half hour during his patrol, and that a murder there must have occurred during the day. He alleged that Frank would not let him finish.

Detectives Black and Scott had arranged the meeting, hoping Frank could persuade Lee to reveal more information. Scott testified that Frank afterward said he had obtained nothing. Lee described the exchange as a warning. Their accounts differed, but Lee's testimony raised the question of why his continued denial would create trouble for his employer.

Frank's Attorneys and the Investigation

Frank had experienced legal counsel while Lee faced repeated questioning as a Black workingman in segregated Atlanta. Attorney Luther Zeigler Rosser attended the coroner's proceedings and later cross-examined Lee aggressively at trial. The defense was entitled to challenge the watchman's recollections, but those attacks did not explain the clock discrepancy or establish that the bloody shirt had been worn during the crime.

The May 9 Constitution recorded a separate controversy involving attorney Herbert Haas. Pinkerton detective Harry Scott testified that Haas wanted the agency's progress reports turned over to him. Scott said he would rather withdraw from the investigation than agree. This is evidence of a dispute over access to the investigators' reports, not proof that Haas suppressed evidence (AC, 2).

Frank was also asked about factory foreman Lemmie Quinn's delayed disclosure of a visit to the building on April 26. Quinn said Frank had suggested discussing it with his attorneys. Frank repeatedly said he could not remember the relevant exchanges. Legal consultation was proper; the unanswered questions about a potentially relevant witness still deserved examination.

Frank's defense also pointed to paperwork to argue that he had been occupied on the afternoon of the murder. Chief clerk Herbert Schiff estimated that the accounting and related tasks required six or seven hours, but acknowledged that he first saw some of the papers on Monday or Tuesday. His estimate could not establish Frank's every movement on Saturday (AC, 2).

What the Coroner's Jury Actually Found

The May 8 hearing did not prove that Frank planted a shirt, falsified the time slip, or ordered the notes written. Nor did it establish that Lee murdered Mary Phagan. Detectives Scott and Black admitted that they had no conclusive evidence and were working from circumstantial clues (AC, 1).

The jury nonetheless recommended that both men be held for further investigation. It was an interim decision in an unfinished murder inquiry.

For Lee, the central problem was that three questionable pieces of evidence could reinforce one another even if none independently proved wrongdoing. The notes pointed toward the night watchman. The irregular punches suggested missing time. The bloodstained shirt offered a possible explanation for what he might have done during that time.

For Frank and his defense, the hardest issue was the Sunday-to-Monday change in the interpretation of the time slip. Frank had handled the clock, said the record was all right, and later suggested gaps that might allow Lee to travel home and back. Detective Black's testimony connected that suggestion to the ensuing search of Lee's residence, although the exact timing was contested.

Conclusion: How Newt Lee Nearly Took the Blame

Newt Lee discovered Mary Phagan's body and called the police. Within days, investigators were weighing evidence that could have turned him from the reporting witness into the accused murderer.

The Atlanta Constitution of May 9, 1913, recorded his account of Frank's warning, the testimony about the bloody shirt, Frank's handling of the time slip, and disagreements involving the superintendent's attorneys. The paper also recorded the detectives' admission that no conclusive evidence had yet been found.

The prosecution later argued that Frank had tried to frame Lee through a combination of missing time-clock punches, a bloodstained shirt, and notes pointing toward the night watchman. The facts justified investigating that accusation, especially Frank's initial assurance that Lee's punches were correct and his subsequent claim that the missing time could allow Lee to go home and return.

But the historical record must keep the allegation separate from proof: Frank's physical alteration of the slip, his involvement in placing the shirt, and his alleged instructions to Conley were all disputed. What cannot be dismissed is the danger to Lee. Three uncertain items of evidence nearly made a Black employee who reported a child's murder appear responsible for it.
