Mary Phagan Case Files | Leo Frank's Negro Scapegoat: 

Newt Lee at the Coroner's Inquest, Atlanta, Georgia

The Atlanta Journal | Wednesday, April 30, 1913 

The Night Watchman Who Discovered Mary Phagan

On Wednesday, April 30, 1913, the Atlanta Journal published a detailed account of Newt Lee's testimony at the Fulton County coroner's inquest into the murder of 13-year-old Mary Phagan.

Newton Jasper Lee (Newt Lee), an African-American night watchman at the National Pencil Company, located at 37–41 South Forsyth Street in Atlanta, discovered the girl's body in the factory basement early Sunday morning at 3:15 a.m., April 27, 1913.

They called him Old Newt Lee

Within days, the man who reported the murder became one of the prime suspects. Detectives questioned his movements, sleep deprived him, fired a gun next to his head at point blank range to rattle him, examined two handwritten murder notes seemingly implicating the nightwatchman, challenged his time-clock record, and discovered a bloodstained shirt at his residence.

His testimony also raised questions about factory superintendent Leo Max Frank, who had summoned Lee to work early, unexpectedly sent him away, handled the time-clock recording slip, and telephoned the factory that evening.

The "Nightwitch" did it!

The central accusation was that Frank attempted to make Lee responsible for Mary Phagan's murder by directing police attention toward contrived evidence that appeared to implicate the night watchman (AJ, 1; AJ, 2).

Where the Coroner's Inquest Was Held

The inquest was conducted by Fulton County Coroner Paul V. Donehoo.

On Monday, April 28, the coroner's jury assembled at P. J. Bloomfield's undertaking establishment at 84 South Pryor Street, examined Mary Phagan's remains, and visited the factory.

On Wednesday, April 30, Donehoo reconvened the jury at the undertaking establishment before marching to Atlanta police headquarters, sequestered by Patrolmen.

The hearing was conducted behind closed doors in the office of the Board of Police Commissioners, beginning at approximately 9:10 a.m.

The six jurors were Homer C. Ashford, foreman; L. Glenn Dewberry; J. C. Hood; Clarence A. Langford; John Miller; and C. Y. Sheats.

Witnesses included Newt Lee, former county policeman Woods White “Boots” Rogers, Police Call Officer William F. Anderson, Sergeants Robert J. Brown and Levi Sanford Dobbs, Mary Phagan's stepfather William J. Coleman, and former factory bookkeeper James Milton Gantt.

Frank's defense attorney, Luther Zeigler Rosser, attended the proceedings (AJ, 1; AJ, 3).

Coroner Paul V. Donehoo (c. 1877–December 1940)

Paul V. Donehoo was approximately 35 years old during the inquest. He lost his eyesight around age six, reportedly following a protracted fever that nearly killed him: meningitis.

Despite his blindness, Donehoo pursued an education, studied law, and became an Atlanta attorney. Around 1908, he became Fulton County coroner, serving approximately 32 years until his death in December 1940, at about age 63. 

He was gifted with near photographic memory.

Widely known for his memory of spoken testimony, Donehoo questioned witnesses about their movements, the factory's operations, and contradictions in the evidence.

His widow, Alverta Benson Donehoo, succeeded him as Fulton County coroner in January 1941 (Martin, 10).

Newt Lee Testifies

At 11:45 a.m., Lee took the witness stand.

He lived at the rear of 40 Henry Street and had worked at the National Pencil Company for approximately three weeks. In other reports Lee told the Coroner he had received three pay three times.

His regular shift began around 6 p.m. He inspected the factory's four floors and registered his movements on a mechanical time clock at half-hour intervals.

A complete round generally required 30 minutes. When time permitted, he also examined the basement.

The clock record became central to the investigation because missing punches could suggest that Lee had failed to make his rounds or left the factory (AJ, 1).

Frank Orders Lee to Arrive Two Hours Early

Lee testified that on Friday, April 25, Frank instructed him to report at 4 p.m. Saturday instead of his customary 6 p.m.

Saturday, April 26, was Confederate Memorial Day, a Georgia state holiday.

Frank reportedly repeated the instruction two or three times.

When Lee arrived at approximately 4 p.m., he found the street entrance unlocked but the interior double doors secured.

Frank emerged from his private office, rubbing his hands. Lee considered the greeting unusual because Frank ordinarily called him inside.

Frank apologized for summoning him early and instructed him to return at 6 p.m.

The Journal quoted Frank:

“I'm sorry, Newt, that I had you come here 
so soon” (AJ, 1).

The sudden reversal raised the question of why Frank repeatedly instructed the watchman to arrive early, then immediately sent him away. And then why the change? Why the hurry up to work and go out of the factory to have a good time? 

One theory was that Frank wanted Lee absent from the factory during those two hours, because he was hoping Conley would return as promised.

Lee's Movements Between 4 and 6 p.m.

Lee walked through downtown Atlanta, describing a route along Forsyth Street, Alabama Street, Broad Street, the viaduct area, Wall Street, and Central Avenue.

He stopped to watch a street gathering where a fat man sold medicine and performers entertained spectators.

He returned shortly before 6 p.m.

His account identified streets and activities detectives could investigate. His absence also resulted directly from Frank's instructions rather than an independent decision to leave work.

Frank remained inside the factory during at least part of that period (AJ, 1).

Frank Handles the Time-Clock Recording Slip

When Lee returned, Frank told him not to punch the clock immediately because its recording slip had been removed.

Frank replaced the paper in the clock. Lee then registered his 6 p.m. punch.

This placed Frank directly at the clock mechanism before the night shift began.

As superintendent, Frank controlled access to the factory's records and equipment. Frank also had the key that could open and close the machine. This fact became important later when Dorsey showed it was possible to open the clock with a key, and make a 12 hour shift on the slip in 5 minutes. 

Frank's custody and handling of the clock became significant when its recording slip subsequently appeared to contain missing half-hour punches (AJ, 1).

James Milton Gantt Arrives at the Factory

Shortly afterward, former factory bookkeeper James Milton Gantt arrived to retrieve shoes left in the building.

Gantt had previously been discharged following a disagreement with Frank.

Lee refused to admit him without permission.

When Frank appeared, Lee believed that his employer looked frightened.

Frank permitted Gantt to enter but instructed Lee to accompany him.

Gantt recovered his shoes, used the telephone, and departed after approximately half an hour.

Lee did not know Frank's exact movements while accompanying Gantt upstairs.

Frank's apparent nervousness attracted attention because it followed his unusual instructions to Lee earlier that afternoon (AJ, 1).

Frank's Unusual Telephone Call

Between 7 and 8 p.m., Frank telephoned the factory.

Lee testified that other employees occasionally called during his shift, but Frank had never personally telephoned him before.

Frank asked whether everything was all right.

Lee indicated that conditions appeared normal.

The call raised questions because Frank had already summoned Lee early, dismissed him, handled the clock slip, and appeared frightened when Gantt arrived.

One theory was that Frank wanted to determine whether Lee had discovered anything suspicious. Another was that Frank was checking security after Gantt's visit (AJ, 1).

Lee Discovers Mary Phagan's Body

Early Sunday morning, April 27, Lee descended through the factory's trapdoor and ladder into the basement.

He carried a lantern and placed it near the basement toilet.

After leaving the toilet, he noticed something beyond a partition. Looking more carefully, he recognized a woman's body.

Frightened, Lee returned upstairs and telephoned the police from the wall phone in Frank's office.

The Journal quoted his reaction:

“It scared me, that body there” (AJ, 1).

Police Call Officer William F. Anderson received the report shortly after 3 a.m.

Lee remained at the factory and guided responding officers to the basement.

His decision to summon police brought investigators directly to the crime scene.

The Contradiction Over the Body's Position

Lee testified that Mary Phagan lay face upward, with her head toward the rear of the building.

Responding officers described her lying face downward, with her head toward the front.

Coroner Donehoo challenged Lee over the contradiction.

Lee answered:

“I didn't turn it over” (AJ, 1).

The conflicting accounts raised questions about whether the body had been moved after Lee's discovery.

The Journal considered whether the murderer remained in the basement when Lee descended and escaped before police arrived.

It also explored whether the killer intended to burn the remains in the factory furnace.

Sergeant Levi Sanford Dobbs Examines the Basement

Sergeant Levi Sanford Dobbs testified about the difficulty of seeing the body from Lee's reported position.

Dobbs attempted to reproduce the view by having another officer lie where Mary Phagan had been found.

Even during daylight, he found the position difficult to see.

Dobbs also observed evidence suggesting that the body had been dragged from the elevator shaft.

He believed an ordinary man would have difficulty carrying a body down the narrow basement ladder.

His testimony raised questions about how the body reached the basement and whether the elevator had been used (AJ, 1).

The Murder Notes That Appeared to Accuse Lee

Two handwritten notes were discovered near Mary Phagan's body.

One was written on yellow paper, the other on rough scratch paper.

Their confused language and unusual spelling included references to a tall Black man and suggested that blame would fall on the night watchman.

The implication pointed toward Lee.

The notes appeared to be messages from the victim, making them potentially damaging evidence.

But their wording also suggested that someone might have written them to direct suspicion toward a Black factory employee (AJ, 1).

Three Handwriting Experts Initially Accuse Lee

The April 30 Journal reported that three handwriting examiners believed Lee had written the notes.

They were Frank M. Berry, assistant cashier of the Fourth National Bank; Andrew M. Bergstrom, assistant cashier of the Third National Bank; and Pope C. Driver, chief bookkeeper in the mail department of the American National Bank.

They compared samples obtained from Lee and Frank.

The examiners identified similarities in spelling and letter formation, including the unusual spelling “slef” for self.

Their conclusions increased suspicion against Lee.

However, weeks later, Jim Conley, another Black factory employee, admitted writing the notes.

Conley alleged that Frank instructed him to prepare them using his own spelling and manner of expression, including the dialect reflected in the documents. Frank asked Conley if he knew Lee. Conley stated he did not. Lee was the intended fall guy for Leo Frank. 

Frank denied the accusation and maintained that Conley was responsible for the murder.

Conley's admission undermined the earlier handwriting accusations against Lee (AJ, 4; AJ, 8).

Sunday, April 27: Frank Says the Time Card Was Correct

The time-clock controversy became one of the most serious questions surrounding Frank.

On Sunday morning, investigators brought him back to the factory to examine Lee's record.

Frank opened the clock and removed the recording slip.

Woods White “Boots” Rogers, who had assisted the responding officers, witnessed the examination.

Others present included Detective John R. Black, factory foreman N. V. Darley, and Lee.

Rogers later testified that he examined the slip and remembered seeing a punch at every numbered position.

He recalled morning punches at approximately 6:01 and 6:32 or 6:33.

Frank initially described the record as satisfactory on Sunday, on Monday he said there were missing punches.

Lee confirmed that statement during the April 30 inquest.

Asked what Frank said about his punches, Lee answered:

“He said it was all right” (AJ, 1).

Darley also acknowledged that every numbered position contained a punch, although closer examination revealed irregular intervals.

Frank retained possession of the recording slip after the Sunday inspection.

This raised questions about why a record initially described as satisfactory subsequently became evidence against Lee (AJ, 5).

The Missing Punches Suddenly Become Evidence Against Lee

By Monday and Tuesday, April 28 and 29, investigators were treating the time card as suspicious.

The April 30 Journal reported regular punches until approximately 9:25 p.m. Saturday.

The next recorded punch appeared at 10:29 p.m., an interval of 64 minutes rather than the expected 30.

Another irregularity occurred between 2 and 3 a.m.

These gaps suggested that Lee had unaccounted-for time during his shift.

Frank explained that he initially overlooked the irregular intervals.

But Lee had testified that Frank originally described the punches as correct.

The dispute raised questions about Frank's handling of the recording slip and whether investigators were examining the same record originally removed from the clock (AJ, 2; AJ, 5).

Frank Says Lee Had Enough Time to Go Home and Return

The most damaging testimony concerning Frank's interpretation of the clock appeared during the July 1913 trial.

On Thursday, July 31, the Atlanta Journal reported Detective John R. Black's testimony.

Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey asked Black whether Frank suggested that the missing punches gave Lee enough time to visit his residence and return to the factory.

Black testified that Frank made that suggestion after examining the time slip a second time.

This connected Frank directly to the theory that Lee could have left the factory without recording his movements.

The 9:25 to 10:29 p.m. interval lasted 64 minutes, approximately 34 minutes longer than the expected half-hour interval.

Under the police theory, Lee could have used that time to travel to his residence on Henry Street, change bloodstained clothing, conceal evidence, and return to the factory.

Frank's statement transformed an irregular clock record into a suggested opportunity for criminal activity. The police would naturally check Lee's home.

The distinction was significant. A missing punch showed that the clock was not registered at the expected time. It did not independently establish that Lee had left the premises (AJ, 6).

Detective Black Connects Frank's Statement to the Search

During the same examination, Dorsey asked Black whether detectives searched Lee's residence before or after Frank directed attention toward the irregular time punches.

Black answered:

“Afterward” (AJ, 6).

Frank had suggested that Lee possessed enough time to visit his residence.

Detectives subsequently searched that residence and discovered a shirt bearing suspected bloodstains.

The time card suggested an opportunity to leave the factory.

The shirt appeared to explain what Lee might have done during that absence.

Together, these two pieces of evidence made the watchman appear more suspicious.

The prosecution later used this chronology to argue that someone had attempted to frame Lee.

The Bloodstained Shirt Found at Lee's Residence

Detectives John R. Black and Fred Bullard found a shirt with suspected bloodstains inside a barrel containing discarded clothing at Lee's residence.

Lee maintained that he had not worn it for approximately two years and that it had no bloodstains when he last saw it.

The April 30 Journal reported that his wife said he had left home wearing the same clothing he wore while detained.

The newspaper also reported that investigators considered whether the evidence had been planted.

The discovery supported the theory that Lee could have returned home during a missing clock interval.

But investigators still needed evidence showing that he actually visited his residence and wore the stained garment (AJ, 2).

The Shirt Appears to Have Been Stained While Unworn

At trial, Atlanta City Chemist Dr. Claude A. Smith examined the shirt.

The Journal reported that it appeared otherwise clean, with suspected bloodstains primarily on the inside.

Smith testified that the garment appeared washed and not recently worn. The condition of the collar and armpits supported his conclusion.

The stains appeared smeared across the inside rather than deposited during ordinary wear.

These findings supported the prosecution's argument that the shirt had been stained while unused and deliberately planted.

The defense challenged that interpretation.

The evidence nevertheless weakened the suggestion that Lee had worn the shirt during a violent struggle (AJ, 7).

Prosecutor Frank Arthur Hooper Connects the Time Card and Shirt

During closing arguments on August 22, 1913, prosecutor Frank Arthur Hooper accused Frank of attempting to make Lee appear responsible for Mary Phagan's murder.

Hooper emphasized the superintendent's initial approval of the time punches, the subsequent discovery of irregularities, and the bloodstained shirt found at Lee's residence.

The prosecution argued that the clock record created sufficient time for Lee to visit home, while the shirt supplied apparent physical evidence of that visit.

Under this theory, the two items reinforced each other and could direct investigators toward a false accusation.

Frank's defense maintained that the clock irregularities had simply been overlooked during the first inspection (AC, 9).

Police Fail to Obtain a Confession From Lee

The April 30 Journal reported that detectives repeatedly questioned Lee, attempting to obtain additional information or a confession.

Lee continued denying involvement.

The newspaper described an incident in which Walter Graham, a nearby prisoner, discharged a small revolver in an adjoining cell.

The gunshot frightened Lee, but further questioning did not produce a confession.

A chemical examination of material recovered beneath Lee's fingernails revealed no blood.

Investigators also determined that apparent bloody fingerprints on Mary Phagan's arm were actually paint marks.

Francis E. Wright, who assisted police in questioning Lee, reportedly believed the watchman was innocent.

These findings weakened the accusations against him (AJ, 2).

Frank and Lee Meet Privately at Police Headquarters

The April 30 Journal reported that detectives arranged a private conversation between Frank and Lee on Tuesday night, April 29.

Rumors circulated that police used a dictaphone to overhear their discussion.

Chief of Detectives Newport A. Lanford and Chief of Police James L. Beavers denied using a dictaphone.

The encounter later became an issue at the May 8 coroner's hearing.

Lee alleged that Frank warned him about continuing to insist that he knew nothing about the murder.

Frank maintained that detectives had instructed him to question Lee.

Detective Black confirmed that police encouraged the meeting but did not corroborate the precise statements Lee attributed to Frank (AJ, 2).

Luther Zeigler Rosser and Frank's Defense

Luther Zeigler Rosser represented Frank during the investigation and subsequent trial, working alongside attorney Reuben R. Arnold.

The defense challenged the prosecution's interpretation of the time card, shirt, and murder notes.

Frank maintained that he initially overlooked the irregular clock intervals.

His attorneys denied that he planted the shirt or directed Conley to write the notes.

They challenged Conley's credibility and rejected the allegation that Frank attempted to make Lee responsible for the murder.

But Detective Black's testimony created a serious question for the defense.

Frank had suggested that the missing punches gave Lee enough time to visit his residence.

Detectives subsequently searched that residence and discovered the suspicious shirt.

The defense's explanation for the clock discrepancy therefore had to be considered alongside Frank's role in directing investigators toward Lee's possible movements (AJ, 6).

How the Three Pieces of Evidence Worked Together

The time card, shirt, and murder notes formed the foundation of the alleged attempt to frame Lee.

The time card suggested an opportunity to leave the factory.

The shirt suggested a reason for visiting his residence.

The murder notes appeared to accuse a Black night watchman.

Each item increased suspicion against Lee.

Yet the clock record had been described differently following Frank's examination, the shirt appeared stained while unworn, and Jim Conley eventually admitted writing the notes.

The prosecution argued that these circumstances represented an effort to redirect suspicion toward the employee who discovered the body.

Frank's defense disputed that interpretation and maintained that the evidence had been misunderstood or resulted from Conley's actions.

Conclusion: The Time Card That Could Have Condemned Newt Lee

Newt Lee entered the investigation as the watchman who discovered Mary Phagan's body and telephoned the police.

Within days, three pieces of evidence appeared to implicate him.

The time card became especially dangerous because Frank suggested the missing punches gave Lee enough time to leave the factory, travel home, change clothing, and return.

A bloodstained shirt discovered at Lee's residence appeared to support that theory.

Two murder notes seemed to accuse a Black night watchman, although Conley subsequently admitted writing them.

The April 30 Atlanta Journal recorded Lee's testimony that Frank had initially declared his clock punches correct.

The July 31 Journal later reported Detective Black's testimony that Frank suggested Lee had enough time to go home and return.

Black also testified that detectives searched Lee's residence after Frank directed attention toward the irregular record.

These circumstances formed the prosecution's argument that someone had attempted to make Lee the scapegoat for Mary Phagan's murder.

Frank's unusual instructions, his control over factory records, and his statements about Lee's possible movements remain central to examining that allegation.

The Atlanta Journal of April 30, 1913, provides a detailed contemporary account of how suspicion developed against Newt Lee and how the evidence later used against Leo Frank emerged during the investigation.

A U.S. Army Air Forces photograph from February 1, 1943, shows a B-17 bomber in flight with its tail almost cut off.

The ten Americans inside were offered the chance to bail out twice. All ten stayed, and all ten walked away from the landing.

The bomber was a B-17F named All American, flown by Lieutenant Kendrick Bragg from a desert base near Biskra, Algeria. That day his squadron bombed the German-held ports of Bizerte and Tunis. The P-38 fighters that were supposed to escort the bombers never joined up.

On the way home, German Bf 109 fighters attacked head-on. Gunners hit one of them, and its pilot could no longer pull away. Bragg and his copilot shoved the nose down. The fighter's wing sliced through the top of the bomber's rear fuselage.

Bragg remembered it as a slight thud, like an engine coughing.

Behind him the left horizontal stabilizer was gone. The intercom, oxygen and electrical systems were damaged. The tail section hung on by a few spars and a strip of skin on the right side. One crewman said, "You could drive a jeep through that hole."

Enough control cable survived to work the rudder and part of the elevator, and the autopilot helped hold the bomber steady. The two pilots throttled back and braced the control yokes with their hands and knees.

The tail gunner, Sam Sarpolus, was sitting in the part that was coming off. He crawled forward to the waist, carrying his parachute.

Other B-17s slowed down and stayed close until the damaged bomber was out of reach of enemy fighters. From one of them, navigator Cliff Cutforth took the photograph.

Biskra was about 90 minutes away. Bragg twice offered his crew the chance to jump. Every man chose to ride the bomber down.

The tail wheel no longer worked. The crew fired three flares, ambulances stood by, and the broken tail dragged across the sand runway. It held.

When the engines stopped, Bragg reported: "No business, Doc."

Later, three visitors climbed inside to look at the damage. One of them asked Sarpolus why she hadn't broken in two. Under the weight of the three men, the tail broke in two right then.

Mechanics fitted a tail from the salvage yard in about six weeks, and All American flew again.

text:
WHEN CULTURE OPENS NEW DOORS! 🌍

══════════════ ❧ ════════════════

CULTURAL DEBUTS 🎭

══════════════ ❧ ════════════════

A CULTURAL TIME CAPSULE ⋆ NOVEMBER 10TH EDITION

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🕒 ESTIMATED READING TIME: 10–12 MINUTES

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎵 Music ⋆ 📺 Television ⋆ 🎬 Film & Animation ⋆ 📚 Publishing & Literature ⋆ 🎭 Theatre ⋆ 📻 Radio ⋆ 🎮 Games & Other Cultural Firsts

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

📜 EPIGRAPH

“Every author, as far as he is great and at the same time original, has had the task of creating the taste by which he is to be enjoyed.” — William Wordsworth, Essay, Supplementary to the Preface, 1815.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎭 THE CURTAIN RISES. THE CLOCK TURNS BACK. THE MAGIC BEGINS!

“Imagination is the beginning of creation. You imagine what you desire; you will what you imagine; and at last you create what you will.” — George Bernard Shaw, Back to Methuselah (1921), Part I, Act I.

November 10 celebrates creations that taught, challenged, entertained, and endured.

A neighborhood opens its doors to the world, and Sesame Street begins a television experiment that will help generations of children learn through laughter, music, and imagination. In Britain, a very different kind of neighborhood welcomes a new vicar—and discovers that Geraldine Granger is about to upset every comfortable expectation.

Rock music finds fresh languages of expression. The Moody Blues combine pop with orchestral color; Patti Smith turns poetry and rock into a declaration; Queen embraces theatrical excess, while The Clash sharpen their political edge.

Literature confronts the human cost of war, Broadway welcomes a musical Noah, and cinema brings audiences the extraordinary true-life story of Christy Brown.

Different stages. Different audiences. One shared power: culture can change what people hear, see, question, and believe.

THE PAST IS CALLING. THE MEMORIES ARE ALIVE. LET US RELIVE THE MAGIC! ✨

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎵 MUSIC

1967 — The Moody Blues Release Days of Future Passed 🎼

On November 10, 1967, the Moody Blues released Days of Future Passed, an ambitious album that helped define the possibilities of orchestral rock.

Built around the passage of a single day—from morning to night—the record placed the band's songs alongside arrangements performed by the London Festival Orchestra. The combination of rock instrumentation, orchestral passages, spoken poetry, and recurring musical themes gave the album a distinctive, almost cinematic shape.

Its best-known track, “Nights in White Satin,” became one of the group's signature recordings. The album also included “Tuesday Afternoon,” “The Day Begins,” and “The Night.”

🧩 TRIVIA: The album's original concept was structured as a complete day, with its movements progressing from “The Day Begins” to “The Night.”

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Sometimes a musical experiment becomes a new way of hearing an entire genre.

───────────────

1975 — Patti Smith Releases Horses 🐎

On November 10, 1975, Patti Smith released Horses, her debut studio album and one of the landmark recordings associated with the emergence of punk rock.

Produced by former Velvet Underground musician John Cale, the album fused raw guitar-driven rock with Smith's poetry, spoken-word intensity, and unconventional vocal delivery. Its opening reinterpretation of “Gloria” announced an artist unwilling to separate literary ambition from rock-and-roll rebellion.

Songs such as “Redondo Beach,” “Birdland,” and “Free Money” moved between punk energy, poetic imagery, and musical experimentation. Horses would influence generations of musicians who saw that rock could be confrontational, intellectual, and emotionally unguarded at once.

🧩 TRIVIA: Horses was inducted into the Library of Congress National Recording Registry in 2009 for its cultural, historical, and aesthetic significance.

🐶 SPOT: The album's stark cover portrait was photographed by Robert Mapplethorpe, a close friend of Smith's whose image became one of rock's most recognizable album photographs.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A new sound can begin when an artist refuses to choose between poetry and noise.

───────────────

1978 — Queen Releases Jazz 🚲

On November 10, 1978, Queen released Jazz, its seventh studio album, a record that moved confidently between hard rock, pop, music-hall humor, and theatrical experimentation.

The album included “Fat Bottomed Girls,” “Bicycle Race,” “Don't Stop Me Now,” and “Mustapha.” Its contrasting styles reflected a band comfortable treating the studio as a place for invention rather than musical restraint.

“Bicycle Race” and “Fat Bottomed Girls” had been released together as a double A-side single the previous month, but the album gathered them into a wider collection of Queen's exuberant and sometimes deliberately outrageous musical ideas.

🧩 TRIVIA: Jazz was released in the United Kingdom on November 10, 1978, with thirteen tracks on its original album.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Creative confidence sometimes means refusing to stay in one lane.

───────────────

1978 — The Clash Releases Give ’Em Enough Rope 🎸

On November 10, 1978, The Clash released Give ’Em Enough Rope, their second studio album and their first to feature drummer Topper Headon.

Produced by Sandy Pearlman, the record expanded the band's sound while retaining the urgency and political edge that had distinguished its debut. Songs such as “Safe European Home,” “English Civil War,” “Tommy Gun,” and “Stay Free” combined forceful rhythms with lyrics attentive to conflict, alienation, and life under pressure.

The album helped introduce the group to a wider international audience and showed that punk could grow in scale without surrendering its bite.

🧩 TRIVIA: Give ’Em Enough Rope reached No. 2 on the UK Albums Chart, becoming the band's highest-charting studio album in the United Kingdom.

🐶 SPOT: The album's producer, Sandy Pearlman, was already known for his work with Blue Öyster Cult—an unexpected bridge between the Clash's punk urgency and American hard rock.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A band can expand its sound without abandoning the convictions that made it matter.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

📺 TELEVISION

1969 — Sesame Street Opens Its Doors to the World 🧸

On November 10, 1969, Sesame Street made its television debut, introducing a new kind of children's program built around entertainment, educational research, and the belief that television could help prepare young children for school.

Created through the work of Joan Ganz Cooney, Lloyd Morrisett, educators, researchers, performers, and television producers, the series brought together live-action scenes, animation, music, and Jim Henson's Muppets. Its lively mixture of short segments was designed to hold children's attention while teaching letters, numbers, and other foundational skills.

The first episode, “Gordon Introduces Sally to Sesame Street,” welcomed viewers into a fictional New York neighborhood where children and adults shared the screen with colorful puppet characters.

🧩 TRIVIA: The first episode aired on more than 180 television stations across the United States.

🐶 SPOT: Sesame Street's educational approach was developed with research and testing; the show was designed not merely to entertain preschoolers, but to help children—especially those with fewer educational opportunities—enter school better prepared.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The most lasting lessons can arrive disguised as play.

───────────────

1994 — The Vicar of Dibley Welcomes Geraldine Granger ⛪

On November 10, 1994, BBC One premiered The Vicar of Dibley with the episode “The Arrival,” introducing Dawn French as Geraldine Granger, a new vicar assigned to a small English village.

The villagers expect a conventional clergyman. Instead, they meet a witty, outspoken woman whose arrival unsettles the assumptions of the parish's traditional-minded residents—especially David Horton, the village's self-appointed authority.

Created by Richard Curtis and written with Paul Mayhew-Archer, the sitcom mixed affectionate village comedy with questions about tradition, authority, faith, and changing social attitudes. French's performance, supported by a memorable ensemble, made Geraldine an enduring television character.

🧩 TRIVIA: The first episode was broadcast at 8:30 p.m. on BBC One.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Sometimes the person who changes a community is the one it never expected.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎬 FILM & ANIMATION

1989 — My Left Foot Reaches Wider Audiences 🎬

On November 10, 1989, My Left Foot: The Story of Christy Brown received its wide theatrical release in the United States.

Directed by Jim Sheridan and starring Daniel Day-Lewis, the film tells the story of Christy Brown, an Irish writer and painter born with cerebral palsy who learned to communicate and create by controlling the movement of his left foot.

Day-Lewis's performance portrayed Brown's determination, anger, humor, and artistic ambition without reducing him to an inspirational symbol. Brenda Fricker co-starred as his mother, whose commitment helped him find ways to express himself in a world that often underestimated him.

The film brought Brown's life and work to a much wider audience and became a major critical success.

🧩 TRIVIA: Daniel Day-Lewis won the Academy Award for Best Actor for his performance, while Brenda Fricker won Best Supporting Actress.

🐶 SPOT: The story was based on Brown's own autobiography, published in 1954, making the film an adaptation of an artist's account of his life rather than a fictionalized disability narrative.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Art can give a voice to someone the world has failed to hear.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

📚 PUBLISHING & LITERATURE

1928 — All Quiet on the Western Front Begins Publication 📖

On November 10, 1928, the first installment of Erich Maria Remarque's All Quiet on the Western Front appeared in the German newspaper Vossische Zeitung.

Published serially over the following month, the novel follows Paul Bäumer, a young German soldier whose experience of the First World War strips away the patriotic language and heroic expectations with which his generation had been sent to fight.

Remarque's direct, unsentimental account brought readers close to the physical and psychological destruction experienced by ordinary soldiers. The novel appeared in book form the following year and became an international bestseller, translated into numerous languages and adapted for the screen.

🧩 TRIVIA: The newspaper serialized the novel from November 10 through December 9, 1928; the book edition followed in 1929.

🐶 SPOT: Remarque had served in the German army during the First World War and was wounded several times. His experience helped inform the novel's portrayal of young soldiers whose lives were consumed by a conflict they had barely understood.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: The most powerful war stories often come from those who expose the distance between patriotic promises and lived reality.

───────────────

1973 — Reports Emerge of Slaughterhouse-Five Copies Burned in North Dakota 🔥

On November 10, 1973, newspapers reported that a school custodian in Drake, North Dakota, had burned copies of Kurt Vonnegut's Slaughterhouse-Five three days earlier, following a school board order to destroy the books.

The novel, published in 1969, follows Billy Pilgrim through a fractured narrative shaped by war, memory, and time. Vonnegut's account of the firebombing of Dresden drew on his own experience as a prisoner of war who survived the destruction while held in the city.

The school board's action became part of the book's long and controversial history in American education, where challenges to its language and treatment of violence repeatedly brought questions of censorship into public debate.

🧩 TRIVIA: Slaughterhouse-Five was published in 1969, four years before the North Dakota book-burning incident.

⚠️ IRONY: A novel condemning the destruction of human life became the target of an act intended to destroy the book itself.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Banning a book does not erase the questions that made it worth reading.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎭 THEATRE

1920 — George Bernard Shaw's Heartbreak House Opens on Broadway 🎭

On November 10, 1920, the Theatre Guild presented the American Broadway premiere of George Bernard Shaw's Heartbreak House at New York's Garrick Theatre.

Subtitled “A Fantasia in the Russian Manner on English Themes,” the play unfolds in a country house on the eve of the First World War. Its eccentric inhabitants debate love, money, politics, social responsibility, and the direction of a society drifting toward catastrophe.

Shaw uses the household as a miniature portrait of an entire social order: clever, privileged, distracted, and unable to recognize the danger gathering beyond its walls.

🧩 TRIVIA: The original Broadway production ran for 125 performances, closing on February 26, 1921.

🐶 SPOT: Shaw's subtitle deliberately invokes the Russian playwright Anton Chekhov, whose plays often used domestic gatherings and apparently ordinary conversations to reveal deeper social unease.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A society can be in danger long before its comfortable rooms notice the approaching storm.

───────────────

1970 — Two by Two Brings Danny Kaye to Broadway as Noah 🛶

On November 10, 1970, Two by Two opened at the Imperial Theatre, starring Danny Kaye as Noah in a musical retelling of the biblical flood story.

With music by Richard Rodgers, lyrics by Martin Charnin, and a book by Peter Stone, the production approached the familiar story through family comedy and the everyday complications of a man charged with building an ark and saving the animals.

The show also featured Madeline Kahn, Joan Copeland, Marilyn Cooper, and Walter Willison. It gave Kaye a major Broadway musical role and offered Rodgers another opportunity to explore a theatrical story built around character and song.

🧩 TRIVIA: An original Broadway cast recording was made shortly after the show's opening, preserving Danny Kaye's performance as Noah.

🐶 SPOT: The musical was based on Clifford Odets's play The Flowering Peach, which had already reimagined the Noah story as a family drama.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Even the biggest assignments in history come with very human family complications.

───────────────

1944 — Lyricist Tim Rice Is Born ✍️

On November 10, 1944, Tim Rice was born in Amersham, Buckinghamshire, England. He would become one of the most successful lyricists in modern musical theatre.

His partnership with composer Andrew Lloyd Webber produced Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat, Jesus Christ Superstar, and Evita. Rice later collaborated with Elton John on Disney's The Lion King and contributed lyrics to Aladdin.

His work helped bring the scale and storytelling of musical theatre to audiences around the world, moving easily between biblical subjects, historical figures, pop music, and animated film.

🧩 TRIVIA: Rice and Andrew Lloyd Webber first met in 1965 after a publisher suggested that the aspiring lyricist collaborate with the young composer.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A great lyric can make a character's story live long after the curtain falls.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🎮 GAMES & OTHER CULTURAL FIRSTS

2000 — Spyro: Year of the Dragon Arrives in Europe 🐉

On November 10, 2000, Spyro: Year of the Dragon was released for the original PlayStation in Europe.

The third main entry in Insomniac Games' platform series sent the purple dragon on a quest to recover 150 dragon eggs stolen by the Sorceress. The adventure expanded the series with new playable characters, varied environments, and a collection of mini-games and challenges.

Its colorful worlds, accessible controls, and playful personality helped make it one of the best-remembered entries in the original PlayStation era.

🧩 TRIVIA: Year of the Dragon was the final Spyro game developed by Insomniac Games before the series moved to other developers.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A beloved game world can keep growing while preserving the character that made players care.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

📚 SOURCES & FURTHER READING

🎵 MUSIC

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

AND WHAT A SHOW IT HAS BEEN! 🎭

November 10 opened a neighborhood that would become a classroom for the world. Sesame Street showed that learning could be joyful, inventive, and welcoming—and that television could serve children as well as entertain them.

Music explored new territory: the Moody Blues joined rock to orchestral ambition, Patti Smith fused poetry with rebellion, Queen embraced musical variety, and The Clash carried punk's urgency to a wider audience.

The Vicar of Dibley turned a village's expectations upside down. My Left Foot brought Christy Brown's extraordinary creative life to wider audiences, while All Quiet on the Western Front gave a generation of readers an unvarnished account of war.

Literature also reminded us that books can be challenged, suppressed, and even burned—but their ideas do not disappear so easily. Broadway welcomed Shaw's social unease, Danny Kaye's Noah, and the early life of a lyricist whose words would travel around the world.

From a children's neighborhood to a dragon's quest, today's creations remind us that culture can teach, unsettle, inspire, and endure.

THE YEARS MOVE ON. THE CREATIONS LIVE ON. THE MAGIC NEVER STOPS! ✨

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

🍬 CANDY

November 11, 1965.

The Beatles return to Abbey Road Studios for the final recording session on their sixth album. In one marathon session, they record two new songs, add finishing touches to two others, and bring the recording of the album to completion.

The album will mark a creative turning point, with more introspective lyrics, richer arrangements, and a sound that moves beyond the group's earlier pop identity.

Which album reached the end of its recording sessions that night? Which two new songs were recorded, and which two earlier tracks received finishing touches? And what made this record such an important turning point?

Tomorrow, we'll step inside the studio for the making of a Beatles classic. 😉

There's another remarkable chapter waiting in tomorrow's cultural time capsule!

Keep discovering. Keep looking closer. The next cultural classic may be waiting to be found.

This is a fascinating story and I take some small amount of umbrage at Klippenstein's mischaracterization of it for political purposes. There is a mountain of context that the manufactured outrage throws by the wayside.

Critical to what's actually happening with this restoration of an enemy war memorial is this: Scouts are bound by an oath and law which (although few modern scouts take these seriously) demand a very high standard of conduct compared to society writ large.

It is multifaceted, but most relevant to this case is that the scout law commands scouts to be reverent in all that they do. This includes having respect for the weak, the infirm, or the enemy; The most difficult commandment that is implicit in this part of the scout law is this: having respect even for your most reviled vanquished foes and their progeny.

Scouts are implicitly forbidden to be motivated by raw hatred or fury no matter how indignant or righteous they may feel. It is an exercise in reverence, honor, and humility to do things like restoring an enemy's war memorial. Historically, scouts have done this as part of US Civil War reconciliations.

Affording honor and respect to the defeated and being able to separate conflict from the people left behind to deal with its ramifications is a critical aspect of fulfilling a scout's obligations to the scout oath and law. It is also an exercise in controlling one's most brutal impulses.

To that end, possessing a degree of universal reverence and restoring memorials that are visited by the children and grandchildren of a vanquished enemy are in keeping with the conduct expected of every scout. This is why the US Army makes a positive note of the event; It is in keeping with the high moral standard that scouts, a pool for the recruitment of military personnel and thus military personnel themselves, should be held to.

It is unfortunate that with the extreme politicization of the Second World War in particular, this virtuous action is made suspect, but I digress from that observation.

I leave you instead with an anecdote which is indicative of this attitude.

An American servicemen was severely wounded at the Battle of Okinawa and had been separated from his compatriots. As his vision began to fade, he saw a young Japanese soldier approach, bayonet readied to render a coup de grace. In a haze, the American offered the three-fingered scout salute in recognition of his approaching killer before losing consciousness. To the man's surprise, he awoke and found a scribbled note reading that the Japanese soldier was himself a scout and could not stomach killing a man who had lost the will to fight. The Japanese soldier had rendered aid to the American and wished him luck in surviving the battle. There is a memorial to this event, and the unknown Japanese scout who almost certainly perished, in Yokohama, Japan which is maintained by scouts to this day.

A scout is reverent.

Mirroring: Copying someone's speech patterns, interests, clothing style, or values to make the target feel like they have met a "soulmate" or an identical match. [1, 2]
Performative Generosity & Virtue Signaling: Displaying public acts of kindness, charity, or moral outrage so that witnesses view them as good, while behaving selfishly or cruelly behind closed doors. [1, 2]
Aggressive Mimicry / Playing the Victim: Feigning vulnerability, helplessness, or victimhood to disarm others, deflect accountability, and gain access to sympathy or protection. [1, 2]
The Savior Complex: Positioning themselves as a protector or fixer in someone's life to establish control and dependency while pretending it is purely out of care. [1]
Selective Empathy & Politeness: Showing extreme charm, calmness, or manners in social settings or arguments, which makes them look reasonable while the other person looks unstable. [1, 2]
Moral Disengagement & Compartmentalization: Convincing themselves that their bad actions are actually justified, necessary, or for a "greater good" so they can bypass guilt and maintain a clean self-image. [1, 2]
How to Spot the Mask Slipping
Lack of Accountability: When confronted, they deflect, blame-shift, or use gaslighting rather than sincerely apologizing and changing behavior.
Conditional Kindness: Goodness appears only when they need a favor, an audience, or leverage, or vanishes the moment things do not go their way.
Private vs. Public Split: How they treat people who cannot do anything for them (service workers, subordinates, or private partners) is vastly different from how they treat authority figures or crowds.
Gut Instincts and Inconsistencies: Small red flags—like subtle degradation, white lies, gossiping about others to you, or quick shifts in tone—often reveal the underlying contradiction.

**Model Act: Informed Consent, Conscience, Religious Liberty, and Reserved Powers Protection Act**

### Section 1. Short Title
This Act may be cited as the “Informed Consent, Conscience, Religious Liberty, and Reserved Powers Protection Act.”

### Section 2. Legislative Findings and Purpose
The Legislature finds that:
- Informed consent and freedom of conscience are foundational to individual liberty. No person should be required to accept any medical intervention against their will.
- Conscience includes religious belief, moral conviction, and the internal sense that an action is wrong. Feeling that something is wrong is a sufficient basis to refuse.
- Legitimate authority rests on the absence of initiated force and fraud. Government may not use force or fraud to compel medical interventions.
- Powers not delegated to the federal government are reserved to the States or to the people under the Tenth Amendment.
- Individuals who report violations of these principles must be protected from retaliation.

### Section 3. Definitions
- **“Informed consent”** means a voluntary decision made after receiving information about the nature, purpose, risks, benefits, alternatives, and uncertainties of a proposed medical intervention.
- **“Conscience”** means a person’s sincerely held religious belief, moral conviction, ethical judgment, or internal sense—including feelings of unease or that an action is wrong—whether or not the person belongs to a religious organization or provides a detailed justification.
- **“Force”** means the initiation of physical violence, threats of violence, or coercive deprivation of property or liberty without consent.
- **“Fraud”** means intentional misrepresentation or concealment of material facts intended to induce another person to act to their detriment.
- **“Medical intervention”** includes any vaccine, drug, treatment, procedure, or experimental therapy.
- **“Covered entity”** includes state and local governments, public institutions, schools, employers receiving public funds, and health care facilities subject to state regulation.

### Section 4. Tenth Amendment Affirmation
(a) The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to this State or to the people.
(b) Federal mandates, regulations, or funding conditions that exceed enumerated powers and compel medical interventions in violation of this Act are void and unenforceable within this State to the maximum extent permitted by law.
(c) State and local officials shall not enforce such federal directives except where required by a final judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction.

### Section 5. No Force, No Fraud Principle
(a) It is the public policy of this State that no person or government entity may initiate the use of force or fraud against another.
(b) No covered entity may use force, threats, penalties, or fraudulent representations to compel any person to accept a medical intervention.
(c) Refusal based on informed consent or conscience may not be overridden by coercion, misrepresentation of risks or benefits, or conditioning of rights and benefits.

### Section 6. Right to Refuse on the Basis of Informed Consent or Conscience
(a) No person may be compelled to receive any medical intervention without their voluntary informed consent.
(b) A person has the absolute right to decline any medical intervention for any reason, including religious belief, moral conviction, personal conscience, or the internal feeling that the intervention is wrong, even if they offer no further explanation.
(c) No covered entity may deny employment, education, public benefits, licensure, or services; impose fines or disciplinary action; or condition any right or privilege on acceptance of a medical intervention because of such a refusal.
(d) A simple statement of decline on grounds of conscience is sufficient. No detailed justification or documentation may be required.
(e) Parents and legal guardians have primary authority to refuse medical interventions for their minor children on the basis of informed consent or conscience, except in a true emergency necessary to prevent death or serious permanent injury where consent cannot be obtained in time.

### Section 7. Conscience and Religious Liberty Protections
(a) Government shall not substantially burden a person’s exercise of conscience or religion unless it demonstrates a compelling governmental interest and uses the least restrictive means.
(b) No covered entity may discriminate against any person for declining a medical intervention on grounds of conscience or religion.
(c) No person or institution may be required to participate in, facilitate, administer, or refer for a medical intervention that violates their conscience.
(d) No person may be punished for expressing conscience-based objections or providing truthful information about risks and alternatives.

### Section 8. Whistleblower Protections
(a) No covered entity may retaliate against any person who, in good faith:
1. Discloses a violation or suspected violation of this Act, the Constitution, or the no-force/no-fraud principle;
2. Refuses to participate in an action they reasonably believe violates this Act; or
3. Provides information or testimony related to such violations.
(b) Protected disclosures may be made to a supervisor, the Attorney General, a legislative committee, law enforcement, or the public (provided no legitimately classified information creating a clear and present danger is knowingly released).
(c) A person who suffers retaliation may bring a civil action for reinstatement, compensatory and punitive damages, attorney’s fees, and other appropriate relief. Protection applies if the person had a reasonable belief that a violation occurred.

### Section 9. Private Right of Action and Remedies
Any person whose rights under this Act are violated may bring a civil action for injunctive relief, compensatory damages, reasonable attorney’s fees and costs, and any other appropriate relief. The Attorney General may also enforce this Act.

### Section 10. Severability
If any provision of this Act is held invalid, the remainder shall not be affected.

### Section 11. Effective Date
This Act takes effect upon passage.

---

This version integrates the Tenth Amendment reservation of powers, the no-force/no-fraud principle, broad conscience protections (including pure internal feeling), and whistleblower safeguards into a single model statute.

text:
New York's new AI companion law has a date problem. The signed text says it takes effect January 1, 2027. The sponsor's office says an amendment accompanying the signature moves that to June 1. That change isn't in the published law, so for now the text says January 1.

Ace's Report Card: AI Companion Features for Minors (NY S9051-B / A10379-C, Ch. 368, 2025-26 session) (signed Oct 28, 2026)

The Deal: AI companion operators can't offer 12 listed "unsafe" features to any New York user unless the user isn't a "covered minor" and the operator has used approved age-assurance methods to determine that. The attorney general enforces it.

Poker Hand: Everyone at the table shows ID before the dealer hands out these cards.

Title Integrity: C. The title says features "unsafe for minors," but the operative ban covers every user who hasn't passed an age check, adults included. Receipt: GBL 1801(1)(a)-(b).
Transparency: C. Feature (h) lets the AG add features by regulation, and the permitted age methods come from Article 45 rules. Receipt: GBL 1800(8)(h); 1801(1)(b); 1803.
Fiscal: C (judgment, unscored). No official fiscal note available; the Assembly record shows no LFIN. It imposes age-assurance costs on operators that no one has estimated, and adds AG enforcement work. (Confidence: Medium) Receipt: Assembly bill record; GBL 1802.
Liberty: C. Age checks touch adults who want these features. Safeguards: operators must offer one method that avoids government ID or keeps the user anonymous to them, and age data must be deleted. Limits on chatbot speech raise open First Amendment questions. (Confidence: Medium) Receipt: GBL 1801; 1804.
Ideological Capture: B. Open and germane. A law using the same age-gate to require features would get the same grade. Receipt: GBL 1800-1801.
Special Interests: B. Common Sense Media backed it; the Business Council of New York State opposed an earlier version. Customer service, research and internal business tools are exempt. Sponsor donor check (NYS BOE) not retrieved. Receipt: GBL 1800 exemptions; Engadget; Law Commentary.
Enforceability: C. The AG has strong remedies (up to $25,000 per violation, disgorgement, deleting data and models trained on it). The effective date conflict and the AG-defined features leave operators unsure what applies and when. Receipt: GBL 1802; Sec. 3.

Hidden Gotchas
- Feature (f): companions can't use a user's health or personal information "acquired from the user more than twelve hours previously or in any previous user session" unless the user is age-verified. (Confidence: High) GBL 1800(8)(f).
- "Covered minor" requires the operator's "actual knowledge" of age, but the ban turns on whether the operator ran an age check. (Confidence: Medium) GBL 1800(9); 1801(1).
- Self-declaration counts "only" if the user declares they're a minor. Adults can't just click "I'm 18." (Confidence: High) GBL 1804(1)(b).

The River Card: Backers cite teen self-harm cases and say companion features are built to hook kids. Critics, including some on the right, say it means age verification for every New Yorker who wants those features. It passed the Assembly 137-0, with Republican cosponsors in the Senate. Ch. 368 was signed with an approval memo.

Ace's Call: Call. Push lawmakers to settle the effective date in the statute itself (the signed text, Sec. 3, says January 1, 2027) and to set the age-assurance standards in law, not just in rules.

Confidence: High on the text; Medium on the effective date and First Amendment exposure.

Journalist Angle Note: Coverage says "for kids," but the gate applies to every user, and the date in the law isn't the date being announced.

Sources Used: NY Assembly bill record (text, votes, actions); Law Commentary; Engadget; IAPP.

Ratan ji, I am not an expert on the Ramayana. I watched the film purely through the eyes of a filmmaker and appreciated its cinematic spectacle and craft.

Yes, there may be creative liberties, and some may even be open to legitimate criticism. But I am neither qualified nor inclined to adjudicate matters of scriptural interpretation, particularly when it concerns something that is a matter of faith and devotion for millions.

I can speak with some authority on contemporary politics and subjects I have researched deeply. But when it comes to the Ramayana, I would rather exercise restraint than offer uninformed opinions or look for faults merely for the sake of criticism.

My appreciation, therefore, is strictly for the film as a cinematic experience. It should not be mistaken for an endorsement of every creative liberty taken by the filmmakers.

text:
Supreme Court Makes a Savage Ruling on Property Rights 

This video, presented by Noelle Randall, warns homeowners about the risks of eminent domain and property easements, explaining how private, for-profit utility companies can legally gain access to private land.

Key Takeaways:

The Legal Trap:  Governments can grant power to private companies to seize property rights, often taking a permanent easement—a "permanent permission slip" attached to your deed—that allows utility companies to access your land 24/7.

The Driver:  The rapid expansion of AI data centers is driving a massive need for power infrastructure, leading utility companies to aggressively pursue transmission routes across private land.

Case Example:  The video cites a dispute involving an Alabama homeowner, Fenn Church, whose property was impacted by a utility project despite an ongoing legal challenge.

Your Property Protection Playbook:

If you receive a certified easement letter, Noelle suggests these three steps:

1.  Negotiate the wording:  Never accept a "blanket easement." Demand a narrow, surveyed strip and add restrictions to prevent third-party usage (e.g., internet/telecom) without your consent.

2.  Fight for fair compensation:  Hire an independent appraiser to determine the true "diminution in value" of your property, as initial offers from corporations are rarely the best.

3.  Challenge the route:  If a more logical path exists, such as existing cleared timber tracts, push for the utility company to reroute.

Finally, Noelle emphasizes the importance of knowing state property laws, seeking qualified legal advice, and using structures like LLCs and trusts to protect your real estate investments.

text:
Four Tigers Who Have Stood Out This Fall

Fall softball offers an early look at what a roster can become. Through the scrimmages I attended, four Tigers consistently caught my attention: Mackenzie Pickens, Sydnee Williams, Ashlin Mowery and Char Lorenz.

Pickens has brought an elite bat with SEC experience, and it shows. The Ole Miss transfer launched a two-run homer at Orange Beach, drove a double off the right-field fence and added a three-run blast at Tiger Park a week later. Her ability to change an inning with one swing has been evident throughout the fall.

Williams arrived with plenty of buzz and has backed it up. The freshman’s scoreboard-clearing grand slams have been a highlight, including one that pushed LSU’s lead to 8-1 on Nov. 1. Her arm has been just as impressive. Watching her throw runners out at the plate from center field multiple times has made her impact on both sides of the ball difficult to overlook.

Mowery has stood out in the circle with an imposing presence and swing-and-miss heat. She was really good in her outing at Orange Beach against the Noles and continued to impress at Tiger Park the following week. Her ability to overpower hitters has been one of the fall’s most encouraging developments.

Lorenz has been among LSU’s most utilized players, moving between catcher and the outfield. Her work behind the plate has particularly impressed me, and her versatility gives the Tigers options as they sort through combinations for the spring.

Alix Franklin, Kylee Edwards and Sierra Daniel also have not missed a beat in the action I have watched. With those familiar contributors and these four standouts, LSU has offered plenty of reasons for encouragement heading toward spring.

text:
$TDW $RIG $VAL $OIH $SLB $XOP $SDRL $NE 

Tidewater Q3 results were much stronger than I anticipated. 

Seeing the leading edge at $27K with spare capacity ~11% of the fleet to reprice opportunistically is also a promising move. 

At 82% util guide for 2027 that assumes a $2,700 increase in day rate but we think that actually undershoots what realized day rates could be in 2027. 

FCF generation is going to allow for continued leverage declines though at a paltry 0.9x leveraged ratio now, we think any focus on debt is simply over thinking the businesses position at this point. 

The buyback is unlimited in its application at these leverage ratios and we continue to believe that will be the case as leverage ratios are something like 0.6-07x by early next year.

Wilsons is closed and integration is expected complete by Q1 2027. That fleet is inherently value add not just in the optionality from access to Brazil but because of the position Brazil is in as a major offshore development hub which importantly is a bipartisan effort regardless of who is in office in Brazil.

Transocean talked about vessels moving from USG > West Africa and Tidewater was no different. Because of sluggish demand in the USG vessels are recontracting for work in Suriname (via Total), Guyana and Africa - markets Tidewater and Transocean remain incrementally bullish on in the next 24 months. 

Asia Pacific has been strong with more projects to come in 2027 in Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia. Indonesia specifically is seeing development pulled forward. 

Projects we think Tidewater management was thinking about for continued demand include: Venus in Nambia, Neptun Deep in Romania, GranMorgu in Suriname, Bonga North Nigeria, Coral North FLNG, Agogo Integrated West Hub development in Angola, Buzios broadly alongside Albacora FPSO + 2 Sergipe FPSOs arriving later in the decade. CPOC Petronas/PTTEP JV in Asia Pacific.

Importantly, the less developed a basin, the more support required and more infrastructure that needs built. This is why we are incrementally bullish on the move out of the USG where intensity on vessels is higher and offer a more nascent development picture at this point - this further adds to our point that Tidewater, in the big picture of multi billion dollar FPSO/Drillships & subsea/SURF tech is a drop in the bucket to project economics. 

Are you going to haggle hard over a few thousand in day rate when you are paying $500K a day for a drill ship and risk project delays and lost cost from untimely drill mud and equipment?  We find that increasingly unlikely.

 The buyback program restarting is a net positive and we think it is notable Tidewater management reasserted the point on buybacks relative to intrinsic value inclusive of Wilsons in our mind, this means they are clearly underwriting the buyback decision on a bigger, better fleet therefore the pace and intensity of buybacks even at $75-80 is highly economic where perhaps it wasn't as promising in 2H 2024-2025. 

Supply that has been ordered largely was repurposed for other industries and different work with just 2 notable deliveries of OSVs from that 2024 order backlog. 

We think supply is going to continue to be hard pressed to bring on and even if one wanted to - who is going to pay for it? OSV operator balance sheets cant support the type of scale required not even at the current leading edge. 

We think Tidewater stands to earn something like $1.3B in cumulative FCF for 2027-2028. For next year, We think EBITDA could be a touch over $800M and using company average EV/EBITDA we think 8-10x is more than fair.

The wild card in our per share FCF is what does the pace of BB look like from here? Management notes vessel secondhand rates have exploded in the last 3 months so M&A is probably harder to get done at the prices Tidewater would hope to achieve. 

That leaves nothing but high FCF generation that, even if done at $100 reduces roughly 10% of the outstanding shares. The business is absolutely statistically cheap and on 1-2 year forward numbers makes us blush. 

We have been buyers throughout the life of this recovery starting back in 2020-2021 and continued to buy in the white space meltdown in 2025. 

We think reactivation risk is far over blown. It stands to reason that if new builds from 2024 are being moved to other types of work that companies with old vessels laid up that haven't worked would be skeptical of spending the kind of money required to retrofit vessels and get them to work. 

Those reactivations are also inhibited by the same shipyard dynamics as new builds. Our EBITDA walk is as follows:

Call it 63,450 working days on 212 vessels (assumes 82% active util includes dry dock).

Day rates of $27,000 give you revenue of $1.71B - the low end of management estimates (1.70-1.75B) - keeping util flat takes day rates required to just under $28,000 a day in rate for 2027. 

Revenue $1.730M
Vessel Opex $825M
Gross Income $900M
Cash G&A $140M
EBITDA $765M
Dry Dock $145M
Capex $45M
Taxes $90M
$480 - $500M FCF
S/O 49M
$9.50 - $10.25 FCF/PS excluding any buyback.
Buyback $475M @ $85 p/s = 5.6M shares retired 
Adj. S/O = 43M

The multiple of FCF is yours to assume but does a growing business with high operating leverage at a strong point in the cycle with no new supply coming justify 12-13x FCF? Perhaps. If it doesnt, rest assured the buyback will benefit shareholders even more.

text:
"Perfection is finally attained not when there is no longer anything to add, but when there is no longer anything to take away."

Antoine de Saint-Exupéry wrote that in 1939, about aircraft design.

It applies well beyond airplanes. A 2021 study in Nature found that when people try to improve something, they default to adding and overlook changes that take something away. They were even less likely to spot a useful subtraction when their minds were busy with something else.

That sounds a lot like running a business.

A slow approval process gets a new tool to track approvals, when it might only need one fewer sign-off. A confusing offer gets another FAQ, when it might need one fewer option.

Next time you're about to fix something, list what you could remove from the problem in front of you: a step, a rule, a product option, a meeting, a form field.

Test a reversible change where it is safe to do so. Keep required approvals, accessibility, security and customer protections intact; removing a step is useful only if the process still does its job.

Sometimes communications are very direct confirmations meant for anons. 

But every now and again— have you ever noticed that President Trump, the White House, or certain military-affiliated accounts or patriots post something that looks oddly out of place—strange misspellings, unusual capitalization, weird numbers, or a statement that doesn’t quite fit the moment?

This is a long-standing form of low-tech communication used by Trump and patriots aligned with him. Sometimes the audience is the public; sometimes it’s specific operators or insiders. 

What I am describing are steganographic or cryptographic signaling.

In these systems, the surface post is ordinary enough to be deniable. The real information is carried by deliberate “errors” or markers that only people with a shared key can read. A misspelling, a specific number, an odd timestamp, or a particular word order acts as a flag. 

Only Recipients who possess the codebook know which markers correspond to which pre-arranged meanings or actions. Think of it as a map and legend that only certain people have. 

Suppose you and a small group of patriots have agreed in advance that when a post contains the specific misspelling “Perade,” the extra “e” is the trigger. That single letter, combined with the time of posting or another agreed signal, tells you which action to take. Everyone else sees a typo. They see an instruction.

This approach offers strong plausible deniability and works over public channels that may be monitored. 

It doesn’t require encrypted apps, secure phones, or special equipment—just a pre-shared understanding and the ability to post or notice a post. 

In environments where conventional communications could be compromised, the method is simple, low-signature, and difficult to prove as intentional after the fact.

Military and intelligence organizations have used similar techniques for decades: open-source signaling, one-time codebooks, and steganographic markers embedded in routine traffic. 

The same principle is definitely being applied within the Trump admin. And Those holding the key see coordinated direction.

But always remember the very obvious comms of reassurance meant for us— such as “PATRIOTS IN CONTROL”

text:
Over this series I've covered JPYSC, Strium, the app and the card. OFK is the part where Startale offers that kind of infrastructure to other companies

OFK stands for Onchain Finance Kit. Startale announced it in July as a set of infrastructure kits for financial institutions and enterprises, with Japan and the US named among the key markets

The problem they point at makes sense to me. Plenty of institutions are working on strategies for stablecoins and tokenized assets, the hard part is turning those strategies into something live under local rules

The release lists five kits
Stablecoin: tooling to run and use JPYSC, with treasury management, reporting and links to existing financial systems
Wallets: account abstraction wallets that work across chains, basically smart wallets, plus the services around them
Privacy: privacy tech powered by Privacy Boost, for compliant and secure onchain transactions
Developer: RPC nodes (the doors apps use to talk to a chain), APIs and the Startale App SDK, so others can build on top of Startale App
Chains: Strium for trading and investment, Soneium for entertainment, enterprise and consumer apps

Two more are planned, one for tokenization and one for institutional custody

The way I'd explain it: instead of building a kitchen from zero, you move into one that already works, and Startale keeps maintaining the equipment
That second half comes straight from the release. Startale owns the modules and keeps improving them across every deployment, and institutions pick only the ones they need

What I like is how much of this is already working. JPYSC, the smart wallets in Startale App and Soneium are all live today
Strium is the one still on the way, its site says the testnet is launching soon

It's a quieter topic than the card, but it's how all of this can reach banks and businesses, not only people with a wallet
