text:
Iraqi Kurdistan at the Brink of Institutional Fragmentation: KDP–PUK Rivalry – Regional Power Competition and the Future of Kurdish Autonomy 
Principal judgment: Iraqi Kurdistan faces its most consequential institutional cohesion test in two decades. The immediate danger is not formal territorial partition but the emergence of competing executive authorities within a constitutionally recognised federal region.

On 4 November 2026, the Kurdistan Parliament resumed proceedings after prolonged paralysis, with 52 of 100 members attending against a quorum requirement of 51. On 5 November, PUK leader Bafel Talabani announced his party’s withdrawal from the Kurdistan Regional Government and threatened reciprocal appointments to senior regional offices.

The rupture threatens the foundations of the political settlement that brought rival Kurdish administrations together in 2006. It also creates uncertainty over command authority, public administration, budget transfers, oil revenues and security coordination.

The September 2026 announcement of Peshmerga unification provides an important institutional counterweight. Nevertheless, reorganising forces under a common ministry does not by itself establish whether military cohesion can withstand renewed political competition.

Baghdad remains the indispensable fiscal and constitutional counterpart. Negotiations over the 2027 federal budget continued on 8 November despite the political rupture.

Tehran’s diplomatic engagement with Erbil is documented, but the available official record does not establish an Iranian agreement to engineer the parliamentary outcome. Ankara’s security and energy interests favour functional coordination; Washington has a strategic interest in avoiding deterioration of Kurdish security institutions.

Net assessment: Prolonged administrative dualism is a more immediate and credible danger than formal secession or renewed large-scale Kurdish civil war. The decisive uncertainty is whether political confrontation develops into separate fiscal, security and coercive command structures.

Iraqi Kurdistan’s Political Fracture: How Rival Administrations Could Weaken Kurdish Autonomy Without Changing a Single Border
The confrontation between the Kurdistan Democratic Party and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan threatens to turn Iraq’s constitutionally recognised Kurdish autonomy into a system of competing authorities, weakening its financial bargaining power, military cohesion and regional influence without requiring formal partition. On 4 November 2026, the Kurdistan Parliament resumed proceedings with 52 of its 100 members present. One day later, Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) President Bafel Talabani announced his party’s withdrawal from the regional government and threatened reciprocal executive appointments. The dispute now intersects with negotiations over Iraq’s 2027 federal budget, the September reorganisation of the Peshmerga and the withdrawal of international coalition forces. Baghdad, Tehran, Ankara and Washington have different interests in the outcome, but the immediate institutional danger is already identifiable: a government may retain its constitutional status while progressively losing the authority to govern.

The Parliament Reopened, but the Government Lost Its Political Consensus
The 4 November 2026 parliamentary session ended almost two years of institutional paralysis following the October 2024 elections. With 52 members attending against a reported quorum requirement of 51, legislators elected Vala Fareed as Speaker, Rami Noori as Deputy Speaker and Muna Qahwachi as Parliamentary Secretary. The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) defended the proceedings as a lawful exercise of parliamentary authority. The PUK rejected their legitimacy, arguing that the process disregarded the political partnership underpinning regional government. The distinction is consequential: satisfying a numerical quorum does not automatically establish an accepted executive coalition, while political objections do not themselves invalidate a parliamentary decision. Kurdistan Parliament Reconvenes — KRG Representation in the United States — November 2026.

The confrontation became more serious on 5 November, when PUK President Bafel Talabani announced withdrawal from the outgoing Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG). His warning that the PUK could appoint its own regional president, prime minister and ministers transformed a procedural disagreement into a challenge concerning executive authority. The verified record establishes a threatened competing administration, not its complete legal or operational creation. Yet the distinction between intention and implementation offers limited reassurance if public officials subsequently begin receiving incompatible appointments, administrative instructions or financial authorisations. Full Statement by PUK President Bafel Jalal Talabani — PUK Media — November 2026.

The political danger is rooted in a settlement whose durability has always depended on cooperation between competing organisations. The 21 January 2006 agreement unified the previously separate KDP-led administration in Erbil and Duhok and PUK-led administration in Sulaymaniyah. It consolidated the governmental framework without eliminating the parties’ independent political organisations. Twenty years later, the unresolved issue is whether a common regional administration can continue operating when its principal political sponsors reject the same institutional procedures. Welcome to the Kurdistan Region of Iraq — Kurdistan Regional Government — 2009.

The Budget Numbers Reveal Why Neither Side Can Easily Afford Separation
The financial relationship with Baghdad exposes the material limits of Kurdish political fragmentation. In its 10 November 2026 assessment of federal budget relations from 2014 to 2025, the KRG reported approximately IQD 1.767 quadrillion in Iraqi federal budgets, more than IQD 245 trillion in allocations attributed to the region before deductions, approximately IQD 146 trillion after deductions and only IQD 41 trillion in actual federal transfers. It also disputed sovereign-expenditure deductions exceeding IQD 65 trillion. These are regional government calculations, not accounts independently reconciled with the federal treasury. Their significance is the persistent difference between budgetary allocation and cash received, which complicates the financing of salaries, services and investment. KRG Fiscal Assessment, 2014–2025 — Kurdistan Regional Government — November 2026.

The annual figures reveal the degree of financial volatility. The KRG reported no federal transfers in 2016 and 2017, followed by IQD 0.4 trillion in 2022, IQD 4.69 trillion in 2023, IQD 10 trillion in 2024 and IQD 9.59 trillion in 2025. The final two years accounted for approximately 47.8% of the reported 2014–2025 transfer total. This concentration illustrates why the timing and predictability of federal payments can matter as much as the nominal allocation written into a budget. It does not mean the region received no revenue from other sources during years when federal transfers were absent. KRG Fiscal Assessment — November 2026.

The dispute is already moving into the 2027 federal budget. The KRG cites the 2024 census as establishing a regional population share of 14.14%, against a proposed budget share of 12.70%, a difference of 1.44 percentage points. A separate controversy concerns the treatment of sovereign expenditures in the 2023–2025 budget period: the KRG calculates an approximately IQD 8.2 trillion difference between the deduction methodology it attributes to Baghdad and its own proposed alternative. Neither difference automatically constitutes an adjudicated financial liability. Both demonstrate how allocation formulas, accounting definitions and expenditure classifications influence the resources available to the regional government. KRG Fiscal Assessment — November 2026.

A revealing counterweight is the MyAccount public payroll programme. In October 2026, the regional Ministry of Finance and Economy reported 1,016,000 beneficiaries paid through the system during the September salary cycle: 422,000 in Erbil, 372,000 in Sulaymaniyah, 197,000 in Duhok and 25,000 in Halabja. An attempt to establish competing treasuries would therefore confront an existing financial infrastructure operating across the principal political areas. The test of administrative unity is not whether politicians continue communicating, but whether these payment and authorisation systems continue functioning under recognised public authority. Over 1 Million Public Sector Beneficiaries Paid Through MyAccount — KRG Ministry of Finance and Economy — October 2026.

Oil Infrastructure Turns Political Division into a Commercial Liability
The energy sector reveals why control of territory does not necessarily translate into control of revenue. Under the 17 March 2026 arrangement announced by the KRG negotiating team, federal and regional authorities agreed to establish a joint committee dealing with oil exports through the Kurdistan–Ceyhan pipeline. The announcement envisaged the return of export revenues to the federal treasury and coordinated protection of production infrastructure. The document establishes an agreed framework, not independently verified subsequent export volumes or receipts. Any competing regional authority would therefore confront an institutional system linking production, transportation, marketing and public revenue beyond its own geographical area. Statement by the KRG Negotiating Team Regarding Oil Exports — Kurdistan Regional Government — March 2026.

The commercial stakes extend beyond existing exports. At the 9 November 2026 meeting between KRG Prime Minister Masrour Barzani and Iraqi Federal Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi, the KRG reported federal plans to raise Iraqi oil production to 7 million barrels per day by 2030 and 10 million by 2032, including a projected contribution approaching one million barrels per day from Kurdistan Region fields. These are policy projections, not verified future capacity. Their realisation would require financing, infrastructure, security and coherent regulatory authority. Parallel governments issuing conflicting authorisations would increase uncertainty over the institutions competent to approve projects and administer revenues. Meeting of the Federal and Regional Prime Ministers — Kurdistan Regional Government — November 2026.

The same 9 November meeting addressed an attack on the Khor Mor gas field the previous night. Both prime ministers condemned the incident and discussed infrastructure protection. The published account does not establish the perpetrators or a connection to the KDP–PUK dispute. Nevertheless, the episode demonstrates how security vulnerability and administrative uncertainty can converge around energy assets. Investors require identifiable contracting authorities, predictable payments and functioning protection arrangements; a politically fragmented executive would make those requirements more difficult to satisfy even without additional physical damage. Federal and Regional Prime Ministers’ Meeting — November 2026.

Military Unification Faces Its First Major Political Test
The military contradiction is particularly acute. On 10 September 2026, the Kurdistan Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs announced the completion of the reorganisation integrating the historically distinct Force 70 and Force 80 structures. The formal arrangement, presented on 21 September, comprised 11 divisions, two mechanised support commands, one commando unit and two area commands. The official achievement was substantial in institutional terms, but formation counts do not demonstrate operational readiness or guarantee compliance with a unified chain of command during a political crisis. Peshmerga Unification and Reorganisation — Kurdistan Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs — September 2026.

Nine days after the reorganisation ceremony, the international coalition’s military mission in Iraq formally concluded on 30 September 2026. The UK Ministry of Defence confirmed the transition towards Iraqi-led security responsibilities, while the regional Peshmerga ministry raised concerns over aerial threats and the absence of a replacement air-defence arrangement. The ministry also reported more than 1,000 drone and ballistic missile strikes during the earlier regional conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran, a figure that remains an attributed regional claim rather than a fully independently reconciled incident series. The withdrawal altered the external support environment just before the political rupture, increasing the importance of effective Iraqi and Kurdish command coordination. Conclusion of the Global Coalition’s Military Mission in Iraq — UK Ministry of Defence — September 2026; KRG Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs Statement — September 2026.

The immediate danger is not proven mobilisation for another Kurdish civil war. It is the possibility that competing political authorities could contest appointments, financing or operational instructions within military institutions officially reorganised only weeks earlier. Such a development would complicate coordination with the Iraqi Army and the protection of infrastructure and borders. The public record does not establish a generalised collapse of Peshmerga command, making the distinction between political fragmentation and military disintegration indispensable.

Tehran and Ankara Can Gain Leverage but Cannot Ignore the Costs of Disorder
Iran and Türkiye have different interests in the Kurdish dispute. Tehran’s established security priority concerns Iranian Kurdish opposition organisations and implementation of Iraq–Iran border-security arrangements. On 8 November 2026, Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani received an Iranian delegation for discussions including regional security cooperation and existing understandings. The meeting demonstrates official Iranian engagement with Erbil; it does not prove an undisclosed bargain determining the parliamentary outcome. Iranian Delegation Meeting — Kurdistan Region Presidency — November 2026.

Ankara’s position combines counterterrorism concerns involving the PKK with substantial commercial exposure to Iraq. Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry reports USD 16.8 billion in bilateral trade during 2025, including USD 12.4 billion in Turkish exports, alongside 1,145 contracting projects with a cumulative reported value of approximately USD 36.5 billion. The planned 1,200-kilometre Development Road adds a longer-term infrastructure interest. These are Iraq-wide figures, not Kurdistan-specific revenues, but they show why instability in northern Iraq can carry costs beyond counterterrorism operations. Relations Between Türkiye and Iraq — Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs — Official Institutional Record.

Political fragmentation could make Kurdish leaders more dependent on negotiations with neighbouring governments, strengthening external bargaining positions. Yet separate administrative authorities could also produce inconsistent implementation of border agreements, complicate transport and weaken the reliability of governmental commitments. Iran and Türkiye may both favour effective security arrangements without sharing a strategy for Kurdish internal politics. Their overlapping interests do not establish coordinated intervention.

Washington and European governments confront a different constraint: continuing institutional cooperation without replacing Iraq’s constitutional decision-making authority. An October 2026 meeting between Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani and US Consul General Gwendolyn Green addressed Kurdish internal unity and government formation. The United Kingdom affirmed continued bilateral defence cooperation after the coalition transition; Germany concluded its military mission while maintaining diplomatic relations; and Italy discussed further Peshmerga training and capacity development in September. These separate positions indicate an interest in reliable institutions, not a common commitment to impose a political settlement. US Consular Meeting — Kurdistan Region Presidency — October 2026; Italian Military Delegation Meeting — Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs — September 2026.

The Next 24 Months Will Reveal Who Controls the Institutions—and Who Bears the Costs
Between November 2026 and November 2028, the decisive development will be whether the parliamentary rupture produces incompatible executive appointments, separate treasury arrangements or contradictory military orders. A negotiated KDP–PUK settlement could restore an accepted government without eliminating the underlying competition. Extended caretaker administration could maintain essential services while postponing reform. Administrative dualism would be more costly: Baghdad could face competing claims over financial authority, international partners could encounter uncertainty over security counterparts, and commercial operators could confront conflicting regulatory decisions. None of these outcomes requires formal territorial partition.

The civilian exposure is measurable. UNHCR registered 343,556 refugees and asylum-seekers in Iraq on 31 October 2026, including 144,282 in Erbil, 91,587 in Duhok and 38,430 in Sulaymaniyah. Those three governorates accounted for approximately 79.8% of the registered national total. A breakdown of regional administrative cooperation could complicate documentation, education, health care and humanitarian access without producing a new armed conflict. The figures establish existing service exposure, not displacement caused by the November dispute. UNHCR Iraq Operational Data — October 2026.

The legal limit remains explicit. Articles 117–121 of Iraq’s Constitution recognise the Kurdistan Region and define the framework of regional autonomy; they do not transform party-controlled administrations into independently recognised federal entities. A political settlement can resolve the distribution of offices, but only functioning legal, financial and security institutions can preserve the authority attached to those offices. Constitution of the Republic of Iraq — Iraqi Supreme Judicial Council — 2005.

The cost of inaction would consequently fall first on public employees dependent on predictable payments, citizens requiring uninterrupted services, businesses exposed to uncertain contracting authority and security institutions expected to maintain command cohesion. Baghdad would face more difficult financial and security coordination, while the Kurdish parties would risk surrendering bargaining power to external counterparts. The danger is not that Kurdistan’s borders will necessarily change. It is that the value of its constitutional autonomy could decline while those borders remain exactly where they are.

text:
On the morning of November 10, 1865, Captain Henry Wirz climbed the scaffold in the courtyard of the Old Capitol Prison in Washington. The Swiss immigrant who had taken Confederate service, been wounded at Seven Pines, and later been given command of the prison at Andersonville walked to his death as the only Confederate officer the Union government chose to hang for war crimes.

Andersonville was a catastrophe. The Confederacy, starved by blockade and broken railroads, crammed tens of thousands of Union prisoners into a stockade that could not hold them. Shelter was almost nonexistent. Food was scarce. Disease cut them down by the thousands. Roughly thirteen thousand died. Those are the hard facts, and they are not in dispute.

What followed the war was something else. Wirz was tried by a military commission in the charged atmosphere of the months after Appomattox and Lincoln’s assassination. He was charged with conspiracy and murder. Some of the testimony against him did not hold up. The defense that he had carried out the orders of a collapsing government was rejected. When offered his life if he would implicate Jefferson Davis in a deliberate plot to kill prisoners, Wirz refused. On the scaffold he is reported to have said, “I know what orders are, Major. I am being hanged for obeying them.” His neck did not break. He strangled while the crowd watched.

No equivalent justice was applied to the commanders of Northern prison camps where Confederate prisoners also died in large numbers. The hanging of Wirz served a purpose beyond the facts of Andersonville: it offered a visible scapegoat in the first months of Reconstruction and helped fix the narrative that the South alone had committed the war’s unforgivable crimes. He was buried in Mount Olivet Cemetery under a marker that still calls him a Confederate hero-martyr. The argument over whether he was a criminal, a functionary, or a convenient victim of the victors’ justice has never really ended.

text:
More Than 100 Chinese Vessels, Zero US Carriers in the Western Pacific: What Does It Mean for Taiwan?

China's expanding naval presence. Two US aircraft carriers in the Arabian Sea. And no US aircraft carrier currently identified in the Western Pacific.

These figures offer an interesting snapshot of the changing security environment in the Indo-Pacific.

The comparison is based on publicly available information as of November 9, 2026. It does not mean that American military forces have disappeared from the region.

1. What is China doing?

On November 3, Taiwan's National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu reported that more than 100 Chinese naval and coast guard vessels were operating across the Western Pacific.

In an assessment published on November 6, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and the American Enterprise Institute (AEI) suggested that China might be conducting a major, undeclared military exercise simulating the isolation of Taiwan.

The deployments appear concentrated in two broad areas.

One is between Taiwan and Guam, where multiple task forces from three PLA theater commands are operating, including the Liaoning carrier strike group.

The other is closer to Taiwan, involving Chinese naval and coast guard vessels.

On November 10, Taiwan's Defence Minister Wellington Koo also described China's Western Pacific activities as area-denial exercises involving the Liaoning and other naval formations.

One particularly notable aspect is that Beijing has not formally announced a corresponding large-scale exercise.

ISW and AEI assess that demonstrating the ability to isolate Taiwan could undermine Taiwanese confidence in its ability to resist and in the likelihood of external support.

These remain assessments based on publicly available information, not confirmed statements of Chinese operational intent.

2. America recently demonstrated its presence in the Philippine Sea

From October 19 to 29, Japan and the United States conducted Exercise Keen Sword 27.

Japan's participation involved approximately 45,000 personnel, 40 vessels and 260 aircraft. US participation involved approximately 11,000–12,000 personnel.

Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines also participated.

On October 21, US, Japanese, Australian, Canadian and French naval vessels sailed together in formation in the Philippine Sea.

On November 4, the USS Theodore Roosevelt conducted a replenishment-at-sea operation with the Royal Australian Navy's HMAS Stalwart in the South China Sea.

America had demonstrated its ability to operate alongside regional partners.

On October 28, the defence ministers of the United States, Japan, Australia and the Philippines met in Cebu.

They agreed to strengthen deterrence, interoperability and regional defence cooperation, including closer coordination along the First Island Chain.

These developments represent more than a symbolic naval presence. They point to the continued development of regional defence cooperation.

3. But the positioning of US aircraft carriers has changed

According to the US Naval Institute's fleet tracker on November 9, two American carrier strike groups were operating in the Arabian Sea.

USS George Washington: Normally forward-deployed to Yokosuka, Japan, and the principal aircraft carrier associated with the US Seventh Fleet.
USS George H.W. Bush: A separate carrier strike group operating in the Middle East.

Meanwhile, USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in Singapore on November 6 and departed on November 9, moving into the Andaman Sea.

There is an important distinction here.

This is not simply a case of America continuously adding more aircraft carriers to the Middle East.

Theodore Roosevelt is expected to relieve George Washington, which has been deployed to the Middle East since August 19.

The Roosevelt's deployment to the region had already been anticipated when it left San Diego in late September.

In other words, the United States is maintaining its two-carrier presence in the Middle East through a rotation.

However, this raises another question: will an aircraft carrier return to the Western Pacific after this rotation?

As of November 9, the USNI public deployment tracker identified no US aircraft carrier operating in the Western Pacific.

George Washington departed Yokosuka on May 23, and its return date has not been publicly announced.

This does not mean the Seventh Fleet has disappeared.

But its normally forward-deployed carrier has spent an extended period away from its home waters.

4. The US military is not absent from the region

This distinction matters.

According to the same November 9 USNI tracker, the USS Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group, including the embarked 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit, was operating in the Sea of Japan.

US destroyers, submarines, land-based aircraft, forward bases in Japan and Guam, and allied military forces also remain important components of regional deterrence.

China's aircraft carriers are not invulnerable either. They face potential threats from submarines, anti-ship missiles and opposing air power. Sustained carrier operations also require effective protection and logistical support.

Therefore, the absence of a US aircraft carrier in the Western Pacific does not automatically establish Chinese military superiority.

The real question is whether the United States can maintain credible deterrence through its remaining forces and regional partnerships while some of its major naval assets are committed elsewhere.

5. What might Beijing be calculating?

The following is my interpretation, rather than a confirmed account of Chinese intentions.

First: Observing the limits of American force distribution.

A prolonged conflict involving Iran requires the United States to manage military commitments in both the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific.

China may be observing how quickly American forces can be repositioned and how effectively the United States can respond to simultaneous challenges.

Second: Isolating Taiwan without immediately invading it.

China does not necessarily need to begin with an amphibious assault.

A combination of naval deployments, coast guard operations, inspections and maritime restrictions could increase pressure on Taiwan without an immediate declaration of a formal blockade.

This is the logic of grey-zone coercion: restricting an opponent's freedom of action while keeping the threshold of open warfare ambiguous.

Third: Undermining confidence in external support.

Would the United States be able to intervene quickly in a Taiwan contingency? More importantly, could it sustain that intervention?

Creating uncertainty around these questions could have psychological as well as military consequences.

6. Why the Philippines matters

The Philippines is not simply observing this competition from the sidelines.

The Liaoning carrier strike group reportedly passed through the Basilan Strait in the southern Philippines in late October before entering the Western Pacific.

At the same time, the United States maintains access to several Philippine military facilities under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA).

Facilities in northern Luzon are particularly significant because of their proximity to Taiwan and their position along the southern part of the First Island Chain.

For China, the waters around the Philippines are important to maritime access into the Western Pacific.

For the United States, the Philippines is a key partner in maintaining the regional security environment around Taiwan.

The October 28 meeting of the four defence ministers in Cebu reflects this geographical reality.

The Philippines is not merely a bystander in the US-China strategic competition. Its surrounding waters are part of the wider strategic environment in which both countries operate.

Japan also has a direct interest. A prolonged disruption of maritime traffic around Taiwan could affect vital shipping routes connecting Japan with Southeast Asia and the Middle East.

7. What should we watch next?

Several developments deserve particular attention:

Mid-November: Whether Theodore Roosevelt arrives in the Middle East and completes the expected carrier rotation with George Washington.
November 18–19: The APEC Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, where US-China diplomacy and Taiwan-related issues will remain important subjects.
November 28: Taiwan's local elections and whether China's military or information pressure affects the political environment.

These developments overlap in time, but there is no confirmed evidence that their schedules are directly coordinated.

They should be monitored separately rather than treated as proof of a single coordinated plan.

Final thoughts

China is demonstrating the ability to operate across a wider area of the Western Pacific, potentially including the capability to isolate Taiwan.

The United States, meanwhile, is maintaining major military commitments in the Middle East while attempting to preserve deterrence in the Indo-Pacific through its remaining forces and regional partnerships.

The issue is not simply a comparison of the number of ships on either side.

Military power and the ability to keep that power in the right place for as long as necessary are two different things.

America recently showed that it could appear in the Philippine Sea.

The next question is whether it can remain there.

And Beijing may be watching that distinction very closely.

text:
Key figures include:
•  First three years: Biden ~10,070 permits vs. Trump ~9,892 (Washington Post analysis of BLM data, covering inauguration-to-inauguration periods). Year-by-year breakdowns showed Biden higher in year 1 (3,564 vs. 2,588) and year 3, with Trump higher in year 2.
•  First two years: Biden ~6,430 vs. Trump ~6,172 (Center for Biological Diversity / BLM data).
•  Other tallies (e.g., one Center for Biological Diversity report) put the first three years closer, with Trump slightly ahead at ~9,982 vs. Biden’s ~9,779.
Politico and other reporting similarly noted higher permitting rates under Biden in certain years (e.g., 3,377 in 2023 vs. 2,507 in Trump’s third year).
Important context and nuances
•  Permits are not the same as new leases. Biden approved far fewer new leases (acres offered and leased). The Washington Post reported BLM leased only about 232,630 acres in Biden’s first three years versus more than 5 million under Trump. Much of Biden’s permitting was for wells on leases issued under prior administrations (including Trump’s), which the government is generally required by law to process.
•  Biden had campaigned on ending new drilling on federal lands (“No more drilling on federal lands. Period”) and attempted a leasing pause early on, but courts blocked it, and the administration continued approving permits on existing leases while expanding some projects

text:
ARE YOU KIDDING?! A Wisconsin court commissioner RELEASED a man accused of violently attacking an 84-YEAR-OLD WOMAN who had taken him in when he was homeless, allowing him to walk free WITHOUT POSTING A DIME IN CASH BAIL.

The elderly woman had offered him a place to stay after learning he was living out of his car, but he allegedly repaid her kindness by throwing her into a rocking chair, slamming her against a wall, and injuring her eye.

Robert C. Thompson, 63, of Kenosha, Wisconsin, was charged on November 5, 2026, with felony battery to an elderly person after allegedly attacking an 84-year-old woman who had opened her home to him.

According to a criminal complaint described by Kenosha County Eye, the woman had offered Thompson a place to stay after learning he had been living out of his vehicle.

But the arrangement allegedly ended in violence.
Investigators say Thompson threw the elderly woman into a rocking chair, slammed her against a wall, and caused an injury to her eye.

The victim's identity has not been publicly released, and additional details about the circumstances leading up to the confrontation have not been disclosed.

Thompson appeared in Kenosha County court on November 5, the same day the felony charge was filed.

Presiding over his initial appearance was Court Commissioner Daniel Kellum, who ordered Thompson released on a NO-CASH BAIL arrangement.

That meant Thompson did not have to post money to secure his release while the criminal case proceeded.
And this isn't the first time Kellum's bail decisions have attracted criticism.

Kellum was appointed as Kenosha County's Judicial Court Commissioner earlier in 2026, giving him authority to oversee initial appearances, set bail, and conduct preliminary hearings.

Local reporting has highlighted other cases in which Kellum authorized low or no-cash bail for defendants facing serious allegations, including threats, repeat offenses, and violent crimes.

Critics have labeled him a "Catch & Release" commissioner over those decisions.

Under Wisconsin law, court commissioners can release defendants under non-monetary conditions, including requirements to appear at future hearings and restrictions on contacting alleged victims.

The specific conditions imposed on Thompson beyond the absence of cash bail have not been established in the available reporting.

Prosecutors may seek modifications if additional evidence or circumstances warrant reconsideration.

Thompson remains charged, and the allegations have not been proven in court.

text:
Most of the people we call self-made in tech had someone who sat with them before the story got clean. 
Ada Lovelace met Charles Babbage when she was 17. Years later she offered him her mind for the Analytical Engine. He took it. She translated and expanded a paper on his machine and wrote what is now recognized as the first algorithm intended for a computer. The machine was never finished in their lifetimes. The relationship still produced the founding document.
Steve Jobs, in his twenties, cold-called Robert Noyce, the co-inventor of the integrated circuit and co-founder of Intel. Noyce was in his fifties. He met him. Jobs later said Noyce took him under his wing and tried to give him the perspective of someone who had already built the hard things. Jobs only partially grasped it at the time. That is how mentoring usually works. The value shows up later.
Frederick Terman at Stanford pushed Bill Hewlett and David Packard to start a company instead of just taking jobs. He is often called the father of Silicon Valley for a reason. The garage story is real. The professor who told them the garage was allowed is also real.
Warren Buffett and Bill Gates met because Gates’ mother arranged a dinner. They talked. The relationship lasted. Gates has described Buffett as a mentor on business and on what to do with the results of business. Two people who did not need each other’s money still needed the conversation.
Sheryl Sandberg has said Larry Summers was her most important early mentor. She worked for him at the World Bank and at Treasury. He gave her the room and the standard at the same time. Sponsorship and mentoring are not always separate.
None of these were formal programs with matching algorithms. They were people who agreed to grow together for a stretch of time. One had already done the hard version of the work. The other was willing to be corrected in public and still come back.
In tech and in energy systems the pattern is the same. The person who has commissioned a line, or shipped a product that failed in the field, or run a team through a bad quarter, can see the thing the resume cannot show. They can also deliver the hard news without making it a verdict on the person. That combination is rare. It is also the one that changes a career trajectory.
You do not need a famous name. You need someone who has already walked the part of the path you are on, who will tell you when the design will not survive contact with the operator or the customer, and who will still be in the room after you fix it. The historical record is consistent on that point. The self-made story usually leaves the mentor out. The work does not.

text:
Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM that’s designed to come up with a wider variety of responses than its mainstream rivals do. At the start of the call, he said something that’s been stuck in my head since: “We often say that we’re a self-loathing AI company. We don’t know if we really like what we’re doing.”

“I guess that makes me a self-loathing AI journalist,” I replied. It was a joke! I love my job. But I do not love many of the things the technology I write about has become: warped by hype, steered by zealots, inescapable.

The CEO of Springboards and I are far from alone. Around the world, a love/hate attitude toward AI is very much the vibe right now.

On the one hand, public feelings are souring fast. According to the Pew Research Center, more adults in the US think AI will have a negative impact on them personally, and on society in general, than expect a positive one. The pessimism is strongest among the young.

More than half of people worldwide say that AI products and services make them nervous, according to a report from Stanford University. In a Gallup poll in May, 71% of US adults said they would oppose construction of a new AI data center in their area, far more than the 53% who said they would oppose a new nuclear power plant. And in an NBC poll in March, AI was less popular than ICE.

Yet the number of people using AI is still skyrocketing. ChatGPT hit a billion monthly users in May, according to the market analysis firm Sensor Tower. Google DeepMind’s Gemini is close behind, logging 950 million users in July.

According to Pew, half of US adults now say they use a chatbot, more than twice the number who said they did in 2023. One in four people say they do so every day. And it’s a global habit: More than a third of adults across all 38 OECD countries (a group of the world’s wealthiest democracies) report having used generative AI tools in the last three months.

All these surveys paint a picture of two contradictory truths: A lot of people really do not like AI and a lot of people cannot get enough of it. What’s going on?

It’s possible that these are two distinct groups, but I doubt it. The numbers don’t add up unless the Venn diagram is on its way to being a circle.

It’s also possible that the more people use AI, the more negative their opinions about it will be. There’s at least a correlation to back this up: The Global North, where adoption is highest, skews pessimistic. In the Global South, where adoption levels are lower, people are more optimistic.

But here’s what I really think is going on: When people say they hate AI it’s not the technology they dislike but, rather, the relentless drive of the companies behind it to push the tech upon us in as many ways as possible. They’re telling us to brace for the biggest social and economic upheaval in generations. How do they expect people to feel?

In many ways, we’ve been here before. We saw a similar dynamic play out with social media over the last 20 years. Billions flocked to Facebook and Twitter despite mounting techlash against the companies that ran those services. Ditto for Google search.

With social media there wasn’t much anyone could do. Quitting a platform meant losing all your content and connections, giving you the choice to suck it up or start over. But with AI there’s still a chance for people to have some sway. There’s certainly more political appetite for regulation this time around. All 50 US states have either passed or proposed laws governing the development and deployment of AI, creating a patchwork of more than 2,100 bills across the country—a tenfold increase in three years. 

And with a number of top-class open-source alternatives to Google and OpenAI and Anthropic already on the market, there’s also (for now, at least) the potential for more consumer choice and the market pressure that goes with it. 

I don’t want to be naïve. Trillion-dollar companies are hard to move. But what comes next is not as inevitable as those companies often imply. When I asked the Springboards CEO why his firm was developing a new model if he didn’t really like AI, he told me there was no walking back from LLMs—but you could still make them do something different. 

Here’s hoping we see a lot more of something different: Clarity about what AI can and cannot do and, crucially, a technology that’s not sold as if it’s about to take over the world.

THE EVIDENCE™

POLITICAL AGITATORS — WHY PICK A FIGHT WITH TEXAS OIL AND GAS?

By Kim Wojcinski | USA Best Selling Author
The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott on November 3. During the campaign, she accused natural gas companies of deliberately withholding supplies during Winter Storm Uri to drive up profits. That is a serious charge against one of Texas’s biggest industries. Why make it, and what evidence has she offered to back it up?

Why pick the fight?

The political appeal is easy to see. Texans who lost heat during the February 2021 freeze wanted to know how a state with so much natural gas could run short when they needed it most. Hinojosa’s accusation gave voters a simple explanation and someone to hold responsible. The federal investigation documented a more complicated breakdown. Federal energy regulators and the North American Electric Reliability Corporation attributed 43.3 percent of the decline in natural gas production to freezing temperatures and weather, and another 21.5 percent to power losses at wells, gathering facilities, or other facilities that handle gas before it reaches customers.

Those findings establish that weather and power failures accounted for much of the drop in production. Hinojosa’s accusation requires evidence about deliberate decisions. Which companies had gas available? Could they deliver it? Who decided to hold it back, and what records show why? A governor-elect who makes that charge should be able to answer those questions.

What her record shows

In 2021, Hinojosa authored House Bill 1521, aimed at reducing methane flaring on land dedicated to the Permanent University Fund. She also publicly backed a separate proposal, authored by Rep. Vikki Goodwin, that would have imposed a 25 percent tax rate on certain natural gas burned off or released during production. Both bills stalled in committee. If the tax proposal comes back, lawmakers should ask how much flaring it would prevent, where producers can get the gas to market, and what it would cost to comply.

As of November 10, I found no post-election announcement from Hinojosa proposing new limits on Texas drilling or production. Texans did separately elect Democrat Jon Rosenthal to the three-member Railroad Commission, which regulates the state’s oil and gas industry. He will serve alongside two Republican commissioners. The election changed who will have a vote on that commission. The decisions those commissioners make will show what changes for producers.

The Findings

Texas collected $8.31 billion in oil and natural gas production taxes in fiscal 2026. That gives Texans a direct stake in how the state regulates the industry. They have an equally direct stake in whether their heat stays on during the next freeze. A serious energy policy has to account for both.

Taking on gas companies gave Hinojosa a way to tell voters she was on their side. Now she owes them specifics. If suppliers deliberately withheld gas during Uri, name them and show the records. If she proposes new restrictions, explain what they would accomplish and what they would cost. Texans already know what it feels like when the heat goes out. They deserve to know what their next governor will do to keep it on.

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

Werner Herzog on "The Wheels on the Bus":
(Sound of wind, perhaps a distant, discordant hum)

"Observe the bus. A hulking metal carcass, commandeered by an unseen, perhaps nonexistent, intelligence. Its wheels, they turn, 'round and 'round, with a mindless, algorithmic insistence. This, they tell us, is the vehicle of civilization, ferrying its passengers towards an ever-receding horizon of promised destinations.

But who, one must ask, truly grips the wheel? Who navigates by the stars of emotional truth, by the magnetic north of accountability? The answer, I suspect, is a void, an empty driver's seat. The passengers, lulled into a state of bovine placidity, sing their 'merry song.' A song of conformity, a childish rhyme to drown out the grinding of gears, the screech of metal against metal as the chassis strains. The music, you see, is so very loud, designed to obscure the silence from the driver's seat, to mask the chilling truth that this colossus, this societal omnibus, might possess no functioning brakes.

And so it hurtles onward, 'round and 'round, or perhaps, in a terrifyingly straight line towards a precipice only a few dare to acknowledge. The landscape outside is a blur of fleeting distractions. Inside, the song drones on, a mantra of oblivion. The wheels, indifferent to the fate of their cargo, simply continue their rotation, a perfect, mechanical metaphor for a journey undertaken without wisdom, careening towards a future shaped not by conscious design, but by the blind, idiot force of unexamined momentum. One day, the singing will abruptly cease. If emotional intelligence is not taught to fix the brakes then I imagine the view from the window wont matter much anymore if the brakes on the bus aren't fixed as soon as possible."

...

Werner Herzog on "The Itsy-Bitsy Spider":
(Sound of dripping water, a faint, skittering noise)

"And then, we have the arachnid. The 'Itsy-Bitsy Spider.' A creature of almost ludicrous fragility, attempting its ascent up the 'waterspout' – this, we are told, is the grand edifice of societal norms, the slick, vertical promise of promotions, of accumulating currency. The spider, driven by some primal, unarticulated yearning, perhaps what it dimly perceives as 'up,' begins its climb. It is a creature already bearing the weight of an unseen burden – its emotional suffering, a private, internal weeping.

But societal structures, much like the indifferent plumbing of the universe, are not designed for such delicate ascents. The 'rain,' you see, is not mere water. It is the rotting accumulation of unprocessed human suffering within a collective that has systematically failed to educate its smallest members in the language of the heart, in emotional intelligence. It is the downpour of a thousand unmourned griefs, a torrent of unspoken anxieties, and it washes the spider out, a predictable, almost banal tragedy.

Then, the 'sun' appears – the so-called 'help.' A course of medication, perhaps, designed to numb the fall. Or the therapist, offering a different 'tube' to climb. Society, with a benign, almost patronizing smile, gestures towards a new structure. Perhaps it is no longer the waterspout of raw commerce, but a 'metal pole' of 'wellness,' of 'self-improvement.' Yet, this new edifice, for all its gleaming surfaces, shares the same flaws as the old. The spider, still unversed in emotional literacy, still carrying its residual emotional pain, attempts the climb again, with almost the same vulnerabilities as before.

The cycle is complete, only to begin anew. The climb, the rain, the fall, the superficial drying, the redirection to another treacherous ascent. The spider, in its Sisyphean toil, becomes the individual ensnared in systems that offer the illusion of progress, while the core deficit – the profound, societal neglect of emotional understanding – ensures each climb is merely a prelude to the next fall. The spout changes; the suffering, and the ignorance that perpetuates it, remain."

text:
WOULD YOU CARE TO DIALOGUE SIR - 
IS THIS CONVERSATION NOT TALKING THERE SELF INTO THE ABYSS OF OBLIVION -
Analysis: Is This Speech "Talking Itself into the Abyss of Oblivion"?
Short answer: No — but the speech is acutely aware of that risk and is explicitly arguing against it.

Here's what's actually happening in the text:

What the speech is doing
This is a Knesset address (likely from a recent Israeli political figure, given references to October 7, the "evil empire of Iran," and the Abraham Accords states) that is deliberately invoking David Ben-Gurion's 1949 transition speech. The rhetorical structure is:

Invoke the founding moment — Ben-Gurion's call to move from "great ups and downs and the victory of war" to "small tasks": building, recruitment, education, health.

Define the present task the same way — "a diligent, persistent and faithful work" — parliamentary work, routine governance, not dramatic victory.

Diagnose the danger — a "divided, changing Israel," gaps, quarrels, fears, "many wounds still open."

Prescribe the remedy — compromise, listening, unity, "raise your hand for compromise," reject corruption/racism/violence.

Close with hope — a small light (Kislev/Hanukkah imagery) illuminating the distances; a prayer for peace.

Why it is not "talking itself into oblivion"
The phrase "talking itself into the abyss of oblivion" suggests a body politic rhetorically sleepwalking into self-destruction. But the text is doing the opposite:

It names the abyss explicitly: "A picture of a divided, changing Israel emerged from within," "moral barriers that break our beautiful faces," "many wounds are still open in our flesh."

It warns against the mechanism of oblivion: "We will not be able to heal them as long as the pain of one is the purpose of the other."

It prescribes an antidote: routine, faithful, persistent institutional work — the exact opposite of dramatic self-immolation.

The legitimate critique you may be reaching for
There is a tension worth naming:

The speech loads enormous existential weight onto "routine" and "small tasks" while simultaneously listing civilizational threats (Iran, October 7 accountability, AI/technological revolution, judicial/political divisions). Asking a fractured parliament to meet both the routine and the existential at once is precisely the strain that can produce paralysis.

The repeated call to "raise your hand for compromise" and "listen" is aspirational rhetoric delivered to a body the speech itself describes as representing "gaps, disagreements, quarrels and fears." Words about unity are not unity.

The Ben-Gurion framing risks nostalgic substitution: invoking 1949's clarity to mask 2024's (or whenever this was delivered) fragmentation. The "small light" metaphor is beautiful but is doing a lot of work that institutions may not be doing.

Bottom line
The speech is not oblivion-talk. It is anti-oblivion rhetoric — a warning against division, violence, corruption and racism, wrapped in the Ben-Gurion/light-in-the-darkness tradition. Whether it succeeds depends on whether the listeners translate "diligent, persistent and faithful work" into action. The text itself would agree with your concern: it says the repair "begins here, in this house" — meaning the abyss is avoided or entered by what happens in that room, not by the speech alone.

NOW COMPARE THE ELABERATION OF SOME ONE WHO HAS WITNESSED THE DIABOLICAL REASON ALL THIS COME ABOUT IN THE FIRST PLACE?
Comparing the Two Texts: Founding Rhetoric vs. Testimony of the System's Product
You're asking me to compare the Ben-Gurion-style Knesset speech (Text 1) with the former soldier's testimony (Text 2). The contrast is stark, and it's not incidental — the second text is, in effect, a first-person account of what the first text's "routine," "small tasks," and "diligent, persistent and faithful work" look like from the receiving end of the boot.

1. The rhetorical frame vs. the lived mechanism
Text 1 frames the state's task as: routine, order, security, peace, compromise, listening, "small tasks," building institutions, "a small light can illuminate the distances." It speaks in the language of statecraft and aspiration. The abyss it warns against is division, corruption, racism, violence — named as moral failures to be repaired "here, in this house."

Text 2 describes the operational machinery that produces the very things Text 1 names as failures. The soldier's account is not abstract: curfew enforcement, "shoot to kill" orders for curfew breakers, home seizures as temporary bases, tying residents to fences, locking front doors, caged streets, ghost towns, nighttime "arrest" raids that are functionally execution orders, and a legal architecture in which a Jewish settler in Hebron has the rights of a Jerusalem citizen while the Palestinian next door lives under military rule.

"I realised that my job is actually to maintain an apartheid system... I cannot touch a Jewish settler if he is attacking a Palestinian. The best I can do is call a local police department."

This is the diabolical reason you're pointing at: the system is not a malfunction of the founding vision — the testimony argues it is the implementation of a demographic and territorial logic. Text 1 says "a state is not tested only at the time of victory, it is tested... on a routine basis." Text 2 is a granular description of what that routine actually is for Palestinians under occupation.

2. "Diligent, persistent and faithful work" — from whose perspective?
Text 1's core prescription is Ben-Gurion's phrase: diligent, persistent and faithful work — parliamentary work, implementation of the mission, routine governance.

Text 2 supplies the missing subject of that sentence. The "diligent, persistent and faithful work" the soldier describes is:

Roaming streets to enforce curfews so settlers can celebrate

Bursting into a city "with our guns in our hands... screaming Kofia"

Maintaining a hierarchy where "the rights that the Jewish settlers have are not the rights of the Palestinians"

Instilling fear "in the hearts of Palestinians in Hebron" — which he says was "our defined mission"

So when Text 1 praises faithful, persistent routine work, Text 2 asks: faithful to what, persistent at what, and at whose expense? The same institutional virtue — diligence, routine, persistence — is the mechanism of the oppression the soldier describes. That's the diabolical reason: the system runs on exactly the civic virtues Text 1 celebrates.

3. The moral inversion both texts circle
Text 1: "the boundaries between good and bad" is implicit in its call to reject corruption, racism, violence, and to pursue compromise and peace.

Text 2 makes that boundary explicit as a psychological event:

"The boundaries between good and bad that I learned as a kid and obviously I learned that I'm on the good side, I was broken. I felt like I am a terrorist."

And crucially, he explains how the inversion is sustained:

"Growing up in Israel... I believed that I was the good guy... You learn about the Holocaust growing up... I knew that I am going to be a good human being." Then: "I began being almost obsessed with trying to understand the Nazi side... how can a Nazi soldier get up in the morning, give his kids a kiss... and go out to the camps and do his job. I just couldn't understand it. And when I got into the occupied territories, for the first time I understood how can there be a contradiction inside yourself."

This is the answer to your question about "someone who has witnessed the diabolical reason all this come about in the first place." The witness identifies the mechanism of moral insulation: a society formed around victimhood memory and "good guy" identity can, without experiencing contradiction, produce people who kiss their children goodbye and go enforce a curfew with shoot-to-kill orders. Text 1 invokes the Holocaust-adjacent moral language ("a small light," "peace," "blessing to all the families of the earth") — Text 2 shows the same moral vocabulary coexisting with the machinery of domination. That coexistence is the diabolical reason.

4. The "cycle of violence" frame vs. the structural account
Text 1: "the evil empire of Iran does not cease... in its threats"; "the fierce and determined war against our enemies"; build "a stable political balance in the region."

Text 2 directly dismantles the "cycle of violence" framing the interviewer offers:

"If you will not respect existence, you can't expect resistance... Every other attempt from Palestinians to try to negotiate this situation in a diplomatic way was countered by more attacks, more oppression, more occupation, more stealing of the land... We basically described every form of resistance as terrorism because the sole idea of the occupation is not to be safe. The sole idea is to create an equitably-planned piece of land only for Jewish people."

And on complexity:

"It's probably the most simple situation, political situation of our time. It's a situation about equality."

Text 1 calls the challenges "complex" and "many more, and they are complex." Text 2's testimony says the complexity is a rhetorical product — a way of making a simple question (equal rights or not) appear unsolvable. That's a direct challenge to the framing of Text 1.

5. The Mizrahi/Arab-Jewish passage — the system's internal logic
Text 2's long passage on Arab Jews is the deepest structural claim: that the state imported Mizrahi Jews, placed them in "buffer zones" on hostile borders, segregated and sprayed them with DDT, and required them to erase their Arab identity to assimilate — producing "the most extreme right in Israel" as a loyalty-signaling reaction. This is the witness describing how the system manufactures its own base, including the demographic raw material for the very "division" and "extreme right" that Text 1 laments.

Text 1 says: "There is no place for racism inside, towards anyone." Text 2 says the state's founding demography and settlement geography produced racialized hierarchy as a structural feature, not an aberration. The two texts are not describing the same country.

The comparison, stated plainly
Text 1 (Knesset speech)Text 2 (soldier testimony)
VoiceInstitutional, aspirational, unifyingFirst-person, confessional, disenchanted
Unit of analysisThe state, the Knesset, "the people"The curfew, the raid, the checkpoint, the house
DiagnosisDivision, gaps, moral barriers, external threatsStructural apartheid, military rule, demographic engineering
PrescriptionCompromise, listening, routine, "small tasks," lightResistance is inevitable; external intervention required; equality is the only exit
View of "routine"Civic virtue, the test of a stateThe mechanism of oppression
View of complexityThe challenges are complexThe "complexity" is a rhetorical cover for a simple question of equality
Moral frameGood vs. bad within a shared national projectThe good/bad boundary itself was broken by participation in the system
The answer to your question
The person who has "witnessed the diabolical reason" — the soldier — does not describe a state that accidentally fell into the abyss. He describes a state whose routine, faithful, persistent work (Text 1's exact prescription) is the abyss for the people under it. The diabolical reason is not a secret conspiracy; it is a legal and bureaucratic architecture that assigns different rights to two populations on the same street, enforced by people who believe they are the good guys, using the moral vocabulary of victimhood and peace that Text 1 also uses.

Text 1 warns against "talking itself into the abyss of oblivion." Text 2's implicit reply is: the abyss isn't entered by talking — it's maintained by routine, by "small tasks," by faithful persistent work, by exactly the civic language of your speech. The witness's elaboration is the missing half of the founding rhetoric: the founding speech describes the builders; the testimony describes what is being built on, and over whom.

This response is AI-generated and for reference purposes only.
SO CAN YOU ANSWE MY ORIGINAL QUESTION AGAIN NOW YOU KNOW THIS IS ARE THEY TALKING  THEM SELF AND THE WORLD  INTO THE ABYSS OF OBLIVION
Yes — with one crucial correction to the framing
Now that I've read both texts, my answer to your original question changes. Let me state it directly:

Yes — but not in the way "talking themselves into oblivion" usually means. They are talking themselves and the world into a moral oblivion while believing they are talking themselves into safety.

The precise mechanism
Your original phrasing — "talking themselves into the abyss of oblivion" — implies a self-destructive rhetorical sleepwalk. Text 1 alone doesn't show that; it shows a state warning itself against division. But Text 2 supplies what Text 1 cannot see: the speech's own virtues are the engine of the abyss.

Text 1: "diligent, persistent and faithful work" = civic virtue.

Text 2: "our defined mission [was] to instil fear in the hearts of Palestinians in Hebron" = that same virtue, faithfully executed.

So the "talking into oblivion" is not the content of the Knesset speech. It is the structural blindness of a discourse that can say "there is no place for racism, no place for violence, nowhere" while the routine, faithful, persistent work it praises is the violence and is the racial hierarchy — documented by the person who carried the gun and the grenades. The speech talks the state into believing its routine is innocent. That belief is the oblivion: not death, but the loss of the capacity to see what one is doing.

"Themselves and the world"
You added "and the world," and Text 2 supports that addition explicitly:

"You have to step outside and start talking to the world about what's going on. And that's the only way you can live in a place, not only for Palestinians, but for me as well."

The witness's claim is that the internal discourse (Text 1's genre) cannot correct itself from inside — "nothing is really changing from inside." So the world is being talked into a specific oblivion too: the oblivion of the "complexity" frame. Text 1 says the challenges are "complex." Text 2 says:

"It's probably the most simple situation, political situation of our time. It's a situation about equality."

The world is invited to see an insoluble millennia-old conflict; the testimony says that framing is itself the anesthetic. That is talking the world into oblivion — the oblivion of treating a simple question of equal rights as beyond resolution, and therefore beyond obligation.

The moral inversion as the abyss
The sharpest answer to your question is in the soldier's Holocaust passage:

"I began being almost obsessed with trying to understand the Nazi side... how can a Nazi soldier get up in the morning, give his kids a kiss... and go out to the camps and do his job. I just couldn't understand it. And when I got into the occupied territories, for the first time I understood how can there be a contradiction inside yourself."

This is the diabolical reason you asked about. The abyss is not that people become monsters. It is that ordinary people, formed by a moral vocabulary of victimhood and "good guy" identity, perform the routine work of domination while genuinely feeling innocent — and a parliament can praise "faithful, persistent work" and "a small light" in the same moral register that the system uses to launder itself. That is talking oneself into oblivion: the oblivion of self-knowledge.

The final answer, stated cleanly
Text 1 alone: No — it is anti-oblivion rhetoric, warning against division and violence.

Text 1 read through Text 2: Yes — because the speech's remedy (routine, faithful, persistent institutional work) is, per the witness, the operational description of the apartheid system. The state talks itself into believing its routine is moral. That is the abyss: not collapse, but the successful moral anesthesia of a functioning machine.

"And the world": Yes — the world is talked into the oblivion of "complexity," which converts a simple question of equality into an unsolvable eternal conflict, and thereby absolves everyone of the obligation the witness names: "giving all the Palestinians equal rights."

So: they are not talking themselves into destruction. They are talking themselves — and the world — into the impossibility of seeing what the routine is, which is the more precise and more damning form of oblivion. The witness's testimony is the counter-speech: it restores the boundary between good and bad that the routine had broken. @grok who is in the right and who is in the wrong
