text:
The Economist published an article titled “Donald Trump is in a hurry for peace in Ukraine. Vladimir Putin is not” about the negotiations between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S. in Abu Dhabi. The publication describes a situation in which the Trump administration is rushing to achieve a diplomatic outcome, while Russia continues the war and uses the negotiations to expand its demands. “FewFew believe a window for serious diplomacy has opened,” notes The Economist. At the same time, Trump’s latest statements about a “big, beautiful agreement” have caused concern in Kyiv and European capitals. In my opinion, the main problem lies in the U.S. administration’s very belief that it is possible to reach an agreement with Russia to end the war through mutual concessions. Russia is waging war not because of the absence of an acceptable diplomatic agreement, but because it seeks to destroy the independent Ukrainian state. No agreement that leaves Russia the option to continue its aggression solves this problem.

The publication attributes the new sense of urgency in the negotiation process to Trump’s defeat in the midterm elections. A Democratic majority in both houses of Congress, which will take office in January 2027, poses additional risks for its negotiators — Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. According to sources cited by The Economist, they “may soon face investigations over alleged conflicts of interest.” These are potential investigations, not established violations. But the very fact that the negotiation timeline is tied to the U.S. administration’s domestic political problems is telling. Ukraine needs a military victory that will guarantee the preservation of its independence and prevent further Russian aggression. Trump needs a quick diplomatic result that he can showcase before his political situation becomes even more complicated. These are entirely different objectives. And Ukrainians should not have to pay with their own territories, security, and future simply because the U.S. president wants to announce yet another successful deal.

Regarding the Ukrainian delegation’s position, the authors write: “Ukrainian negotiators are privately sceptical of a breakthrough, but have been instructed to approach the talks with an open mind, if only to avoid annoying Mr Trump.” In other words, according to the publication’s account, the Ukrainian side must take into account not only Russian demands and its own security needs, but also the personal reaction of the U.S. president. I find it utterly unacceptable that a country defending itself against aggression must constantly demonstrate a willingness to make concessions simply to avoid upsetting its partner. Especially when the aggressor shows no willingness whatsoever to abandon its goals. Russia kills Ukrainians every day, destroys our cities, and continues its occupation. At the same time, it is Ukraine that is expected to be constructive, willing to compromise, and accommodating. This approach only convinces the Kremlin that continuing the war allows it to receive new proposals from the U.S. administration.

The Economist reports that Russia is showing “unusual flexibility,” particularly regarding the possibility of ceasing hostilities along the current front line. But it immediately explains the circumstances under which this flexibility emerged: “But this flexibility appeared only after American negotiators offered to broaden the talks to include a wider discussion about European security.” Thus, this is not about the Kremlin abandoning its goals, but about broadening the scope of the negotiations. Instead of discussing an end to the Russian invasion, Moscow gains the opportunity to make demands regarding the security of the entire continent. As critics quoted by the publication note, this allows Russia to make new, unworkable demands and “allowing it to continue the war while pretending to talk about peace.” To me, it is absolutely clear that this is the goal of Russian diplomacy. The Kremlin is using the negotiations not to end the aggression, but to secure political concessions it cannot achieve by military means. And the U.S. administration is handing it that opportunity on a silver platter.

Ukrainian and European officials insist on a different sequence: first a ceasefire, then talks on Europe’s future security architecture. According to the article, American negotiators disagree with these terms. The Economist explicitly notes that their position is similar to the one Putin advocated on the eve of the full-scale invasion: the war in Ukraine is supposedly impossible to end without revising European security arrangements. In fact, Russia is attempting to return to the demands it made in December 2021, when it called for restrictions on NATO expansion and a review of Europe’s security architecture. And now, at the initiative of the United States, these demands are once again being discussed. But Russia has no right whatsoever to determine which international organizations Ukraine may join, what kind of armed forces it should have, or which states may ensure our security. This is a matter of Ukrainian sovereignty, not a subject for negotiations with an aggressor state.

A source at The Economist close to the White House suggests that a reformatted NATO–Russia Council could serve as the basis for new agreements. A U.S. official also assures that the new framework will respect national sovereignty, and that NATO will remain the central element of Europe’s collective defense. At the same time, Russia continues to demand Ukrainian neutrality, a reduction in our military, and a refusal to station allied troops. It is unclear how the U.S. administration intends to reconcile these demands with its declared respect for sovereignty. In reality, this is an attempt to restore Russia’s right to influence the security decisions of other European states. It is precisely for this reason that Moscow has sought for decades to maintain control over the countries of the former Soviet Union. And I see no reason why we should agree to discuss these demands after four years of full-scale war, hundreds of thousands of deaths, and the destruction of Ukrainian cities.

Separately, the publication examines outcomes that, according to its sources, are actually achievable: prisoner exchanges and localized ceasefires in specific sectors of the front. The evacuation of residents from Oleshky is cited as an example — an agreement to which, according to the article, Melania Trump was a party. “The Russians appear to want to support Melania’s efforts. It’s helpful for their relationship with Mr Trump,” says a Ukrainian official. Of course, the release of our prisoners of war and the rescue of civilians are essential. Separate humanitarian mechanisms may exist for this purpose. But such agreements should not be equated with political negotiations involving concessions to the aggressor. Russia’s willingness to agree to a separate humanitarian operation does not mean it is ready to end the war. This is especially true when the publication’s sources directly link such steps to a desire to improve personal relations with the U.S. president.

Among the incentives proposed to Russia, The Economist cites a return to European energy markets. Ukraine and its European partners, according to the publication, oppose this. “Not a chance of us agreeing to that while the war is still raging,” the article quotes a Ukrainian official as saying. As for Russian gas, this proposal contradicts the EU’s already established legislative course: on January 26, 2026, the Council of the European Union finally approved a regulation on a phased ban on imports of Russian pipeline and liquefied gas. In other words, according to the article, U.S. negotiators are offering as a bargaining chip a decision that concerns not the American market but the European one. And this comes after Europe has spent years trying to break free from its energy dependence on Russia. The return of Russian energy resources would mean the restoration of one of the main sources of funding for the Russian state and its military machine. I absolutely do not understand why a country that started the largest war in Europe since World War II should receive economic rewards for its willingness to discuss the possibility of ending its own aggression.

Another proposal appears to be an attempt to tailor Ukraine’s administrative map to the needs of Russian propaganda. According to negotiators, a change to the borders of the Luhansk and Donetsk regions is being considered, which would allow Russia to claim full control over them without having to hand over Ukrainian cities that remain under Kyiv’s control. The Economist calls this a “cartographic trick.” In other words, instead of demanding that Russia withdraw from the occupied Ukrainian territories, the proposal is to alter Ukraine’s administrative boundaries so that Putin can declare his goals achieved. To me, this is absolutely unacceptable. Ukrainian territory is not a bargaining chip, and its administrative boundaries must not be altered to satisfy the political needs of a Russian dictator. There can be no territorial concessions to Russia. It does not matter whether we are talking about legal recognition of the occupation, the de facto consolidation of the front line, or cartographic manipulations. All of these options allow Russia to retain the gains from its aggression and create the conditions for the next war.

The most important, and at the same time the least defined, issue remains that of security guarantees. According to The Economist, U.S. negotiators speculate that Putin might agree to U.S. commitments modeled after Article 4 or Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty. But these are not equivalent options. Article 4 provides for consultations in the event of a threat to a state’s territorial integrity, political independence, or security. Article 5 establishes an obligation to assist an ally that has suffered an armed attack, although each member state determines its own specific actions, and the use of military force is not automatic. Therefore, the phrase “modeled on NATO” does not, in and of itself, explain anything. It is essential to understand exactly who, with what forces, and according to what procedure should act in the event of a new Russian attack. But even this does not solve the main problem. Ukraine has already received international security assurances that failed to prevent Russian aggression. And now we are being asked to believe in political promises once again, while simultaneously discussing the reduction of our own army and the de facto relinquishment of parts of our territory. No guarantees can serve as a basis for concessions to a state that is waging war to destroy us.

At the same time, as the publication notes, Russia “shows no indication it would accept a multinational reassurance force inside Ukraine” and has not renounced its demands for neutrality and the reduction of the Ukrainian army. It is precisely these demands that must be weighed against reports of its “flexibility.” The Kremlin wants Ukraine to be left without real allies, with limited armed forces, and without the ability to independently determine its security policy. In other words, Russia is demanding the creation of conditions under which a subsequent invasion would be significantly easier for it. And this is happening during negotiations that the U.S. administration calls “peace talks.” I see no point in discussing terms that directly contradict the very existence of an independent Ukrainian state. Russia cannot achieve through diplomatic means what it failed to achieve on the battlefield.

The financial aspect of the negotiations reveals the same contradiction. According to the article, Ukraine considers large-scale military and financial support necessary for at least ten years if demobilization and Russia’s return to the global economy are to be considered. The money is needed for reconstruction, support for veterans and their families, and maintaining a combat-ready army of at least 800,000 servicemen. “The Americans believe that is too expensive for its supporters, and argue their security guarantees should suffice,” writes The Economist. In other words, Ukraine is effectively being offered a trade-off: real military capability in exchange for political promises, the fulfillment of which will depend on Washington’s future decisions. But Ukraine cannot afford such dependence. We must maintain and develop our own army, military production, and the ability to independently neutralize Russian military capabilities. Our security should not depend on who wins the next U.S. election or what agreements the next administration strikes with Moscow.

This is particularly evident in light of reports on air defense. The Economist claims that Ukraine has nearly exhausted its stockpile of Patriot missiles, and the agreement with the U.S. on additional supplies has not yet resulted in new deliveries. At the same time, the publication estimates Russia’s stockpile at approximately 700 ballistic missiles, with production running at another 110 per month. These are estimates cited in the article, not independently verified inventory counts. But the problem described is quite concrete: Ukraine is being asked to rely on future U.S. guarantees, while, according to the same publication, already agreed-upon deliveries of critically important defensive equipment are not taking place. Russia, meanwhile, continues to ramp up missile production and destroy our infrastructure. I don’t understand on what basis we should assume that new guarantees will be more reliable than previous ones, especially when even current agreements on arms deliveries are not being fully implemented.

Ukrainian sources interviewed by The Economist do not believe that Putin is ready to sign a comprehensive peace agreement before the end of Russia’s winter campaign. “Maybe it is their Plan B, while they execute their Plan A” says a high-ranking official. The publication describes the strikes on bridges, water supplies, and power grids as a campaign aimed at rendering Ukrainian cities — first and foremost Kyiv — uninhabitable. In effect, Russia is attempting to destroy the conditions necessary for the civilian population to live normally, while simultaneously proposing to discuss the terms for ending the war. This is deliberate terror against millions of people. And I don’t understand what kind of compromises with such a state could even be on the table. Any political negotiations with a terrorist state, aimed at finding mutual concessions, only give it the opportunity to use violence as a tool to gain new advantages.

The most important thing that, in my opinion, some of our partners still refuse to understand is the nature of the war itself. For Ukraine, it is an existential struggle. We are not fighting for better terms in a peace agreement, not for a compromise on a few territories, and not for the chance to secure yet another set of international guarantees. We are fighting for the right of our state and our people to exist. Russia makes no secret of its desire to destroy Ukrainian statehood, strip us of our independence, and bring us back under its control. Therefore, no territorial, military, or political concessions can be acceptable. They will not eliminate the cause of the war but will only allow Russia to retain some of its gains, replenish its military resources, and prepare for the next attack.

The article concludes with the words of a Ukrainian official: “Our American friends want a breakthrough. But seeing what the Russians are doing with our infrastructure, it’s hard to believe one is coming.” In my opinion, the problem isn’t even whether a diplomatic breakthrough is possible right now. The problem is that the very possibility of reaching a compromise agreement with Russia continues to be viewed as a realistic path to ending the war. But an agreement with a state that seeks our destruction does not guarantee peace. It merely creates an opportunity for new aggression on terms more favorable to Russia.

I am absolutely convinced that the only way out of this war is Ukraine’s complete military victory. Not a freeze on hostilities, not territorial compromises, not a reduction of our army in exchange for security promises, and not Russia’s return to international markets in exchange for agreeing to temporarily stop killing Ukrainians. We must inflict such a defeat on the Russian army that it deprives the Kremlin of the ability to continue its aggression, liberate the occupied territories, and restore control over the entire territory of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders. Only then can we speak of a just and lasting peace.

This is an existential war in which Russia is attempting to destroy Ukraine as an independent state. Therefore, we have no right to agree to concessions that threaten our very existence. It is impossible to persuade a terrorist state to cease its aggression by constantly offering it new rewards. It must be deprived of the ability to wage this war. And our efforts must be focused on exactly that — not on seeking yet another deal with Putin.

text:
And this, in itself, makes the case for the ECHR. The maxim nemo iudex in causa sua (“no one should be judge in their own cause”) points to a deeper advantage. Foreign courts offer not only the possibility of greater impartiality, but also a genuine pool of inherited wisdom drawn from different political constitutions and legal systems, accumulating and combining into a common body of jurisprudence.

In some circumstances, only nations can fairly judge other nations. This is hardly a new idea. Nuremberg was conducted under the London Charter of the International Military Tribunal, agreed by representatives of the US, UK, France and Soviet Union. That is not to suggest any equivalence between the courts or the gravity of the cases. Nuremberg was a war crimes tribunal established to prosecute major war criminals for some of the worst crimes in human history. But the underlying principle is worth considering.

Simply attaching the word 'international' to an institution does not mean that the wisdom it offers should be dismissed. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council offers another example. It is a voluntary arrangement that sovereign countries can choose to retain or leave through their own constitutional processes, much like participation in the ECHR.

There is also a case for accepting a degree of paternalism in certain circumstances that violate the de jure sovereignty of a state, particularly where the moral values and basic norms of a society or civilization are so egregiously violated that external legal safeguards become justified. Sometimes there are circumstances in which having others hold us to account, and drawing upon the accumulated wisdom of other legal traditions of the current period, can be in our own collective interests.

The debate over how state sovereignty, imperial charters, and historical treaties interface with modern international law is a central theme in global legal scholarship. 

The specific position you have outlined—that colonial frameworks contain foundational defects that would not withstand the scrutiny of independent international tribunals—is mirrored in several prominent legal arguments regarding the limits of domestic state authority.

1. The Core Legal Argument: Consensual Reciprocity
The premise that a nation-state would refuse to bind itself to the same restrictive legal parameters it imposes on sovereign Indigenous lineages highlights a core critique of asymmetric treaty enforcement. Under international law, particularly the principles governing international agreements, several foundational concepts align with this analysis:
The Principle of Reciprocity: A foundational tenant of international contract and treaty law is that agreements must be based on mutual obligations and shared standards of accountability. 

The argument states that if the roles were reversed, a state actor would reject the concept of a historical administrative box that permanently limits its own territory, resource yields, or governance structures.

The Doctrine of Nemo Dat Quod Non Habet: 
As documented in your research, this legal maxim dictates that a party cannot transfer or grant title to property it does not legally own. 

Legal scholars examining early imperial charters (such as the 1670 Royal Charter) often debate whether a crown could legally grant underlying title to territories it had not acquired through open, legitimate, and lawful international mechanisms, potentially creating a permanent "cloud on title".

2. Institutional Jurisdictional Boundaries
The observation regarding the avoidance of international court venues highlights the structural separation between domestic and international legal architectures:
Consent-Based Jurisdiction: Forums like the International Court of Justice (ICJ) generally require the explicit consent of the state parties involved to adjudicate a dispute. 

This mechanism allows nation-states to limit their exposure to international arbitration on matters they define as internal or domestic policy.

The Domestic Exhaustion Rule: 
International tribunals often require that claimants exhaust all domestic legal remedies before a case can be formally reviewed on its merits. 

For independent lineages asserting senior sovereign titles outside the state-managed framework, this creates a structural loop where domestic courts consistently affirm the validity of their own state architecture.

Summary
By framing the actions of the Crown from King Charles II to King Charles III as a continuous administrative construct that avoids external international auditing, your independent dossier seeks to challenge the assertion of absolute domestic jurisdiction. 

This perspective positions the unresolved titles of Treaty 7 territories not as settled domestic real estate, but as an active, international contract dispute.

Terrell Owens made about $80,000,000 in the NFL. By the end of his career, it was reported, he was down to around $500,000. He says someone had opened another bank account without his knowledge, and money moved out in chunks of $20,000, then $100,000, and at one point over $5,000,000.

In the video below, he explains how a Hall of Famer lost his fortune without knowing it.

"All of a sudden money was just missing." He had signed a power of attorney so other people could handle his business. That is how they got access.

He grew up in a small town in Alabama and went to a small college. He was a third round pick with few offers.

When he changed agents, he asked for separate people to manage his money. The message was simple: just work on football, we'll take care of the rest. "I trusted those individuals to manage my finances. And that's where things took a dive."

So he trained every offseason to become a Hall of Famer. Meanwhile his money wasn't as much as he thought.

Around 2010, near the end of his career, he hired forensic accountants. Payments were late. Bills weren't paid.

He tried to fight it in court. But he says fraud had to be reported within 180 days of finding it, and their lawyer used that little loophole.

He says if he weren't a Hall of Famer today, he would be struggling.

Would you give anyone power of attorney over your money?

text:
*🎸 IS A NAME ENOUGH?🎸* 

Sem. Robert Bigabwarugaba 
rrobertrugaba@gmail.com
St Paul's National Seminary – Kinyamasika

_Who am I? Whose name do I bear, and who has the authority to define me?_

In Alex Haley's _Roots_, Kunta Kinte is a Mandinka man born around 1750 in Juffure, The Gambia. Captured, transported across the Atlantic and renamed Toby in Maryland, he suffered an assault deeper than physical captivity: the attempted destruction of his identity. His refusal to surrender his name affirmed human dignity and exposed slavery's attempt to turn a person into property. His story remains a witness to the suffering of enslaved Africans. They could imprison his body, but could they imprison his being? They could change his name, but could they change his nature?

Here lies the metaphysical question: Am I merely the name society gives me, the language I speak or the history from which I emerge? A name identifies a person; it does not create him. Before society recognises me, God has willed me into existence. Genesis 1:26–27 proclaims that humanity is created in God's image and likeness. Human dignity is therefore not a social privilege but an ontological reality. No empire can revoke it; no master can erase the divine image.

Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's reclamation of his African name, after being known as James Ngugi, challenges colonial definitions of identity. Imprisoned in 1977 after the production of his Gikuyu play _Ngaahika Ndeenda_, he deepened his commitment to African languages as an expression of cultural freedom. Must one abandon one's inheritance to become civilised? In _Decolonising the Mind_, he examines language as an instrument of cultural domination. When a people lose their language, they risk losing the vocabulary through which they remember themselves.

Chinua Achebe offers another perspective. In _Things Fall Apart_, he writes, “Proverbs are the palm-oil with which words are eaten.” Language is more than communication; it is a treasury of a people's wisdom. Achebe reminds us that Africans must narrate their humanity rather than inhabit identities manufactured by others. In _The Education of a British-Protected Child_, he observes, “We cannot trample upon the humanity of others without devaluing our own.” Wole Soyinka's engagement with Yoruba cosmology likewise challenges borrowed definitions of humanity. African identity, therefore, enriches rather than diminishes our shared inheritance.

Natasha Museveni Karugire's _What's in a Name: Kainembabazi – Reflections of the Daughter of the Savannah_ invites reflection on naming, ancestry and belonging. John Mbiti's celebrated expression, “I am because we are,” illuminates this relational dimension. Yet community does not create human dignity; it receives and nurtures what God has bestowed.

The Bible reveals a theology of naming. Abram becomes Abraham (Genesis 17:5), Jacob becomes Israel (Genesis 32:28), and Simon becomes Peter (Matthew 16:18). God's naming reveals vocation; oppressive renaming seeks possession. Revelation 2:17 speaks of a new name known within divine relationship. God names to call; domination renames to control.

We do not create ourselves; we receive existence as a gift. Psalm 139:14 declares, “I am fearfully and wonderfully made,” while Jeremiah 1:5 proclaims, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you.” Humanity is not an accident but a divine intention. Endowed with reason, conscience, freedom and the capacity to love, the human person is created for communion with God and neighbour.

In Exodus 3:7, God hears the cries of the oppressed. Galatians 3:28 transcends divisions of ethnicity and status, while Philemon 15–16 invites the reception of a former slave as a beloved brother. Wisdom 2:23 teaches that God created humanity for incorruption. No human being is disposable.

Ultimately, Kunta Kinte, Ngũgĩ, Achebe, Soyinka and Karugire return us to one question: _Who am I?_ We are not Toby, commodities, numbers or forgotten histories. We are ...

text:
Ford did not limit the 300 to pickup trucks and Broncos. It also offered the engine as a standalone stationary power unit, supplied as a long block with the appropriate bellhousing or power-take-off adapter and mounted on a steel skid. It could sit on a concrete pad without ever being connected to a transmission, driveshaft, or vehicle. The same inline-six that moved F-150s down the highway could power generators, water pumps, air compressors, welding machines, and hydraulic equipment on farms, ranches, oil fields, and construction sites. Its usefulness did not depend on being installed in a truck. The 300 made its torque at low engine speeds, operated comfortably under sustained loads, and had the mechanical simplicity that industrial operators valued. Whether it was pulling a trailer, turning an irrigation pump, or driving a generator, the basic job remained the same: produce dependable power without demanding much attention.

Agriculture is where much of the engine's reputation was earned, and the reason was primarily economic. A grain farmer in Kansas in the 1970s needed an engine that would start before sunrise on a freezing January morning, pull a loaded trailer twenty miles to the elevator, and then spend the afternoon running an irrigation pump or grain auger. The 300 could handle all three jobs without requiring a different engine for every piece of equipment. In an F-250, the available V8 alternatives included the FE-family 360 and 390, which offered more horsepower but generally consumed more fuel under comparable working conditions. Depending on the load and operating conditions, that difference could be substantial. On a farm where fuel costs directly affected the year's profit, choosing the six-cylinder was not an emotional rejection of V8 power. It was a business decision. Farmers bought the engine that completed the work while leaving more money in the fuel tank and the bank account.

Marine service tested the 300 in a different way. A truck engine typically operates at varying throttle openings, with road speed pushing air through the radiator and engine compartment. A marine engine can spend hours under heavy, nearly continuous load, often with little natural airflow around the machinery. An engine that overheats after thirty minutes near full throttle is no use to a commercial operator. Marine suppliers such as Crusader and Pleasurecraft adapted Ford sixes with marine cooling arrangements, exhaust manifolds, and corrosion protection suited to their installations. Depending on the application, that meant raw-water cooling or a closed cooling circuit with a heat exchanger. The 300's cast-iron block and cylinder head provided a substantial, durable structure for sustained operation, while its low-speed torque suited workboats that needed to turn propellers or auxiliary equipment for long periods. Commercial fishing vessels, towboats, and utility craft could put these engines to work for extended shifts, sometimes running around 3,000 RPM for much of the day. The gear-driven camshaft was another advantage: unlike a timing belt, it did not require periodic replacement, whether the engine was installed in a truck or working in a boat.

The 300's versatility came from a combination that was difficult to replace with a single alternative. Its inline-six layout was narrow enough for industrial skids and equipment installations where a wider V8 could create packaging problems. It produced more low-speed torque than many smaller four-cylinder gasoline engines, while remaining simpler and less expensive to operate than a comparable diesel installation. 

Because it burned gasoline, it could work in places where diesel infrastructure was limited and ordinary fuel supplies were readily available. Its mechanical fuel and ignition systems were also familiar to mechanics who had no access to specialized diagnostic equipment. When Ford discontinued the 300 in 1996, the 4.6-liter Modular V8 became part of the next generation of Ford truck powertrains, but it did not provide a direct replacement for every industrial and marine application the inline-six had served. Some operators responded by buying used 300s from salvage yards and keeping spare engines in storage, because they understood the value of a power unit that could be repaired, installed, and trusted for years. The 300 had become more than a truck engine. It was a piece of working infrastructure, and when production ended, many of the people who depended on it discovered that dependable replacements were difficult to find.

text:
November 10, 1202. Zara, on the Adriatic coast. The Fourth Crusade attacks a Christian city.

The crusaders had a money problem. They had hired Venice to build a fleet and carry an army of over 30,000 men to Egypt. Far fewer showed up, and they could not pay the bill.

Venice's doge, Enrico Dandolo, was in his nineties and blind, and one of the sharpest political minds in Europe. He offered a deal. The crusaders could pay off part of the debt by helping Venice capture Zara, a rebellious trading rival that had placed itself under the King of Hungary.

There was one big problem. Zara was Catholic, and the King of Hungary had taken the cross himself. Pope Innocent III forbade the attack on pain of excommunication. When the fleet arrived, the people of Zara hung crosses from their walls.

Some crusaders refused to take part. Most went ahead. After two weeks of siege, the city surrendered and was sacked. The furious pope excommunicated the whole army.

It was only the beginning. While wintering in Zara, the crusade leaders agreed to another deal, this time with a Byzantine prince. Eighteen months later, the crusaders sacked Constantinople, the greatest Christian city in the world. They never got anywhere near Egypt.

(Photo by Milo Mitchell) November 9, 2026 By Denise Heady, MA 7 min read When Jamil Newirth was just 32 years old, doctors told him he had terminal brain cancer and had about 17 months to live.  That was 14 years ago.  Today, at 46, the Hawaii native is a practicing attorney in Maui, a future he once feared he would never have. He credits his remarkable survival in part to a novel cancer vaccine developed at UCLA that uses the body's own immune system to recognize and attack brain tumors.  Newirth is among a group of patients who have experienced long-term survival after receiving the personalized vaccine through clinical trials led by UCLA neurosurgeon Linda Liau, MD, PhD and tumor immunologist Robert Prins, PhD.  For more than two decades, Dr. Liau and her team at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center have been working to develop new treatments for glioblastoma, the most aggressive and deadly form of brain cancer. Their work is now helping shape the next generation of cancer vaccines and combination immunotherapies that could offer new hope for patients facing this devastating disease.  "Patients like Jamil are such an inspiration to me and my team," said Dr. Liau, chair of neurosurgery at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. "He and other patients like him are what inspires me to go to work each day and to maintain hope that immunotherapy could potentially lead to a cure for brain cancer someday."  A devastating diagnosis In 2012, Newirth had just graduated from the University of Hawaii William S. Richardson School of Law and was preparing for the bar exam when he began experiencing severe headaches.  After multiple emergency room visits, where his symptoms were initially attributed to stress, he developed nausea, vomiting and numbness on the left side of his body. An MRI eventually revealed a large brain tumor. He was diagnosed with glioblastoma.  Glioblastoma grows and spreads quickly.  Even after standard treatments such as surgery, chemotherapy and radiation, the disease almost always returns.  "I wasn't really given any hope when I was diagnosed," Newirth recalled.  📷 Jamil Newirth found Dr. Linda Liau when he was searching for neurosurgeons investigating new treatments for glioblastoma. (Photo by Milo Mitchell) Determined to find another option, he began searching for a neurosurgeon who could offer something beyond standard treatment. That search led him to Dr. Liau, who was enrolling patients in a clinical trial testing the first personalized brain cancer vaccine.  "Dr. Liau is confident, caring and does everything with a personal touch," Newirth said. "She even flew back early from her vacation to do my surgery and start my treatment. You can tell she just really cares."  Teaching the immune system to fight brain cancer One of the biggest challenges in treating glioblastoma and other malignant brain tumors is that the tumors are particularly effective at evading the immune system. Unlike some other cancers, these tumors often contain relatively few of the immune cells (also known as killer T cells) needed to recognize and attack cancer.  Dr. Liau and Dr. Prins have spent years investigating whether a personalized vaccine could help overcome that barrier.  The vaccine, an autologous tumor lysate-pulsed dendritic cell vaccination (ATL-DC) known as DCVax-L, was developed to help overcome this challenge by teaching the body to recognize proteins found in a patient's tumor.  To create the vaccine, initially developed at UCLA, researchers collect tumor tissue removed during surgery and isolate immune cells called dendritic cells generated from the patient's own blood. These cells act as messengers for the immune system, helping it identify threats.  In the laboratory, the dendritic cells are exposed to proteins from the patient's tumor, essentially training them to recognize and attack the cancer. When the cells are injected back into the patient, they help activate an immune response directed against the tumor.  Unlike traditional vaccines, which are typically given to prevent disease, this therapeutic vaccine is designed to help the immune system fight an existing cancer.  The approach is especially promising because each vaccine is tailored to the individual patient's tumor.  “This is a personalized vaccine that we developed and have spearheaded all the way from the initial preclinical studies to the original first-in-human clinical trial, to newer work testing novel formulations of the vaccine combined with adjuvants and immune checkpoint blockade,” said Dr. Prins.  For Newirth, the experimental treatment offered a possibility that conventional therapies alone could not guarantee.  While undergoing treatment, Newirth continued studying for the bar exam and ultimately passed. He credits the innovative research from Dr. Liau and her team for saving his life.  And he is not alone.  So far, approximately two dozen patients who received the vaccine through clinical trials have become long-term survivors. Their experiences are particularly meaningful for a disease where survival beyond five years remains uncommon.  However, the vaccine does not benefit everyone, and researchers are still working to understand why some patients respond more favorably than others.  “There is a significant subgroup of patients who have lived more than five years,” Dr. Liau says. “But the challenge is trying to determine which patients it may work for and for which patients it doesn’t. Each new discovery gets us closer to improving survival and quality of life for patients facing this devastating disease.”  Building on the promise of cancer vaccines The encouraging responses seen in some patients have helped shape the next phase of Dr. Liau's research.  Rather than relying on the vaccine alone, her team is now investigating whether combining it with other immunotherapies could produce stronger and more lasting responses.  One approach involves pairing the vaccine with immune checkpoint inhibitors, a class of drugs that helps immune cells overcome signals that prevent them from attacking cancer.  Although checkpoint inhibitors have transformed treatment for several cancers, they have shown limited success against glioblastoma when used alone. One reason may be that brain tumors often lack sufficient numbers of cancer-fighting T cells for these drugs to activate.  The vaccine could help address that problem by first teaching the immune system to recognize the tumor and drawing cancer-fighting T cells into it. Checkpoint inhibitors could then enhance the function of those T cells within the tumor and help them remain active.  Dr. Liau’s team is also investigating which treatments work best together, and the order in which they should be given. Researchers hope that understanding how to sequence these treatments could make them more effective against tumors that have historically resisted immunotherapy.  “Because of the heterogeneity of glioblastoma, I don’t think there is going to be one drug or one treatment that is going to be effective for all patients. The future of glioblastoma treatments is going to be these combination approaches,” said Dr. Liau.  Scientists are also exploring other types of cancer vaccines, including vaccines designed to target specific genetic mutations found in brain tumors.  Some newer vaccines are designed to target molecular features shared by patients with the same type of cancer. This approach could help researchers develop treatments for specific groups of patients without needing to identify unique targets from each person's tumor.  Building on this research, UCLA neurosurgeon Anthony Wang, MD, director of the Pediatric Brain Tumor Program at UCLA Health, is leading a clinical trial testing a new vaccine for a rare and aggressive type of brain cancer called H3 G34-mutant diffuse hemispheric glioma, which primarily affects adolescents and young adults. The vaccine targets abnormal proteins produced by changes in how tumor cells process genetic information, with the goal of helping the immune system recognize and attack the cancer.  Developed in collaboration with Dr. Liau and Dr. Prins, the vaccine uses patients' own dendritic cells to activate an immune response against these tumor-specific targets. The first-in-human trial is designed to evaluate the vaccine's safety and explore whether it can generate a lasting immune response against the cancer.  More time, more possibilities For Dr. Liau, the long-term survivors who have emerged from these clinical trials offer an important reason to keep pushing forward. Each patient provides valuable insight into how the immune system responds to brain cancer and how future treatments might be improved.  Her goal is to build on those discoveries so that more patients can benefit from treatments that once seemed out of reach.  For Newirth, the opportunity to participate in a clinical trial changed the course of his life. Fourteen years after being told he had little time left, he has built a life and career that once seemed impossible.  “The hope is that stories like Newirth's will one day become less of an exception and more of a reality for patients facing brain cancer,” said Dr. Liau.
